PREFACE 

In 1875, the Supreme Court stated that if the federal government "comes down from its position of sovereignty and enters the domain of commerce, it submits itself to the same laws that govern individuals there."* That statement, however, is no longer true either technically or substantively; if it were, there would be no need for a separate textbook on government contract law. 

The compelling fact is that, to quote Dean Pound, "the bigness of everything"** has left its indelible mark on this subject as well as on virtually everything else. Within the last twenty-five years, with the demands or threats of war on the one hand and the strides of science on the other, the federal government has emerged as the principal buyer, as well as a principal seller, of goods and services; as the principal owner and occupier of land; as one of the principal sources of credit; and, all in all, as the most important single business factor in the entire national economy. And this transition in function of the United States Government has had a corresponding impact on the law applicable to dealings with the Government, with the result that there has now arisen and clearly exists a special body of legal principles with a distinct personality of its own which, in many circles at least, is called "government contract law."

It is relatively new, however, and it is still not sufficiently well understood by contractors or the Bar. Indeed, it is common knowledge in certain government circles, at least, that many contractors make silly but costly mistakes because of ignorance of the applicable rules. These mistakes are not in the interest of the Government or the taxpayer any more than they are in the interest of the contractor himself. They constitute sheer waste. And part of the reason for this lack of understanding of the subject has been the lack of availability of written materials. It is thus our hope that this second edition of NAVY CONTRACT LAW will help to further a better understanding of the subject. 

The first edition of this work, published in 1949 when Hudson B. Cox was General Counsel, reflected the great changes in procurement authority and practice wrought by the Second World War and described, in organized form, the system of government contract law then used in *Cook v. United States, 91 U.S. 389, 398 (1875). 

**Pound, Foreword to Symposium on Twenty-five Years of Federal Administra tive Law, 16 FED. B. J. 445 (1956).

III 

947134

PREFACE 

the Navy. It was well received and has been extensively used by government lawyers and procurement officials. 

As in the first edition, the chapters in this one have been written by lawyers, past and present, of the Office of the General Counsel of the Navy. There have been substantial changes and developments in government contract law since 1949, and these have required major revision of most of the original chapters. Much credit is due to George M. Coburn, the editor of this edition, who has labored tirelessly to make it a more valuable and useful work. Also we are grateful to Lawrence E. 

Chermak, Counsel for the Navy Comptroller, who prepared the index and tables-a major undertaking-and made many helpful suggestions for improving the book generally. The views expressed should be considered those of the individual authors rather than as official pronouncements by the Office of the General Counsel or by the Department of the Navy.

Notable features of the second edition include a textbook arrangement of material with numbered section headings and a form of binding that will permit the inclusion of supplementary material. In this way the book may be brought up to date regularly and the material kept reasonably current. In addition, while the first edition was issued only for government use, the present edition will also be available, at modest cost, to the public through the Government Printing Office. This is on the theory indicated earlier that the principles of government contract law should be as well known to the Bar and the public as to government officials. Contractors and their lawyers must understand these principles if they are to know what they are getting into when a contract is executed with the Government, and to avoid errors in the course of its performance. And these principles must be especially so understood if we are to have those clear understandings and that speedy and smooth performance of government procurement which mean economy and financial savings to the contractor, and also to the Government and the taxpayer. 

MARCH 30, 1959. 

F. TROWBRIDGE VOM BAUR, General Counsel.

Admiralty Claims Jurisdiction Over Maritime Contract Suits $ 1.1. Introduction: The Role of the Government Lawyer 

The government lawyer, like his counterpart in private practice, must maintain that constructive viewpoint of endeavoring to find a legal way for his client to do what he wants to do. Thus, as with the lawyer in private life, the role of the government lawyer is to get things done in the legal field. True, it is not always possible for the lawyer to approve what the client wishes, and then the client must be so advised, in candid if polite terms. But however the chips may fall, the government lawyer must at least always seek to precipitate legal problems on to a solution and to expedite the client's programs, rather than hold them up indefinitely because of the presence of a legal problem or bog the client down with fuzzy and ambiguous advice. 

Inherent in this process, as in the private practice of law, is a concept of very great importance, that the lawyer in Government should be brought in by his client at the very outset or inception of a program. When that is done, the lawyer not only has more time to think things out; in addition, he can work his legal thinking into the early planning of the program and so keep it on a safe legal course. Other- wise, without early legal advice, a program may start to march boldly down the field only to be met suddenly by an insuperable legal obstacle, and with resultant crises, backtracking and hurt feelings. 

These considerations apply to the Navy. For today there is much more to the Navy than its fast carrier task forces ranging the seas of the world, jet planes, and guided missiles. Apart from its fighting capabilities and grey-hulled ships at sea, the Navy is also a vast industrial enterprise. It is far bigger than a combination of several of the largest corporations of America, and it does much the same things that they do. It purchases an enormous variety of items-ships, planes, 2

INTRODUCTION: THE ROLE OF THE GOVERNMENT LAWYER $ 1.1 

ordnance, electronics, petroleum, medical supplies, etc. It manages industrial plants, real property, and shipping. It disposes of great quantities of surplus property. It maintains extensive systems of fiscal control. And it enters into contracts of the most varied nature. Current procurement alone in the Navy averages some five to six billion dollars annually, requiring the writing of some 48,000 contracts per year in Washington, and another 20,000 contracts in the field. Some of these contracts run into millions or even hundreds of millions of dollars. Just as a large corporation requires a substantial corps of lawyers to enable it to get things done in the legal field, so as a large industrial organization the Navy maintains a law office-the Office of the General Counsel-for the same purpose. 

However, the role of the lawyer advising an operating agency of the federal government, such as the Navy Department, has one striking difference from that of the lawyer in private practice. The latter is frequently guided by the principle: What are the things my client can and cannot safely do without running afoul of some statutory or regulatory restriction? The government lawyer, on the other hand, finds that his first question inevitably becomes: What is the authority under which my client can proceed? And only after he has found the affirmative authority does he look for the conditions, restrictions and limitations. The reason is elementary. The federal government is one of delegated rather than of so-called natural powers, and the executive agencies, in turn, have only that authority which Congress or the President has chosen to grant out of their respective constitutional powers.' 

Narrowing the focus of this general observation to that of the lawyer called upon to advise and guide the Navy Department through the legal intricacies of doing annual business with American industry on a multi-billion dollar scale, the lawyer soon finds that he must early familiarize himself with a field of law somewhat different from those learned in the classroom or in the private practice of law. He must know the statutes under which the Navy derives its authority to acquire the ships, planes, materials, and supplies necessary to equip and to keep modern the most potent naval force in history; he must know the limitations on the availability of public funds; and he must be thoroughly conversant with the decisions of the Court of Claims, the 

Armed Services Board of Contract Appeals and the Comptroller Gen eral, which are of immediate relevance to the law of government contracts. 

It is the purpose of these several chapters to outline some of the more important phases in the field of Navy procurement and contract law. Without striving to be encyclopedic in discussing subjects of 

1 For an instructive application of this principle in the field of government contracts, see Federal Crop Insurance Corp. v. Merrill, 332 U.S. 380 (1947). 3

$ 1.

numerous facets and refinements, the authors will endeavor to portray a substantively correct panorama of applicable law, practice and fact. 

Thus, there will be considered such topics as procurement by formal advertising, procurement by negotiation, types of contracts, fiscal problems in procurement, contract termination, renegotiation, the acquisition of industrial facilities, property disposition, standard contract clauses, and contracting in the field of research and development. This introductory chapter will attempt to lay the groundwork for these topics by reviewing briefly the development of the Navy's current procurement authority and practices both before, during and following World War II, thereby furnishing a frame through which to view current Navy contract law practice. In addition to being broadly historical in perspective and general in its scope of review, special attention will be focused in the latter part of this chapter to legal aspects of the ocean shipping services now operated by the Navy. 

At the outset, it should be explained that while the Navy has been less prone than some government agencies in creating or using novel terms which perplex the American businessman, there are two expressions which will recur frequently throughout these chapters that are foreign in some degree to the general usages of the commercial world. 

The term "procurement" is used as a generic expression to denote the purchase or acquisition by the Government of property or services from others, and the term "facilities" is employed to describe property acquired or used by others in aid of production for the Government. 

A “facility” may be anything from a screwdriver to an industrial plant, and it may be government-owned or privately owned. $ 1.2. 

Logistics and the Navy

In his dual capacity as the nation's chief executive officer and Commander-in-Chief, the President of the United States has ultimate direction of the defense establishment and its logistics functions. The basic law of the land created that responsibility.2 In 1789, the first year of our national history, the first Congress established the Departments of War (including naval affairs) and the Treasury, and in 1792 vested the latter with responsibility for purchases and contracts for the Army. More than 160 years ago, in 1794, the Congress passed and President George Washington approved an act to provide a naval armament.5 The Barbary Pirates, who were corsairs from Morocco, Algiers and Tripoli, were capturing and pillaging American merchant ships, and the infant American nation had to construct and send war-

The following year a Purveyor of Public Supplies was established in the Treasury to act as the Government's first purchasing agent. His duties included the procuring of all arms and military and naval stores as well as "generally all articles of supply, requisite for the service of the United States." But the growing importance of naval affairs was recognized in 1798 by the establishment of a separate Department of the Navy. The same year Congress declared that "all purchases and contracts for supplies or services for the military and naval service of the United States, shall be made by or under the direction of the chief officers of the Departments of War and the Navy, respectively." It was further provided that the Purveyor of Public Supplies would execute all orders received from the military departments for providing stores and supplies.

Widespread abuses of this broad grant of authority caused the enactment in 1808 of a law still in effect requiring the insertion of a clause in every government contract that no member of Congress might benefit therefrom. In the following year, there was enacted the first of a long series of laws implementing the congressional power to control the expenditure of public funds by imposing a general requirement for the use of formal advertising in the procurement of supplies and services. That statute 10 provided that all purchases and contracts by the Secretaries of the Treasury, War and Navy would be made "either by open purchase or by previously advertising for proposals respecting the same." In an opinion to the Secretary of the Navy, the Attorney 

General described the purpose of the statute as preventing favoritism and giving the Government the benefit of competition by formal advertising." In still another opinion regarding this act and two more of like purpose, the Attorney General described the congressional intent against the notorious mischief of making contracts privately as distinguished from public advertising for proposals." 12 Ultimately, two lines of legislation developed with respect to government purchasing by formal advertising. One involved laws regarding procurement in general which culminated in Rev. Stat. § 3709 13 and

It was in World War II that the United States Navy became the world's most potent naval force. Logistics was in the ascendancy, and the Navy Department was able to obtain the ships and the planes, the equipment and the weapons, the supplies and the services needed for victory over aggression.

Since World War II the United States Navy has continued to be the most modern as well as the largest naval force, and its influence as a force for peace has been profound. The Navy's 2800 ships include atomic-powered submarines, aircraft carriers and guided-missile cruisers. 

Its 17,000 aircraft, many of them jet-propelled, evidence its adaptation to the age of air power. Research is under way in fields which challenge the imagination. All this requires ingenious planning, competent personnel, combat effectiveness, and the ability to procure the many things which must be bought in an orderly fashion within the framework of the law.

As the past is the prologue without which the present cannot be understood, let us view what has gone on before in the field of pro curement we call Navy Contract Law. 

I. HISTORICAL BACKGROUND § 1.3. Restrictions on Contracting Procedures Before World War II 

Prior to World War II, Navy procurement was governed by an astonishing mass of undigested and uncoordinated legislation-statutes that had accumulated on the books over a period of more than one hundred years. Many were completely archaic, many were conflicting, and not a few had been enacted to serve special and now forgotten interests. In the aggregate they presented an obstacle to efficient and speedy purchasing that must have been the lament of many a supply officer. Shoes, brooms and brushes had to be purchased from the federal penitentiary at Leavenworth before they could be bought elsewhere." 

Brooms and mops had to be purchased from non-profit agencies for the blind unless procured for use outside the United States or required by any law in effect on June 25, 1938, to be procured from any fed-

Wartime Procurement Liberated From Unrealistic Restrictions

II of that act permitted the President to authorize any department or agency of the Government engaged in the war effort "to enter into contracts and into amendments and modifications of contracts heretofore or hereafter made and to make advance, progress and other payments thereon, without regard to the provisions of law relating to the making, performance, amendment or modification of contracts, whenever he deems such action would facilitate the prosecution of the war." 

The President was quick to extend to the Armed Services this emancipation from statutory confusion and restriction. On December 27, 1941, Executive Order 9001 authorized the War and Navy Departments and the U.S. Maritime Commission to exerise the full powers and freedom contemplated by Congress in Title II of the First War Powers Act. 

In fact, but for the reverberating shock of Pearl Harbor, this extreme change must have seemed no less than heretical to many an old-time government lawyer. In addition to lifting the bars completely on all the time-honored limitations on government contracting, it authorized the War and Navy Departments, and the United States Maritime Commission, to “enter into agreements with contractors and/or obligors modifying or releasing accrued obligations of any sort, including accrued liquidated damages or liability under surety or other bonds" whenever such action in the judgment of the Services or of the Maritime Commission would facilitate the prosecution of the war. Amendments and modifications of contracts could be made with or without consideration and "irrespective of rights which may have accrued under the contract." 

The second half of Executive Order 9001 carried a few sobering limitations. A prohibition against racial discrimination was required to be inserted in all contracts; assignments of claims against the United 

States might be made only in accordance with the Assignment of Claims Act of 1940; 33 advance payments under contracts could be made only where they would promote the national interest, and were required to be carefully scrutinized; contractors had to warrant that they were not paying commission agents any fee for soliciting or securing the contract; the cost-plus-a-percentage-of-cost system of contracting was prohibited (as it was by the First War Powers Act itself); existing ceilings upon profits and fees were retained, and the fee in cost-plus-fixed-fee contracts was limited to seven percent of the estimated cost of performance; finally, the sanctity of the Walsh-Healey,34 Davis-Bacon 35 and 

Copeland 36 Acts was preserved, and the Eight-Hour Law, as amended on September 9, 1940,37 was continued in effect.

$ 1.4 

This virtually complete emancipation from peacetime procedural limitations on contracting, accomplished by the First War Powers Act and Executive Order 9001, had been foreshadowed, in part at least, by modified relaxations upon contracting procedure during the two and one-half year period of defensive preparation preceding the outbreak of hostilities on December 7, 1941. The Public Works Act of April 25, 1939,38 in aid of the burgeoning defense activities of the nation (particularly the construction of off-shore bases), authorized the Secretary of the Navy to negotiate for the construction of public-works projects to be located outside the continental limits of the United States and to have such work performed on a cost-plus-fixed-fee basis, the permissible fee being limited to 10 percent of the estimated cost of the work. That this first step was timidly taken is evidenced by the safeguards which Congress threw around the authority it granted. The approval of the President himself was necessary for the validity of any contract made under the new relaxed rules; the fee, as noted, was limited by statute; before a contract could be let, negotiations had to be conducted with three or more contractors regularly engaged in construction work of the type and magnitude contemplated; and a naval officer had to be permitted to participate in meetings of the Board of Directors of the contractor "for the purpose of safeguarding the interests of the United States." 

The same act also authorized the employment on a negotiated basis of outside architectural or engineering firms for the preparation of designs, plans and specifications for any public-works project or for the construction of any naval vessel or aircraft.

From this small beginning, other legislation, loosening in part the restrictive bonds of peacetime purchase procedure, found favor with Congress and paced the intensifying defense effort of the country. In July of 1939 the War Department was permitted to negotiate for the procurement of aircraft parts, instruments, and accessories without regard to formal advertising when their classified nature was such that they should not be publicly divulged. A certificate of secrecy made by the Secretary of War was a necessary condition precedent, and an award might be made only after the proposal had been submitted to at least three reputable concerns for their respective bids.³⁹ 

In March of 1940 the "Multiple Awards Act" 40 authorized the Secretaries of the War and Navy Departments, in the interests of national defense and as an aid to expanding aircraft production, to award contracts for aircraft, aircraft parts and accessories not alone to the lowest responsible bidder but to the three lowest bidders dividing the work among them and avoiding the overloading of aircraft production facilities.

Expansion of Procurement Authority and Reorganization of the Navy's Procurement Structure 

Three months later, contemporaneously with the fall of France, and on June 14, 1940, Congress gave authorization for an 11 percent expansion in the size of the Navy.41 In the following month it gave authorization for a 70 percent expansion, the authority for the two-ocean Navy.42 

Between the effective dates of these two authorized increases in naval strength, Congress passed a bill, H.R. 9822, which was approved by the 

President on June 28, 1940, as Public Law 671, 76th Congress.43 Although superseded and greatly overshadowed by the First and Second War Powers Acts, Public Law 671 (colloquially and not inappropriately called the "Speed-up Act") was the cornerstone upon which much of our wartime procurement authority and practice was erected. It authorized advance payments to contractors up to 30 percent of the contract price; it authorized contracts for the acquisition, construction, repair or alteration of naval vessels and aircraft, or any portion thereof, to be made by negotiation without regard to existing requirements for competitive bidding and award to the lowest bidder; and it was the basis upon which preference ratings were founded by providing for priority of deliveries of material under Army or Navy contracts over deliveries for private account or export. An amendment dated May 31, 1941,44 provided for allocations of all materials as to which a shortage threatened, from which allocation requirement there later emerged the system of rationing. The Act of June 28, 1940, also authorized the Navy Department to construct and provide for the construction of plant facilities, including extensions and additions to private plants, and to take over and operate any existing manufacturing plant or facility necessary for the national defense whenever a satisfactory agreement with the owner for its use or operation for defense purposes could not be arrived at a grant of authority which, though not exercised until after the outbreak of war, illustrated eighteen months before Pearl Harbor a realization on the part of Congress that the approaching war clouds justified drastic measures. Public Law 671 in large measure, therefore, was the vehicle which first converted the country from a peacetime to a wartime. footing.

As a further stimulus to the expansion of private industrial capacity for war production, Congress by the Second Revenue Act of 1940, approved October 8, 1940,45 provided for the accelerated amortization over a five-year period of emergency facilities constructed or acquired after

As might have been expected, the increasing volume of the Navy's procurement during the eighteen months intervening between the increased tonnage authorizations in the summer of 1940 and the onset of hostilities in December of 1941 gave rise to some far-reaching changes in the Navy's procurement practices. As noted above, substantially all 

Navy procurement was required to be made by formal advertising "when the public exigencies do not require the immediate delivery of the articles, or performance of the service," 46 and with very few exceptions (as in the case of contracts for the construction of vessels, of guns, or of facilities) the Navy's purchases were made by the Bureau of Supplies and Accounts on contracts executed by that Bureau. $ 1.6.

President's Delegation of Authority to the Secretary of the Navy 

Section 2(a) of the so-called "Speed-up Act" provided:

That whenever deemed by the President of the United States to be in the best interests of the national defense during the national emergency declared by the President on September 8, 1939, to exist, the Secretary of the Navy is hereby authorized to negotiate contracts for the acquisition, construction, repair, or alteration of complete naval vessels or aircraft, or any portion thereof, including plans, spare parts and equipment therefor, that have been or may be authorized, and also for machine tools and other similar equipment, with or without advertising or competitive bidding upon determination that the price is fair and reasonable. .47 (Emphasis added) 

By a letter dated June 29, 1940, the President formally "deemed [it] to be in the best interests of the national defense during the national emergency" for the Secretary of the Navy to be authorized after June 28, 1940 (the date of the approval of the act) to negotiate the contracts specified in the act without formal advertising. The 

President, however, placed certain limitations upon such authority which did not appear in the act. The first of these limitations was expressed in the alternative and required a personal finding by the Secretary of the Navy that either (i) the bids which would be received after formal adver- 

47 See § 1.5, n. 43 supra. 

46 REV. STAT. § 3709 (1875), 41 U.S.C.

tising would not represent the operation of effective competition or (ii) formal advertising for a reasonable time would seriously hamper, impede and delay the procurement. Neither of such findings was expressly or impliedly required by the act.

The act, however, did require that there be a "determination that the price is fair and reasonable." It did not require the Secretary of the 

Navy to make such determination, but the letter of June 29, 1940, from the President required that prior to the execution of any negotiated contract the Secretary of the Navy shall find and determine that the price or prices included therein are fair and reasonable. 

The effect of this non-delegable grant of authority to the Secretary necessitated the establishment of procedures whereby he could make the requisite determination (i) that the price was "fair and reasonable” and (ii) that formal advertising would not result in the operation of effective competition or that it would seriously hamper, impede and delay the procurement. By Navy directive dated July 5, 1940,48 provision was made for the submission of all negotiated contracts to the Secretary's office for execution by him, each such contract being required to contain a certification as to the facts upon which the Secretary could predicate the required determinations.

This procedure was further amplified by a directive of June 20, 1941,49 which required, rather than a simple certification by the technical Bureau of the ultimate facts, a request to the Secretary for "Authority to

Negotiate," which request had to recite sufficient facts to serve as a sound basis for the determinations that the Secretary under the President's letter was required to make. The laborious procedure involved in first investigating and ascertaining facts which would justify the required determinations, in setting forth these facts at length and processing through channels to the Secretary the request for Authority to Negotiate, in then negotiating the procurement, and finally in preparing and forwarding the resulting contract or letter of intent to the Secretary's office for execution, was manifestly unsatisfactory and a material impediment to that expedition in procurement which the worsening world situation increasingly demanded. Tedious and retarding though they must have been, these requirements for personal determination and action by the Secretary himself nevertheless laid the groundwork for the program of centralized control and coordination of procurement in the Secretary's office that proved so successful during the war.

Furthermore, in determining the reasonableness of price, consideration was to be given to the objectives of the Executive Order, so that a higher price might be justified if the effect of the proposed contract would be to spread defense production over a wider area and out of tight labor markets. $ 1.7.

The exercise of central control in the Secretary's office, which had been engendered by the non-delegable nature of the negotiation authority conferred on the Secretary of the Navy by the President's letter of June 29, 1940, was retained in the directive of December 28, 1941, by requiring that authority to contract by negotiation must continue first to be obtained from the Secretary in connection with any contract or amendment involving the payment of $200,000 or more. This limitation upon the Secretary's delegation, it should be noted, provided one of the cornerstones upon which rested the Navy's wartime system of checks and balances on procurement. The request for authority to make contracts under the new directive differed materially from the Request for Authority to Negotiate under the "Speed-up Act." No longer was emphasis placed on reasonableness of price or the type of procurement; the information now required was essentially statistical: the name of the proposed contractor, the kind of supplies being purchased, the price to be paid, the location of the producing plant or site of the proposed facility, and the certificate of the contracting officer that the article or facility was necessary for the prosecution of the war. Navy procurement was required to be made by formal advertising "when the public exigencies do not require the immediate delivery of the articles, or performance of the service," 46 and with very few exceptions (as in the case of contracts for the construction of vessels, of guns, or of facilities) the Navy's purchases were made by the Bureau of Supplies and Accounts on contracts executed by that Bureau. $ 1.6. 

President's Delegation of Authority to the Secretary of the Navy 

Section 2(a) of the so-called "Speed-up Act" provided:

That whenever deemed by the President of the United States to be in the best interests of the national defense during the national emergency declared by the President on September 8, 1939, to exist, the Secretary of the Navy is hereby authorized to negotiate contracts for the acquisition, construction, repair, or alteration of complete naval vessels or aircraft, or any portion thereof, including plans, spare parts and equipment therefor, that have been or may be authorized, and also for machine tools and other similar equipment, with or without advertising or competitive bidding upon determination that the price is fair and reasonable. (Emphasis added) 47 

By a letter dated June 29, 1940, the President formally "deemed [it] to be in the best interests of the national defense during the national emergency" for the Secretary of the Navy to be authorized after June 28, 1940 (the date of the approval of the act) to negotiate the contracts specified in the act without formal advertising. The 

President, however, placed certain limitations upon such authority which did not appear in the act. The first of these limitations was expressed in the alternative and required a personal finding by the Secretary of the Navy that either (i) the bids which would be received after formal adver- 

47 See § 1.5, n. 43 supra. 

46 REV. STAT. § 3709 (1875), 41 U.S.C. 

§ 5 (1952). 

11

$ 1.

tising would not represent the operation of effective competition or (ii) formal advertising for a reasonable time would seriously hamper, impede and delay the procurement. Neither of such findings was expressly or impliedly required by the act. 

The act, however, did require that there be a "determination that the price is fair and reasonable." It did not require the Secretary of the 

Navy to make such determination, but the letter of June 29, 1940, from the President required that prior to the execution of any negotiated contract the Secretary of the Navy shall find and determine that the price or prices included therein are fair and reasonable. 

The effect of this non-delegable grant of authority to the Secretary necessitated the establishment of procedures whereby he could make the requisite determination (i) that the price was "fair and reasonable" and (ii) that formal advertising would not result in the operation of effective competition or that it would seriously hamper, impede and delay the procurement. By Navy directive dated July 5, 1940,48 provision was made for the submission of all negotiated contracts to the Secretary's office for execution by him, each such contract being required to contain a certification as to the facts upon which the Secretary could predicate the required determinations.

This procedure was further amplified by a directive of June 20, 1941,49 which required, rather than a simple certification by the technical Bureau of the ultimate facts, a request to the Secretary for "Authority to Negotiate," which request had to recite sufficient facts to serve as a sound basis for the determinations that the Secretary under the President's letter was required to make. The laborious procedure involved in first investigating and ascertaining facts which would justify the required determinations, in setting forth these facts at length and processing through channels to the Secretary the request for Authority to Negotiate, in then negotiating the procurement, and finally in preparing and forwarding the resulting contract or letter of intent to the Secretary's office for execution, was manifestly unsatisfactory and a material impediment to that expedition in procurement which the worsening world situation increasingly demanded. Tedious and retarding though they must have been, these requirements for personal determination and action by the Secretary himself nevertheless laid the groundwork for the program of centralized control and coordination of procurement in the Secretary's office that proved so successful during the war. 

Needed relief from the stringent requirements of the President's letter of June 29, 1940, was forthcoming through the medium of Executive 

Order 8891 issued on September 4, 1941. This Executive Order created

Furthermore, in determining the reasonableness of price, consideration was to be given to the objectives of the Executive Order, so that a higher price might be justified if the effect of the proposed contract would be to spread defense production over a wider area and out of tight labor markets. $ 1.7.

Thus by the beginning of World War II some experience in negotiating contracts for the Navy's requirements had been gained and the concept of central coordination in the Secretary's office of contracts made by the technical

The day following the Executive Order the Secretary issued his directive of December 28, 1941,52 putting the new war contract procedures into effect in the Navy. Under this directive there was delegated to contracting officers in the Department (¿.e., those authorized by the Chiefs of their respective Bureaus to contract on behalf of the Bureau) authority to execute contracts and amendments and modifications of contracts without regard to the requirements for formal advertising and without limitation as to form or substance except for the following contractual provisions: (1) those required for classified contracts, (2) in the event of progress payments, appropriate provision for a lien in favor of the Government in accordance with the Act of August 22, 1911,53 (3) labor provisions required by the Walsh-Healey, Davis-Bacon, and Copeland "Anti-kickback" Acts refered to above, (4) racial non-discrimination, (5) employment of aliens, (6) assignability, if any, under the Assignment of Claims Act,54 (7) in cost and cost-plus-fixed-fee contracts, provision for the preservation of records, and (8) required patent and patent infringement clauses. The exercise of central control in the Secretary's office, which had been engendered by the non-delegable nature of the negotiation authority conferred on the Secretary of the Navy by the President's letter of June 29, 1940, was retained in the directive of December 28, 1941, by requiring that authority to contract by negotiation must continue first to be obtained from the Secretary in connection with any contract or amendment involving the payment of $200,000 or more. This limitation upon the Secretary's delegation, it should be noted, provided one of the cornerstones upon which rested the Navy's wartime system of checks and balances on procurement. The request for authority to make contracts under the new directive differed materially from the Request for Authority to Negotiate under the "Speed-up Act." No longer was emphasis placed on reasonableness of price or the type of procurement; the information now required was essentially statistical: the name of the proposed contractor, the kind of supplies being purchased, the price to be paid, the location of the producing plant or site of the proposed facility, and the certificate of the contracting officer that the article or facility was necessary for the prosecution of the war. President, in Executive Order 9001, had to all intents and purposes made the finding of facilitation of the prosecution of the war required by section 201 of the First War Powers Act, thereby obviating the necessity for an individual finding in connection with each contract. 

Finally, the directive of December 28, 1941, was explicit on the point that it was not designed to "change or affect in any way the present distribution among the several Bureaus and Offices either of business or authority to make or execute contracts." This statement was not entirely gratuitous. With the rapidly increasing volume of Navy procurement, considerable opposition was being manifested to the historical distribution of procurement authority whereunder the Bureau of Supplies and Accounts, with only limited exceptions, did all of the Navy's buying upon requisition from technical Bureaus. At a time when substantially all Navy purchases had been effected by formal advertising, the centralization of the procurement function in one Bureau had been entirely logical and satisfactory. With the advent of negotiated procurement, however, the buying function could not be wholly disassociated from the persons familiar with the technical requirements involved. 

As a result of increasing material shortages, rigid specifications became subordinated to the capacity of an available supplier to produce the item. Negotiations covered not only price but time of delivery, specifications, use of substitute materials, preference ratings, and the like, thereby requiring the presence and views of persons in the Bureau actually charged with responsibility for the item. Furthermore, the vastly increased volume of procurement and the necessity for utmost economy in manpower required that any duplication of effort between the technical Bureau and the Bureau of Supplies and Accounts as the buying agency be reduced to a minimum or eliminated. 

In December of 1941 the time was not ripe for any radical change in the division of procurement responsibilities between the Bureaus. 

During the summer and fall of 1942, however, the preparation, execution and administration by the Bureau of Supplies and Accounts of contracts which of necessity had to be negotiated in the technical Bureaus became increasingly anomalous and wasteful with the result that on December 13, 1942, a directive 56 was issued which had as far reaching and significant an effect on the division of the Navy's procurement responsibilities as the First War Powers Act had on the Navy's procurement practices. Briefly, this directive authorized the Chief of any 

Bureau having technical cognizance over materiel and services to be procured to determine in his discretion the extent to which contracts embodying the terms of such procurement should be negotiated, pre-

$ 1.

pared and executed in his Bureau and the extent, if any, to which the Bureau of Supplies and Accounts should be availed of for the purpose. 

Thus, the procurement function within the Navy became decentralized, whereas at the same time procurement policy, as will be noted below, remained centralized. $ 1.8. 

Bureau Offices of Counsel 

The directive of December 13, 1942, also gave formal recognition to the establishment within each Bureau (other than Medicine and Surgery, which had no procurement function) of an Office of Counsel for the Bureau. Counsel for each respective Bureau was charged with the preparation or approval of all contracts, and with furnishing all necessary legal advice and services to the Bureau in matters of procurement. 

The various Counsel were answerable jointly to the Chief of the Bureau and to the Under Secretary of the Navy through the Chief of the "Procurement Legal Division" in the Under Secretary's office. While the procurement function was decentralized by the December 13, 1942, directive, centralized coordination over the mechanics of procurement was obtained through the respective Offices of Counsel and the Procurement Legal Division. Similarly, as we shall see, centralization of procurement policy control was obtained through the Office of Procurement and Material. 

$ 1.9.

The Office of Naval Material and the Office of the General 

Counsel 

Executive Order 9024, issued on January 16, 1942, established the

War Production Board, which superseded the Supply Priorities and Allocations Board and the Office of Production Management, and which was vested with the broadest possible powers to "exercise general direction over the war procurement and production program." All federal departments and agencies were instructed to "comply with the policies, plans, methods and procedures in respect of war procurement and production as determined by the Chairman" of the War Production Board. 

To meet the need for a central coordination of program planning within the Navy Department, and to provide a single agency in the Department as its representative before the War Production Board in arranging priorities, obtaining allocations and securing permission for new or converted facilities, the Secretary of the Navy, by General Order 166, established the Office of Procurement and Material on January 30, 1942. 

This Office was charged with the duties of coordinating all the material procurement activities of the Department, supervising procurement programs, and estimating and scheduling requirements.

Although historical in approach, this brief review is of more than purely historical interest for, as will be seen, so satisfactory did this organizational distribution of procurement functions prove, and so successful was the Navy's record of negotiated purchasing during the war, that they have set the pattern for the present peacetime operations of the Department.  II. FINANCING PRODUCTION FOR THE NAVY $ 1.10. Plant Expansion and Working Capital 

The tremendous expansion demanded of American industry to meet the requirements of total war, as well as the costly conversion from peacetime to war production, could not have been met without extensive financial assistance from the Government. As has been indicated briefly above, and as will be developed in a later chapter,63 this assistance was provided in large part through government financing of plant expansion, with the Government itself constructing additional industrial plants and shipyards or paying for additions and extensions to existing privatelyowned production facilities.64 It was furnished, in addition, through the medium of accelerated amortization under Certificates of Necessity pursuant to section 124 65 of the 1939 Internal Revenue Code, to which reference has already been made.❝6 

However, important as was the expansion of the nation's productive capital assets, the furnishing of working capital to enable industry to meet the financial burden of greatly expanded sales, labor force and inventory, and the expenses incident to tooling up and preparing for an entirely new type of production were no less important. Mention has been made of the fact that the "Speed-up Act" 67 authorized advance payments up to 30 percent of the contract price, and that under the First War Powers Act advances might be made up to the full amount of the contract price. Specific statutory authority in this respect was necessary because of the restrictions of section 3648 of the Revised Statutes (derived from an Act of January 31, 1823)68 prohibiting advances of public moneys and payment for services or articles which have not at the time of payment been rendered or delivered. The Navy had had statutory authority since 1911, however, to make contractual provision for payments under its contracts as the work progressed, taking a lien upon all materials and work in progress in connection with which payment is made."⁹ While the making of progress or partial payments did not have the effect of increasing the contractor's net working capital, it did afford a means of effecting payment up to 80 or 90 percent of the contract price without compelling the contractor to carry the entire financial burden

§ 1.11. Advance Payments 

The 30 percent advance payment authority under the "Speed-up Act" and the 100 percent of the contract price advances authorized by the First War Powers Act provided the necessary wartime legislative sanction for government financing of the contractor's initial outlay. In order to retain control over the use made of such advances, it was customary to require their payment only into "controlled accounts," out of which withdrawals could be made by the contractor upon the countersignature of a Navy representative. By April 2, 1942,71 it was established policy to require a payment in the nature of interest at the rate of 22 percent per annum on the unliquidated balances of advances in order to avoid discriminating in favor of producers enjoying government financing over those employing their own capital or securing private financing. Under the provisions of the Defense Contract Financing Regulations,72 the interest rate on advance payments, having been first established at 4 percent per annum of the unliquidated balance, has now been increased to 

5 percent. 

In order to afford uniform application of policy and control over advance payments, a Finance Section (later Finance Division) was established in the Office of Procurement and Material from which the contracting Bureaus had to secure approval to make advances. It was the function of the Finance Division to determine whether or not financial assistance should be rendered to Navy contractors, the form that such assistance should take, and the terms upon which it might be granted.73 

The Division was staffed during the war with civilians and reserve officers having wide business and banking experience; and although government financial assistance was by its very nature extended for the most part to those credit risks to whom private financing was not available, the Navy's experience of losses was less than one-twentieth of one percent, a loss ratio which was offset more than seven times by the interest return to the Government.

The Armed Services Procurement Act 74 extends to present peacetime procurement the authority to make advances up to the full amount of the contract price when approved by the "agency head" (the Secretary of the Navy, the Under Secretary, or an Assistant Secretary), or his designee thereby furnishing evidence of congressional satisfaction of the use

The Finance Division, which was continued as a part of the Office of the Fiscal Director, is now under the control of the Assistant Comptroller, Accounting and Finance. $ 1.12. Prohibition Against Contract Assignments; Assignment of

Claims Act 

Whenever practicable, however, the use of private capital to finance defense production was and still is encouraged in preference to direct government financing. A serious obstacle to the use of private financing lay in the prohibition against the transfer of government contracts or the assignment of claims against the Government. Section 3477 of the Revised Statutes,75 which rendered void any attempted transfer of assignment of any claim upon the United States or of any interest therein, and section 3737 of the Revised Statutes," which prohibited the transfer of any contract or interest therein to which the United States was a party, effectively precluded the hypothecation of valuable government production orders as security for private loans. Historically, the purpose of these statutes was to prevent the scandalous trafficking in contracts and claims against the Government. On October 9, 1940, the Assignment of Claims Act was approved 77 as an amendment to sections 3477 and 3737 of the Revised Statutes to permit the assignment to financial institutions of all moneys due from the Government under any contract in excess of $1,000. Pursuant to the provisions of that act, as subsequently amended in 1951,78 payments to be made to an assignee after May 15, 1951, of any moneys due or to become due under the contract shall not be subject to reduction or set-off for any liability of any nature of the contractor to the Government which arises independently of the contract, or for any liability of the contractor on account of (i) renegotiation under any renegotiation statute or under any statutory renegotiation clause in the contract, (ii) fines, (iii) penalties (which term does not include amounts which may be collected or withheld from the Contractor in accordance with or for failure to comply with the terms of the contract), or (iv) taxes, Social Security contributions, or the withholding or non withholding of taxes or Social Security contributions, whether arising from or independently of the contract.

THE SETTLEMENT OF DISPUTES UNDER NAVY CONTRACTS $ 1.14

While the Assignment of Claims Act of 1940 did much to promote private financing of war production, the necessity for utilizing all American industry in the war effort required the extension of financial assistance to many companies engaged in war production that were poor credit risks even under the most liberal banking criteria. To make private capital available to these financially shaky segments of war industry, Executive Order 9112,79 issued on March 26, 1942, authorized the Army, Navy and Maritime Commission (i) to guarantee or participate in loans or commitments made to contractors whose business was found to be necessary or convenient to the prosecution of the war, or (ii) to make direct loans to such contractors. The Federal Reserve 

Banks were designated as the fiscal agents for the Army and Navy in carrying out the program of government guarantee and participation in war industry loans, and on April 6, 1942, the Federal Reserve Board issued the Regulation which gave its name to this method of government financing, the well-remembered "Regulation V-Loans." The authority to make V-Loans was revived with the passage of the Defense Production Act of 1950 and is currently employed by the Navy Department. However, the authority to make direct loans was not similarly extended. 

V-Loans 

The approximate total of advance payments authorized by the Navy during the war was $2,000,000,000 and during the same period guaranteed loans in the amount of $2,215,000,000 were authorized. Although the authority to make direct loans, as opposed to the making of advance payments and the guaranty of private loans, was strictly a wartime measure and is not now exercised, the lessons learned and the procedures established will be valuable precedents in any future emergency period wherein that authority may be reinstituted to meet the special needs of certain contractors.

With logistics ever increasing in importance in the measurement of the nation's capacity for defense, the ability and the means to finance Navy production will probably become increasingly significant elements in the procurement plan which will attend any major mobilization effort. 

III. DISPUTES UNDER NAVY CONTRACTS $ 1.14. The Settlement of Disputes Under Navy Contracts 

Another innovation of wartime procurement which has left its mark upon the peacetime procurement practices of the Navy is the resolution 

79 This Executive Order was given legislative ratification by the Act of June 11, 1942, 56 Stat. 351. 

80 64 Stat. 801 (1950), 50 U.S.C. App. § 2092 (1952), extended to June 30, 1960, by the Act of June 28, 1958, 72 Stat. 241, 50 U.S.C. App. § 2166 (1958). The use of government-guaranteed loans is discussed in 88 4.39-4.41 infra. 21

of disputes under Navy contracts. Since about 1920, it has been customary in government contracts to provide that all disputes concerning questions of fact arising under the contract shall be decided by the contracting officer, subject to a right on the part of the contractor to appeal the decision to the head of the agency within a limited period of time (usually thirty days). The disputes clause further requires the contractor to proceed with his performance under the contract notwithstanding the pendency of a dispute. Such a provision, calling for unilateral determination of disputed questions of fact, is valid and does not render the contract unenforceable for lack of mutuality. It does require, however, that the decision or determination be made by the officer or person referred to in the disputes clause. In brief, the contractor is entitled to the unbiased and impartial judgment of the contracting officer himself and cannot be bound by the substituted judgment of another authority, the contracting officer's duty so to decide the dispute being that of a fiduciary.83 

$ 1.15. The Armed Services Board of Contract Appeals 

82 The tremendous increase in the volume of procurement during the war, coupled with the necessity for speed in procurement and the introduction to government contracting of persons hitherto strangers to public contracts, necessarily gave rise to a vastly increased number of disputes between the Navy and its contractors, and necessitated the adoption of a standard appeal procedure. Under the earlier form of disputes clause, appeal by the contractor was permitted to the Secretary of the Navy, whose decision on disputed questions of fact was by contract made final and conclusive on the parties.84 This procedure required the personal determination and decision of the Secretary of the Navy himself, although the Compensation Board of the Navy was charged, in addition to its several other functions, with the duty of looking into the facts and making recommendations to the Secretary. During the war, the form of disputes clause was changed to provide for appeal

to the Secretary "or his duly authorized representative," which permitted the decisions of the Compensation Board and of its immediate successor, the Navy Board of Contract Appeals, to be final and conclusive and obviated the necessity for personal action by the Secretary. 

In 1944 the Navy Board of Contract Appeals issued detailed procedural regulations making provision for the filing of briefs and the conduct of hearings before the Board, providing within the Navy Department an impartial tribunal for the hearing and determination of disputed questions under Navy contracts. In addition to disputed ques tions of fact, the Board on behalf of the Secretary of the Navy, also determined the allowability of items of cost under cost-reimbursement type contracts which had been disallowed by the Cost Inspection Service of the Bureau of Supplies and Accounts and by the Chief of that Bureau. 

Following enactment of the Armed Services Procurement Act of 1947 85 

and to ensure uniformity in procedures and decisions of the military departments in settling contract disputes, a tribunal called the Armed Services Board of Contract Appeals was administratively established in 1949 as a joint board of the Departments of the Army, Navy and Air Force. The Board was to be the authorized representative of the 

Secretaries of the Army, Navy and Air Force and was to be responsible to them for the proper performance of the delegated authority conferred in a charter approved June 17, 1949, by the three military departments.86

Basically, the Board finally determines claims which arise under contracts of the Departments concerned. Thus it hears, considers and determines as fully and finally as might each of the Secretaries, appeals by contractors from decisions on disputed questions by contracting officers or their authorized representatives, or pursuant to the provisions of any directives whereby the Secretary of a Department has granted a right of appeal. When an appeal is taken in connection with a contract which provides only for appeals from decisions on questions of fact, the Board may in its discretion hear and decide all questions of law necessary for the adjudication of the issue. Unless the contract provides otherwise, when in the consideration of an appeal it appears that a claim for unliquidated damages is involved, so far as the evidence permits the Board may make findings of fact with respect to such claims without expressing an opinion on the question of liability. When a contract requires the Secretary of a Department personally to render a decision on the matter in dispute, the Board submits its findings and recommendations to the Secretary of the Department concerned. 

There are three Panels of the Board, one each for the Army, Navy

(1958). 

86 ASPR, App. A (Jan. 3, 1955). 23

and Air Force, and appeals are assigned for decision to the Panel of the Department whose contract or procurement is directly involved. 

Each of the Panels acts in divisions which normally consist of three or more members of the Panel. Hearings may be held by a division, a designated member, or a duly authorized examiner. The decision of a majority of a division constitutes the decision of the Panel and of the Board, provided all three Panel Chairmen signify that in their opinion a review by the full Board is not required. If one or more Panel 

Chairmen do not waive review by the full Board, determination of the appeal is made by a majority of the members of the full Board. 

In consequence of a meeting called by the General Counsel of the Navy in 1954 and attended by the representatives of the Departments of the Army, Navy, Air Force and of the District of Columbia, Federal and American Bar Associations, studies and conferences took place aimed at revising the Rules of the Board. The work of the conferees received added impetus when the President of the United States, in acknowledging a report from a general conference he had called on Administrative Procedure, took occasion on March 3, 1955, to request each agency in the Executive Branch of the Government to consider ways in which its procedures could be improved. On June 30, 1955, the Board's 

Rules, in effect for the previous six years, were officially revised. Employing terms of accepted legal usage, the Rules described with clarity how appeals are to be taken, the content of a notice of appeal, the duties of the contracting officer, the complaint, the answer, amendments to proceedings, motions, depositions, interrogatories, prehearing conferences, the hearings themselves, examination of witnesses, briefs, etc.

$ 1.16. Finality of Decisions

Over the years, problems arose with respect to the finality and scope of judicial review of administrative decisions under the disputes clause. 

As a result of a series of cases in the Supreme Court " and in the Court of Claims 90 and based upon some want of clarity on the general subject, legislation was introduced in the Congress after publication in 1951 of the widely discussed case of United States v. Wunderlich." 

In that case, it was held that a finding by the head of a Department on a disputed question of fact, under a contract containing a standard disputes clause, may not be set aside unless it was founded on fraud, alleged and proved. The Supreme Court took the occasion to say that if another view should be deemed desirable it would be appropriate for the Congress to enact legislation. After extensive hearings, Congress enacted a statute, approved May 11, 1954, that no provision of any contract entered into by the United States relating to the finality or conclusiveness of any decision of a department head or board involving a contract question may be pleaded in any suit to be filed as limiting judicial review of any such decision to cases where fraud by the official or board is alleged. The statute provided that any such decision shall be final unless the same is fraudulent, capricious, arbitrary, so grossly erroneous as necessarily to imply bad faith, or is not supported by substantial evidence. IV. REQUESTS FOR RELIEF UNDER NAVY CONTRACTS $ 1.17. The First War Powers Act 

Somewhat allied to the subject of disputes under Navy contracts was the question of requests for relief under the First War Powers Act of 1941. It will be recalled that Executive Order 9001 provided that the 

War and Navy Departments and the U.S. Maritime Commission "may modify or amend or settle claims under contracts heretofore or hereafter made and may enter into agreements with contractors and/or obligors, modifying or releasing accrued obligations of any sort, including accrued liquidated damages or liability under surety or other bonds, whenever, in the judgment of the War Department (now the Department of the Army), the Navy Department, or the United States Maritime Commission, respectively, the prosecution of the war is thereby facilitated." It also went on to provide that "amendments and modifications of contracts may be with or without consideration and may be utilized to accomplish the same things as any original contract could have accomplished hereunder, irrespective of the time or circumstances of the making of or the form of the contract amended or modified or of the amending or modifying contract, and irrespective of rights which may have accrued under the contract, or the amendments or modifications thereof." 

Under this authority of Executive Order 9001 the Navy Department could relieve a contractor from an improvident commitment and could amend, modify or reform contracts without regard to the classic requirements for adequate consideration or mutuality of mistake, and notwithstanding the well-settled rules that an officer of the Government may not give away or surrender a right vested in the Government by contract 95 or modify the terms of a contract in a manner prejudicial to the best interests of the United States.9%

THE FIRST WAR POWERS ACT 

$ 1.17

In order to ensure some uniformity of policy in the granting of extraordinary relief under the First War Powers Act, the Office of Procurement and Material was required to approve requests or applications for relief, such action being taken only on the recommendation of the contracting officer and with the opinion of Counsel for the Bureau concerned that the requested relief might legally be granted under the First War 

Powers Act and Executive Order 9001.97 All such amendments or modi fications without consideration were required to be supported by a clear finding that the prosecution of the war would be facilitated thereby, which meant generally that the applicant for relief had to be an essential producer of war materials whose continued productivity was necessary to the war effort. Navy caution, prompted by OGC lawyers, was demonstrated in the directive of July 7, 1943, which warned against generosity to careless contractors and against relief based upon diminution of anticipated profits. Relief was authorized not only where a contractor's continued production was needed for the war effort but also where fairness, equity, and the consequent encouragement or stimulation of war production required the rectification of such inevitable instance of wartime procurement as serious (but honest) mistakes and reliance upon technically unauthorized requests or representations of government officials.98 Standardized procedures were established for passing upon contractors' application for this type of extra-contractual aid commonly known as "requests for relief." 99

Careful screening of requests for relief resulted in extraordinary relief being granted, as a matter of grace, in some 65 cases out of many hundreds of applications received, a further illustration of the restrained exercise by the Navy of the powers extended to it by Congress and the 

President during the war emergency.

$1.18. The Lucas Act 

This sudden cessation on V-J Day of the military departments' entertaining requests for relief meant that certain claimants whose requests might have been pending at that time, and upon which favorable action would have been taken but for the Japanese surrender, were victims of the fortunes of war. In order to extend relief to these persons, Congress in August of 1946 enacted legislation 2 sponsored by Senator Scott Lucas of Illinois and commonly referred to thereafter as the Lucas Act. This statute authorized those Departments to whom the extraordinary prerogatives of the First War Powers Act had been extended to entertain claims for war contract losses on the part of persons who had filed written requests for relief with the Department prior to August 14, 1945, and upon which final action had not been taken. Actually the statute had a very limited application, being confined to an authorization to the Departments to go forward and act upon claims for relief under the First War Powers Act which were pending on V-J Day and to afford them the same consideration that they would have been given but for the Japanese surrender on August 14, 1945, and the ending of hostilities. The legislative history of the act, and the President's regulations ³ issued thereunder, amply confirm this somewhat narrow application. Unfortunately, the act was not drafted with all the clarity that might have been desired, and it gave rise to a rather general misapprehension on the part of a number of contractors that it was a green light to the Departments to make good all losses incurred by persons engaged in war production. Proof of the Lucas Act's intimate connection with the First War Powers Act discretionary relief was found not only in its history but also in its wording and structure. Only agencies empowered to grant War 

Powers Act relief could grant Lucas Act relief, and only contractors who filed "requests for relief" the special designation for War Powers Act applications—before V-J Day could claim under the new act. Similarly, the new statute characterized awards as "relief," with the requisite that

At no time was there any real indication of a broad purpose alleged in various quarters of a concept which, if true, would be unprecedented in our history, namely to guarantee all war contractors against loss, or of a congressional desire to provide a special forum for the relitigation of all manner of claims usually within the jurisdiction of the Court of Claims or the District Courts. The Navy Department War Contracts Relief Board, established in the Secretary's office to consider claims filed under the act (and the equivalent Army Board), had to deny substantially all claims presented to it as not qualifying for relief under the narrow orbit of the statute. With the cessation of active hostilities on V-J Day this authority was returned to the General Accounting Office as required by its rules.?

The authority of the First War Powers Act of 1941 aided immeasureably in bringing about the successful prosecution of World War II, and its lessons motivated the Department of Defense, at the outbreak of the Korean conflict, to request that Title II of that act be revitalized. 

The Congress responded by enacting legislation which made Title II effective until June 30, 1952. Thereafter this legislation was successively extended until June 30, 1958.⁹

Without the authority of Title II or equivalent authority it would be difficult or impossible to employ some of the special procurement techniques which are necessary in times of partial mobilization. This authority has been used by the military departments in a number of ways. 

Provisions have been included in defense contracts to indemnify private contractors against losses due to war risks and other special hazards, without which contractors would not have undertaken the projects requested or would have had to include in the contract price exorbitant contingency allowances for such risks.12 This is best illustrated in the case of commercial aircraft transporting military cargo to combat areas such as in Korea. The possibility of being suddenly faced with a similar commercial airlift problem is not too remote for consideration.

Title II likewise has been used, as the need arose, to authorize the making of advance payments in existing contracts, including those awarded by formal advertising; the extension of delivery dates under existing contracts in appropriate cases; the expediting of ammunition production; the erection of nonseverable facilities in contractor-owned plants; the emergency sale of government-owned spare parts to civilian airlines to keep them in operation; and the making of toll agreements with scrap metal smelters whereby waiver is made of the usual legal requirement that the identical scrap metal received by the smelter from the Government be contained in the reclaimed ingot being returned to the Government.

Amendments without consideration have been granted where an actual or threatened loss on a defense contract would impair the productive ability of a contractor whose continued operation as a source of supply is found to be essential to the national defense. OFFICE OF NAVAL RESEARCH ESTABLISHED 

$ 1.21 alties and patent infringements. The all-pervasive scope of production for total war and defense inevitably meant that the Government and its contractors were compelled to avail themselves of patented techniques and processes on an unprecedented scale, posing problems of negotiating innumerable license agreements at royalty rates that would not be exorbitant and of protecting the Government against potential infringement claims 27 that could well have run into billions of dollars.28 In addition, means had to be devised of reconciling a needed stimulation for inventiveness and for improved techniques for war and defense production with the fact that what the taxpayers were paying for should belong to all the people and not become the patent monopoly of the inventor. 

The Navy's patent organization in the days of peace preceding World War II was more or less haphazard and uncoordinated. The Bureau of Ships, the Bureau of Ordnance and the Bureau of Aeronautics each had patent sections of their own with little integration of activity or coordination of effort between them. They were staffed for the most part with persons technically qualified in patent law occupied principally with questions of novelty, validity, patentability, infringement, and the like. However, since agreements affecting patents or licenses negotiated by the patent section of one Bureau affected not only the whole Navy Department but frequently the entire Government, some centralized coordination over the handling of patent matters became essential. 

$ 1.21. Office of Naval Research Established 

On August 15, 1942, the Secretary of the Navy directed 29 that all patent matters relating to or affecting procurement should be coordinated and handled in the Procurement Legal Division which established a patent section for that purpose. Subsequently, active administration over all patent matters in the Navy Department was taken over by a new office, the Office of Patents and Inventions, which in turn was superseded seven months later by the Office of Research and Inventions, in a desire to wed the greatly increased research activities of the Navy to the patents and inventions group. By Public Law 588 of the 79th 

Congress, approved August 1, 1946,30 statutory permanence was accorded this organizational development by the establishment of the Office of Naval Research which was charged with the supervision over and coordination of all research within the Navy and over patents, inven- 27 The Government's consent to suit for patent infringement is granted by 28
