$ 1.22. Patent Indemnification and License Agreements 

In an effort to reduce the substantial potential liability of the Government for patent infringement, the Navy Department early in World War II adopted the policy of securing from its contractors indemnity against liability for patent infringement arising out of the performance of the contract,32 an exception being made where the infringement resulted from direct and necessary compliance with written specifications or instructions developed and furnished to the contractor by the Government. Although industry evinced some reluctance to accept this risk itself, the Navy succeeded in making patent indemnification a condition of virtually all of its procurement.

From the holders of privately-owned basic patents whose use was essential to war and defense production a concerted effort was made to secure license agreements which were either royalty-free or provided for a reduction or limitation of royalties. That the effort proved eminently successful was due principally to industry's patriotic support and in part to the recurrent threats on the part of Congress to open all patents to royalty-free government use for the period of the war with a compensatory pro tanto extension of the life of the patent after the conclusion of the war.

With respect to any such license entered into subsequent to 

September 9, 1939, by Public Law 694, 81st Congress, Congress, in 1950, authorized the cancellation thereof by virtue of changes in circumstances which occurred since the granting of such license.33 In short, it appeared to be the equitable thing to do.

However, the most vexatious question with respect to patent rights which grew out of the Government's extensive participation in and financing of industrial production during World War II was that of defining the rights to be acquired by the Government and the contractor respectively in inventions conceived, or of developments and improvements made in prior conceptions, during the course of performance of work paid for by the Government. The problem became particularly acute as greater intensification of effort and emphasis was placed upon government-sponsored research and development. The solution espoused by some, particularly the Attorney General, was that all inventions resulting from the performance of work paid for by the Government 

31 SecNav Inst. 5430.20 (June 24, 1954). 

32 NPD 13,821 (1943 ed.). 

33 64 Stat. 448 (1950). 34

PATENT INDEMNIFICATION AND LICENSE AGREEMENTS 

$ 1.22 should belong to the Government and not be the subject of patent monopoly. The difficulty with this approach was, first, that by withdrawing the reward it went far toward eliminating all incentive for inventiveness at a time when the rapidly advancing techniques of war required a maximum stimulation of inventive effort. Second, it over-simplified the problem. The units of industry selected for research into particular fields were principally those with the most experience in that field, staffed with experts in the particular area of science in which lay the problem that the Government wished to have solved. Thus, in the case of many an invention conceived during the course of performance of the government work, it was both impossible to segregate and inequitable to ignore years of prior experimentation and development in the field for which the Government did not pay. Furthermore, a patented invention in the abstract is of little real value: it is the constant development and reduction to practice which lends value to the invention. If it is to fall into the public domain, available to all comers, the incentive which the patent holder would otherwise have constantly to develop and give practical application to his invention either dies or the incentive must be furnished by the Government itself financing the endeavor through a series of developments contracts. 

During the war, the Navy Department developed a policy, reflected by its standard contract patent clauses, of asking only for a non-exclusive, royalty-free license for governmental purposes under inventions made, conceived or reduced to practice in connection with the performance of work under government-financed research and development contracts, leaving title to the patent with the contractor. The same policy was followed, of obtaining so-called "shop rights" or implied licenses, with respect to inventions of employees, except with respect to those inventions flowing directly from the project and purpose for which the employee was hired.

Having established a policy for the treatment of inventions first actually reduced to practice at government expense under a contract, the problem remained, however, of adequately defining, as a matter of contract draftsmanship, the inventions to which the "shop rights" policy should be applied. An invention is more frequently the result of a continuous process of experimentation and growth of ideas than it is a spontaneous conception. Hence, it became necessary carefully to delimit from the application of the "shop rights" principle those concepts which in fact were the result of a contractor's work and development in the field prior to the time of the Government's sponsorship under a research or development contract. For some time the approach was employed of arbitrarily excluding from the application of the "shop rights" clause inventions on which applications for patent had been filed prior to the date of the contract (a constructive reduction to practice) or on which so- 35

$ 1.

called "paper" patents had issued. However, this approach ignored the fact that after the filing of an application or even after the issuance of a patent there usually remains considerable refining and development before practical use can be made of an invention. If the Government pays for this development and "actual reduction to practice," should it still have to pay royalties for the right to employ the invention? Accordingly, it has been decided to adopt the principle of requiring a nonexclusive license, for governmental purposes, under all inventions actually reduced to practice in connection with performance under the contract unless in a particular case the equities of the situation clearly justify an exception. 

§ 1.23. Patent Secrecy 

The problem of security and patents, similarly, has not been easy of solution. Applications pending in the Patent Office are preserved in secrecy and are not open to public inspection, but copies of Letters Patent, when issued, can be purchased by anyone for 25 cents a copy. Manifestly, in connection with inventions of a classified nature, some means had to be found of preserving the secrecy not only by withholding the issuance of the patent but by charging the inventor and those in privity with him with an obligation not to reveal the invention. This required reconciling the rights of an inventor under the patent laws with the public interest against disclosure of his work. In July 1940 Congress amended the Patent Secrecy Act of 1917 to authorize the Commissioner of Patents, whenever he deemed that disclosure might be detrimental to the public safety or defense, to order an invention to be kept secret and to withhold the issuance of a patent thereon for such period as the national interest might require.34 In order that the Commissioner of Patents might be advised which disclosures of inventions might be prejudicial to national security, contractors performing work under classified Navy contracts were required to submit all applications for patents relating to the subject matter of the contract to the contracting officer in advance, or at the time of filing in the Patent Office, in order that he might make appropriate recommendations relative to their being held in secrecy. As an additional security precaution provision was made in contracts classified as "secret" or higher for an assignment to the Government of all the contractor's right, title and interest in all patent applications disclosing the subject matter of the contract or any part thereof. The assignment is one in trust with provision for reverter to the contractor when secrecy is no longer important. By virtue of the assignment, notwithstanding the expiration of the Secrecy Statute upon the termination of the war, issuance of the patent could be indefinitely delayed, without abandonment on the part of the applicant, by reason of the special provisions of sec-

THE ROYALTY ADJUSTMENT ACT OF 1942 

$ 1.24 tion 4894 of the Revised Statutes.35 By renewing the certification required by this statute every three years, an application could be kept pending indefinitely, and publication of the invention by the grant of a patent could be indefinitely postponed. The wartime Secrecy Statute was repealed and superseded by the Invention Secrecy Act of 1951.36 

The Invention Secrecy Act is permanent legislation, and under its provisions the Commissioner of Patents is authorized to maintain an invention secret and withhold the grant of a patent for successive one-year periods upon notification by the head of the department or the chief officer of the agency who caused the order to be issued that an affirmative determination has been made that the national interest continues so to require. In periods of national emergency the act does not require yearly determination to achieve this end. Accordingly, in order indefinitely to postpone the grant of a patent, it is no longer necessary to have recourse to reverter assignments and special statutory provisions 37 with respect to contractors' applications for patents relating to the subject matter of classified contracts. 

$ 1.24. The Royalty Adjustment Act of 1942 

Finally, in order to eliminate the payment of excessive patent royalties which the Government was called upon to pay for the use of patented inventions in connection with war procurement and to permit the Government to utilize patented and unpatented inventions through the medium of any desired source of supply without having to pay more than a fair and just compensation to the owners of such inventions, Congress, in October of 1942, passed the Royalty Adjustment Act.38 The primary purpose of the act, as stated by the Supreme Court, was to reduce royalties for which the United States was ultimately liable, from prewar rates to rates appropriate to the volume of production in wartime.39 The authority conferred by the act on the Secretary of the Navy to revise and adjust patent royalty rates was delegated by him to the Patent Royalty 

Revision Board composed of the Chief of Naval Research as Chairman and seven members selected and appointed by the Secretary of the Navy from personnel of procurement bureaus having a general background in contractual and procurement matters coupled with some knowledge of production and frequently also experienced in legal or patent matters. 

For the Department of the Navy all matters relating to royalty payments as an item of cost to the Government are forwarded to, and are reviewed and administered by personnel in the Office of the Assistant Chief of

VI. POST-WAR PROCUREMENT LEGISLATION $1.25. The Armed Services Procurement Act of 1947 

The lessons learned under the wide latitude of the First War Powers Act-that negotiated contracts, far from leading to higher prices or the concentration of procurement in the hands of larger and more favored producers, more often than not led to lower costs and to a wider distribution of suppliers would have gone into the discard upon the termination of the First War Powers Act authority 44 and the Navy would perforce have had to revert to the mechanical process of securing its requirements only after formal advertising.

Two things were clearly apparent at the end of the war: first, that the Services had demonstrated an ability to use with judgment, discretion, and sound business sense the broad procurement powers granted them during the war; and, second, that to compel a return to the inflexible procedures of formal advertising would mean that supplying the needs of the military would soon revert to a relatively small group of professional government suppliers, with the consequent loss of the invaluable "know-how" and ability to furnish military requirements acquired by industry during the war years. The outstanding lesson of the war was that industrial power is a critical factor of no less value than trained manpower and that the obligations of those government agencies concerned with national defense cannot be met without the maintenance of a powerful industrial structure.

THE ARMED SERVICES PROCUREMENT ACT OF 1947 

$ 1.25 

In order that government peacetime procurement might become an instrument for keeping this vital weapon in a state of readiness, the War Production Board, through its Procurement Policy Board, recommended in November 1945 that the government agencies propose procurement legislation to take effect when the emergency procurement legislation expired. The proposed legislation, while retaining for the most part the formal advertising method of procurement, was to make provision for broad authority to negotiate the price and other contract terms when judgment and circumstances so dictated and was to dispense entirely with formal advertising during any future national emergency. 

The report of the Procurement Policy Board pointed to a number of fields in which formal advertising was either inadequate or costly: the report adverted, by way of illustration, to contracts required for security reasons to be kept secret, to contracts for research and development work where experience in the field and capacity to conduct the research preclude effective competition, to contracts for items involving high starting load costs, to contracts for items for which assurance of a source of supply is required, to contracts for items for which it is desirable to prevent the supply from becoming concentrated in a few sources or in dangerous areas, and to contracts for items where the limited sources of supply preclude effective price competition. The report adverted further to the lack of authority to negotiate when necessary to secure protection against the many practices which result in non-competitive or unreasonable prices under formal advertising. 

In accordance with these recommendations a bill was prepared and introduced in the 80th Congress on January 27, 1947, as H.R. 1366, the 

Armed Services Procurement bill. The bill had the effect of pulling all Army and Navy procurement authority together under one statute, sweeping out archaic laws in the process and paving the way for coordination and uniformity of practice between the Armed Services in the field of military procurement in consonance with the purposes of unification.45 It made no radical departures but rather preserved sound and tested wartime methods of procurement when appropriate or desirable for reasons of economy or national security.

With few significant changes of substance but with several perfecting modifications during the legislative process, H.R. 1366 was finally approved by the President on February 19, 1948, as Public Law 413 of the 80th Congress, but only after very full and careful review and analysis by the Armed Services Committees of both the House and Senate, each of which held extended hearings on the bill. It became effective as to all procurement of the Armed Services ninety days after enact-

VII. OCEAN TRANSPORTATION $ 1.26. The Military Sea Transportation Service 

Just as the Navy's combat ships protect the United States on the sea lanes of the world, so the Navy provides the shipping services on those lanes to transport personnel and supplies vital to the success of military missions abroad. Ships were chartered for this purpose as long ago as the Mexican War, with the Army Transport Service and the Collier Service, forerunner of the Naval Auxiliary Service, being established in 1898. During World War II the Army and the Navy operated individual ocean shipping services, but as the result of a study initiated thereafter by the Joint Chiefs of Staff, a more centralized and uniform control of the ships of the military establishment was directed and the Military Sea Transportation Service was established. 

The duties of the agency encompass the transoceanic movement of and logistic support for all Army, Navy and Air Force military forces outside the United States and for other government agencies when such transportation is sponsored by the Department of Defense.

APPLICABILITY OF ADMIRALTY LAW

It is important to note in this respect that admiralty law, with its roots in the civil and general maritime law of Europe rather than in common law, embodies numerous principles which are completely foreign to the general scheme of common and statutory law with which we in the Navy are most familiar.64 Some of these are discussed below. 

Admiralty law is essentially federal law and relatively uniform as to substance and practice throughout the United States. The Constitution itself includes jurisdiction over maritime matters in the judicial power granted to the federal government.65 The extent of this jurisdiction has been determined by the maritime nature and relations of the subject matter involved, the purpose of the Constitutional assignment thereof to the federal government, the scope of jurisdiction as it has existed among maritime nations throughout the world, and its development in America.66 

Maritime liens, specifically provided for by federal statute," are enforced in the case of privately-owned vessels by the assertion of a right in rem against the vessel itself. One who has a contract, to which a ship is bound, and which is breached, or who, through the instrumentality of the ship, has suffered a wrong that is within the maritime jurisdiction, has by way of security or redress an enforceable interest in the ship itself. 

The mode of enforcement is that the ship is condemned and sold under a decree which, as it is founded on dominion over the res, binds not only

Admiralty procedures and principles take into consideration the mobile nature of ships and the necessity of protecting against both the possibility of vessels stealing away and interference with their use. Thus, in admiralty the means of payment is secured before liability has been determined, the reverse of the more usual occurrence at common law. The assurance that payment can be made is accomplished by use of the in rem and attachment process referred to above. Similarly, separate rules of court for admiralty have been promulgated," rules which provide for a less complicated and more expeditious system 70 than obtains in other federal court proceedings.

Contrary to the generally accepted common-law principle of contributory negligence, admiralty courts may divide damages on the basis of mutual fault. In collision cases, when both parties are determined to have been at fault, the damages are divided equally regardless of the degree of fault." Likewise, in maritime personal injury cases, a doctrine of comparative negligence is sometimes applied with resulting diminution in the amount of recovery.72 $ 1.29. General Average

General average 73 is a concept unique to the maritime law. A general average act is defined as any extraordinary sacrifice or expenditure intentionally, reasonably and successfully made or incurred for the common safety in order to preserve the common maritime venture. The several interests engaged in the maritime venture are required to make good the loss by contributing to the extraordinary sacrifices or expenditures in proportion to the share of each in the adventure.74 

The obligation to contribute is now invariably imposed by a contractual provision which is incorporated in all commercial contracts for the water 68 There is no in rem remedy against United States Government vessels. LIMITATION OF LIABILITY 

$ 1.30 carriage of goods; however, a similar obligation could arise under admiralty law, as a matter of equity, entirely independent of contract. Before there can be a valid claim for general average contribution, it is necessary that the ship and cargo should have been placed in a common, imminent peril, that there should have been a voluntary expenditure or sacrifice of property to avert the peril and to accomplish the safe prosecution of the voyage, and that by that sacrifice or expenditure the safety of the contributing property should have been successfully attained. 

Contribution, if all the necessary conditions prevail, is based upon the principle that whatever is sacrificed for the common safety should be made good by all the interests which were exposed to the common peril and which were saved from that common danger by the sacrifice. The contributing interests are primarily the vessel, the cargo, and the freight, the latter meaning the sum the ship is able to earn as a result of the successful sacrifice.

General average may be declared as the result of practically any type of marine casualty or misadventure, such as fire, jettison of cargo, voluntary and involuntary stranding, damage to hull, machinery and boilers, heavy weather, salvage, foundering, and collision. 

$ 1.30. - Limitation of Liability 

The law of the maritime nations agrees that a shipowner should not be forced to commit himself to greater liability than the value of his ship in the event of maritime casualty or disaster. The concept is based on the desire to nurture shipping by protecting the vessel owners and operators against risking all their resources in a single venture.75 

By legislation in the United States, this liability has been somewhat increased. While an owner may limit his liability against all manner of claims to the amount or value of his interest in the vessel which gave rise to the claims, if that interest is insufficient to pay all losses in full, and if personal injury or loss of life is involved, his liability is increased to an amount equal to $60.00 per ton of the vessel's tonnage. This right to limit liability is given to an owner irrespective of fault of himself or his servants. However, that limitation is broken if the owner, or in the case of a corporation, the managing officials, have imputed to them personal privity or knowledge of the condition which caused the loss. Incidentally, a limitation proceeding not only permits an owner to limit his liability but also serves the useful purpose of consolidating all claims in one action and having those claims tried in one forum.

Admiralty Claims 

The essentially maritime nature of issues arising under MSTS contracts can perhaps best be illustrated by citing a few examples of the many types of maritime claims with which the Navy is concerned. 

(1) Cargo Claims. Commercial carriers are liable under appropriate circumstances for pilferage, damage and short-landings of government cargo carried under MSTS commercial contracts. By the 

Carriage of Goods by Sea Act,82 which is applicable to all foreign voyages from or to United States ports, a carrier's liability is limited to losses caused by a failure of due diligence to make the carrying vessel seaworthy prior to the start of the voyage or by a failure of care and custody of cargo during the voyage. There is no liability for damage caused by fire unless such fire was caused by circumstances within the personal privity and knowledge of the owners or managing officials of the carrier. The carrier is expressly exonerated from liability for damage caused by errors in navigation or management of the master or owner's other servants aboard the carrying vessel. Even in cases in which the carrier is liable, liability is limited to $500 per package or customary freight unit for unpackaged goods. 

(2) General Average. All MSTS contracts for the carriage of government cargo by commercial vessels provide, as do comparable contracts for the carriage of private cargo, for the payment of contribution in general average and for salvage. General average by contract provision is adjusted in accordance with York-Antwerp Rules 83 which were agreed upon by international convention among the various maritime nations. 

General average contribution is payable by the Government as cargo owner regardless of fault or negligence by the vessel's owner or servants except where the incident was caused by a failure to exercise due diligence to make the vessel seaworthy. This result is achieved in the United States by a standard clause known as the

(3) Unsafe Berth Damage. Under MSTS contracts, the Govern ment is responsible for the loading and discharging of its cargo aboard commercial vessels. It warrants the safety of loading and discharging berths in conformance with customary commercial practice and must respond in damages for any breach of its warranty resulting in damage. $ 1.32. Jurisdiction Over Maritime Contract Suits 

To attorneys concerned with MSTS contracts, perhaps the most important area of difference between maritime contracts and other government contracts is that of jurisdiction and the statutory basis for suits against the Government. The Suits in Admiralty Act 86 and the 

Public Vessels Act 7 afford the exclusive remedy against the Government in all cases to which they are applicable. This is particularly significant to MSTS contractors since the period of limitations under both of these Acts is two years rather than the six-year period which pertains to suits in the Court of Claims and District Courts under the Tucker Act.89 It has not been uncommon, in the recent past, for government contractors suing on maritime claims to learn to their sorrow that jurisdiction does not exist under the Tucker Act and that their action is time-barred.90

statute of limitations makes for unique litigation problems. Administrative processing is frequently not completed at the end of the twoyear period of limitation. This places contractors on the horns of a dilemma. A failure to file suit at that point will defeat any judicial action; on the other hand, a suit can be dismissed as premature on general principles of administrative law for failure to exhaust administrative remedies. Admiralty Courts have met this problem by stating that while the time limitation starts running when the breach occurs and not upon the exhaustion of administrative remedies, litigation will not be dismissed because suit was filed prior to the completion of the administrative processing procedure." Instead, such litigation will be held in suspense pending completion of the administrative processing unless the suit has been filed so prematurely that it is possible for administrative processing to be completed before the end of the two-year statutory limitation. In the latter case at least one court has dismissed the litigation without prejudice with permission to refile the litigation within the two-year period, if it should be necessary.92 Also, somewhat contrary to the usual custom, the Department of Justice and the Navy have an understanding that, because of the short limitation period, MSTS should continue to process claims administratively, even though litigation has been filed, if the libelant stipulates that protective litigation was filed only to avoid the defense of time-bar.

Traditionally, as noted earlier, ship-repair contracts are maritime and cognizable in admiralty. This has made for some doubt as to the jurisdictional basis for suits against the Government arising out of the repair of government-owned public vessels. The Suits in Admiralty 

Act is applicable if the vessel has a merchant vessel status. However, this statute does not cover most MSTS public vessels. The Public 

Vessels Act, the other jurisdictional statute providing for admiralty suits against the Government, permits suit for "damages caused by a public vessel." 93 If ship repair claims under the master ship repair contract are considered to be "damages caused by a public vessel," the District Courts are the only proper forums and the two-year limitation period controls. If, on the other hand, ship repair contract claims cannot be brought within "damages caused by a public vessel," these claims should be brought in the Court of Claims or in the District Courts under the Tucker Act, and a six-year limitation period is applicable. The First Circuit has indicated that a ship repair claim against the Government could probably not be brought under the Public Ves-

Combinations of Items VIII. AWARD OF CONTRACT $2.1. Introduction 

99 1 Since 1809 most federal government contracts for supplies and services have been required by statute to be made by advertised competitive bidding, a procedure generally known as "procurement by formal advertising." Comparable requirements have long prevailed for state and municipal contracts.2 Since May 19, 1948, the procurement of supplies and services by the military departments and certain other federal agencies has been governed by the Armed Services Procurement Act of 1947.3

On August 10, 1956, this act was codified into positive law as Chapter 137 

of Title 10, United States Code.3 The provisions of this act relating to procurement by formal advertising by the military departments are codified in 10 U.S.C. §§ 2304 (a) and 2305. § 2304 (a) provides that: 

Purchases and contracts for property or services covered by this chapter shall be made by formal advertising. However, the head of an agency may negotiate such a purchase or contract, if-4 § 2305, in turn, provides: (a) Whenever formal advertising is required under section 2304 of this title, the advertisement shall be made a sufficient time before the purchase or contract. The specifications and invitations for bids shall permit such free and full competition as is consistent with the procurement of the property and services needed by the agency concerned. (b) The specifications in invitations for bids must contain the necessary language and attachments, and must be sufficiently descriptive in language and attachments, to permit full and free competition. If the specifications in an invitation for bids do not carry the necessary descriptive language and attachments, or if those attachments are not accessible to all competent and reliable bidders, the invitation is invalid and no award may be made.5 (c) Bids shall be opened publicly at the time and place stated in the advertisement. Awards shall be made with reasonable promptness by giving written notice to the responsible bidder whose bid conforms to the invitation and will be the most advantageous to the 

United States, price and other factors considered. However, all bids may be rejected if the head of the agency determines that rejection is in the public interest. (d) If the head of the agency considers that any bid received after formal advertising evidences a violation of the antitrust laws, he shall refer the bid to the Attorney General for appropriate action. 

The considerations of public policy underlying procurement by means of formal advertising have been stated as follows:

The purpose of these statutes and regulations [requiring formal advertising] is to give all persons equal right to compete for Government contracts; to prevent unjust favoritism, or collusion or

The statutory procedures of procurement by formal advertising quoted above are amplified by the Armed Services Procurement Regulation (hereinafter "ASPR”), which reflects many of the detailed requirements of competitive bidding prescribed by statutes antecedent to the Armed Services Procurement Act and administrative practices and rulings under these prior statutes, especially under section 3709 of the Revised Statutes (hereinafter Rev. However, many questions of law remain and invite recourse to opinions of the Attorney General, to administrative rulings of the Comptroller General, and to judicial decisions concerning public contracts, officers and funds. In a brief survey of some of these questions, this chapter will consider procedures and precedents concerning (i) advertising for bids, (ii) the submission of bids and the firm-bid rule, (iii) mistakes in bids, (iv) rejection of all bids, (v) nonconforming bids, (vi) responsible bidders, (vii) the evaluation of bids as to price and other factors, and (viii) the awarding of contracts.

I. ADVERTISING FOR BIDS $ 2.2. Methods of Advertising 

It has been repeatedly held under Rev. Stat. § 37097 that the selection of a particular method of advertising is left to agency discretion. ASPR 

2-202.2⁹ provides for displaying a copy of the invitation for bids in the purchasing office or other appropriate public place and mailing or delivering invitations for bids to a representative selection of prospective bidders. This procedure has been approved by the Comptroller General.10 

In the use of this method the purchasing office provides prospective bidders with the following standard forms: Invitation for Bids and Bid 

(S.F. 30), Schedule (S.F. 31), and General Provisions (S.F. 32). The contract with the successful bidder consists of the invitation for bids, the bid, and the award.

Paid advertisements in newspapers are seldom used by the Navy for the solicitation of bids; when used, the invitation for bids must also be mailed

In the cases discussed below, the advertisement for bids was found by the Comptroller General to be inadequate because of (i) the method of solicitation adopted, (ii) the time allowed for bidding, or (iii) the distribution given the invitation for bids.

Invitation for Bids

An invitation for bids states the Government's terms of a proposed contract for the procurement of specified supplies or services and requests suppliers to offer (by bids in sealed envelopes, such bids to be received before a time fixed for public opening) to furnish such supplies or services in accordance with such terms. A bid conforming to the essential terms of the invitation becomes a contract to furnish the offered supplies or services upon its acceptance by the Government within the specified acceptance time.

The invitation must disclose fully the precise requirements of the Government concerning each item to be furnished, but avoid improperly restrictive specifications or conditions that would justify protest by prospective bidders or invalidate the resulting award. Further, the invitation should state any factors of bid evaluation, other than price, that may determine the award,22 such as provisions that time of delivery is an important factor, that bids be on a minimum quantity or combination of items, that bid samples are required, or that bidders' qualification of their

SPECIFICATIONS 

$ 2.4 products prior to opening of bids is a condition of eligibility for award. 

If the invitation provides that time of delivery is an important factor and may result in award to other than the low bidder, the invitation should also make appropriate provision for the Government to recover the difference between the low bid price and the contract price if the promised delivery time is not met.23 $2.4. Specifications

As a general rule, the specifications of the invitation for bids must define the item to be furnished in sufficiently definite terms to assure that each bid made in compliance therewith will be for substantially the same product or service, so that all bidders may compete on a common basis and assure the Government of the lowest available price.24 Specifications must be drawn with regard for the actual minimum needs of the Government and may not reflect mere administrative preferences for a particular make or brand,25 or favor the product of any individual or class of suppliers over others, the test being what is required, not what may be desired.26 Nor may requirements be advertised repeatedly on varying specifications to gain a preferential result.27 

It is not proper to prepare the invitation in a manner that will permit or require bidders to draft their own specifications without any standard as to the Government's minimum needs, for this not only prevents competition but fails to furnish a common basis for the evaluation of bids.28 

For example, an award for drapery material was voided because the invitation merely asked bidders in effect to display their wares, leaving the contracting officer free to "shop around" among the samples and select preferred material.29 However, a requirement for bid samples in conjunction with adequate specifications may be allowed if necessary to determine whether offered items will in fact conform.30 

Specifications may not be limited to particular makes or brands unless

Further, the deceptively easy course of referring to particular commercial articles, "or equal," has been criticized as a general practice, even where problems of considerable difficulty are presented in the drafting of proper specifications, for it amounts to a requirement that, unless otherwise specified, compliance with every detail of the specified commercial article is necessary to meet the needs of the Government. By analogy, competitive bidding may not be evaded by the preferential use of renewal options,56 or extension of existing contracts,57 or by the improper addition of new work by contract amendment.58 $ 2.6. Bidder's Experience 

The often difficult problem of determining the responsibility of bidders prior to award has led to attempts to define in the invitation minimum standards for a bidder's eligibility in terms of experience or past performance of work of a comparable kind and magnitude. The Comptroller 

General has sharply restricted this practice, holding that an invitation usually may not condition the right to bid upon a showing of minimum requirements for eligibility for award, or otherwise restrict the eligibility of suppliers by unreasonable requirements as to past experience.59 Nevertheless, the application of this general principle has varied in different categories of cases. Where the construction of public works was involved, the requirement that a bidder must show two comparable installations that had been in operation for at least two years was not questioned, and the disregarding of a bidder organized only eight months previously was approved.60 And a similar decision states that it is proper to require bidders to give satisfactory evidence of having been regularly engaged in performing the kind of work in question and to have examples of such work available for examination in the local area or elsewhere in the country. Where supplies or technical equipment affecting safety or health are involved, more latitude has been allowed than in other cases. 

Thus the Comptroller General reviewed without objection the requirement of an invitation for the furnishing of chlorination equipment that bids would be accepted only from persons experienced in water sterilization by chlorine who had been in such business for at least five years and had made other satisfactory installations.62 Again, where the procurement of special skilled services alone is involved, greater latitude has been permitted in restricting competition to experienced suppliers. COMPLIANCE WITH FEDERAL AND STATE LAWS 

$ 2.7 ample, in proposed procurements of technical services to prepare documentary motion pictures and to perform building management services, the Comptroller General held that it would be proper to limit the competition to qualified suppliers, either by stating the necessary qualifications in the invitation or by restricting the circulation to persons or firms known to possess the necessary equipment and requisite degree of skill.63 $ 2.7. 

Compliance With Federal and State Laws 

Invitations for bids may not impose conditions that tend to limit competition unless required by statute or otherwise permitted in the public interest.64 For example, the Comptroller General has held that there was no authority to provide for compliance with the National Labor Relations Act, there being no statute requiring compliance with that act as a condition of doing business with the Government.65 However, where the possession of an ICC permit would be a necessary prerequisite to the performance of interstate armed-car services and thus affect the bidder's ability to perform, it was held that ordinarily the invitation should restrict competition to the holders of such permits, but if no qualified bidders responded, upon readvertisement the invitation might permit the submission of bids conditioned upon the obtaining of a permit by the successful bidder prior to award.“

The principle that competition may not be restricted unnecessarily applies also with respect to stipulations in invitations requiring compliance with state laws. It was long the position of the Comptroller General that all contracts with the federal government were subject to an implied constitutional immunity from any state regulation and that all bidders therefore were free to perform such contracts without regard to otherwise applicable state requirements. Accordingly, it was consistently held improper to restrict competition by provisions in invitations specifying bidders' compliance with state regulations, such as those concerning the licensing of carriers 67 and compliance with established transportation rates 68 or minimum prices for milk.69 The Supreme Court has limited the broad constitutional premise of that position, but the principle stands where particular grounds of federal immunity are applicable.70

Competitive Bidding Limited to Small Business Concerns 

Arrangements between the Department of Defense and the Small Business Administration created by the Small Business Act of 1953 71 provide for the award of certain procurements to small business concerns by means of "Small Business Restricted Advertising," conducted generally in the manner prescribed by Section II of ASPR and subject to the same legal requirements,72 except that the invitation restricts bids and awards to small business concerns and the contract is awarded pursuant to section 214 of the Small Busine. s Act of 1953. $2.9. Information to Bidders

No person employed by the Government may render assistance to any bidder in the preparation of his bid or otherwise act to the prejudice of any other bidder or the interests of the Government. Information that may impair competition, such as the estimated cost of the supplies or services, may not be included in the invitation or otherwise disclosed. 

And the principle that all bidders must be afforded equal opportunity to compete requires that no disclosures or commitments may be made to any bidder that might give him an advantage over others.73 Subject to these limitations and the restrictions concerning the divulging of classified security information, information concerning the supplies or services to be procured, including the right to examine standard samples, plans, or specifications not set forth in the invitation, should be furnished upon request to any potential bidder. If ambiguities or inconsistencies in the invitation that might cause nonresponsive bids are discovered, they should be corrected by issuing a timely amendment to the invitation for bids or by cancelling the invitation prior to the time for opening of bids. $ 2.10.

Revision or Cancellation of Invitations for Bids 

The invitation may be revised or cancelled prior to the opening of bids as the interest of the Government may require. Invitation amendments or modifications are displayed with the posted copy of the invitation and are furnished to all recipients of the invitation, with the instruction that acknowledged copies must be returned to the issuing office prior to the time set for bid opening. The opening date is extended when necessary to allow the timely return of acknowledged amendments. In the event of cancellation, all bids received are returned unopened to the bidders.

II. BIDDING $2.11. Bidder's Legal Position Prior to Acceptance of Bid 

The authority to advertise for bids implies the power to prescribe reasonable terms and conditions.74 Nonconformance of a bid to such terms ordinarily requires its rejection.75 Under the "firm-bid rule," discussed in § 2.17, the bidder, after bid opening and prior to award, is bound by his bid as submitted, subject to important exceptions.76 The 

Government, however, is not bound by an invitation for bids or by any resulting bid since laws concerning the advertising and award of public contracts are for its benefit and protection, and no bidder acquires enforceable rights thereunder until the valid acceptance of his offer by an official authorized to do so.77 $ 2.12. Alternative Bids

Offers of alternative bids for source or destination delivery are proper when requested by the invitation; and unless forbidden by the invitation, bidders may offer alternative bids, one for each item and another on condition of an "all or none" award of a specified group of items.78 Alternative offers must be clearly stated to permit proper evaluation, and as with other conditions of the bid, ordinarily they may not be withdrawn or modified after bid opening." 

§ 2.13. Execution of Bids 

The authority of a person to execute a bid is of particular importance because a bidder may not elect after bid opening whether or not to be bound. As a general rule, a bidder may, after bid opening, establish the authority or lack of authority of its agent or employee at the time of bid execution, but may not be permitted to cure an earlier lack of authority by ratification after bid opening." The United States does not contract with undisclosed principals, and the failure of an agent to disclose the agency may render him liable as the principal contractor.82 The terms of the invitation provide that bids signed by an agent must be accompanied by evidence of his authority, but this requirement, protecting

Telegraphic Bids

The printed terms of the invitation preclude telegraphic bids unless expressly authorized, but permit bid modification by telegraphic notice received prior to the time set for bid opening. However, the Comptroller General has ruled that an unauthorized but timely telegraphic bid could be considered where the bidder clearly could not have had any knowledge of the other bids and thereby have gained an advantage over other bidders. Ordinarily, telegraphic bids are authorized only when bidders would not have sufficient time to prepare and submit bids on the prescribed forms and the short opening time is otherwise proper. The invitation must clearly state the conditions of any such authorization and require telegraphic bids to identify the invitation and items bid upon, and, except as specifically qualified in the telegram, to state the bidder's acceptance of all terms and conditions of the invitation, schedule, and general provisions. $2.15. In one case a crafty bidder during the opening of bids walked up and down the hall in front of the bid room, exclaiming, "Where can that messenger boy be with my bid?" At length the messenger arrived and gave an envelope to the bidder who handed it to the contracting officer. 

This bid proved to be the lowest. Becoming suspicious, the contracting officer interrogated the messenger who confessed that his delivery of one of two envelopes depended upon a prearranged hand signal, and the bidder's attempt to secure an unfair advantage over other bidders by the use of this "one if by land, two if by sea" system of signalling was frustrated.

 $ 2.16. Bid Opening 10 U.S.C. § 2305 (c) (formerly § 3(b) of the Armed Services Procure ment Act) provides that "Bids shall be publicly opened at the time and place stated in the advertisement." ASPR 2-401 and 2-402 95 provide procedures for the security of bids and the opening, reading (aloud when practicable), and recording of bids. If bids are opened prematurely and other bids are subsequently received prior to the set time, the rejection of all bids ordinarily is required; but in one such case it was held that a timely bid received after an inadvertently premature opening could be considered without readvertisement upon full proof that no advantage thereby accrued to the bidder and no prejudice to other bidders in fact resulted.9%

In a case under Rev. Stat. § 3709, the Attorney General said that the designation of 2 o'clock for the opening of all proposals means only that such proposals shall not be opened before 2 o'clock and does not preclude consideration of a bid received by mail shortly after 2 o'clock, provided it is certain that the later bid was not prepared and submitted with knowledge of the terms of other bids. In this case the bid was mailed in time to reach the purchasing office in the usual course of the mails prior to the hour of opening."7

Although the contracting officer should not permit a bid to pass out of the hands of an official of the Government (except, as provided in ASPR 2-401, when a duplicate bid cannot be made available for public inspection, and then only under the immediate supervision of a government official and under proper safeguarding conditions), nevertheless a bid which was erroneously returned unopened to a bidder at the time of the opening could be taken back and considered when there was no possibility of prejudice to the other bidders. In this case it appeared that the bidder had not left the bid room and could not have changed his bid." 

$2.17. The Firm-Bid Rule 

Although statutes in derogation of the common-law rule of revocability of offers prior to acceptance are clearly valid," early opinions of the Attorney General cast doubt upon the power of the executive departments to provide by regulation or procedure for the irrevocability of advertised bids in the absence of express statutory authorization.' However, in Scott v. United States.2 where the Court of Claims upheld the forfeiture of a required bid deposit in consequence of withdrawal of a bid, the court declared, by way of dictum, that the irrevocability of

THE FIRM-BID RULE 

$ 2.17 advertised bids for a reasonable time was supported by the following considerations of public policy: 

The agents of the Government stand upon a different footing from private individuals in the matter of advertising for the letting of contracts in behalf of the United States. They have no discretion. 

They must accept the lowest or the highest responsible bid, or reject all and readvertise. Private individuals are not required thus to act. Hence it is apparent that government agents should be allowed a reasonable time after the opening of bids before they are allowed to be withdrawn, so they can be afforded opportunities to ascertain whether collusion or fraud had been perpetrated against the United States by the parties engaged in the bidding. It is also apparent that if the rule of allowing immediate withdrawals after the results of the bidding are made known [should be adopted], frauds innumerable could be perpetrated against the United States, and thus public justice would be greatly hampered.3 

The Attorney General soon reversed his earlier position and relied upon the reasons of public policy declared in the Scott case to uphold the general irrevocability of advertised bids by virtue of express provisions of the invitation and bid alone, without benefit of statute or regulation.4 

This result was justified further in terms of consideration based on mutual promises:

This seems, therefore, to be a case of mutual stipulations, the commission agreeing to receive and consider all bids submitted only if the bidders would agree not to withdraw them capriciously, and give security to that effect, while the bidders made this concession because of their understanding that the commission would treat their bids with the fair and impartial consideration incumbent on public officers.5

In Refining Associates, Inc. v. United States, the plaintiff attempted to withdraw its bid during the acceptance period due to unspecified circumstances alleged to be beyond its control. The Government accepted the bid and later collected damages for plaintiff's nonperformance of the contract by set-off against payments otherwise due plaintiff. In plaintiff's suit to recover this sum, the issue was the validity of the attempted revocation. The position of the Government was stated by the court to be that the common-law rule as to the revocability of offers did not apply, "either because of regulations pursuant to which plaintiff's bid

430 OPS. ATT'Y GEN. 56 (1913). And see statement to same effect in the Massman Construction Co. v. United States, 102 Ct. Cl. 699, 718-19 (1945).

In denying recovery, the court placed primary reliance upon the requirement of ASPR 2-303 that bids may not be withdrawn after opening. Also, the court implied that consideration to support the irrevocability of the bid during the time specified, as expressly provided in the invitation and bid might be found in the plaintiff's "right of having its bid considered on its merits.”7 

The firm-bid rule is inapplicable where the invitation for bids does not stipulate against bid withdrawal, unless otherwise provided by published regulations. Also, the rule has a number of recognized exceptions. 

Some are based upon the interests of the Government, as in the cases discussed in § 2.33 infra concerning the curing of informalities in bids. 

Another exception was considered in Leitman v. United States, where the court held that the contracting officer in his discretion could consider a late downward modification of the bid price of an already low and eligible bid because it was in the interest of the Government to do so and other bidders were not prejudiced. Other exceptions to the rule involve the application of remedies for mistake (reviewed in detail in the following Part), fraud, misrepresentation, illegality, frustration, impossibility, and gross injustice. Thus, for example, in United States v. Sunshine Dairy, Inc.,¹º a bidder offered to sell milk at prices lower than the minimum prices established by the State of Oregon and was threatened with proceedings for injunction and possible penalties. The court recognized the firm-bid rule but granted relief on the ground of the apparent impossibility of performance. Other court decisions, in which bidders were relieved from contract obligations because of mistake where bid withdrawal was attempted before award, necessarily assume the validity of the firm-bid rule, for otherwise relief grounded on mistake would not be necessary."1 10

ADMINISTRATIVE PROCEDURES 

$ 2.18

III. MISTAKES IN BIDS 

$2.18. Administrative Procedures

Although most bidders are aware of the firm-bid rule in advertised competitive bidding, mistakes in bids are frequent and give rise to requests for correction or withdrawal of bids or for cancellation or amendment of contracts if award has been made prior to the allegation of the mistake. Few cases of mistakes in bids are litigated; most are settled administratively. Until 1950 most cases of bid mistake alleged before award were decided by the Comptroller General.12 Since decision by the 

Comptroller General would gain for the Government the benefit of low prices when claims of mistake were determined to be without merit, or when clearly established intended prices in a mistaken bid would still be the lowest, the mechanical rejection of allegedly mistaken bids was not permitted.13 However, when time was of the essence contracting officers were authorized to accept allegedly mistaken bids subject to determination by the Comptroller General of the question of mistake.14 

By early exceptions to the general procedure of submission of mistake in bid cases to the Comptroller General, contracting officers were permitted to disregard erroneous bids on articles purchased for resale when mistake was alleged and clearly established before delivery,¹5 and to allow bid correction in a limited class of obvious clerical errors.16 Later, the substantial increase in the volume of bid mistake cases following the general return to advertised procurement after World War II led the Comptroller General to authorize the General Service Administration and the Department of Defense to decide these cases on condition that exercise of the authority would be centralized in each department, that the Comptroller General reserved the right to question the correctness of any decision, and that bidders would not be denied the opportunity to have any case decided by the Comptroller General on request.17 De-

$ 2.19. Elements of Mistake 

Actions induced by mistake-which is defined as "a state of mind not in accord with the facts" 19—have various legal consequences. Some mistakes may prevent the formation of contracts; 20 others may justify relief, such as reformation or rescission,21 or provide defense against nonperformance; 22 and still others may be without legal effect. $ 2.19 other's mistake.25 Mistakes also are classified as those of fact and those of law.26 However, such definitions and the related general rules and exceptions found in decisions and texts are not always a sufficient basis for predicting how the Comptroller General or a court will decide a particular case. It is often necessary, therefore, to weigh and evaluate various factors in the light of past decisions involving comparable factors.27 For example, results may vary depending upon whether the risk of the mistake was assumed by one of the parties by agreement or custom; 28 whether the mistake concerned a material matter; 29 whether it was induced by a third party; 30 the nature and degree of negligence involved; 31 whether one party induced or knew, or should have known, of the other's mistake; 32 and the relief sought-whether damages, restitution, specific performance, rescission, cancellation, or reformation.33

§ 2.20. Notice of Mistake in Bid 

In the making of contracts no person may in good faith "snap up" another's offer, too good to be true, involving a mistake actually or constructively known to the offeree, and profit thereby.39 In advertised competitive bidding this principle represents a major exception to the firm-bid rule. Further, when price disparity or other circumstances give constructive notice of possible mistake, bid confirmation must be requested to prevent the award of an unenforceable contract.40 In one case, a claim for the actual loss in performing a contract was allowed where the contracting officer had consciously refrained from asking confirmation of a doubtful bid. In another case, it was said to be unconscionable for a contracting officer to attempt to apply the bid price for future additions or reductions in the amount of work when he had notice of the fact of mistake before awarding the contract.42

After confirmation of a questioned bid, the bidder usually cannot charge that it is snapped up in bad faith,43 and the contracting officer usually has no duty to inquire further and may consider the bid for award on the confirmed basis.44 However, the bidder is not foreclosed thereafter from alleging and proving mistake before award. Relief has been afforded after bid confirmation and award where the offered price was grossly out of line, ambiguous specifications caused mistakes by other Courts of equity are reluctant to grant rescission where the status quo of the parties cannot readily be restored.

The fact that bid confirmation is requested does not decrease the required measure of proof of mistake or insure that relief will be afforded.46 

In one decision it was held that a contracting officer acted properly in denying a bidder's attempt to confirm unit prices that were at variance with the extended prices, where the bid would have been low only on that basis. In another unusual decision it was held that when the bidder alleged mistake but thereafter agreed to extend an expired bid acceptance time without referring to the allegation of mistake, the extension constituted a new offer on the original terms and was in effect a confirmation of the bidder's willingness to perform on that basis.48 

$ 2.21. Remedies for Bid Mistake: Moffett v. City of Rochester 

In the case of Moffett v. City of Rochester,49 Moffett bid on public work advertised pursuant to a city ordinance that "neither the principal nor sureties on any bid or bond shall have the right to withdraw or cancel the same until the board shall have let the contract. 

After the bid opening the bidder alleged one mistake involving a bid of 50¢ per cubic yard for excavating in trenches, instead of the intended price of 70¢ that was offered for the same work elsewhere in the bid; and a second mistake involving a bid of $1.50 per cubic yard for tunnel excavation, instead of the intended price of $15.00, showing that the offered price included only the cost of digging and loading earth with no allowance for tunnel work and that other bids ranged from $12.00 to $15.00. The city board rejected the claims of mistake and demanded execution of a formal contract at the prices bid, or forfeiture of a $90,000 bid bond. 

The bidder sued in equity praying either "reformation" of the bid to reflect the intended prices or its "rescission" and an injunction against enforcement of the bond. The trial court denied "reformation" of the bid since the board had awarded part of the work to another bidder, but decreed rescission on grounds of clear, explicit and undisputed evidence of mistake.50 As to the unilateral nature of the mistake, the opinion stated that although equity will not reform a contract unless both parties were mistaken, it may interfere to prevent the enforcement of an unjust agreement induced by the mistake of one. The requirement of the city ordinance forbidding bid withdrawal was disposed of with the following statement later adopted by the U.S. Supreme Court: 

The complainant is not endeavoring to withdraw or cancel a bid or bond.' The bill proceeds upon the theory that the bid upon which

In other words, that the proposal read at the meeting of the board was one which the complainant never intended to make, and that the minds of the parties never met upon a contract based thereon. If the defendants are correct in their contention there is absolutely no redress for a bidder for public work, no matter how aggravated or palpable his blunder. The moment his proposal is opened by the executive board he is held as in a grasp of steel. There is no remedy, no escape. If, through an error of his clerk, he has agreed to do work worth $1,000,000 for $10, he must be held to the strict letter of his contract, while equity stands by with folded hands and sees him driven to bankruptcy. The defendant's position admits of no compromise, no exception, no middle ground.51

The Court of Appeals reversed the decree of rescission, holding first that the ordinance gave to the bid attributes of finality greater than those pertaining to ordinary contracts and beyond the reach of equity doctrines concerning relief for mistake; and second, that in any event, a court of equity may no more rescind than reform a contract because of the mistake of one party.52 The Supreme Court reversed this decree and affirmed the decree of rescission. It ruled, adopting the above quotation, that the principles and standards for reforming and rescinding contracts because of mistake applied equally to the bidder's obligation under the ordinance and bid and that the bidder's negligence would not preclude relief where the proved mistakes otherwise justified it.53 On the question of unilaterial mistake, the court repeated the statement in its earlier decision in Hearne v. Marine Insurance Company 54 that a mistake on one side may be a ground for rescinding but not for reforming a contract, but said that here "reformation" of the bid was prevented only by the board's prior award to another bidder. $ 2.22.

Decisions granting contract rescission because of mistake alleged or considered after award are, a fortiori, pertinent in cases of mistakes in bids alleged before award when the mistake is similar since the probability of relief after award is seldom greater but often is lessened by such factors as waiver, laches, and change of position. Correction of Bid Mistakes 

The Comptroller General has explained the higher standard of proof required for bid correction in a decision involving a mistake in price computation: 

The question of whether a bidder may change a bid-after the bids have been opened because of error therein always presents a matter of serious concern in a factual situation such as is here present. 

In order for this Office to be in a position to authorize such action by decision, the record submitted here should contain evidence conclusively establishing not only the existence of error, but its nature, how it occurred, and what the bidder actually intended to bid. The form of such evidence necessarily will vary with the circumstances of particular cases, but it should always be the best evidence available. A mere statement that the administrative officials themselves are satisfied that an error was made ordinarily will not suffice.68 

Numerous unpublished decisions of the Comptroller General have permitted bid correction before award. In one of the few published decisions a timely letter modifying a bid did not fully describe certain items. 

The contracting officer requested confirmation, and the bidder was permitted to clarify his intent.69 Correction was also authorized where the invitation called for tax-inclusive prices but the bidder in error omitted the tax and the intended price was still the lowest.70 And several decisions holding that allegedly mistaken bids should not have been rejected without review indicate circumstances in which correction perhaps would have been authorized." Excepting some of the cases of obvious clerical error, the published decisions do not include cases concerning requested correction of other than the low bid that would make it the lowest. It is doubtful that such relief would be authorized except in most unusual circumstances where the possibility of bid recomputation or election in light of the bidding was clearly precluded.

The following decisions of the Comptroller General define the limited class of cases in which contracting officers may permit bid correction if mistake is alleged or confirmed before award and the error involved is apparent on the face of the bid.72

$ 2.24. Denial of Relief Before Award 

The denial, before award, of relief for alleged mistake is usually based upon the failure of the evidence to support the allegation of a mistake in the bid or to establish both the mistake and the intended bid when bid correction is sought.76 Some decisions have emphasized negligence, such as a bidder's carelessness in preparing the bid or reading the specifications as an additional reason for denying relief." However, since there is a measure of negligence in almost all cases of mistake, it would seem that this factor ordinarily is not controlling." 78

Relief is sometimes denied in cases where the alleged mistake occurred in transactions between the bidder and a third person. Where relief was

Denial of Relief After Award

Partial or full performance of an awarded contract or other changes in position often make rescission impracticable,83 and reformation is not available where the Government did not intend to contract at more than the awarded price. Once a contract has been made, the sufficiency of proof of mistake is not the controlling factor, the question then being whether one of the parties to a contract may properly be charged with unanticipated or unaccepted costs because of the other's mistake. Often, therefore, such cases are not good precedents for deciding questions as to alleged bid mistake.

Occasionally a bidder gives notice of a mistake that would perhaps justify relief, but thereafter executes a required formal contract or takes other action inconsistent with the continued prosecution of the claim. In a leading case of this kind, the bidder alleged before award that a figure of $88,000 on an estimate sheet was overlooked in computing the bid price of $367,000. The intended bid would have been lower than the others, which ranged from $620,400 to $935,000. The contracting officer refused correction, but advised the bidder that a claim could be filed with the Comptroller General. However, in order to keep on good terms with the Government, the bidder signed a formal contract, performed the

IV. REJECTION OF ALL BIDS $ 2.26. Rejection of All Bids In implementation of 10 U.S.C. § 2305 (c),7 ASPR 2-403 provides in part that: 

All bids may be rejected by the contracting officer (i) when rejection is in the interest of the Government, or (ii) when he finds in writing that the bids are not reasonable, or were not independently arrived at in open competition, or are collusive, or were submitted in bad faith. . . .⁹

Although the terms of the invitation also reserve to the Government the right to reject any or all bids, the Comptroller General has ruled that an invitation for bids does not obligate the Government to accept any bid, whether or not such a reservation is stated.10 The right to reject all bids should of course be exercised when the procurement requirement no longer exists or is substantially modified. 

Further, it is in the Government's interest to reject all bids when necessary to protect the competitive bid system. Thus, the rejection of all bids has been approved or required by the Comptroller General where specifications were unduly restrictive or otherwise improper;" where incorrect specifications were furnished by mistake to some bidders; ¹² and where the invitation was held insufficient to permit the evaluation of bids offering supplies of partially foreign origin.13 The rejection of all bids has sometimes been approved when a nonconforming bid discloses that the Government's minimum needs may be met under reduced speci- 12

V. NONCONFORMING BIDS $2.27. Nonconforming Bids: General Principles 

The provisions of 10 U.S.C. § 2305 (c) limiting awards to bids that conform to the invitation for bids narrows considerably the scope of otherwise acceptable bids and largely restricts the contracting officer from accepting nonconforming bids or making counteroffers.18 Read literally, this limitation would forbid acceptance of any nonconforming bid, but the Comptroller General has ruled that this requirement was "not intended to deprive contracting officers of the Government of the right to waive informalities in bids as had been the practice for many years.

NONCONFORMING BIDS: GENERAL PRINCIPLES 

$ 2.27 requirements of the Invitation for Bids, shall be rejected (but see ASPR 

2-404)." In turn, ASPR 2-404,21 authorizes the contracting officer to waive or permit bidders to cure informalities or minor irregularities in bids.

Whether the nonconformance of a bid goes to the form or the substance of the invitation for bids, and the policy considerations requiring rejection of essentially nonconforming bids, have been analyzed by the 

Comptroller General in a leading decision: The question as to whether deviations from the requirements of advertised specifications might be waived after the opening date has been before this Office many times; and it has been consistently held that such deviations may be waived provided they do not go to the substance of the bid or work an injustice to other bidders. In other words, the primary question for determination in this and similar cases is whether the deviation proposed to be waived goes to the substance of the bid so as to affect either the price, quantity, or quality of the articles offered and therefore is prejudicial to the rights of other bidders or is merely a matter of form or some immaterial variation from the exact requirements of the specifications such as would not affect either the price, quality, or quantity of the articles offered. .. To insure to the Government the benefits of such competition it is essential that awards of contracts be fairly made upon the basis of the essential requirements of the specifications submitted for competition. While the Government reserved the right in the invitation for bids to waive any informality in bids received, the informalities which may be waived are those of form and not of substance, or of some immaterial and inconsequential defect in or variation of a bid from the exact requirements of the advertised invitation and specifications. As was stated in 17 Comp. 

Gen. 554, 558, 559- . . . To permit public officers to accept bids not complying in substance with the advertised specifications or to permit bidders to vary their proposals after the bids are opened would soon reduce to a farce the whole procedure of letting public contracts on an open competitive basis. The strict maintenance of such procedure, required by law, is infinitely more in the public interest than obtaining an apparently pecuniary advantage in a particular case by a violation of the rules. As was said by the court in City of Chicago v. Mohr, 216 Ill. 320, 74 N.E. 1056666 Where a bid is permitted to be changed [after the opening] it is no longer the sealed bid submitted in the first instance, and, to say the least, is favoritism, if not fraud-a direct violation of lawand cannot be too strongly condemned." 22 (Emphasis added.)

Alternate Bids

Bids offering unauthorized alternate (i.e. nonconforming) supplies usually must be rejected. Thus where specifications called for the use of steel per specification No. 352a, a bid offering steel conforming to specification No. 352 could not be accepted, although the bidder after bid opening offered to meet the specification.25 Further, a bid was properly rejected for nonconformance although the bid stated that in the bidder's opinion the article offered was in strict compliance with the specifications and that any deviation therefrom should be considered as an error in the bidder's specifications and not an exception to the invitation.26 

The rule is different, however, for alternative bids. Where a bid on a circuit breaker offered both a nonconforming and a conforming item, the latter being labelled as an "alternative specification," the Comptroller General held that the offer of the conforming item could be considered since the prohibition of the invitation against alternate bids is concerned only with the acceptance of something other than that called for by the specifications. In another case where the bidder bid on all items of construction work but did not submit a requested alternative bid on one item of the invitation, it was held that the bid was complete on one alternative and need not be rejected if the contracting officer determined that the award should be on that basis.28 

$2.29. Bid Samples

Where bid samples are properly required by the invitation, a materially nonconforming sample submitted with an otherwise conforming bid is an integral part thereof and requires rejection of the bid.29 However, where a required sample is not submitted with the bid, rejection of the bid for failure to submit the sample with the bid will not be approved except in unusual cases. To support a proper requirement for bid samples it must be shown that, because of the intricacy or novelty of the article to be purchased, the specifications could not be set forth with

Indefinite Price

Bids indefinite as to price usually must be rejected, as their acceptance would impose an uncertain and indefinite liability upon the Government." But bids providing for price variation in relation to particular contingencies and within a specified maximum usually may be considered. 

Rejection was required where a bidder failed to specify in the bid, as clearly required by the invitation, whether the prices offered were firm or subject to the escalation clause of the invitation. If construed as a firm price, the bid was low. To the bidder's contention that this omission should be cured as an informality the Comptroller General replied: 

In the present matter, it clearly appears that the deviation from the advertised requirements was of such substance as to affect not only the price of the units offered by the bidder, but also was prejudicial to the rights of other bidders in that it obviously would enable the [bidder] subsequently to make an election to its own advantages. 

To permit a bidder thus to clarify its original bid after opening would soon reduce to a farce the whole procedure of letting public contracts on an open competitive basis.32 

An early decision held that the bidder's deletion of a provision of the invitation for price adjustment to reflect future increases or decreases in applicable taxes did not require rejection, since the clause was in the nature of a concession in the bidder's favor to make a contingency allowance unnecessary.33 Later unpublished decisions concerning the deletion. by bidders of up and down escalation clauses of invitations for bids have sustained bid rejection since the provision for downward adjustments may not be deleted as a provision for the bidder's sole benefit.34 $ 2.31. - Delivery Terms

Invitations commonly state only the desired time of delivery, permitting bidders to offer other delivery time. In such cases, a low bid offering reasonable delivery may not be rejected in favor of another offering earlier delivery, since there is no notice to bidders that time is an essential element of the proposed contract.38 The rule is otherwise when the invitation indicates that delivery is "required," or a "must," or "shall be made," or is "mandatory," on or before a specified time.39 When time is thus clearly made of the essence, bids offering delivery beyond the specified period may not be changed so as to conform, after the opening of the bids, but must be rejected as nonconforming, unless no bid offers the required delivery schedule.40 For example, where an invitation specified "mandatory" delivery at destination before a given date, a bid offering delivery f.o.b. carrier at the bidder's plant three days before the specified date was required to be rejected because the bidder, by shifting to the Government the risk of delay in transit, would thus make a better deal than that offered generally to all bidders.41 Again, where an invitation required delivery to begin within 60 days, a bid offering to commence delivery within 75 days should have been rejected. Where the addenda covered additional work to be included in a lump-sum bid, rejection was required under the principles of materiality and post-opening election; 68 but where the manner of bid preparation inferred the adoption of one addendum, and the other involved little if any additional cost, waiver of the omission as an informality was authorized.“⁹
