VI. RESPONSIBLE BIDDERS $2.34. Responsible Bidders: In General The legislative history of the Armed Services Procurement Act explains the requirement for contracting with responsible bidders 75 as follows:

Other matters which may properly be covered by administrative regulations include the rejection of offers of any person who as principal or surety has been a defaulter on previous contracts with the Department, rejection of bids having nominal or fictitious prices, and barring as a contractor a person who is not a manufacturer or a regular dealer in the articles which he offers to supply. 

Section 3(b) states that contracts shall be awarded to the lowest responsible bidder The question whether a particular bidder is a 'responsible bidder' requires sound business judgment, and involves an evaluation of the bidder's experience, facilities, technical organization, reputation, financial resources, and other factors. The service concerned with the procurement of goods of the type dealt in by the bidder is naturally best qualified to make this evaluation, and broad discretion is accordingly reserved to the service in this respect.76

Prior to the award of any contract for supplies or services, the contracting officer must determine whether the prospective contractor meets all the criteria of responsibility set forth in ASPR 1-307.77 These define a responsible prospective contractor to be a person or firm who (i) is a manufacturer, construction contractor, or regular dealer, if the contract or order calls for supplies (see ASPR 1-201.9); (ii) has adequate financial resources, or ability to secure such re sources (see Defense Contract Financing Regulations, Part II, AR 

715–6, NAVEXOS P-1006, AFR 173–133, 17 December 1956); (iii) has the necessary experience, organization, and technical qualifications, and has or can acquire the necessary facilities (including probable subcontractor arrangements) to perform the proposed contract (where a bidder is proposing to use the facilities of an affiliate

Manufacturer or Regular Dealer

Contracting officers have long endeavored to eliminate speculation in government contracts. One attempted means was by clauses in invitations limiting awards of supply contracts to manufacturers and to legitimate dealers having stocks of the offered supplies and warehouses or shops from which sales thereof were made to the public as well as to the Government. Lists of debarred bidders also were used. These efforts, however, were not wholly successful.78 Additional government protection against contracting with irresponsible bidders was afforded by the enactment, in 1936, of the Walsh-Healey Public Contracts Act,79 which requires, inter alia, that every government contract exceeding $10,000 for the manufacture or furnishing of supplies shall include a stipulation that the contractor is either the manufacturer of or a regular dealer in such supplies.80 The standard form of invitation and bid for supplies requires a representation by the bidder that he is a regular

Regulations of the Department of Labor have defined the terms "manufacturer" and "regular dealer" as follows: (a) A manufacturer is a person who owns, operates, or maintains a factory or establishment that produces on the premises the materials, supplies, articles or equipment required under the contract and of the general character described by the specifications. (b) A regular dealer is a person who owns, operates, or maintains a store, warehouse, or other establishment in which the materials, supplies, articles, or equipment of the general character described by the specifications and required under the contract are bought, kept in stock, and sold to the public in the usual course of business.82 

Section 29 of the Labor Department's Rulings and Interpretations No. 3 

of April 30, 1953, under the Walsh-Healey Act provides further that:

(a) The responsibility of determining whether or not a bidder is qualified as a manufacturer or as a regular dealer under the Public Contracts Act rests in the first instance with the contracting agency. 

However, any decision which the contracting officer might make is subject to review by the Department of Labor which is charged with the administration of the Act. The Department of Labor may determine the qualifications of a bidder in the first instance in the absence of any decision by the contracting officer. 

If a dealer awarded a contract subject to the Walsh-Healey Act causes a manufacturer to deliver the supplies required thereunder directly to the Government, the dealer will be considered as an agent of the manufacturer in executing the contract and the manufacturer will be deemed to have agreed to the stipulations contained in the contract.83 Nothing in the Walsh-Healey Act, the Armed Services Procurement Act, or regulations thereunder prohibits award to an otherwise eligible supplier who contemplates subcontracting, if the proposed subcontractor is qualified to perform the work and the bid is otherwise proper.84 $ 2.36. Akin to speculative bidding is the occasional practice of a bidder submitting more than one bid under different names in response to the same invitation. The right of the Navy to reject such bids was formerly provided by statute which provided in part : 

If more than one bid be offered by any one party, by or in the name of his or their clerk, partner, or other person, all such bids may be rejected. . . .⁹0

Objections to multiple bidding by the same bidder were evident in cases in which dishonest bidders would submit multiple straw bids under names of fictitious organizations, omitting the required bid security, with the purpose of qualifying only the highest bid found after bid opening to be low enough to secure the award." Where a corporation and its wholly owned subsidiary submitted bids on the same supplies, the Comptroller General has advised that "no bidder should be permitted the advantage of double bidding hereafter." 92 However, it would seem that

§ 2.38. Contracts With Government Employees 

An officer or employee of the United States is not by statute prohibited from contracting as a principal with the United States when the subject of the contract is in no way connected with the performance of official duties.93 Nevertheless, the Comptroller General has long declared a general rule of public policy that the Government shall not contract with its own employees, unless the needs of the Government cannot otherwise reasonably be met.94 In one case he ruled that an electron microscope could be purchased from a Bureau of Standards employee who had previously constructed it, since it was the only one of its kind and no other equipment would meet the needs of the service.95 $ 2.39. Performance Capability and Integrity

In determining whether or not a bidder is responsible the courts have construed the word "responsible" to mean more than a bidder's pecuniary ability. It includes also his judgment, skill, ability, capacity, and integrity. The courts and the Comptroller General recognize that broad discretion rests with the contracting officer in his determination of the lowest responsible bidder." However, under section 3709 of the Revised

Statutes, the Comptroller General has held that the determination of the contracting officer in this respect must be reasonably supported by the facts of the particular case.98 It should again be pointed out that the committee reports on the Armed Services Procurement Act indicate that broad discretion should be given to contracting officers in deciding who is and who is not a responsible bidder." 

The contracting officer should not award a contract to a bidder who clearly lacks financial resources sufficient for performance. However, where the contracting officer questions a bidder's financial ability, he may require the bidder to submit a performance bond as a condition of the

Manufacturer or Regular Dealer

Contracting officers have long endeavored to eliminate speculation in government contracts. One attempted means was by clauses in invitations limiting awards of supply contracts to manufacturers and to legitimate dealers having stocks of the offered supplies and warehouses or shops from which sales thereof were made to the public as well as to the Government. Lists of debarred bidders also were used. These efforts, however, were not wholly successful.78 Additional government protection against contracting with irresponsible bidders was afforded by the enactment, in 1936, of the Walsh-Healey Public Contracts Act," which requires, inter alia, that every government contract exceeding $10,000 for the manufacture or furnishing of supplies shall include a stipulation that the contractor is either the manufacturer of or a regular dealer in such supplies.80 The standard form of invitation and bid for supplies requires a representation by the bidder that he is a regular

Regulations of the Department of Labor have defined the terms "manufacturer" and "regular dealer" as follows: (a) A manufacturer is a person who owns, operates, or maintains a factory or establishment that produces on the premises the materials, supplies, articles or equipment required under the contract and of the general character described by the specifications. (b) A regular dealer is a person who owns, operates, or maintains a store, warehouse, or other establishment in which the materials, supplies, articles, or equipment of the general character described by the specifications and required under the contract are bought, kept in stock, and sold to the public in the usual course of business.82 

Section 29 of the Labor Department's Rulings and Interpretations No. 3 

of April 30, 1953, under the Walsh-Healey Act provides further that: (a) The responsibility of determining whether or not a bidder is qualified as a manufacturer or as a regular dealer under the Public Contracts Act rests in the first instance with the contracting agency. 

However, any decision which the contracting officer might make is subject to review by the Department of Labor which is charged with the administration of the Act. The Department of Labor may determine the qualifications of a bidder in the first instance in the absence of any decision by the contracting officer. 

If a dealer awarded a contract subject to the Walsh-Healey Act causes a manufacturer to deliver the supplies required thereunder directly to the Government, the dealer will be considered as an agent of the manufacturer in executing the contract and the manufacturer will be deemed to have agreed to the stipulations contained in the contract.83 Nothing in the Walsh-Healey Act, the Armed Services Procurement Act, or regulations thereunder prohibits award to an otherwise eligible supplier who contemplates subcontracting, if the proposed subcontractor is qualified to perform the work and the bid is otherwise proper.84 § 2.36. Akin to speculative bidding is the occasional practice of a bidder submitting more than one bid under different names in response to the same invitation. The right of the Navy to reject such bids was formerly provided by statute which provided in part : 

If more than one bid be offered by any one party, by or in the name of his or their clerk, partner, or other person, all such bids may be rejected.

Objections to multiple bidding by the same bidder were evident in cases in which dishonest bidders would submit multiple straw bids under names of fictitious organizations, omitting the required bid security, with the purpose of qualifying only the highest bid found after bid opening to be low enough to secure the award." $ 2.38. Contracts With Government Employees 

An officer or employee of the United States is not by statute prohibited from contracting as a principal with the United States when the subject of the contract is in no way connected with the performance of official duties.93 Nevertheless, the Comptroller General has long declared a general rule of public policy that the Government shall not contract with its own employees, unless the needs of the Government cannot otherwise reasonably be met.94 In one case he ruled that an electron microscope could be purchased from a Bureau of Standards employee who had previously constructed it, since it was the only one of its kind and no other equipment would meet the needs of the service.95 $2.39. Performance Capability and Integrity 96 In determining whether or not a bidder is responsible the courts have construed the word "responsible" to mean more than a bidder's pecuniary ability. It includes also his judgment, skill, ability, capacity, and integrity. The courts and the Comptroller General recognize that broad discretion rests with the contracting officer in his determination of the lowest responsible bidder." However, under section 3709 of the Revised

Statutes, the Comptroller General has held that the determination of the contracting officer in this respect must be reasonably supported by the facts of the particular case.⁹8 It should again be pointed out that the committee reports on the Armed Services Procurement Act indicate that broad discretion should be given to contracting officers in deciding who is and who is not a responsible bidder."

Unless unusual technical skills are involved, the contracting officer's determinations of responsibility usually should be made only in terms of the bidder's present capability. Thus it was held proper to require a showing by the bidder of business and technical organization and financial resources sufficient to perform a large building contract, but not a showing that the bidder had built a building within four years costing at least a specified minimum amount.2 Also, objection has been raised to the use, in procuring repair services, of such artificial standards of capability as a bidder's status as an "authorized or approved" agency of the equipment manufacturer.3 However, as illustrated by a number of decisions sustaining rejections, the application of the general rule varies with the facts of each case.

Rejection of a low bidder on x-ray solution was upheld where bidder was not listed in the telephone directory, the number given in the bid was not answered, and a visit to the address revealed an unoccupied private home listed "For Sale."4 In a procurement of highly technical water chlorination equipment, where public health considerations were present, an award to a higher bidder offering equipment of known dependability and superior quality was sustained when justified by detailed technical findings showing the unreliability of the low bidder's product. In another case, rejection of the bid of a bidder organized only eight months was approved, with no comment concerning a requirement of the invitation that bidders must show two prior installations of comparable technical equipment."

In the procurement of services, greater emphasis on factors of experience and special skill is appropriate. In a decision concerning the procurement of janitorial services for a large office building, the invitation stated that a factor of responsibility would be the bidder's current performance of large scale cleaning operations in the area. A preaward survey disclosed that this condition was not met and that the bidder did not have the staff or experience to perform work of the magnitude involved. Rejection of the bid was sustained, with the following remarks: 

Of course, while hiring ability is a factor in determining potential operating capability, it does not insure adequate performance to the same extent as experience.

As to the effect of state laws and regulations upon a bidder's responsibility, decisions of the Comptroller General until 1943 followed the earlier doctrine that those who contract to furnish supplies or services to the United States are within the implied constitutional immunity of the federal government from taxation and regulation by the States. 

Under that broad doctrine the question of a bidder's responsibility to perform such contracts was to be determined without regard to state requirements such as licensing of business occupations or price control." 

However, the limitation of that doctrine by the Supreme Court with regard to nondiscriminatory state taxation 18 and regulation 19 of government contractors requires that in determining a bidder's responsibility precise analysis must now be made of the legal effect of particular state laws and regulations upon the bidder's ability to perform the proposed contract. A number of factors may affect this determination. Thus, express or implied exemptions of the federal government may be available under the state law or regulation,20 or specific grounds for claiming constitutional immunity may be present, as in cases where the contractor is constituted an agent of the Government,21 or the contract is to be performed within an enclave under the exclusive jurisdiction of the United States, 22 or the legal incidence of a tax is upon property or purchases of the Government.23 Immunity also may be established in consequence of specific federal legislation that excludes the operation of state regulatory laws on the subject.24 The extent to which federal procurement legislation may have had this result, however, is somewhat uncertain. On the other hand, in the Penn Dairies case (see § 2.40, n. 19 supra), the Court upheld a Pennsylvania statute fixing minimum prices for milk and declined to read in the federal procurement statutes a prohibition against selling to the Army at prices below the minima set by state law. One may wonder how a state's setting of milk prices paid by the federal government is different from a state's setting of intrastate transportation rates to the federal government. In Penn 

Dairies, the Court concluded that the state regulation "imposes no prohibition on the national government or its officers", and in the instant case the Court said that "the conflict between the federal policy of negotiated rates and the state policy of regulation of negotiated rates seems to us to be clear." But the controlling difference between Penn

Dairies and the instant case is found in the extent to which the state actions in question interfered with performance of federal functions. As Mr. Justice

Harlan put it, having noted that he could "see no constitutional distinction between state regulation of milk the government must buy and of the price at which the Government must ship the milk it has bought," "the constitutional validity of this California statute depends entirely on its noneconomic impact upon the Government—that is, upon a determination whether this statute interferes with the performance of governmental functions by military personnel or other federal employees." To the majority of the Court, there appeared a probability that the transportation of military supplies, especially in time of emergency, would be delayed pending state action in classification of the heterogenous items of military shipments for tariff purposes or for approval of negotiated rates. This, to the majority, was, in effect, state "prohibition" of an essential federal function. In Penn 

Dairies, on the other hand, the state action, at most, had an economic impact on the price of federal purchases. In this view Penn Dairies is distinguishable and its holding remains intact. The Court of Claims is reported to have reopened its decision in Hughes Transportation, Inc. v. United States, 128 Ct. Cl. 221 (1954), which sustained state regulation of the transportation of federal property.

 VII. EVALUATION OF BIDS: PRICE AND OTHER FACTORS 

$2.41. In General 

That 10 U.S.C. § 2305 (c) requires consideration of "price and other factors" in making award presupposes that bid evaluation should not be limited to the arithmetic determination of the low bid. Factors for consideration in addition to price include urgency of need, and lowest ultimate cost-factors that do not necessarily require bid rejection but may be considered in evaluating otherwise eligible bids. Notwithstanding legislative emphasis upon the exercise of broad business discretion,28 decisions of the Comptroller General indicate that the principle of fairness to bidders may limit the consideration in bid evaluation of most factors other than measurable costs, except to the extent that bidders are otherwise apprised in the invitation 29 and in cases of equal low bids. $ 2.42. Price and Other Cost Factors

In evaluating bids to determine the lowest cost to the Government, bid prices must be adjusted to reflect such immediate and measurable cost factors as discounts, credits for returned containers, etc., government transportation costs, price escalation, and taxes. Also bids offering supplies of foreign origin are subject to special adjustment to determine whether the lowest domestic bid is unreasonable by comparison. $ 2.43. Discounts

Bid prices must be reduced by any separately stated trade or quantity discount,30 and by the amount of any offered prompt payment discount unless it is known with reasonable certainty that the Government cannot take advantage of it within the time specified," or the invitation expressly precludes consideration of the offered discount in the evaluation of bids. Where a bidder fails to state any period for earning an offered discount, it can be considered in bid evaluation since a reasonable time is implied.32 Where otherwise equal bids offer the same rate of discount, the one allowing the longer time for payment should be accepted. Thus a payment time of 30 days is considered more advantageous than a provision for payment "10th proximo," as the former usually will allow more time.33 Ordinarily, invitations provide that the discount period

Credit or Bonus 

A credit or bonus based upon contingent events may not be considered in evaluation,35 but a definite credit or bonus, such as those sometimes offered in the procurement of stenographic reporting services because of the exclusive sale of transcripts to the public, must be considered unless prohibited by the invitation.36 In these stenographic reporting cases, where the cost to the Government varies between bids, the proposed charge to the public may not be considered unless it exceeds a maximum specified in the invitation or is exorbitant.37 Where only no-charge bids for government copies are offered, however, proposed charges to the public may be considered as a factor in evaluation.38 As in other cases, any basis of evaluation stated in the invitation must be strictly followed, to prevent prejudice to bidders by "changing the rules of the game after the opening whistle.” 39 

$ 2.45. Government Transportation Costs 

Where the invitation requests bids on either an origin or destination basis, origin bids are adjusted for evaluation by adding the lowest transportation cost to destination reasonably available to the Government,40 under the principle that the cost of delivery is always a factor in determining which is the lowest bid.41 The Government as a shipper, by virtue of section 22 of the Interstate Commerce Act,42 is authorized to negotiate with common carriers for the rates for the transportation of government property that are lower than the tariff rates prescribed by the Interstate Commerce Commission. Thus not only for the purpose of bid evaluation but also from the standpoint of minimizing transportation costs, it may make a great difference whether or not the Government takes delivery of the supplies at origin or at destination. But in the absence of a special freight rate available to the Government under section 22 of the Interstate Commerce Act, the Government stands on no different footing than do private shippers so far as having to pay applicable freight rates regulated under either federal or state law.43

Specific offers by bidders to equalize transportation costs, in relation to section 22 rates or other known factors, may be recognized in the evaluation.44 However, a general offer of equalization in terms of meeting the delivered price of any other bidder is improper and may not be considered.45 

§ 2.46. 

Price Escalation

Provisions for price escalation are not ordinarily included in invitations for bids. Where an approved clause is included, providing for escalation both downward and upward and with a specified ceiling, bids taking no exception to the clause are evaluated without adjustment. If a bidder specifies a higher ceiling, the bid is adjusted for evaluation by increasing the price by the difference between the percentage specified in the invitation and that offered by the bidder to determine whether it would still be the lowest. If a lower ceiling is offered, the bid price is evaluated without adjustment, although the lower ceiling will be stated in the award if the bid is accepted. As noted above, if the bidder deletes a clause of the invitation providing for both upward and downward escalation, the bid must be rejected as nonresponsive.47 

When the invitation does not include an escalation clause, bids offering prices subject to escalation with no upward ceiling ordinarily must be rejected as indefinite offers.48 Those subject to a specified ceiling are adjusted for evaluation by applying the maximum percentage increase. 

The contracting officer should request the bidder in such cases to accept an approved form of escalation clauses, but if that is refused, award ordinarily may be made on the bid as submitted. $ 2.47. 

Taxes

Federal and state taxes such as excise taxes and use taxes must be considered in the evaluation of bids. In this connection it should be noted that the invitation for bids may request, but may not require, bidders to quote prices free of taxes or to consent to the deduction of included taxes from otherwise acceptable low prices.49 When the invitatransportation tax) and contractorowned property (which was subject to the transportation tax).

BIDS OFFERING SUPPLIES OF FOREIGN ORIGIN 

$ 2.48 tion is silent as to taxes and the bid does not specify that applicable taxes are excluded, the bid is presumed to include such taxes.50 

Different procedures obtain for the evaluation of bids as between applicable federal excise taxes on the one hand and applicable state and local taxes on the other hand. Since exemptions from certain federal excise taxes may turn on the bidder's status as a manufacturer or retailer and since tax-inclusive bids often do not show the amount of the tax included therein, all bids are adjusted on a basis inclusive of applicable federal excise taxes for evaluation, whether or not an exemption is available.51 As to applicable state and local taxes, bids are evaluated upon the basis of ultimate cost to the Government.52 Hence a bid exclusive of applicable state and local taxes is adjusted by the amount of the tax where no exemption is available and the bid may be properly read to shift the burden of the tax to the Government.53 On the other hand, bids inclusive of unspecified amounts for applicable state and local taxes are evaluated as submitted notwithstanding available exemptions since what amount to deduct is uncertain. But bids inclusive of specified amounts for applicable state and local taxes may be evaluated exclusive of such taxes where the purchase may be made upon a tax-exempt basis.54 $2.48.

Equal Low Bids

The rule has long been that the selection of the bid to receive award should be made by drawing lots when two or more low bids are equal, all factors considered." However, selection should not be made by lot if there is any determining factor of advantage to the Government, not excluded from consideration by provisions of the invitation, in choosing between bids of equal amounts," as where material offered is not of equal quality, or delivery time may be saved because of the bidder's location," or advantages to the Government will result from having various distribution points,82 or the risk of loss or delay in transit will vary with source or destination delivery. Further, where services such as property management are involved, the relative responsibility, competence, capability, and experience of each bidder may be considered.*3 84 The above principles are now reflected in ASPR 2-406.4, which also makes special provision for preliminary drawings between equal bidders offering the product of the same manufacturer, and has additional requirements giving preference, for tie-breaking purposes only, first to concerns (whether or not small business) that will perform the contract in a labor surplus area, and then, where labor surplus areas are not involved, to small business concerns.86 85 $2.53. ACCEPTANCE OF BIDS 

$ 2.54 with that bidder to reduce the price. 

If the bidder agrees to reduce the price to an amount that is fair and reasonable, the bid may be modified in writing to reflect such reduction and the award will accept the bid as modified. Negotiations of this kind are to be distinguished from the correction of informalities in bids and may not be undertaken unless the bidder is already clearly eligible for award. As to matters other than price, negotiations with the bidder clearly eligible for award may not depart from the essential requirements of the invitation or permit modification of the bid in any manner prejudicial to other bidders. The resulting contract is entered into by advertising and is not a negotiated contract.

VIII. AWARD OF CONTRACT 

$ 2.54. Acceptance of Bids

A bid must be accepted within the time specified by the bidder or, if none be specified, within a reasonable time. The standard form of invitation and bid specifies an acceptance time of sixty days unless otherwise provided by the bidder, and stipulates further that acceptance will be effected by mailing (or otherwise furnishing) the award to the bidder." The latter provision is in accord with the well established principle of private contract law in the United States that where an offer is made by mail and does not specify differently as to acceptance, the mailing of a properly addressed and responsive acceptance creates the contract whether or not it reaches the offeror." Action short of mailing, such as the preparation of an acceptance letter or the notation of acceptance on government records is not sufficient," and the untimely mailing of an acceptance thereafter cannot create a contract without the bidder's acquiescence or consent.92 Further, the Comptroller General has ruled that the statutory requirement for a written notice of award clearly forbids the consummation of an advertised contract by word of mouth, 87 Comp. Gen. Dec. B-74013 (unpubl.), dig. 4 CCH CONT. CASES FED. ¶ 60,492 (1948), quoting Leitman v. United States, 104 Ct. Ordinarily, in the formation of private contracts by offer and acceptance, the offeree terminates his power to accept an ordinary offer by words or conduct communicated to the offeror which manifest an intention not to accept the offer.94 But where bids are solicited for simultaneous opening or consideration together, a bidder usually would be deemed reasonable in supposing that his bid is rejected when one of the competing bids is accepted.95

A common question is whether a contracting officer, subsequent to the expiration or rejection of a bid, may properly request or permit the bidder to reinstate his bid. In theory acceptance of the reinstated bid would constitute the making of a contract without advertising." Acceptance of a reinstated bid was authorized where only one day after erroneous rejection of all bids and a month after bid opening had elaspedall bids having offered 60 days for acceptance-and the agency had determined that the price was reasonable and readvertisement might well have brought higher bids." In another case, revival of the low bid 35 days after rejection of all bids was approved where the requisition had been cancelled inadvertently, the Government's need in fact had continued, and acceptance of the low bid was clearly in the Government's interest." Where a bidder extends an expired bid and timely acceptance is then made, he has no standing to challenge the validity of the revival of the bid, since the extension will be deemed either a proper revival of the bid or a new offer on the same terms and conditions that may be accepted under ordinary circumstances without advertising." 

In the absence of a bidder's reinstatement of a rejected or expired bid, it would seem that the Government, by accepting such a bid, would be unable to bind that bidder to a contract. However, in one unusual case, the contracting officer rejected all bids and readvertised to obtain a possible slight savings on a small increase in quantity, the possibility of such a savings having been disclosed by a late telegraphic bid. The original low bidder protested this action to the agency head who found that the rejection of all bids in these circumstances was arbitrary. The rejection of all bids was then rescinded and the original low bid was accepted.

Ordinarily the successful bid is accepted by preparing and mailing U.S. Standard Form 263 signed by the contracting officer. The form is completed by entering the date, contract number, contractor's identification, payment office, and the item numbers, descriptions, and prices. 

The award also sets forth discounts, delivery and inspection provisions, and other information from the bid necessary to provide a complete statement of the resulting agreement in the combined invitation, bid, and award, without further reference to the bid. If award is to other than the low bidder on the basis of delivery time, the price and delivery time offered by the low bidder ordinarily are set forth in the award to aid in administration of the contract. Great care must be taken to avoid any new term or condition in the award that would constitute it a counteroffer and result in a legal rejection of the bid rather than the intended acceptance. For the same reason any apparent ambiguity in the bid should be clarified before award.5

When time does not permit the initial issuance of the standard form of award, a preliminary notice of award in letter form signed by the contracting officer may be used, provided that it also incorporates all terms, conditions, and information necessary to accomplish a legally sufficient acceptance of the bid. Records of mailing awards and preliminary notices are maintained for evidence in disputes as to the fact or time of mailing.

For all procurements by advertised competitive bidding, regulations of the General Accounting Office require an administrative certification of award to the lowest bidder or a detailed statement of justification for acceptance of other than the low bid on U.S. Standard Form 1036, 136 COMP.  $3.1. Introduction 

From the initial enactment in 1861 of what later became section 3709 of the Revised Statutes' down to World War II, government contracts for the procurement of supplies and services were entered into for the most part by means of formal advertising-that is to say, by the solicitation of competitive bids and formal award to the lowest responsible and responsive bidder. And despite certain exceptions to the strict requirement of Rev. Stat. § 3709, whether those exceptions grew out of interpretations of that law by the Comptroller General or out of a few specific statutory authorizations for negotiation, it is unquestioned that until the enactment of the First War Powers Act late in 1941 2 the use of negotiation as a method of procurement- that is to say, a method of procurement unencumbered by the formalities and procedures applicable to advertised procurement and designed to give scope to the use of normal purchasing practices in the making of procurement contracts-was rare. 

From the date of the enactment of Title II of the First War Powers 

Act in 1941 until May 19, 1948, the effective date of the Armed Services 

Procurement Act of 1947,3 the Armed Services used and cited Title II 

of the First War Powers Act as the negotiation authority for all contracts. With the outbreak of the Korean War, the Department of Defense requested that Congress revitalize Title II of the First War Powers Act. 

This was done by the enactment on January 12, 1951, of Public Law 921, 81st Congress, which made Title II effective until June 30, 1952. Subsequent legislation continued this authority until June 30, 1958.5 

From May 19, 1948, until Title II was revitalized in January 1951, it was universally considered that the Armed Services Procurement Act of 1947 had suspended the negotiation authority provided by Title II. 

The broad authority provided by Title II was used by the Navy, until its expiration on June 30, 1958, primarily in cases involving (i) amendments without consideration, (ii) correction of mistakes in contracts, and (iii) the formalization of informal commitments. It was also used by the Navy as negotiation authority in only a few instances where it was considered more appropriate to enter into the contracts under the broad authority provided by Title II of the First War Powers Act, as amended, rather than under the Armed Services Procurement Act. This restrictive usage of the negotiation authority provided by Title II was based on the policy statement contained in the Joint Regulations of the military departments governing the authority to contract under Title II of the First War Powers Act, as amended, that it was the general policy of each military department to continue to effect its procurement pursuant

INTRODUCTION 

$ 3.1 to the authority of the Armed Services Procurement Act of 1947 rather than pursuant to the authority of Title II of the First War Powers Act." 

The principal reason why the negotiation authority provided by Title II was not used was that ample authority for negotiation of contracts was provided by the Armed Services Procurement Act. No comparable nego tiation authority outside of Title II of the First War Powers Act existed during World War II. 

Title II of the First War Powers Act, as revitalized in January 1951, finally expired on June 30, 1958. However, by the Act of August 28, 1958, Congress enacted a new law providing permanent authority during time of national emergency for certain defense agencies "to enter into contracts or into modifications of contracts . . . without regard to other provisions of law relating to the making amendment or modification of contracts whenever [the President] deems that such action would facilitate the national defense... "7 While the Act of August 28, 1958, is similar to and was based on Title II of the First War Powers Act, it differs markedly from the Title II authority in that Congress has explicitly provided that it may not be used for "the negotiation of purchases or of contracts for property or services required by law to be procured by formal advertising and competitive bidding." Accordingly, whenever reference is made in this chapter to negotiation authority under Title II of the First War Powers Act, as amended, that reference may not be taken as also applying to the Act of August 28, 1958.

Although the Armed Services Procurement Act of 1947 provides for procurement by formal advertising as well as for procurement by negotiation, and in fact emphasizes that the former is the rule and the latter the exception, no consideration will be given here to the procedures and problems of procurement by formal advertising. That subject has been. thoroughly covered in Chapter 2. This chapter, therefore, will (i) consider the nature and operation of negotiation as one of the two principal methods of procurement, (ii) analyze in some detail each of the sixteen exceptions to the rule of advertising under which negotiation is permitted by that act (as well as the few additional exceptions covered by the act's reference to negotiation in any situation "otherwise authorized by law”), (iii) discuss the various conditions or restrictions imposed upon the use of · •

negotiation as a method of procurement, with particular emphasis on the condition precedent of Determinations and Findings under certain circumstances, and (iv) indicate something of the Navy's actual operation under this part of the Armed Services Procurement Act, as well as some of the purchasing problems which have arisen in connection with procurement by negotiation.

At the outset, it is important to stress the difference in the nature and extent of the negotiation authority given by the Armed Services Procurement Act as compared on the one hand to the rigid situation under Rev. 

Stat. § 3709 and on the other hand to the liberal authority granted by 

Title II of the First War Powers Act of 1941 and its implementing Executive Order 9001. Section 3709 of the Revised Statutes presented the one extreme of strict rules of formal advertising for nearly every govern ment purchase; Title II of the First War Powers Act of 1941 with its blanket authority to enter into contracts (and amendments or modifications thereof) "without regard to the provisions of law relating to the making, performance, amendment, or modification of contracts," represented the other extreme of almost complete freedom as to purchasing methods, and resulted in the inevitable fact that throughout World War II, at least so far as the Armed Services were concerned, no attempt was made to comply with the formalities of procurement by formal advertising. 

Between these two extremes stands the Armed Services Procurement Act of 1947 with its combined authority for procurement by advertising and procurement by negotiation, thereby achieving the harmonious and compromise result of authorizing the more liberal purchasing method of negotiation in those situations which seemed to warrant or compel negotiation, but requiring the restricting formalities of the advertising method of procurement in all other situations. 

The Armed Services Procurement Act of 1947 had many objectives other than authorizing the negotiation of contracts under certain circumstances. Among these more important other objectives were the following: (1) unifying the procurement authority throughout the Department of Defense; (2) consolidating within the framework of one statute the basic procurement authority for the three military departments; (3) assuring small business an opportunity to secure a fair proportion of the total value of military purchases; (4) re-establishing formal advertising as the preferred and usual method of procurement, but expressly permitting consideration of "other factors" besides price in making an award; (5) permitting in negotiated procurement the use of that type of contract which in each instance will promote the best interests of the Government; (6) granting a limited authority for the use of advance payments; (7) giving finality to the decisions of a department head in his use of the authority granted by the act; (8) authorizing, by assignment of procurement responsibility or by mutual agreement, joint procurement 114

NEGOTIATION DISTINGUISHED FROM ADVERTISING 

$3.2 between the Departments as well as procurement by one Department for another; and (9) repealing archaic and unnecessary procurement statutes.

As already stated, the Armed Services Procurement Act of 1947 has been the governing procurement statute for the military departments since May 19, 1948. But on August 10, 1956, this act technically lost its separate identity and popular name with the codification of substantially all laws relating to the Department of Defense and the military departments into a new Title 10, United States Code, entitled "Armed Forces." What was the Armed Services Procurement Act has been codified into positive law in Chapter 137 of this title.10 And with this codification the Armed 

Services Procurement Act as such has been repealed." This codification of the Armed Services Procurement Act has made many changes in the language of the original act, particularly with reference to the provisions of that act concerning procurement by negotiation. In this chapter we shall refer to and quote from the act as so codified. And for reasons of convenience and familiarity we shall continue to refer to the body of law now codified in Chapter 137 of Title 10, U.S. Code as the Armed Services 

Procurement Act, but particular sections of that act will be identified by reference to the appropriate section of Title 10, U.S. Code. 

I. NEGOTIATION AS DISTINGUISHED FROM ADVERTISING $ 3.2. Negotiation Distinguished From Advertising 

Before considering each circumstance permitting negotiation as enumerated in the Armed Services Procurement Act, it is advisable first to discuss briefly just what negotiation is, what it entails, and how it differs from formal advertising as a particular method to be used for the procurement of supplies and services. As pointed out in Chapter 2, procurement by formal advertising entails the solicitation of bids by the Government, the submission of sealed bids by qualified suppliers, the public opening at a set hour and the recording of bids by the Government, and the awarding of a contract by the Government "to the responsible bidder whose bid conforms to the invitation and will be the most advantageous to the United States, price and other factors considered." 12 In connection with these four main steps in the process of procuring by means of formal advertising, the emphasis is consistently placed on balancing the interest in speedy and efficient procurement procedures against the interest in the maximum opportunity to compete and the avoidance of favoritism and fraud in the making of public contracts. Only under rare and special conditions may a bid be accepted that takes exception to the 

9 Act of Aug. 10, 1956, 70A Stat. 1 

(1956). 

10 10 U.S.C. §§ 2301-2314 (1958). 

11 Act of Aug. 10, 1956, § 53, 70A Stat. 

677. 

12 10 U.S.O. § 2305 (c) (1958). 

115

$3.

invitation for bids or may a bid be changed after the public opening; and only under peculiar circumstances may mistakes or irregularities in bids be rectified. Seldom can such important bargaining factors as quality, price, and business reputation be unrestrictedly considered by the Government's purchasing officer; and seldom can there be any give and take, between buyer and seller, over the inclusion and wording of contract clauses. Each transaction is entered into at arm's length and is carried out with virtually no opportunity for negotiating the deal itself or the particular terms of the deal. 

When the Government buys something as a result of negotiation, however, whether under the relatively few statutory and interpretative exceptions to Rev. Stat. § 3709 or under the circumstances permitting negotiation which are specifically enumerated in the Armed Services Procurement Act, the formal procedures and rather rigid rules for procurement by advertising need not be observed. It is important to remember, however, that there is bargaining and competition when this is feasible; but instead of the mailing or public posting of formal invitations to bid, quotations or proposals (supported by statements of estimated cost or other satisfactory evidence of reasonable price) are requested from qualified sources of supply for the particular supplies or work being procured. Thereafter, on the basis of these quotations or proposals, and without any public opening, the contracting officer for the Government negotiates a contract with that supplier or suppliers who offer the best deal to the Government. In this negotiation many different factors are considered and weighed, such as: comparison of prices, and consideration of other prices for supplies and services similar to those which are being procured; negotiation of cost and profit elements in prices quoted; comparison of the business reputations and responsibilities of the various suppliers who submit informal quotations or proposals; consideration of quality, and of the satisfaction of technical requirements; consideration of delivery possibilities, of the extent and nature of expected subcontracting, and of the most favorable type of contract (usually in terms of a fixed-price contract as compared with a contract of the cost-reimbursement type). Individual bargaining is usually conducted by mail or conference; but award may also be made as a result of competitive negotiation without bargaining by accepting the most favorable offer initially received if the contracting officer regards it to be fairly and reasonably priced.13 In short, with procurement by negotiation the Government is, generally, free, like any other purchaser, to do business with whichever supplier seems to offer the most satisfactory terms. 

13 The procedures for "competitive negotiation" are set forth in ASPR 3-805 (Sept. 18, 1958). 116

CIRCUMSTANCES PERMITTING NEGOTIATION 

$ 3.3 

This privilege or freedom of purchasing supplies and services by means of negotiation is permitted under the Armed Services Procurement Act only to a limited degree. Not only must certain Findings and Determinations often be made in justification of the use of this method of procurement (as will be discussed below), and not only must certain procedural and contracting formalities be observed with this kind of procurement, but also and fundamentally-must the contemplated purchase fall within one of the categories or kinds of circumstances permitting negotiation specifically set forth in the Armed Services Procurement Act. For it must be constantly remembered that, although the authority of the First War Powers Act of 1941 gave to the Armed Services and also to several other government purchasing agencies a virtually unlimited right to procure by negotiation "across the board," nevertheless under the compromising provisions of the Armed Services Procurement Act, Congress declared that all purchases and contracts for supplies and services for the Armed Services (and also for the United States Coast Guard and the National Aeronautics and Space Administration) must be made by advertising except that such purchases and contracts may be negotiated by anyone of those government agencies without advertising provided the contemplated procurement falls within some one of the circumstances or situations set forth in the act. 

II. CIRCUMSTANCES PERMITTING NEGOTIATION 

$3.3. In General

Although the Armed Services Procurement Act, as indicated previously in this chapter, provides in effect that procurement by advertising is the rule and procurement by negotiation the exception, nevertheless that act, as codified in 10 U.S.C. § 2304 (a), enumerates sixteen individual and different exceptions under which purchases and contracts may be negotiated without resort to advertising. Consequently, subject to such limitations on the use of certain of these so-called "exceptions" as will be indicated later in this chapter, and subject to the basic requirements governing the execution of any contract for the Government in general and for the Navy in particular, procurement may be carried out by means of negotiation, and contracts may be entered into as a result of that negotiation and irrespective of advertising, under any one of the exceptions set forth and discussed subsequently in this chapter. 

To begin with, 10 U.S.C. § 2304 (a) (formerly section 2(c) of the Armed 

Services Procurement Act) provides that Purchases of and contracts for property or services covered by this chapter shall be made by formal advertising. However, the head of an agency may negotiate such a purchase or contract, if— 117

$ 3.

and goes on to authorize negotiation under sixteen explicit exceptions, and a seventeenth which reads "negotiation of the purchase or contract is otherwise authorized by law."

The first ten of the exceptions set forth in 10 U.S.C. § 2304(a) (and also, by definition, the seventeenth exception-"otherwise authorized by law”), as exceptions to the standard method of procurement by advertising, are for the most part restatements of similar exceptions to this method of procurement which, prior to the Armed Services Procurement Act of 1947, had been authorized by Congress or which had been recognized as exceptions under administrative or judicial interpretations of Rev. Stat. § 3709. 

The remaining six exceptions—that is, exceptions (11) to (16) inclusivewere recommended to Congress by the Armed Services as a result of their extensive procurement experience during World War II and under the 

First War Powers Act. These six additional exceptions, permitting six kinds or categories of contracts to be negotiated, were carefully considered by the Committees and Houses of Congress, and were accepted for inclusion in section 2(c) of the Armed Services Procurement Act 14 because it was felt that negotiation under each of these exceptions or circumstances would result in monetary savings to the Government or was essential from the point of view of national defense or public interest. 

As will be pointed out, each of these six additional exceptions to the requirement of procurement by advertising is hedged about with the safeguard that its use requires a personal finding and determination by the head of the department concerned before the exception may be invoked; and in two of these permitted fields of negotiation, periodic reports as to their use must be furnished to Congress. 

$ 3.4. National Emergency 10 U.S.C. § 2304 (a) (1) (formerly section 2(c) (1) of the Armed 

Services Procurement Act) authorizes the negotiation of purchases and contracts ifit is determined that such action is necessary in the public interest during a national emergency declared by Congress or the President;

This exception is designed to permit the negotiation of contracts in times of national emergency in recognition of the fact that during a national emergency or wartime the placing of contracts by advertising might not be compatible with the emergency responsibilities of the military departments for speed in procurement, for maintaining specialized skills and for broadening the industrial base of suppliers. Since it was over two years after the outbreak of World War II in Europe that the Armed Services were given full authority to negotiate contracts under the First

War Powers Act, it was the opinion of Congress in considering the Armed Services Procurement bill that minimum preparedness required that statutory authority be already enacted and available to permit the shedding of peacetime procurement procedures simultaneously with the declaration of a new national emergency. It was decided by the Armed Services, however, and was in effect agreed to by them with the Congress in connection with the hearings on the Armed Services Procurement bill, that the negotiation authority of exception (1) would not be used during the national emergency then in effect.

On December 16, 1950, the President declared the existence of a new national emergency.15 On December 18, 1950, the Assistant Secretary of the Navy made a formal blanket determination to utilize exception (1) and by directive authorized Navy contracting officers to negotiate contracts under the authority of exception (1) during the period of the new national emergency. The Assistant Secretary in his directive stated, however, that procurement by formal advertising would continue to have a definite place in the Navy's procurement program. Similar blanket determinations under exception (1) were made by the Secretaries of the Army and Air Force. Copies of these determinations were forwarded to the General Accounting Office and no further determinations were required for the negotiation of individual contracts under this exception. From December 1950 until January 1956, all contracts negotiated under the Armed Services Procurement Act by the Armed Services cited this exception in contracts as the negotiation authority rather than the other numbered exceptions. 

With the suspension of hostilities in Korea, the Assistant Secretary of the Navy determined in the early part of 1954 that it was appropriate to place definite restrictions on the use of exception (1) since there was then less justification for the broad usage of this exception than existed in December 1950 when the present national emergency was declared. 

Pursuant to a directive issued by the Assistant Secretary of the Navy, a memorandum for the file justifying the use of negotiation was required for each negotiated procurement in excess of $5,000. While exception (1) continued to be cited in contracts as the actual negotiation authority until January 1956, justification of negotiation generally had to be found in the particular exception under which the procurement would have been negotiated had exception (1) not been available for use. Certain of these determinations could be made at the level of the contracting officer, while those utilizing exceptions (11) through (16) were required to be made by the head of the contract division of the procuring activity. In those instances where negotiation would not have been justified on any

By an amendment to ASPR 3-201.2 which became effective January 1, 1956, the use of exception (1) during the present national emergency was further limited to (i) procurements made pursuant to labor surplus and disaster area programs, (ii) procurements made in aid of small business programs, (iii) procurements of nonperishable subsistence supplies, and (iv) procurements for research and development and of supplies related thereto for $100,000 or less when placed with organizations other than educational institutions. $ 3.5. Public Exigency 10 U.S.C. § 2304 (a) (2) (formerly section 2(c) (2) of the Armed Serv ices Procurement Act) authorizes the negotiation of purchases and contracts ifthe public exigency will not permit the delay incident to advertising;

This authority is a restatement or adaptation of that portion of Rev. Stat. § 3709, as amended, which permitted negotiation "when the public exigencies require the immediate delivery of the articles or performance of the service."

In order for this negotiation authority to be used, the need or exigency must be compelling and of unusual urgency, irrespective of whether that emergency could or should have been foreseen. Two conditions would have to exist in order to justify the use of this authority: the Government would have to be seriously injured, financially or otherwise, if the supplies or services were not furnished by a certain time; and procurement by advertising would not result in the supplies or services being furnished by the necessary date. Some of the situations in connection with which this authority might be used are the following: (1) where supplies or services are needed at once because of a fire, flood, explosion, or other disaster; (2) where essential equipment for or repair to a ship is needed at once in order that the ship may carry out its sailing orders; (3) where essential

$3.9. Purchases Outside the United States 10 U.S.C. § 2304 (a) (6) (formerly section 2(c) (6) of the Armed 

Services Procurement Act) authorizes the negotiation of purchases and contracts if— the purchase or contract is for property or services to be procured and used outside the United States and the Territories, Commonwealths, and possessions; 35

A similar exception, for the Navy Department, was contained in section 3721 of the Revised Statutes which authorized the Navy to purchase without advertising "supplies which might be necessary to purchase out of the United States for vessels on foreign stations." Hence, this earlier 

Navy authority granted by Rev. Stat. § 3721, which was expressly repealed by section 11 (a) of the Armed Services Procurement Act,36 was substantially reincorporated in exception (6) and at the same time was extended to the other Armed Services. 

Although this exception, as originally set forth in the Armed Services Procurement Act, applied "outside the limits of the United States and its possessions," nevertheless the Armed Services took the position that the phrase "United States and its possessions" necessarily and logically includes territories, and was therefore tantamount to the phrase "United States, its Territories and possessions." This interpretation was adopted in the codification of the Armed Services Procurement Act in 10 U.S.C. § 2304 (a) (6).37 Accordingly, the negotiation authority of this exception (6) is used by the Armed Services only for the procurement of supplies or services which are actually purchased and used outside the limits of the United States, its Territories, Commonwealths and possessions (irrespective of the actual place of negotiation or execution of the contract), but when applicable it is used in lieu of any other exception.38 

In the main, this provision would apply to the purchase of supplies, construction, or services for overseas installations or for the use of overseas forces. PERISHABLE OR NONPERISHABLE SUBSISTENCE SUPPLIES $ 3.12 

Although this exception provides for what is literally a new grant of authority, nevertheless it is intended (and so stated in ASPR 3-208.2) that this authority will be used ordinarily only for purchases of articles with brand names or of a proprietary nature, as requested by personnel authorized to make purchases from such military agencies as Navy ships' stores and commissaries. So limited, exception (8) amounts to little more than a specific application of the general exception to Rev. Stat. § 3709 for proprietary purchases where it was impracticable to secure competition. 

In any case, the negotiation authority afforded by this exception (8) is to be used only for purchases for resale where appropriated funds are involved; it will have no application to purchases made with nonappropriated funds, such as purchases by military exchanges. (These were formerly designated "Army post exchanges" and "Navy ships' service stores.") With respect to purchases from funds appropriated for Navy ships' stores and for Army and Navy commissaries, however, it was felt that such purchases were generally not made by specifications but by brand names, with a view toward accommodating the brand preferences of personnel authorized to use such facilities; and hence, as indicated above, the authority to negotiate was deemed necessary because of the proprietary nature of the brand name articles. Furthermore, exception (8) should not be used if the procurement is also covered by exception (3) or by exception (6).45

As in the case of negotiation of contracts for medicine or medical supplies pursuant to exception (7), suitable advance publicity of the proposed purchase must be given whenever the probable cost of supplies purchased for authorized resale under this exception will exceed $10,000. Also, as with negotiated purchases of medicines or medical supplies in excess of $10,000, the form and extent of the publicity is left up to each Department, except that the advance publicity or notification must be given for a period of at least fifteen days wherever practicable. This requirement, it may be recalled, is imposed by 10 U.S.C. § 2304(d) and is expressly incorporated in ASPR 3-208.2.

With respect to perishable subsistence supplies, it was felt to be desirable, and in fact virtually essential, to enlarge this area of negotiation to cover all perishable subsistence supplies, many of which could not be described or given specifications adequately to provide a basis for advertising for bids. The only businesslike method of buying such perishable supplies is by evaluation after visual inspection at the time and place that these supplies are offered, and then by purchase at current wholesale prices. 

It is clear that the delay of only a few days in marketing such common produce items as tomatoes or lettuce would seriously and adversely affect their "freshness," which is a paramount factor in determining quality and hence in determining a reasonable price. 

The negotiation authority afforded by exception (9) was originally limited to perishable subsistence supplies. But by an amendment effective August 28, 1958,49 exception (9) was broadened to cover nonperishable subsistence supplies as well, apparently for the reason that the marketing methods employed for such nonperishables as canned goods and frozen foods had demonstrated the need to negotiate the requirements for such supplies while in the crop stage, something not feasible under procurement by formal advertising.50

ASPR 3-209.3 denies the use of exception (9) in cases in which the procurement may also be negotiated either under exception (3) or exception (6).51

It was felt by Congress that the experience gained before and during World War II proved without doubt that the continuation of programs for research and development was of prime importance to the Armed Services and that the very nature of such programs and of contracts related thereto was inconsistent with procurement by formal advertising. 

Not only was the field of possible contractors in many cases very limited, but also a research or development contractor would usually have to be selected on the basis of special skills and exceptional facilities in much the same manner that an individual would seek the services or professional advice of an expert. Furthermore, in research and development contracts it is frequently impossible to make accurate forecasts of costs, thereby making it necessary to enter into cost-reimbursement type contracts, which on the one hand are not permitted with respect to contracts entered into by advertising and on the other hand require greater care and independence of contracting than would be necessary in the case of fixedprice contracts or would be possible in the case of procurement by advertising.

It should be noted that the negotiation authority given by this exception (11) is basically twofold: on the one hand, applying to experimental, developmental, or research work; and on the other hand, applying to the furnishing of supplies for such work. With respect to the former, the authority may be used for (i) contracts relating to theoretical analysis, exploratory studies, and experimentation in any field of science or technology; (ii) developmental contracts calling for the practical application of investigative findings and theories of a scientific or technical nature; and (iii) services, tests, and reports incidental to such experimental, developmental, or research work. With respect to the second part of exception (11), as indicated above, the authority may be used for the purchase of such equipment and supplies (including parts, accessories, patent rights thereto, and drawings or designs thereof) as are necessary for and as are used in connection with any existing research or development program. Navy procuring activities do not, however, use this exception for the purchase of all supplies which are used in experimental, developmental or research work. For example, if coal or fuel oil is required for the purpose of heating a building in which research work is done or is used in connection with testing research equipment, procurement of the coal or fuel oil is effected by formal advertising and not by negotiation under this exception. Moreover, the negotiation authority of this exception (11) is not to be used for any contract for quantity production (other than such kind of contract for supplies needed in connection with a research

$3.15. Classified Purchases 10 U.S.C. § 2304 (a) (12) (formerly section 2(c) (12) of the Armed 

Services Procurement Act) authorizes the negotiation of purchases and contracts by the Secretary ifthe purchase or contract is for property or services whose procurement he determines should not be publicly disclosed because of their character, ingredients, or components; 

Although this exception is substantially a new negotiation authority, at least in its broad coverage and in its extension to all of the Armed Services, nevertheless there have been in existence three Army statutes (all expressly repealed by section 11 of the Armed Services Procurement Act) which granted certain negotiation authority along the lines of the authority granted by this exception (12). Thus, the Act of May 11, 1908,63 authorized the War Department to purchase ordnance equipment in such a manner as was deemed most economical and efficient, whenever the public interest would be injured by publicly divulging the character or ingredients of such equipment; the Act of May 15, 1936,64 extended the aforementioned authority to cover chemical warfare and signal property; and the Act of Juy 13, 1939,65 extended the authority to cover aircraft parts, instruments and aeronautical accessories.

It was the view of Congress that broad discretion should be given to the Armed Services to determine when and whether the considerations of national security or safety required that procurement by means of advertising, with its unavoidable publicity and disclosure, should be rejected in favor of the more guarded and controllable method of procurement by negotiation. Accordingly, ASPR 3-212 provides that this authority may be used for purchases or contracts classified "Confidential" or higher, or where because of other considerations, the purchase or contract should not be publicly disclosed; but also provides that this authority shall not be used when negotiation is authorized by any other exception, except that if a procurement may be negotiated either under

§3.16. Technical Equipment Requiring Standardization and Interchange ability of Parts 

10 U.S.C. § 2304 (a) (13) Services Procurement Act) 

contracts by the Secretary if- (formerly section 2(c) (13) of the Armed authorizes the negotiation of purchases and the purchase or contract is for equipment that he determines to be technical equipment whose standardization and the interchangeability of whose parts are necessary in the public interest and whose procurement by negotiation is necessary to assure that standardization and interchangeability;

This exception is entirely new and unprecedented (other than, of course, that purchases of this sort, and in fact any kind of purchase, could have been made by negotiation under the First War Powers Act of 1941. This negotiation authority grew out of the pressing need on the part of the Armed Services to be able to negotiate purchases of additional units, spare parts, and replacement items, the initial procurement of which would for the most part be made by advertising and would result in the standardization for general use of the particular equipment of that supplier whose bid was accepted. The argument was advanced to Congress, and was accepted by Congress, that the military importance of and the financial savings resulting from standardized equipment and interchangeable parts made it important for the Services to be able to standardize on major items of technical equipment, and that thereafter additional or replacement units thereof, as well as interchangeable spare parts therefor, should be obtainable by means of negotiation. 

The present policy governing the use of this exception is prescribed by ASPR 3-213.67 This policy recognizes that in certain instances it is necessary in the interest of standardization of technical equipment and the interchangeability of parts for such equipment to procure from one supplier or a limited number of suppliers technical equipment which, although available from a number of suppliers, would, if procured from a number of sources, have such varying characteristics (notwithstanding detailed performance specifications and rigid inspection) as would prevent standardization and interchangeability of parts. Since the standardization of equipments ordinarily restricts normal competition and in most cases results in noncompetitive procurement, determinations to standardize
