 $ 3.17. Technical Equipment Requiring Substantial Initial Investment or Extended Period of Preparation for Manufacture 10 U.S.C. § 2304 (a) (14) (formerly section 2(c) (14) of the Armed 

Services Procurement Act) authorizes the negotiation of purchases and contracts by the Secretary ifthe purchase or contract is for technical or special property that he determines to require a substantial initial investment or an extended period of preparation for manufacture, and for which he determines that formal advertising and competitive bidding might require duplication of investment or preparation already made or would unduly delay the procurement of that property; 

This exception, too, is entirely new and unprecedented, other than formerly being included within the broad negotiation authority of the First War Powers Act of 1941. Somewhat as in the case of exception (13), the negotiation authority afforded by exception (14) grew out of the essential need on the part of the Armd Services to be able to negotiate contracts for such technical and complex items as aircraft, tanks, radar, missiles, rockets, and other such items of specialized equipment. It was felt that to have to award contracts for such items after advertising not only would be timeconsuming and wasteful but also would leave the procuring Service with no assurance that it would obtain supplies of the proper quality. In other words, technical and specialized items of the kind listed above can generally be purchased to the best advantage from that supplier who, as a result of having developed the item for production, has already done a considerable amount of preparatory work and has already acquired the necessary know-how and shop practices which are fundamental to all mass production techniques used for the rapid and less expensive production of intricate mechanisms of high quality. Procurement by advertising and award to the lowest bidder under such circumstances would often mean either, on the one hand, that the award would be made to the untrained contractor who would have to go through all over again the timeconsuming and uncertain processes of development and education, or on the other hand that the award would be made to the trained contractor whose bid would only have to be low enough to shade any other untrained bidder and thereby might result in unreasonable profit growing out of repetitious charges for tooling and other preparatory work that had already been paid for by the Government under the development contract. 

As indicated above, the negotiation authority of this exception (14) is for the most part used in situations where it is preferable to place a production contract with the supplier who had developed the equipment. 

This assures to the Government the benefit of the techniques, tooling, and equipment already acquired by that supplier; and it avoids undue delay arising from the fact that a new supplier would have to acquire such techniques, tooling, and equipment. The use of this exception generally 136

NEGOTIATION AFTER ADVERTISING 

$3.18 involves such background factors as (i) high starting costs, (ii) preliminary engineering and development work not usable by any other supplier, (iii) elaborate special tooling, (iv) substantial time and effort already expended in prototype development; and (v) the likelihood of important design changes. And as emphasized in ASPR 3-214,69 the use of this negotiation authority is limited to the procurement of technical or specialized supplies (examples of which have already been listed above), major components thereof, and supplies necessary for their use or operation.

With respect to the use of this exception (14), just as was the case under exception (13), the Armed Services Procurement Regulation prescribes the particular determinations which the Secretary of a Department must personally make before any contract may be negotiated under the authority of this exception (14). First, he must specifically determine that the supplies being procured under a proposed contract are of a technical or special nature. Second, he must specifically determine that the supplies being procured are such as to require either or both a substantial initial investment and an extended period of preparation for manufacture. And third, he must specifically determine that procurement of the supplies in question by means of advertising and competitive bidding either, on the one hand, might require duplication of investment or preparation already made, or on the other hand would unduly delay procurement of the supplies, or both. $3.18. Negotiation After Advertising 

10 U.S.C. § 2304 (a) (15) (formerly section 2 (c) (15) of the Armed Serv ices Procurement Act) authorizes the negotiation of purchases and contracts by the Secretary ifthe purchase or contract is for property or services for which he determines that the bid prices received after formal advertising are unreasonable as to all or part of the requirements, or were not independently reached in open competition, and for which (A) he has notified each responsible bidder of intention to negotiate and given him reasonable opportunity to negotiate; (B) the negotiated price is lower than the lowest rejected bid of any responsible bidder, as determined by the head of the agency; and (C) the negotiated price is the lowest negotiated price offered by any responsible supplier; 

This exception, also new and unprecedented (apart from its inclusion formerly under the broad authority of the First War Powers Act of 1941), was deemed to be necessary in order to protect the Government in situations where formal advertising is at first used, but results in excessive or collusive bids. In either of these two kinds of situations the only effective course of action for a contracting officer to take is to negotiate 

69 Ibid. 137

$3.18

with one or more of the bidders in an effort to break the price line and thereby to obtain the desired supplies at reasonable prices. Even though resort might be made in certain instances to the antitrust laws, any relief obtained therefrom would usually be too slow, and too late to be of practical use. As it is, resort to the negotiation authority afforded by this exception (15) would permit prompt and economical procurement of the supplies in question and at the same time would still permit the initiation of corrective action to prevent recurrence of collusive bidding in any instance where further investigation revealed that violations of the antitrust laws were involved. In this latter connection, 10 U.S.C. § 2305 (c)⁰ expressly requires that any such evidence of violation of the antitrust laws, based on a consideration of bids received after advertising, shall be referred by the head of a procuring agency to the Attorney General for appropriate action.

As specifically provided in this exception (15), the Secretary of a Department must himself determine that the bid prices received after formal advertising either were not reasonable as to all or part of the requirement or were not independently reached in open competition. 

Furthermore, no contract may be negotiated under this authority unless and until three further conditions have occurred: (1) the contracting officer has notified each responsible bidder of intention to negotiate and given him reasonable opportunity to negotiate; (2) the Secretary has made an additional determination that the contemplated negotiated price is lower than the lowest rejected bid price of any responsible bidder; and (3) the contemplated negotiated price is in fact the lowest negotiated price offered by any responsible supplier. It is proper to make an award under the invitation for those items or quantities as to which the bid prices are reasonable and have been independently arrived at, whereupon the balance of the procurement may be negotiated under this exception. 

There is some question as to whether or not the price of the proposed negotiated contract could properly be determined by the Secretary to be "lower than the lowest rejected bid price of any responsible bidder” if the base price as negotiated was in fact lower but at the same time was subject to upward escalation or redetermination to an extent that might conceivably take it above the amount of the lowest rejected bid price. 

In this situation the Services have agreed that such a negotiated price could properly be determined to be lower only if there was a ceiling or maximum limit on the amount of authorized upward escalation or redetermination which would prevent that negotiated price from ever exceeding the amount of the "lowest rejected bid price of any responsible bidder."

$3.19. Purchases in the Interest of National Defense or Industrial 

Mobilization 

10 U.S.C. § 2304 (a) (16) (formerly section 2(c) (16) of the Armed 

Services Procurement Act) authorizes the negotiation of purchases and contracts by the Secretary ifhe determines that (A) it is in the interest of national defense to have a plant, mine, or other facility, or a producer, manufacturer, or other supplier, available for furnishing property or services in case of a national emergency; or (B) the interest of industrial mobilization in case of such an emergency, or the interest of national defense in maintaining active engineering, research, and development, would otherwise be subserved; 

Although this exception is virtually a new one, at least in its broad coverage and extension to all of the Armed Services, nevertheless its underlying principle had been previously recognized in the Act of June 16, 1938," under which the Secretary of War was authorized, subject to the approval of the President, to place so-called "educational orders" for special munitions with selected commercial concerns for the purpose of familiarizing them with the manufacture of such munitions, and accessories and parts thereof. The experience gained during World War II made it essential that the Armed Services have the authority given by this exception (16). Since in a national emergency, such as the one declared on December 16, 1950, there is not time for the reorganization of industrial strength so as to become speedily adapted to the needs of war, this important negotiation authority is necessary to serve as an instrument of preparedness by permitting the development of industrial facilities and production know-how necessary to keep abreast of the industrial requirements arising out of the discovery and application of new weapons, and also by permitting consideration to be given to such important military factors as geographical location in the interest of dispersal, avoidance of overconcentration in a few companies, and maintenance of a basic core of plants, facilities, skills, and personnel around which there can be expansion when and if urgently needed.

The negotiation authority of this exception (16) is used to carry out such plans and programs as are evolved under the direction of the Secretary of a Department to provide incentives to manufacturers to maintain, and to keep active, not only engineering and design staffs but also manufacturing facilities available for mass production. It is used, therefore, whenever it is deemed necessary to keep vital facilities or suppliers in business or to make them available in the event of a national emergency. 

It is also used when it is deemed necessary to train selected suppliers in the furnishing of critical supplies to prevent the loss of their availability 

71 52 Stat. 707 (1938). 139

$3.

and employee skills, or to maintain active engineering, research, and development work. Furthermore, it has been used when it was deemed necessary to maintain properly balanced sources of supply for meeting the requirements of procurement programs in the interest of industrial mobilization.

The authority granted by this exception (16) might be said to complement and in a sense to parallel the principles underlying the Strategic and Critical Materials Stock Piling Act; 72 and although in this connection use of the authority may result in contracts which do not represent the most economical purchase of particular items, nevertheless the national security requires the use of this exception. Without it, the plants, facilities, skills, and personnel needed during a war or national emergency might atrophy or might not be ready for use in a time of critical need. 

As with the five preceding exceptions, here too the Armed Services 

Procurement Act requires, and ASPR 3-216 73 sets forth in detail, specific determinations to be made personally by the Secretary of a Department before using the authority of this exception (16). These determinations, in the alternative, are as follows: (1) the Secretary must specifically determine that it is in the interest of national defense to have a particular facility or supplier available for furnishing supplies or services in the event of a national emergency; or (2) the Secretary must specifically determine that the interest of industrial mobilization (in the event of a national emergency) would be promoted by procurement by negotiation with a particular supplier; or (3) the Secretary must specifically determine that, in maintaining active engineering, research, and development, the interest of the national defense would be promoted by procurement by negotiation with such a supplier. As discussed in § 3.16 in connection with exception (13), procurement assignments have been made among the military departments whereby one Department procures all of the requirements of the military departments for certain supplies. In certain instances where a procurement is effected by a Department other than the Requiring Department, the Secretary of the Requiring Department makes the formal Determinations and Findings under this exception (16) and the Secretary of the Purchasing Department is not required. to make further Determinations and Findings.

$ 3.20. Otherwise Authorized by Law: In General 

10 U.S.C. 2304(a) (17) (formerly section 2(c) (17) of the Armed Services Procurement Act) authorizes the negotiation of purchases and contracts ifnegotiation of the purchase or contract is otherwise authorized by law.

This exception preserves the statutory authority to negotiate contracts as contained in permanent legislation not repealed by section 11 of the Armed Services Procurement Act. As has been previously indicated, section 11 expressly repealed nineteen statutes in their entirety; it designated portions of five other acts that were repealed; it provided that three acts (including in particular Rev. Stat. § 3709) shall not apply to the procurement of supplies or services by any of the agencies subject to the provisions of the Armed Services Procurement Act; and it contained the relatively common and general provision that "all other laws and parts of laws to the extent that they are inconsistent with this Act are hereby repealed." 76 It is also important to note that the negotiation authority contained in this exception (17) would have the effect, in addition to preserving and virtually incorporating into the Armed Services Procurement Act such negotiation authority as was available under earlier laws not thereby repealed, of permitting negotiation under any relevant after-enacted law, such as Title II of the First War Powers 

Act as it existed during the period of its revitalization until its expiration in 1958. Since any such after-enacted law might take the form of general legislation and might omit any reference to the Armed Services Procurement Act, this exception (17) would forestall a statutory construction that would deny to the Armed Services the benefits of such later general legislation on the basis of earlier specific legislation. Both in the committee hearings and in the committee reports with respect to the Armed Services Procurement bill, six relatively major pre-existing acts were specifically referred to as being illustrative of earlier laws under which the authority to negotiate contracts would be preserved by virtue of exception (17). These six acts are considered in §§ 3.21-3.25 infra.

The Aircraft Procurement Act of 1926 78 

This act, in general, sets out a method for procuring by negotiation aircraft and aeronautical material under certain limited circumstances. 

More specifically, under the provisions of this act as codified in 10 U.S.C. §§ 2274 and 2275, the rules of competitive bidding with respect to aeronautical material are relaxed for the Army, Navy and Air Force, not only by authorizing each of the Secretaries to award production contracts to that bidder found by the Secretary to be the "lowest responsible bidder who can satisfactorily perform the work to the best advantage of the United States," but also by permitting experimental contracts to be placed without competition. $ 3.22. 

Architectural or Engineering Services: Act of April 25, 1939 7 

This act gives to the Secretary of the Navy the authority to contract with any individual, firm, or corporation, without formal advertising and without regard to the laws relating to the compensation of government employees, to furnish architectural or engineering services for designs, plans, drawings and specifications required on the one hand for the construction or alteration of Naval public works or utility projects or on the other hand for the construction of Naval vessels or aircraft or parts thereof, whenever the Secretary deems that such action is advantageous to the national defense and that the existing facilities of the Navy Department are inadequate. A specific limitation imposed on the use of this negotiation authority is that in no case shall the charge for any service procured under this act exceed 6 percent of the estimated cost of the project to which such charge is applicable. By the Act of August 7, 1939, the Secretaries of the Army and Air Force were granted substantially the same authority given to the Secretary of the Navy by the aforementioned Act of April 25, 1939. $ 3.23. 

Transportation Services by Common Carriers: The Trans portation Act of 1940

Section 321(a) of the Transportation Act of 1940 is supplementary to the Interstate Commerce Act and authorizes the procurement by negotiation of transportation services whenever the services required are procured from any common carrier lawfully operating in the territory where such services are to be performed. However, this authority may not be used for the procurement of transportation services from other than such a common carrier.82

III. DETERMINATIONS AND FINDINGS IN JUSTIFICATION OF NEGOTIATION AND OF CERTAIN TYPES OF CONTRACTS $3.29. Determinations and Findings Required by the Armed Services Procurement Act 

Although it was indicated in the introduction to this chapter that the various conditions or restrictions imposed upon negotiation would be considered together, it seems advisable to take up separately that condition or restriction which throughout the military departments goes by the name of "Determinations and Findings" and which has been frequently alluded to in the immediately preceding part of this chapter in connection with the desire of Congress to hedge about with adequate safeguards the use of the newer and more important negotiation exceptions, and in that connection to require a personal finding and determination by the head of the department concerned before any one of these special exceptions may be invoked. Furthermore, the other conditions or restrictions administratively imposed upon the use of negotiation, which will be discussed in the next succeeding part of this chapter, apply almost equally to contracts entered into as a result of advertising. The "condition precedent" of 

Determinations and Findings is peculiar to procurement by negotiation, and not only is spelled out carefully in the Armed Services Procurement Act (now 10 U.S.C. §§ 2304 (a), 2306, 2307, 2310, 2311) but also is referred to frequently and relied on extensively throughout the consideration of the Armed Services Procurement bill in the various committee hearings and committee reports. In this connection, too, the matter of Determinations and Findings is treated at some length in Part 3 of Section III of the Armed Services Procurement Regulation; and, as shall be referred to later, is the subject of a Navy-wide directive" containing instructions as to the proper form and use of the different determinations and findings required throughout the Armed Services Procurement Act. 

The determinations and supporting findings by the agency head that are referred to in the statute, in the Armed Services Procurement Regulation, and in this Chapter 3 usually appear in the form of the statement “if he determines . . ." or "which he determines. . . ." Thus, as has been pointed out in the discussion of exceptions (11) through (16), each of those exceptions contains some reference to a determination by the head of on the use of negotiation for construction work in the continental United States. 

So viewed, negotiation authority for construction work is granted only by 10

U.S.C. § 2304(a), and the "unless" clause of 2304 (e) merely refers back to the use of negotiation for construction work outside the continental United States otherwise authorized by § 2304 (a).

While reasonable arguments can be made in support of each of these interpretations, this latter interpretation has been adopted by the Department of Defense and is reflected in the revision to ASPR 

3-218 issued on June 11, 1958.

So too, 10 U.S.C. § 2306 (c) 2 provides that neither a cost nor a cost-plus-a-fixed-fee contract nor an incentive-type contract shall be used unless "the head of the agency determines that such a contract is likly to be less costly to the United States than any other kind of contract or that it is impracticable to obtain property or services of the kind or quality required except under such a contract." And 10 U.S.C. § 2307 provides for advance payments under negotiated or advertised contracts if the agency head determines that such provision is in the public interest.93 Although there are other references throughout the Armed Services Procurement Act to matters requiring determination by the agency head (such as in 10 U.S.C. § 2304 (d), relating to the practicability of giving suitable advance publicity before negotiating contracts in excess of $10,000 for medical supplies or for supplies for resale; and such as in 10 U.S.C. § 2306 (b) which provides that every negotiated contract shall contain a warranty, or covenant against contingent fees, "determined to be suitable by the head of the agency"), nevertheless the only three kinds of situations where use of the word "determines" is important (both procedurally and authoritatively) are (i) its use in 10 U.S.C. § 2304 (a) (11) through (16) as a condition precedent to the authority to negotiate under those special circumstances, (ii) its use in 10 U.S.C. § 2307 (c) as a condition precedent to a provision for advance payments, and (iii) its use in 10 U.S.C. § 2306(c) as a condition precedent to the use of a particular method of contracting.

In two other situations where the requirement of determinations is important (namely, with respect to advance payments and method of contracting) the power to make the determination and findings may be delegated down to the operating level of the contracting officer. 

Although 10 U.S.C. § 2310(a) permits determinations to be made for classes of contracts as well as for individual contracts, nevertheless a Navy directive generally limits this privilege to determinations made personally by the Secretary, and even then, only in special cases and for a specified period of time."

To repeat, only the Secretary of the Department may make the necessary determinations and findings in support of the authority to negotiate under exceptions (11) through (16), except that a chief officer responsible for procurement' may make the necessary determination and findings for any research or development contract not over $25,000. IV. CONTRACT CLEARANCE REQUIREMENTS $3.30. Contract Clearance Requirements in General 

In addition to the statutory requirement for certain determinations and findings precedent to the exercise of certain negotiation authority, there are other conditions or restrictions upon the use of the negotiation and advertising methods of procurement imposed by ASPR 1-403,5 called "Requirements to be Met Before Entering Into Contracts," in which connection it is provided that no contract (by whatsoever method effected) shall be entered into unless and until (i) applicable requirements of law, of the Armed Services Procurement Regulations, and of individual Department procedures have been complied with, and (ii) business clearance or approval has been obtained in accordance with Department procedures. In connection with the first of the aforementioned requirements, not only do numerous federal statutes require the inclusion in all public contracts of certain contract clauses or provisions, but also the Armed Services Procurement Act itself specifically requires the inclusion of certain contract clauses and the compliance with certain federal statutes requiring the inclusion of other contract clauses. These requirements are discussed in detail in Chapter 9 infra. $3.31. Negotiation Clearance

Negotiation clearance, as its name implies, is the requirement for obtaining authority to negotiate certain individual contracts or classes of contracts under exceptions (11) through (16) of the Armed Services

Procurement Act. Obtaining such authority generally requires a determination by the Secretary, and negotiation clearance is obtained by the submission of a "Request for Authority to Negotiate" (Negotiation 

Clearance Memorandum) to the Secretary of the Navy via the Office of

Naval Material. This request transmits a draft of the formal Determination and Findings which is to be executed by the Secretary and is required to set forth, among other matters, the following: (a) the justification for the use of negotiation; (b) the extent of informal competition which will be sought as a basis for selecting the proposed contractor, or if no competition is intended, a statement as to the reasons for the absence of competition; and (c) such other pertinent information not included in the Determination and Findings as will assist the reviewing authorities in the proper understanding of the necessity for granting the proposed exception to advertising. The request is required to be initialed by legal counsel to show that the Determination and Findings has been reviewed and approved as to form and legality. 

5 Jan. 3, 1955.

$3.

$3.32. Business Clearance

A business clearance, which is also referred to as "authority to contract" is granted by the Office of Naval Material based on a "Business Clearance Memorandum" submitted by the procuring activity making the purchase. 

This memorandum details the justification of the price and other business aspects of the proposed contract. It is accompanied by supporting datasuch as a statement of the proposed contractor's financial stability; a complete cost estimate ("cost breakdown"), together with the negotiator's analysis of the estimated cost; a justification of the reasonableness of the proposed contractor's estimated profit or fixed-fee; a price comparison with previous purchases for the same or similar supplies or services; copies of proposed special clauses affecting the contract price which have not been authorized for general use, together with a statement that such clauses have been approved by counsel for the procuring activity involved; a brief description and the estimated value of any Government-furnished equipment, materials and facilities; on all proposed contracts involving $5,000,000 or more, a statement as to the extent of subcontracting of complete units or major components; a statement as to the number of sources requested to bid; and a list of persons and firms which submitted formal bids, proposals or quotations (together with their respective bids, proposals or quotations).

Navy directives require that business clearance must be obtained from the Office of Naval Material prior to contract execution except that contracts for utility services are referred to the Bureau of Yards and Docks. 

Business clearance is required for the following principal types of negotiated procurements: (a) Each letter contract, letter of intent, or other incomplete preliminary contractual instrument, or any unpriced amendment thereto effecting new procurement, regardless of dollar value. Business clearance is also required on the conversion to a definitive contract of any such preliminary instrument where the definitive contract obligates the Government to pay $300,000 or more. If the conversion to a definitive contract obligates the Government in an amount less than $300,000, notification of the transaction is required by memor andum to the Office of Naval Material. 

(b) Each new contract or amendment effecting new procurement which by itself, or by the exercise of any option or options contained therein, would obligate the Government in the sum of $300,000 or more. (c) Any agreement or amendment for redetermination of the price of a contract for which business clearance has previously been required notwithstanding the fact that the redetermination is proposed at no change in the existing contract price.

$4.1. Introduction 

This chapter discusses the fiscal problems that arise in connection with the procurement of property and services for the Navy, the various methods by which the Navy assists in the financing of its contractors, and the legal position of the United States as a creditor in matters involving debt collection. The fiscal problems, as the term suggests, relate to the appropriation of funds by the Congress for Navy use, the obligation by contract of funds so appropriated, the subsequent expenditure of these obligated funds for all of the property and services which are required for the support of the Navy, and indeed, to the entire subject of financial management in the Navy. The fiscal process is a specialized and technical subject, circumscribed by both statutory and administrative controls that place many restrictions, both procedural and substantive, on the conduct of the Navy's business. This chapter will outline the subject in a general way in order to afford the student as well as the practitioner new to the ways of Government a background for dealing with any fiscal, financing or debt collection problem relating to Navy procurement. In approaching any specific problem, however, reference should be made to current reference material since the statutes, regulations, and other authorities cited in the text are constantly shifting and changing.'

 I. THE BUDGET PROCESS 

$ 4.2. In General

The fiscal problems relating to Navy procurement arise long before the appropriations for procurement are made by Congress, and they continue long after such appropriations are obligated. These problems are first encountered in the budget process, which is concerned not only with the steps leading up to the enactment of the appropriation act each year, but also with the execution of the budget or use of the money appropriated by the several departments and agencies. The budget process affords a striking illustration of the division of power between the Executive Branch of the Government and the Congress. Preparation of the budget, is, of course, the sole responsibility of the Executive Branch. When a government-wide budget has been developed by the President and presented to the Congress, it is then the responsibility of the Congress to decide how much money is to be appropriated for each of the Government's activities. 

When the appropriations have been made, the control of obligations and expenditures shifts back to the executive agencies, which are responsible for obligating and spending the appropriations according to law and subject to the general control exercised by the President through the Bureau of the Budget. The conduct of the fiscal affairs of the Government is controlled by the same tools of management that are commonly found in large business organizations, that is, the budgeting, accounting, auditing, and statistical reporting systems, by which both the Congress and the President are enabled to provide for the legal and efficient use of appropriated funds. In the Navy, as in many business organizations, these tools of financial management are the responsibility of a comptroller.3 A re-

PREPARATION OF THE NAVY'S BUDGET 

$ 4.3 view of the budget process in the Navy, then, necessarily involves all of the devices for insuring fiscal control. Since this process has a counterpart in all agencies of the Government, there is a standard fiscal terminology prescribed by the Bureau of the Budget 4 which the newcomer to this field should master in order to deal adequately with the subject matter of this chapter. The basic fiscal terms will be introduced in the text and defined in the footnotes as the subject matter requires. 

$ 4.3. Preparation of the Navy's Budget 

The Navy's budget is based upon planned programs and objectives developed each year by the Chief of Naval Operations within the framework of the strategic concepts and force levels prescribed by the Joint Chiefs of Staff. After the Secretary of Defense has stated the general policies and guidelines covering the preparation of the budget, budget estimates based on these policies and guidelines are submitted by the Navy Bureaus and Offices to the Comptroller of the Navy for his review. 

When this review is completed and a budget satisfactory to the Secretary of the Navy has been worked out, the budget is transmitted to the Assistant Secretary of Defense (Comptroller) who holds hearings on it in order to weigh the Navy's budget request with those of the Army and the Air Force. Thereafter, a single budget for the Department of Defense is approved and submitted by the Secretary of Defense to the Bureau of the Budget. That agency reviews the estimates and justifications and balances the proposed budget for the Department of Defense against the competing claims of other agencies of the Government. After the Bureau of the 

Budget has completed this process of reconciliation, it incorporates all the executive agencies' budgets, including the Navy's, into the President's budget document for presentation to the Congress. Fully three-quarters of a year is consumed during this stage of the budget process, and another half year at least is required for the succeeding stage which culminates in the enactment of the appropriation act. Thus, since a given budget relates to only one fiscal year, it frequently happens that two budgets are in preparation at the same time, in addition to the budget that has been incorporated in an appropriation act and which is being executed.

 § 4.4. The Appropriation of Funds To Support the Navy: Congressional Hearings 

The President's budget document contains a detailed statement of the estimates of the appropriations, with supporting data, which each of the agencies of the Executive Branch will require for one fiscal year. Since this document has both the physical proportions and fine print of a rather large metropolitan telephone directory, it is transmitted to the Congress by a budget message in January of each year to afford the President an opportunity to outline its scope and highlight its salient features. At this point, the "DOD" Subcommittee of the Appropriations Committee of the House of Representatives begins its consideration of the Navy's budget as the first step in the appropriation of funds for the Navy for the ensuing fiscal year beginning on 1 July. In order to obtain a detailed knowledge of the Navy's budget estimates as a basis for recommending appropriations to the full Committee, the Subcommittee schedules hearings for representatives of the Navy, or witnesses as they are called, who appear before it with narrative justification, charts, statistical data and any other information which will be helpful to understanding the program which the President has decided upon for the Navy. Traditionally, the first Navy witnesses include the Secretary and the Chief of Naval Operations, who explain the Navy's budget in terms of anticipated accomplishments within the context of the nation's strategic planning. They are followed by witnesses from the Bureaus and Offices, who go over their programs in detail with the Subcommittee. During these hearings, Navy witnesses are governed by the estimates for their activities as contained in the President's budget document. To insure an orderly and uniform presentation to the Appropriations Committees of both Houses, the Office of the Comptroller of the Navy coordinates the estimates and written justifications of the Bureaus and Offices and serves as the principal point of contact for the Navy with the Committees. The Appropriation Bill 

In drafting the Navy's appropriation bill, Counsel for the Office of the Comptroller of the Navy takes the previous year's appropriation act as a starting point and incorporates any changes which may be either desired by the Navy or directed by higher authority. The appropriation language thus framed appears in the President's budget document, together with the estimates and related justifications. In the nature of things, this process assures a basic continuity in the Navy's appropriation structure. Before a new item may be included in the Navy's appropriation bill, it is required by House Rule XXI to be otherwise authorized by law unless it has the effect of retrenching expenditures." This rule was first adopted in 1837 in order to prevent delay of appropriation bills on the floor of the House because of contention over propositions of legislation that had not theretofore been considered.10 It also has the effect of maintaining a proper distribution of legislative responsibility among the standing committees." For example, a new Navy program such as the construction of a new shipyard is properly the subject of legislation developed by the Armed Services Committees while the provision of funds necessary to carry out the program after it is authorized is a matter

The drafting of appropriation language consummates the preparation of the budget estimates. The language of an appropriation is important not only as a source of information to the Congress and the public with respect to the programs for which the appropriation is made, but also because it determines the legal availability of the funds appropriated. 

In this latter connection, it should be noted that budget estimates and related justifications are not controlling in deciding questions of availability or restrictions on the use of appropriations, unless they are incorporated either directly or by reference in the act making the appropriation.14 

$ 4.6. Execution of the Navy's Budget: The Administrative Machinery 

The Navy's appropriations are made in the Department of Defense appropriation act each year.15 In the appropriation act for fiscal year 

1958, these appropriations were made under 19 separate appropriation heads, each of which has a title and language describing the purposes as well as the time period for which the appropriation made thereunder is available. These separate appropriation heads are phrased in terms of broad functional purposes, and as a general rule there is no machinery provided for in the appropriation act for controlling the use of these appropriations. In effect, the legislative function is complete when the funds have been appropriated; thereafter, it remains for the Navy to use the appropriation for the purposes and within the time limit of the appropriation as specified by the Congress in the appropriation act.

EXECUTION OF THE NAVY'S BUDGET 

$ 4.6 the so-called Anti-Deficiency Act, in such a way as to establish a system of administration control over the funds of all executive agencies at all echelons. Thus, even though Congress should appropriate $100,000,000 under the head "Aircraft and Facilities, Navy" for the fiscal year 1959, the funds, once appropriated, would be available for use by the Navy not in excess of the amounts that have been apportioned by the Bureau of the Budget at the request of the Navy.18 And no obligation may be incurred by the Navy, regardless of the apportionment, until after the Secretary of Defense has approved scheduled rates of obligation.19 The apportionment, which reflects the budgetary control at the presidential level over the use of funds, is made on a quarterly or other periodic basis. to avoid a need for deficiency or supplemental appropriations which might otherwise arise during the fiscal year. In the example given, the apportionment for the first quarter of fiscal year 1959 under the "Aircraft and Facilities" head might be $20,000,000, if the rate of use is to be kept constant during the year. The remaining $5,000,000 would then be set aside by the Bureau of the Budget for contingencies or to effect savings wherever possible.20

ample, the appropriation head "Aircraft and Facilities" is subdivided into subheads covering the purposes of station operations, fleet operations, aircraft overhaul, alteration and replacement of facilities, and so on. 

Each subhead account is given a number which identifies the allocation made within the appropriation. The other appropriation heads of the

Navy appropriations, by means of a contract for goods or services, or otherwise, must in any case await an allocation, allotment or suballotment of funds adequate to cover the obligation.24 Sometimes an obligation is also preceded by a commitment, which is a firm administrative reservation of funds by a Bureau or Office to authorize its subsidiary activities to set in motion the action leading to a procurement obligation.2 

Commitments and allotments, then, are the fiscal devices by which the authority to obligate and expend Navy money is transmitted by a Bureau or Office to its lower operational echelons. 

The Anti-Deficiency Act 26 provides that no government officer or employee shall authorize or create any obligation or make any expenditure in excess of an apportionment, or administrative subdivision of appropriated funds, and that the executive agencies shall prescribe regulations which will make it possible to fix responsibility for creating such overobligations or overexpenditures." To enforce this prohibition against overobligating and overexpending funds, the act requires administrative discipline of those who inadvertently exceed their authority and criminal penalties for those who knowingly and willfully do so.28 Accordingly, a government officer or employee will exceed the funds made available to him in an allotment, suballotment or commitment at his peril, notwithstanding the administrative nature of the authorization. In this fashion, both Congress and the President are assured of planned and orderly fiscal management in the executive departments and agencies.

THE GENERAL ACCOUNTING OFFICE 

$ 4.7 ! 1 tive Branch headed by the Comptroller General, and responsible solely to the Congress. The functions of the General Accounting Office are worth noting here because of the key role that this agency plays in the fiscal administration of the Navy as well as the Government generally. 

It seems clear from the act which created it and its legislative history that it was the general intention of Congress to establish an agency, independent of the Executive Branch, through which it might ascertain whether public funds were being expended in accordance with appropriations.30 This is essentially the independent or "external" audit function which the Congress established in response to the need it felt for closer supervision over the executive departments in the matter of fiscal administration. To perform this independent audit function Congress gave the 

GAO investigative and reporting powers that were somewhat similar to those of a congressional committee. Briefly, the Congress directed the 

Comptroller General to investigate all matters relating to the receipt, disbursement, and application of public funds, and to report to the President and to the Congress thereon with his recommendation concerning the legislation he thinks necessary to improve the fiscal management of the Government. The Comptroller General was also directed to make such special investigations and reports as shall be ordered by either House of Congress or by any committee of either House having jurisdiction over revenue, appropriation, or expenditures, and to report to Congress every expenditure or contract made by any department in any year that is in violation of law. Finally, he must report to the Congress on the adequacy of the fiscal administration in the executive departments." In performing these broad functions, he was by statute clothed with an independence that is unique in the Government; that is, he was required to exercise his functions "without direction from any other officer." 32 Underscoring the independence of the Comptroller General is the statutory provision regarding his appointment by the President, under which he may not be removed, once his appointment has been confirmed by the Senate, during his term of 15 years except by joint resolution of Congress for specified reasons or by impeachment.33

The final power of the Comptroller General worthy of mention is his statutory authority to "settle and adjust" public accounts and all claims by or against the Government.34 It is on this impressive power that the 

Comptroller General has placed primary reliance in exercising such a large measure or control over not only the procurement activities but also the general fiscal management of the Navy. To satisfy this settlement requirement, Navy disbursing officers must send an account of every expenditure made by them, with a few exceptions not pertinent here, to the GAO for approval. A disallowance of a particular item in an account by the Comptroller General is final and conclusive upon the Executive Branch 35 and may result in a charge against the disbursing officer who made the expenditure. Since the latter becomes personally accountable to the Government therefor, it is not difficult to see why the Navy's fiscal and procurement policies have been so strongly influenced by the Comptroller General. In performing his settlement function, the Comptroller General makes an independent determination of the propriety of any given expenditure, since in the exercise of this power he is responsible directly to Congress. He may consider the views of lawyers in the Navy, or of the 

Attorney General, but he refuses to be bound by such views and he will disregard them when they conflict with his own opinion of the legality of the Navy's action. Similarly, he has refused to be bound by precedents of the Court of Claims and other inferior federal courts, although he accepts the finality of a decision of the Supreme Court of the United States. The Comptroller General performs other functions relating to fiscal administration in the Executive Branch, such as prescribing the general principles for accounting systems throughout the Government.

The following year

Congress approved another bill with substantially the same removal provisions, and it became law when President Harding signed it. The constitutional question raised by President Wilson, therefore, remains unresolved to this day. II. APPROPRIATIONS FOR THE NAVY A. IN GENERAL $4.8. The Constitutional Background: The Source of Authority for 

Appropriations

Each annual Navy appropriation act represents an authorization of funds by Congress in an amount which in the opinion of that body will be required for the support of the Navy for the fiscal year concerned. The authority of Congress to make this decision is derived from Article I, Section 8, Clause 1 of the Constitution, which provides that Congress shall have the power "To lay and collect Taxes, Duties, Imposts and Excises, to pay the Debts and provide for the common Defence and general Welfare of the United States. . . ." Congress is also empowered by 

Clause 13 of the same section "to provide and maintain a Navy," and by Clause 18 "to make all Laws which shall be necessary and proper for carrying into Execution the foregoing Powers, and and all other Powers vested by this Constitution in the Government of the United States, or in any Department or Officer thereof." These provisions enable Congress, to the exclusion of the Executive and Judicial Branches, to decide what appropriations are needed for the Navy. For example, the Supreme 

Court has said that the decision by Congress to recognize a claim founded on a merely equitable or honorary obligation as a debt of the United States is not usually subject to review by the Judicial Branch of the Government.39 The clause of the Constitution which gives Congress authority to provide and maintain a Navy was not inserted, therefore, for the purpose of endowing the national government with this power, but rather to designate the department of government which should exercise this power. Story, in his Commentaries, emphasized that this provision, and its companion provision relating to the support of armies, grew out of the conviction that the Executive should be deprived of the sole power of raising and regulating fleets and armies which the King had originally had under the British Constitution. Story wrote: "Our notions, indeed, of the dangers of standing armies, in time of peace, are derived in a great measure from the principles and examples of our English ancestors. In England, the King possessed the power of raising armies in the time of peace according to his own good pleasure. And this 

38 See § 4.7, n. 36 supra. 

39 See United States v. Realty Company, 163 U.S. 427, 440 (1896). 165

$ 4.9

prerogative was justly esteemed dangerous to the public liberties. Upon the revolution of 1688, Parliament wisely insisted upon a bill of rights, which should furnish an adequate security for the future. But how was this done? Not by prohibiting standing armies altogether in time of peace, but (as has already been seen) by prohibiting them without the consent of Parliament. This is the very proposition contained in the 

Constitution; for Congress can alone raise armies; and may put them down, whenever they choose." 40 $ 4.9. 

The Requirement for Appropriations 

Article I, Section 9, Clause 7 of the Constitution provides that: 

No money shall be drawn from the Treasury, but in Consequence of Appropriations made by Law; and a regular Statement and Account of the Receipts and Expenditures of all public Money shall be published from time to time. 

This provision epitomizes the constitutional concept of the legislative control of the purse; it is, in effect, a limitation upon the powers of the 

Executive Branch and does not restrict Congress in appropriating monies from the Treasury." For example, the Supreme Court has held that no officer of the federal government is authorized to pay a debt due from the United States, whether reduced to judgment or not, until an appropriation has been made for that purpose.42 In addition to the power to appropriate money, Congress has the concomitant power to regulate the making, spending and accounting for appropriations.43 The purpose of an appropriation, as well as the terms and conditions on which it is made, are matters solely within the discretion of Congress.44 These terms and con-

$ 4.10 ditions may be expressed in provisos attached to the appropriation," or in general provisions separately stated at the end of the appropriation act. In pursuance of this power, Congress has also enacted many permanent statutes which are applicable to all appropriations. The Constitutional provisions, the related regulatory statutes, and the appropriation acts, together with the decisions of the courts and the Comptroller General construing them, constitute the body of law governing the use of Navy appropriations. $ 4.10. The Legislative Framework for the Use of Appropriations 

Before any officer in the Executive Branch can spend public money of the United States, there must have been an Act of Congress appropriating the money and defining the purpose for which the appropriation was made. Accordingly, an appropriation has been defined as a statutory authorization to make payments out of the Treasury for specified purposes. In addition, an appropriation carries with it the authority to enter into contracts for goods or services, or, in other words, to obligate the Government to make future payments within the amounts provided and for the purposes specified in the appropriation act.48 

The legislative framework governing the use of funds appropriated for the Navy is found in part in the annual Department of Defense appropriation acts and in part in permanent legislation. A glance at some of the more salient items of this permanent legislative framework will illustrate the manner in which Congress has exercised its control over the purse.

 § 4.11. Fiscal Management 

Over the past several years, there has been an unusual amount of concern, both in Congress and in the Executive Branch, for the improvement of fiscal management in the Government.62 This concern undoubtedly reflects the increased size and scope of government operations that have continued after World War II. The basic laws providing a framework for fiscal management are the Budget and Accounting Act of 1921 63 and the Budget and Accounting Procedures Act of 1950.64 These two laws relate to the budget process,65 which is the process by which the executive agencies plan their requests for appropriations and carry out their programs after the money has been appropriated. The recommendations of the First Hoover Commission prompted the enactment of Title IV of the National Security Act Amendments of 1949, which established a Comp troller in each of the military departments as well as in the Office of the Secretary of Defense, and provided for a more flexible and up-to-date system of financial management throughout the Department of Defense. 

In this connection, Title IV among other things called for the adoption of performance budgets,67 and authorized the establishment of working capital funds 68 for financing inventories of supplies as well as certain industrial operations in the military departments, and management funds.69 More recently, the Second Hoover Commission has made suggestions for further improvements in the fiscal management of the Government. The most significant items of legislation resulting from the recommendations of this group are laws calling for the development and use of cost information in government budgeting and accounting 70 and authorizing limits to be placed in future appropriations on the amount of annual accrued expenditures thereunder."

Because the law authorizing accrued expenditure limitations may have a considerable effect on the Navy's ability to make payments to its contraetors, its mechanics should be briefly noted. The purported purpose of this law is to provide for greater congressional control over the amount of annual government spending. Very substantial government expenditures each year are made in liquidation of obligations incurred under appropriations made in prior years especially under contracts for weapons that require two or more years for manufacture and delivery-with the result that the amount appropriated as new obligating authority for

To enable Congress to bring government expenditures each year in closer balance with estimated revenues for that year, this law has proposed that appropriations hereafter impose limits on the accrued expenditures that may be made each year under such appropriations. -The Appropriation Acts 

The remaining aspect of the legislative framework governing the use of Navy appropriations is the legislation found in the annual Department of Defense appropriation acts. As a general rule, the basic Navy appropriations are made in this act each year, but if changes are required to alter the period for which the appropriations are available, as well as their purpose or amount, a deficiency or supplemental appropriation act may be passed. Such an act is available for the same purposes and is subject to the same terms and conditions, as the original act, unless otherwise provided. However, if the deficiency or supplemental appropriation act provides for a new function not provided for in the basic act for the fiscal year, the availability of the money appropriated for the new function takes effect on the date of enactment of the deficiency or supplemental act, in the absence of a clear intention to the contrary.” 

Since the appropriation acts are enacted each year, the money that they appropriate, as well as the legislative provisions embodied in them, are effective only for the fiscal year concerned, unless the appropriation or legislative rider expresses a contrary intention. Thus, if the appropriation for "Ships and Facilities" merely indicates an amount of money appropriated for the function that is described under this appropriation head, the money must be intended to serve the purposes only of the fiscal year in question. Likewise, a legislative rider or "general provision' in the appropriation act will be temporary in its effect whether or not it is so labeled." And a limitation of an appropriation act has been held not to repeal or even suspend an existing statutory obligation." From time to time, however, some of these general provisions have been enacted into permanent law, usually by the device of incorporating in them the word "hereafter" or some other word or phrase that clearly imports futurity.80

B. PERIOD FOR WHICH AVAILABLE $4.13. One-Year and Multiple-Year Appropriations: Period Available for Obligation

In exercising its constitutional power over appropriations, the Congress usually provides limits on the time period for which appropriations are available. Thus, appropriations for the Navy fall into one of the following three categories: one-year, multiple-year, or no-year. These time limits define only the period for which the appropriations are available for obligation, since the present appropriation structure of the Government rests on an obligation rather than an expenditure basis." A multiple-year appropriation is treated exactly like a one-year appropriation except that the period of availability for obligation is extended to the period specified in the appropriation. To illustrate, part of the unexpended balance of the appropriation "Ordnance and Facilities" for the fiscal year 1951 was extended by law so as to make the appropriation available for obligation for certain procurement during the fiscal year 1952. That part of the appropriation that was extended in this fashion became a multiple-year appropriation and was available for obligation during two fiscal years. Once the period of availability for obligation has passed, the appropriation, whether one-year or multiple-year in character, is said to expire," whereupon the unobligated balance in the appropriation reverts to the general fund in the Treasury."¹ $ 4.14.

Navy for an unlimited time to liquidate existing obligations.92 By way of illustration, suppose that Congress appropriated $100,000,000 to the Navy for the maintenance and operation of the fleet for the fiscal year 1960 under the appropriation head for this purpose. Among other things, this money is available for the procurement of equipment and supplies incident to this purpose. If such supplies were placed under contract in the fiscal year 1960, but the supplies were not delivered until the fiscal year 1962, the 1960 appropriation, having been properly obligated within the year for which it was made, would be available to liquidate the obligation.

On June 30 of the second full fiscal year following the fiscal year or years for which the appropriation is available for obligation, the obligated but unexpended balance of each one-year and multiple-year appropriation is transferred from separate appropriation accounts to what is termed "successor" or "M" accounts of the Navy.93 These "M" accounts are established to cover the same general purposes as the appropriations they succeed. Thus all "Military Personnel, Navy" appropriations are transferred to a "Military Personnel, Navy" "M" account. All other annual appropriations are similarly transferred to their respective "M" accounts. 

Into each "M" account are merged the obligated but unexpended balances of all comparable Navy annual or multiple-year appropriation accounts for the same or prior fiscal years and for the same general purposes, with the result that for expenditure purposes annual and multiple-year appropriations lose their fiscal year identity two years after they no longer are available for obligation."4 The Navy's "M" accounts are available to the 

Navy without fiscal year limitation for the payment of obligations chargeable against any of the appropriations from which the particular "M" account was derived.95

Regulations prescribed by the Comptroller General under 31 U.S.C. § 702 provide that claims chargeable to successor (M) accounts may be paid, or may be administratively denied, without action by the General Accounting Office, except for those claims which involve "doubtful questions of law or fact" or are otherwise expressly required by statute or GAO regulation or decision to be settled before payment in the General Accounting Office or are barred by an applicable statute of limitations."

Claims against the Government that are required by statute to be settled by the General Accounting Office are "barred unless such claim, bearing the signature and address of the claimant or of an authorized agent or attorney, shall be received in said office within ten full years after the date such claim first accrued. . . ." Claims that may be paid administratively under 31 U.S.C. § 702 without reference to the General Accounting Office are subject to this limitation since 31 U.S.C. § 71 requires all claims to be settled in the General Accounting Office. This settlement is usually accomplished when the General Accounting Office settles the accounts of disbursing officers covering all appropriations and funds, including "M" accounts.

The foregoing procedure concerning "M" accounts and their availability without time limits for the liquidation of obligations properly incurred under annual and multiple-year appropriations was established by Congress, on the recommendation of the second Hoover Commission, by the Act of July 25, 1956," which greatly changed the then existing law in regard to fiscal year limitations on the availability of annual and multipleyear appropriations for expenditure." For, under the Surplus Fund 

Certified Claims Act of 1949,¹ expenditures from annual and multipleyear appropriations could be made administratively only for an additional two years after the fiscal year or years for which such appropriations were available for obligation. Upon the expiration of this two-year period annual and multiple-year appropriations were said to lapse, and expenditures from lapsed appropriations could be made only if the Comptroller General first certified the payments to be lawfully due. This was a cumbersome procedure which led to unreasonable delays in making payments under contracts financed by annual or multipleyear appropriations where the period of contract performance extended beyond two years. These restrictions on the administrative availability of annual and multiple-year appropriations for expenditure were removed by the Act of July 25, 1958, as described above. $ 4.15. The Needs Theory

A basic test for the validity for obligations is that the supplies or services contracted for must be intended to serve a bona fide need of the fiscal year for which the appropriation is made. The Comptroller General has stated the principle as follows: "The general rule for lawfully obligating a fiscal year appropriation is that the supplies or services are intended to serve a bona fide need of the fiscal year in which the need arises or to

THE NEEDS THEORY 

$ 4.15 replace stock used in such fiscal year."3 Accordingly, where a need for the transportation of household effects arose in fiscal year 1940 and a valid agreement was entered into during that year with a carrier, the appropriation for fiscal year 1940 was said to be properly obligated even though the actual transportation occurred in fiscal year 1941.4 This rule applies even though payment may not take place, or the exact amount payable is not known, until the following fiscal year or years. Another illustration of the needs theory is afforded by contracts or obligations for services, which are normally chargeable to the appropriation for the fiscal year in which they are rendered. However, services in a period overlapping two fiscal years may be charged to the appropriation for the first fiscal year if there is involved only one undertaking which is determinable both as to the services needed and the price to be paid therefor at the time the contract is entered into. The essential distinction to be observed is whether the contract is severable or entire; if the former, the services must be charged to the appropriation current at the time they are rendered. 

As previously noted, the needs theory has been extended by the Comptroller General to include stock or inventory requirements. On this basis, it is permissible for the Navy to maintain a two-year stock on hand of certain articles, for example, and to replace such stock from time to time as necessary, charging the appropriation then current, even though the replacements are not intended for use during that fiscal year. In other words, the replacement of the stock, rather than its actual use, is considered to serve a bona fide need of that fiscal year. However, when instead of a contract for such stock replacement an intragovernmental order or requisition is issued, it may be treated as an obligation under the then current appropriation only if it requests prompt delivery of specific available stock items for a stated consideration and is formally accepted by the supplying agency. Formal evidence of acceptance is not required for common-use standard stock items carried on hand for sale at published prices. 10

Finally, leases of property to the Government are considered severable by fiscal years, unless there is specific statutory authority authorizing leases for a term longer than one year. Thus, the courts and the Comptroller General have consistently maintained that, in the absence of specific statutory authority to the contrary, the Government can execute a lease only to the end of the fiscal year concerned, and that the execution ticipation of future appropriations. Fiscal Year Chargeable 

There are several special situations involving the needs theory in which it is sometimes difficult to determine which fiscal year appropriation should be charged with a given obligation. The first of these situations occurs when a contractor defaults in the performance of a contract and the contract is relet in a succeeding fiscal year on the same basis. Under these circumstances, the appropriation obligated by the original contract remains available for payment under the new contract.13 But if the contract is canceled by mutual agreement or terminated for the convenience of the Government,14 or if there is undue delay in terminating the defaulting contractor and repurchasing against his account,15 a similar contract relet in a succeeding fiscal year is not regarded as an obligation of the prior fiscal year. And the same result will obtain where the new contract is on a different basis from the original." The theory which the Comptroller General has developed in this line of cases is that in the default situation the repurchase is made against the account of the defaulting contractor, who, of course, holds a valid obligation which by definition satisfies the bona fide needs of the appropriation for the earlier fiscal year. On the other hand, where the contract is canceled or terminated for convenience, or where the new contract is on a different basis, the repurchase is made against the account of the United States and must be charged to the then current appropriation. 

The second special situation in which it may be difficult to determine which fiscal year appropriation is chargeable concerns the amendment of a contract after the appropriation has expired. In this connection, the first determination that has to be made is whether the contract is sever-

SCHEDULING DELIVERIES UNDER SUPPLY CONTRACTS 

$ 4.17 able or entire." A severable contract must always obligate the appropriation for the fiscal year then current; while an entire or nonseverable contract, on the other hand, is chargeable in full to the appropriation current at the time the contract was entered into.18 Where it is desired to add additional funds to an entire or nonseverable contract, appropriations subsequent to those obligated by the contract may not be used without a corresponding increase in the scope of the contract.19 The theory upon which this rule is based is that an entire contract, like any other obligation, may neither be in excess of the amount available in the appropriation concerned nor may it anticipate the enactment of subsequent appropriations. In other words, new money may not be used to pay old bills. Similarly, if a change order issued in a subsequent fiscal year does not change the scope of the contract or increase the quantity of supplies called for thereunder, the appropriation originally obligated will be available for the cost of the change order. This rule is subject to the following conditions: first, provision for the issuance of the change order must be made in the original contract and the change order must comply with the terms of the changes clause; second, the work done under the original contract must be utilized and form a part of the work to be done under the contract as changed; and third, the purpose of the change must be not to enlarge the scope of the original contract, such as by increasing the quantity of supplies called for by the original contract.20 $ 4.17. 

Scheduling Deliveries Under Supply Contracts 

In compliance with the needs theory, careful attention should be given to the schedules of deliveries called for under supply contracts to avoid extending the deliveries to such an extent that the supplies may be presumed not to satisfy a need of the fiscal year in question. Thus, where a delivery schedule for a readily obtainable item of supply called for deliveries starting one year and ending two years after the fiscal year for which the appropriation obligated by the contract was made, the Comptroller General ruled that the contract did not satisfy the bona fide needs of that fiscal year.21 Normally, deliveries should not be initially called for in a contract to be made more than two years after the expiration of the related appropriation for obligation purposes. To do so may raise a presumption that the contract does not satisfy a need of the fiscal year for which the appropriation obligated by the contract was made, and hence the contract may violate section 1 of the Surplus Fund-

$ 4.18. No-Year Appropriations 

A no-year or continuing appropriation is available for an indefinite period of time, both for the purpose of incurring obligations and making expenditures. In each of the Navy appropriations of this kind, the words "to remain available until expended" appear after the indication of the sum which is appropriated. An express provision signifying continued availability is required in each case to avoid the statutory presumption in favor of one-year availability.24 The Navy's no-year appropriations are usually made for long lead-time construction and procurement programs, such as the shipbuilding, ordnance and aircraft programs, and the construction of airfields or other Navy shore facilities, where the time required for procurement will usually exceed the oneyear period of availability for obligation that the one-year appropriations have. No-year appropriations, as the term suggests, continue until their funds are exhausted or until the purpose for which they were made has been fulfilled. Before 1956 it was necessary for Congress to terminate no-year appropriations by law in order to take the account off the books of the Treasury and return the funds to the general fund of the Treasury. 

Under the law now in effect, no-year appropriations may be terminated whenever the head of the agency concerned determines that the purpose for which the appropriation was made has been fulfilled; termination is automatic, however, whenever disbursements have not been made out of the appropriation for two full consecutive fiscal years.25

(Emphasis added.) Hence when a contract is made that does not satisfy the bona fide needs of the fiscal year to which the appropriation obligated by the contract relates, payments under that contract may not be made from the appropriation thus sought to be obligated. DEFINITION OF THE PURPOSE OF AN APPROPRIATION $4.19 $4.19. Appropriation Symbols 

In order to indicate the period during which an appropriation is available for obligation, and otherwise to identify the appropriation in contracts or elsewhere, accounting symbols have been assigned to the appropriations of the various government agencies. These symbols identify an appropriation with respect to the agency responsible for its administration, the period for which it is available for obligation, the appropriation head, and the bureau or office that has the management responsibility therefor. Navy appropriations are always prefaced by the number 17.26 

The next digit or letter signifies the fiscal year or years in which the appropriation is available for obligation. If this digit is the number 9, for example, it signifies that the appropriation is available for obligation during the fiscal year ending in that number, or 1959. If this digit is followed by a slanted line, the appropriation is a multiple-year appropriation which is available for obligation in the fiscal year beginning with the year designated by the digit before the slanted line and ending in the fiscal year designated by the digit after the slanted line. Thus 

8/9 would represent a multiple-year appropriation available for obligation during fiscal years 1958 and 1959. If the letter X follows the first two digits of the appropriation symbol, a no-year appropriation is indicated. The letter M designates a successor account to a lapsed appropriation. The remaining digits in the appropriation symbol designate the bureau or office to which the appropriation is assigned, as well as the particular appropriation head. Thus, in the appropriation symbol 

1711803, the first two digits, 17, designate the Navy Department, the third digit, 1, designates the fiscal year 1951, the fourth and fifth digits, 18, designate the Bureau of Supplies and Accounts, and the last four digits, 1803, designate the appropriation "Service-Wide Supply and Finance."

C. PURPOSES FOR WHICH AVAILABLE 

$ 4.20. Definition of the Purpose of an Appropriation 

The purposes for which Navy appropriations are available are specified in the annual appropriation acts. To make doubly sure that these purposes will be observed, Congress has provided that:

Except as otherwise provided by law, sums appropriated for the various branches of expenditures in the public service shall be applied solely to the objects for which they are respectively made, and for no others.28 

26 See 7 GAO Ch. 1000 (1958) for a full explanation of the symbolization of appropriation accounts. Other military appropriations are indicated as follows: 

Army, 21; Air Force, 57; and Department of Defense, 97. 

27 For a discussion of successor or "M" accounts see § 4.14 supra. 

28 REV. STAT. § 3678 (1875), 31 U.S.C. 

§ 628 (1952). 181

$ 4.

Accordingly, if appropriations are not used for the particular purposes designated by Congress, it is a fundamental rule that they cannot be used for any other purpose.29 The Comptroller General has said that, in the performance of his statutory function of settling and adjusting all accounts and claims in which the United States is concerned, he is not concerned with the apparent general merit of the proposed expenditure but rather with the question whether the Congress, controlling the purse, has authorized the expenditure.30 Furthermore, he has noted that the accounting officers have been as quick to question the administrative omission from contracts of provisions required by law to be included therein as they have been to question the inclusion of provisions not authorized by law and outside of appropriations. The principle involved, he stated, depends entirely "on the fundamental basis that it is for the Congress to say how and on what conditions public moneys shall be spent." 31 In order to determine the purposes for which an appropriation is made, reference must be had to the express language of the appropriation itself. Inclusion of an item or program in the budget justifications cannot enlarge the purpose of an appropriation established by the statutory language of the appropriation act.32 However, a long continued course of conduct by an agency under a particular appropriation, with the apparent knowledge and sanction of the Congress, may be sufficient to bring that practice within the purpose of the appropriation, even though it is not expressly provided for by the statutory language of the appropriation.33 

$ 4.21. The Performance Budget 

The Navy's appropriation act for the fiscal year 1951 was completely redrafted to conform to the performance-type budget structure called for by Title IV of the National Security Act of 1947, as amended.34 Title 

IV required the budget estimates of the Department of Defense to be prepared, presented and justified, and authorized programs administered, in such a manner as to account for and report the cost of performing readily identifiable functions and activities, with segregation of operating and capital programs. As reflected in the Navy's appropriation acts, all of the costs of maintaining and operating the fleet, for example, are grouped under the appropriation head, "Ships and Facilities." Likewise, the appropriations of the pay and allowances for the Navy and
