THE PERFORMANCE BUDGET 

$ 4.21

Marine Corps are stated separately for ready identification. Capital programs, such as those for the procurement of aircraft, ships, ordnance, and facilities of the Navy's shore establishment, are also carried in appropriations that are segregated from the so-called maintenance and operating appropriations. In this fashion the performance budget is intended to focus attention upon the general character and relative importance of the principal functions to be performed and services to be rendered rather than upon particular objects of expenditure unrelated to the use to which they are to be put. The most important aspect of such a budget structure is to show the work or services that are to be accomplished and what that work or services will cost.

Before 1951, the Navy appropriation acts enumerated many specific items of expenditure. These items were eliminated for the most part on the basis of decisions by the Comptroller General to the effect that where an appropriation is made for a particular object or function, by implication it confers authority to incur expenses which are necessary or incident to its execution.35 This rule assumes that there is no other more specific appropriation provision for such expenditures, and that such expenditures are not otherwise prohibited by law. The performance budget of the 

Navy treats primarily with functions rather than objects. Therefore, the test of the legal availability of an appropriation for a particular obligation is whether the function of the appropriation has been followed rather than whether the obligation has been related to particular objects or programs justified before the Appropriations Committees. This broad test depends in turn on the lump-sum nature of most of the Navy's appropriations, which do not specify the amount of the entire appropriation that may be used for each object thereunder. Therefore, the programs justified to the Appropriations Committee need not be followed if intervening events dictate such a course of action, but if they are not, Navy representatives keep in close touch with the Committees and inform them of each significant departure from the original program. This process is generally referred to as "reprogramming".36

In the Navy's appropriation structure, then, examples of expenses which are considered to be authorized by implication include the following: supplies and materials; office and laboratory equipment; freight carrying vehicles; furniture and furnishings; tools and implements;

Committees closely informed of proposed changes. And, of course, to the extent that the authorizing legislation specifies the location, nature, cost, or other features of the program, reprogramming is thereby precluded. 183

$ 4.22

repair and alterations; parts and accessories; utility services; communication services; and travel and subsistence expenses. In order to achieve uniformity in the budget structure in the three military departments, the Department of Defense has established eight major budget categories as follows: 

1. Military personnel costs 

2. Maintenance and operation 

3. Major procurement and production costs 

4. Acquisition and construction of real property 

5. Civilian components 

6. Research and development 

7. Industrial mobilization 

8. Establishment-wide activities

Of these categories, the first two cover annual recurring costs, while the third, fourth, and sixth categories require expenditures comparable to capital expenditures in industry. The segregation of these capital expenditures from the annual recurring cost of the military departments is, of course, one of the principal purposes behind the adoption of the performance budget. 

$ 4.22. The Rules of Statutory Construction 

To ascertain the purpose for which an appropriation is available the ordinary rules for statutory interpretation are applicable. In compliance with the rules of procedure of both Houses of Congress, legislation, as distinguished from the appropriation of funds for otherwise authorized programs, is not usually included in an appropriation bill. The authority for a Navy program, therefore, is generally expressed in an act other than an appropriation act. However, if Congress appropriates funds for an otherwise unauthorized program or purpose, the appropriation of money carries with it the authority to accomplish the program or purpose that is the subject of the appropriation, since an appropriation act is as authoritative as any other act of Congress which makes the law of the land.38

Even though the Navy's appropriation acts are based on the performance budget structure, with appropriations for functions rather than objects of expenditure, the language of a particular appropriation may make that appropriation available for a specific purpose, such as the charter and hire of vessels under the appropriation "Ships and Facilities." 

In such a case, other more general appropriations may not be used for this purpose. In the words of the Comptroller General, "an appropriation for a specific object is available for that object to the exclusion of a more general appropriation" which would otherwise be available for the

Most of the Navy appropriations are lump-sum appropriations in which a rather large sum of money is made available for a multiplicity of objects needed for the performance of a broad function such as the maintenance and operation of the fleet. Therefore, it may happen that either of two appropriations are available for objects not specifically mentioned under either. In such a case, the Comptroller General has said that he would not question the administrative determination as to which of the two appropriations should be used, but when the determination has been made, the continued use of the appropriation selected, to the exclusion of the other for the same purpose, will be required in the absence of any change in future appropriation acts." Of course, the administrative discretion in the use of appropriations may not go beyond the statutes nor may it be exercised for the accomplishment of purposes outside the scope of an appropriation.42

There is another consequence of the nature of a lump-sum appropriation concerning the effect of an overobligation on a contractor holding a contract thereunder. It is well established that in the case of a specific appropriation, that is, an appropriation made for a single purpose, a contractor is limited to the amount of money in the appropriation since he is held to have had notice of the limitations on the authority of government officials to bind the Government to pay more than the amount appropriated.43 However, if a lump-sum appropriation is involved, it has been held that a contractor is not chargeable with knowledge of the condition of the appropriation or its apportionment between him and other contractors.44 The exhaustion of such an appropriation, of course, would require a government officer to stop the contractor's work just as in the case of a specific appropriation. D. PROJECT ORDERS, ECONOMY ACT ORDERS, AND TRANSFERS BETWEEN APPROPRIATIONS 

$ 4.23. In General

It is essential to the control exercised by Congress over the purse that appropriations be used for the purposes for which they are made and for no others.46 Accordingly, any transfer of funds between appropriations must be authorized by law before it can be made; otherwise an illegal augmentation of the receiving appropriation will result. transfer of funds between appropriations unaccompanied by an order for goods and services is a nonexpenditure transaction which withdraws amounts available for obligation and expenditure from one appropriation account for credit to another.48 Such a transfer is authorized, for example, under the appropriation head "Emergency Fund" in the Department of Defense Appropriation Act for the fiscal year 1958. The sum of $85,000,000 is appropriated under this head for transfer by the Secretary of Defense to any military appropriation available for research. and development.49 This type of transfer is to be distinguished from a transfer of funds from one appropriation to another in return for goods or services received or to be received. The latter is treated as an expenditure transaction and is accomplished in the Navy by project orders and 

Economy Act orders.50 $4.24. Project Orders 

The military departments have statutory authority to issue intra-governmental orders for work or material which have the same general effect as a contract placed with a private contractor.51 These orders are termed project orders, and since they obligate funds in the same manner as con-

Project orders may be issued only to those government activities which are substantially in a position to manufacture supplies and equipment or to render services. For instance, most of the project orders issued by the 

Navy are placed with industrial installations such as shipyards, ordnance plants, and printing plants. Subsidiary orders or subcontracts issued under a project order must be incident to and necessary for the completion of the project order.53 A project order must not result in an overobligation of funds.54 Since project orders obligate funds in the same manner as contracts, they must serve a bona fide need of the fiscal year in which they are issued. Finally, in the absence of any provision to the contrary in the law authorizing project orders, no advance of funds may be made under a project order. 55, 

$4.25. Economy Act Orders 

In addition to project orders, Navy appropriations may be obligated by orders placed with other bureaus and offices or other government agencies under the authority of section 601 of the Economy Act of 1932.56 

Economy Act orders resemble project orders in that they represent expenditure transactions by which Navy funds are transferred from one appropriation account to another in return for goods and services. Section 601 provides, in general terms, that one agency of the federal government may, if it has funds available for the purpose and if the department head determines that it is in the interest of the Government, place an order with any other agency for "materials, supplies, equipment, work, or services, of any kind that such requisitioned Federal agency may be in a position to supply or equipped to render." 57 Payments under Economy 

Act orders are authorized by law to be made either in advance or upon completion of the order. Finally, the Navy is authorized, by a 1942 amendment to section 601, to place Economy Act orders on other federal agencies that are in a position to obtain the requisitioned supplies or services by contract, as distinguished from performing the work itself 52 Detailed regulations on project orders are contained in ¶¶ 023400-023414, NAVY COMPTROLLER MANUAL (Feb. 4,

with its own resources.58 In general, the rules applicable to creating valid obligations by contract apply to Economy Act orders, as in the case of project orders.59 Thus, an Economy Act order must satisfy the bona fide needs of the fiscal year in which it is issued; the order must be specific, definite and certain, it must not result in an overobligation of available funds, and it must call for supplies or services that are within the purposes of the appropriation that is charged."1 60 In 1950, however, Congress altered the pre-existing rule regarding the obligating effect of Economy Act orders by restricting the use of funds transferred under such orders to the period provided in the appropriation charged.62 As a result, the requisitioned agency is placed in the same position as the ordering agency in respect to the obligation of its own funds in carrying out the order,63 and it must, therefore, perform the work under the Economy Act order, or place the work under contract, before the appropriation concerned expires for obligation purposes. If it does not, a new order obligating new funds must be issued to complete the work originally called for. The Comptroller General has held that the statutory restriction on the obligating effect of Economy Act orders does not affect project orders.64 Accordingly, if an advance payment under an intra-governmental order is desired, the use of an Economy Act order is indicated; but if continued availability of the funds past the expiration date of the appropriation charged is desired, the transaction should be covered by a project order.

To illustrate, the Navy Stock Fund has a corpus which is available until expended. E. THE CONCEPT OF OBLIGATIONS §4.27. The Significance of Obligations 

The rule that an appropriation can be obligated only during the fiscal year for which it is made was adopted in the first general appropriation for the Government for the service of the year 1789,70 and, except as otherwise specifically provided by law, it has been followed consistently since that time." As a result, the concept of obligations plays a central role under the present system of appropriating money for the needs of the Government on the basis of the total amount of obligating authority that will be required for each program of the Government. Recording Obligations

In section 1311 of the Supplemental Appropriation Act, 1955, the Congress established certain legal criteria and procedures, applicable to all of the agencies of the Government, for recording and reporting obligations of appropriated funds.74 The administrative criteria which had previously been prescribed for recording obligations 75 had been based upon the total expenditures ultimately required to complete the job initiated by the issuance of an obligating document. This test was not only too broad, but also it failed to establish the desired uniformity of application in the various agencies of the Executive Branch. Accordingly, specific legal criteria were prescribed by section 1311 which had the effect of limiting the recordable amount of an obligation to the legal liability of the United States at the time the obligation was created. Unless an obligation satisfies these criteria, it may not be recorded as an obligation; and no appropriation which is limited for obligation purposes to a definite period of time is available for expenditure after the expiration of that period except for liquidation of amounts obligated in accordance with these criteria.76 Section 1311 also requires the head of each Federal agency, not later than September 30 of each year, to report, as to each appropriation or fund under the control of the agency, the amount remaining obligated but unexpended and the amount remaining unobligated on June 30 of that year." Copies of these reports are forwarded to the Appropriations Committees of both Houses of Congress, the Comptroller General, and the Director of the Bureau of the Budget." 

The importance of this reporting function is underscored by the additional requirement that each report under section 1311 be (1) certified by the officials designated by the agency head, who may not redelegate their responsibility, and (2) supported by records of obligations in such form as to facilitate audit and reconciliation.79 Finally, any statement of ob-

Since the overall purpose of section 1311 was to restrict the amounts recorded as obligations, the Comptroller General has ruled that obligations may be recorded under this subsection only in those cases where there is no question as to the Government's liability and the pending litigation is for the sole purpose of determining the amount of such liability."⁹

RECORDING OBLIGATIONS: SPECIAL PROBLEMS 

$ 4.30 

$ 4.30.

Special Problems 

The adoption of section 1311 has necessarily demanded certain adjustments in the matter of recording obligations." The most significant of the problem areas are as follows: 

(1) Fixed-Price Contracts With Escalation, Price Redetermination or Incentive Provisions: When a fixed-price contract contains escalation, price redetermination or incentive provisions, obligations are recorded under section 1311(a) (1) in the amount of the fixed price stated in the contract, or the target or billing price in the case of a contract with an incentive clause.92 The amount so recorded is increased or decreased to reflect price revisions at the time such revisions are made or determined pursuant to provisions of the contract. The practice of recording the target or billing price in incentive contracts, rather than the maximum estimated cost, is intended to show the most realistic appraisal of the liability of the Government under the contract. 

(2) Contracts Authorizing Variations in Quantity: In the case of a contract authorizing variations in the quantity of supplies to be delivered thereunder, the obligation to be recorded under section 

1311(a)(1) is the price of the quantity specified for delivery, exclusive of the permitted variations.93 The problem here is analogous to that involving fixed-price contracts which provide for contingent liabilities such as escalation or price redetermination. In either case, because of the possibility of an increase of the obligation, the Navy avoids an overobligation of its appropriations and discharges its responsibility for meeting its ultimate liability by means of administrative reservations of funds in amounts sufficient to cover the contingencies involved. (3) Spare Parts: In view of the requirement of section 1311 (a) (1) that an agreement must be for specific goods before it may be recorded as an obligation, a contract calling for spare parts may be recorded only where a spare parts list is incorporated in the contract or where the contract contains a formula which permits a spare parts list to be worked out without further action by either of the parties. 

Otherwise, obligations are recorded only after the Navy's requirements of spare parts are determined by provisioning teams and specific orders are placed on the contractor. 

(4) Change Orders: Orders for contract or engineering changes involving increased costs may be recorded as obligations under section 1311(a) (1) at the time of their issuance, if the Government has the right unilaterally to issue such change orders under the contract. 

In the absence of such a provision, the increase in the amount of the obligation may be recorded only after a bilateral amendment is executed, in view of the requirement of a binding agreement in writing between the parties thereto. If there is no change in the scope

(5) Letter Contracts and Letters of Intent: The maximum liabil ity of the Government shown in a letter contract or letter of intent is that amount necessary to cover expenses to be incurred by the contractor prior to the execution of a definitive contract. If the letter contract or letter of intent is accepted in writing by the contractor, and if it is sufficiently specific to show the purposes and scope of the contract finally to be executed, this maximum liability, rather than the predicted ultimate costs of the definitive contract, may be recorded as an obligation under section 1311(a)(1).95 The difference between that amount and the predicted ultimate costs of the contract may be recorded for administrative purposes as a commitment until the letter contract or letter of intent is converted to a definitive contract. 

(6) Authorizations To Proceed Pending Contract Execution: The pre-existing practice of recording obligations based solely on authorizations to proceed with the work under an unexecuted contract was in effect prohibited by section 1311(a) (1), which provides that before an obligation may be recorded it must be supported by a binding agreement in writing by the parties, in a manner and form authorized by law. However, an authorization to proceed, when accepted by performance, would give rise to a unilateral contract. 

Such a contract would presumably satisfy the requirement of section 1311(a) (8), which permits the recording of any legal liability of the United States against an appropriation legally available therefor. (7) Purchase Orders: Before a purchase order may be recorded as an obligation under section 1311(a) (4), it must be (i) necessitated by public exigency, (ii) for perishable subsistence supplies, or (iii) for services or supplies in an aggregate amount of not more than $2,500.% A unilateral order other than those described above may qualify as an obligation under section 1311 (a) (8), to the extent that it has been accepted by performance; but if the order is to be charged against fiscal year funds and performance is not expected to be completed before the end of that fiscal year, timely obligation may be assured by requesting the written acceptance of the order by the contractor while the fiscal year appropriation is still available for obligation. This written acceptance, of course, would satisfy all the requirements for a recordable obligation under section 1311 (a) (1).9 (8) Termination Costs: The fiscal year appropriation obligated by a contract is available for all costs incident to that contract, including costs under termination agreements whether executed before or after the expiration of the appropriation. III. NONAPPROPRIATED FUNDS 

An interesting and unusual problem in fiscal management has existed for some time, within both the Navy and other military departments, concerning the legal liability of the United States for the torts and contracts of certain activities such as Navy and Marine Corps exchanges, civilian food services and related activities, and commissioned officers messes, which although federally sponsored and regulated are financed principally by nonappropriated funds. LEGAL STATUS OF NONAPPROPRIATED FUND ACTIVITIES $ 4.32 

All of these nonappropriated fund activities are created and governed by carefully detailed regulations prescribed by the Secretary of the Navy. 

Their activities have been repeatedly recognized as governmental by the Congress, the courts and the Comptroller General, and they are administered in their day-to-day operations by members of the uniformed services in the course of their military duties. Despite these elements of control and the obvious principal-agent relationship between the Secretary of the Navy and the activities which these elements represent, there has been a division of opinion in the lower federal courts as to the legal rights and liabilities of the United States for the torts and contracts of these activities. Some courts have adopted the view that these nonappropriated fund activities are arms of the federal government, so as to make the United States liable for claims sounding in both tort and contract arising out of their activities, to the same extent that the United States has consented generally to be sued in such matters." Other courts have held that, even though nonappropriated fund activities are instrumentalities of the United States, the general waivers of sovereign immunity by the Congress do not extend to them.18 Since it is well established that these activities are not legal entities and have no standing to sue or be sued in their own name," the practical result of the latter view is to deny both contract and tort claimants a forum in which to pursue their claims. This result is in marked contrast with the willingness of the Government to assert, in the name of the United States, claims held by these activities against their contractors in bankruptcy proceedings, for example. Although this question has not been finally resolved, the two following sections will present a rationale which not only offers a consistent and workable pattern for dealing with these nonappropriated fund activities, but at the same time affords their tort and contract claimants an opportunity to have their claims considered on their merits. 

$ 4.32. Legal Status of Nonappropriated Fund Activities 

The various elements of control exercised by the Secretary of the Navy over certain nonappropriated fund activities, such as Navy and Marine

Corps exchanges, civilian food and related services, and commissioned officers messes, have been outlined in the preceding section. Where similar elements of control were present, the Supreme Court has held in the leading case of Standard Oil Co. of California v. Johnson, that Army post exchanges were, as a matter of federal law, integral parts of the War Department.20 This case involved an appeal from the decision of the 

Supreme Court of California upholding a license tax which had been levied by California tax authorities on a distributor who sold gasoline to United States Army post exchanges in California. Section 10 of the 

California Motor Vehicle Fuel License Tax Act stated that the act is inapplicable to "any motor vehicle fuel sold to the Government of the United States or any department thereof for official use of said Government." The Supreme Court reversed the decision of the state court on the ground that the question whether post exchanges were "the Government of the United States or any department thereof" was a matter controlled by federal law, and that as a matter of federal law post exchanges were integral parts of the War Department. In the course of the opinion, which was unanimous, the Court stated: 

From all of this, we conclude that post exchanges as now operated are arms of the Government deemed by it essential for the performance of governmental functions. They are integral parts of the War Department, share in fulfilling the duties entrusted to it, and partake of whatever immunities it may have under the Constitution and federal statutes. In concluding otherwise, the Supreme 

Court of California was in error.21

The only question decided by the Court was the legal relationship between Army post exchanges and the Government of the United States. 

Having decided this relationship, the Court made it clear that the post exchanges were exempt from the California tax by the terms of the California Tax Act itself, and that it was unnecessary to decide the question as to whether the California tax, if applied to Army post exchanges, would be unconstitutional. The rule of the Johnson case is equally applicable to Navy, Marine Corps and Air Force exchanges, which are established under regulations similar to those governing Army post exchanges,22 civilian food services boards,23 and other nonappropriated

fund activities, the governing regulations of which establish a degree of control by the department over their operations similar to that upon which the Supreme Court relied in reaching its decision in the Johnson case.24

If the nonappropriated fund activities of the sort described are integral parts of the United States, it follows that they have no separate legal status from that of the United States, and that therefore, they are not suable entities. As to this corollary of the rule enunciated in the Johnson case, there seems to be general agreement both in the courts 25 and within the Department of Defense. It also appears to be well established that nonappropriated fund activities have the same immunity as the federal government itself so far as state and local taxes are concerned.26 And as has been already observed, claims of such activities have frequently been asserted in bankruptcy proceedings in the name of the United States. 

The only matter as to which there is any disagreement relates to the application of the rule of the Johnson case to claims asserted against the United States in tort and contract growing out of operations of these nonappropriated fund activities. The problem is usually presented in the form of the Government's motion to dismiss the action for want of jurisdiction based on the sovereign immunity of the United States.27

Effect on Claims Arising Out of Their Operations 

The Congress has waived the sovereign immunity of the United States in tort 28 and contract.29 In both instances the statutory waivers relate to the United States as such, rather than to specified agencies or departments of the Government. In view of the nature of these statutory waivers of the sovereign immunity of the United States, it is perfectly sound to suppose that they necessarily extend to all constituent parts of the Government of the United States, including such nonappropriated fund activities as fall within the rule of the Johnson case so as to be regarded as integral parts of the Government.30 While there has been a division of opinion as to the correct application of the rule in court decisions after the Johnson case, there is good authority for the view that the general waiver of the sovereign immunity of the United States extends to claims arising out of the operation of nonappropriated fund activities both in contract and in tort.31

Johnson case.36 $4.34. Protecting the Interests of the United States in Matters Involving the Operation of Nonappropriated Fund Activities 

If the United States is liable in matters of tort and contract growing out of the operations of nonappropriated fund activities, it becomes necessary to consider how the interests of the United States can best be protected. A fundamental condition of the establishment of these activities is, of course, that their operating expenses will be defrayed largely out of their nonappropriated funds. In matters of contract, this problem may be resolved by a provision in the contract to the effect that the contract and claims for breach of it shall be paid only out of nonappropriated funds available to the activity, and shall not be construed to obligate appropriated funds of the United States in any way." If a claimant under such a contract pursues his claim to judgment against the United States, the courts could consistently require the judgment to be paid only 34 This point is strongly asserted in dissent. 116 F. Supp. 873, 879.

European exchange system.

$ 4.34

out of the special fund which the claimant has agreed to look to for satisfaction of his claim.38 If sufficient funds are not available to satisfy the judgment, it would follow that appropriated funds of the United States would not be available to supply the deficiency.39 A similar result is reached in an analogous situation under the special fund doctrine in the law of revenue bonds. Under this doctrine, the obligation incurred, represented by the bond issue, is payable wholly out of the income and revenue of the enterprise which it finances, and the bond claimant is not entitled to look to the general funds of the governmental unit that issued the bonds when the special fund proves inadequate to meet the obligation.40 In the leading case approving the special fund doctrine, the court noted that the city there concerned was not in any manner required to repay the obligation except out of moneys in this special fund, since this was a basic part of the contract under which the obligations were issued."¹ 

The problem of protecting the interests of the Government against tort claims arising out of nonappropriated fund activities is complicated by the fact that tort claimants do not agree in advance to look to a particular fund of the United States for satisfaction of their claims. However, even though nonappropriated funds do not originate in the Treasury, they are nonetheless public funds of the United States in the sense that they are derived from the operation of duly authorized activities which are established and carefully regulated by the Secretary of the Navy with the tacit consent of the Congress.42 And, as noted by the

$4.36. Contract Financing Policy

The policy relating to the financing of Navy contractors is established by regulation; 52 the most significant aspects of this policy are restated here as a matter of convenience. Since the Navy's contract financing policy is prescribed by the Department of Defense, it is applicable as well to the Army and Air Force; and it is the general policy of the 

Department of Defense that uniformity of procedures be followed in the three military departments to the extent practicable. 

Contract financing is to be regarded as a useful tool that may be employed to the benefit of the Government for expediting the performance of defense contracts and subcontracts. The contract financing system is designed to make possible production in volume that could not otherwise be accomplished. Prudent contract financing will be used to foster small business by providing such funds as are necessary to supplement other funds available to it for contract performance. PRIVATE FINANCING 

$ 4.37 should be so administered as to avoid a risk of monetary loss to the Government to the extent compatible with aiding essential procurement. 

To this end, the financing and procurement functions are required to be performed by separate organizations (in the Navy, financing is the responsibility of the Comptroller, while procurement is handled by the bureaus and offices), but close cooperation between the two groups is preserved at all times. Any disagreement that arises between the financing office and the interested procuring activity in a particular case as to whether, to what extent, or in what form, financing should be furnished will ultimately be submitted to the Secretary of the Navy for resolution. 

In placing contracts, procuring activities must give due regard to the financial capabilities of the supplier. Navy assistance will be given a contractor only if, and to the extent, it is reasonably required for the prompt and efficient performance of government contracts and subcontracts. It is recognized that if the Government gives adequate protection against the financial impact of terminating contracts and subcontracts for the convenience of the Government, the effect should be to encourage suppliers to invest their own funds in the performance of their contracts. In addition, financing for such termination purposes is considered to be an important aid to the reconversion of industry to peacetime production. Accordingly, termination financing may be made available, with appropriate protection of the Government's interest, either in connection with or independently of performance financing. 

The Navy's assistance in the matter of contract financing is aimed primarily at either the performance or termination of defense contracts, rather than at plant expansion necessary to enable its contractors to perform their contracts. As a matter of policy, then, loans will not be guaranteed by the Navy to support the expansion of a contractor's facilities, except where the expansion is of a minor or incidental nature. And since both advance payments and progress payments are designed to be self-liquidating from contract performance, they are not used to finance the acquisition of fixed assets by the contractor. This policy, of course, does not apply to Navy contracts providing for the acquisition or expansion of plant facilities for government ownership. $4.37. Private Financing

The Navy does not give any direct aid to its contractors in obtaining loans from private banks or lending institutions. However, before other 

Navy financing aids, other than customary progress payments,53 are made available to a contractor, the Navy Comptroller's Office must as a general rule determine that the contractor has been unable to obtain adequate private financing, after making reasonable efforts to do so. This private

Assignment of Claims Under Navy Contracts 

Before 1940 the assignment of claims under government contracts was prohibited by law,55 in order to prevent speculation in government contracts by bidders who have neither the intention nor the ability to perform them,56 to enable the Government to secure the personal attention and services of the contractor of its own selection,57 and to avoid harassment of the Government by multiplying the number of persons dealing with it.58 With the advent of World War II, the Congress modified this prohibition by enacting the Assignment of Claims Act of 1940,59 in order to permit the assignment of claims under defense contracts and thereby encourage the participation of banks in the financing of government contractors under the defense program of that time. This legislation permitted contractors to assign to financing institutions moneys due or to become due under their government contracts, and it assured the assignee banks that, when payments by the Government were due under such assignments, and it was so provided in the contract, the payments would not be subject to reduction or setoff on account of any claims the Government might have against the contractor arising independently of the assigned contract. Under this provision, banks were enabled to finance defense contractors on the security of an assignment of their contracts where other forms of collateral were not available, especially in the case of the marginal contractor with relatively few tangible assets. Such assignments were the principal form of security for loans made by banks to war contractors under the V-loan program of World War II.

After the end of the war, however, certain restrictive interpretations of the statute by the Comptroller General created such uncertainity as to the rights of assignee banks as to discourage their participation in the financing of government contractors and thus defeat the purpose of the statute.60 Accordingly, shortly after the outbreak of Korean hostilities, the Assignment of Claims Act of 1940 was amended 61 in order to give assurance that a bank or other financing institution taking an assignment of claims under the act would not be subject to later recapture by the Government of amounts previously paid to the bank as assignee. A second feature of the amendment was to enlarge the protection of the assignee afforded by the 1940 act to make it clear that, if an assigned contract contained a "no setoff" clause,62 the assignee bank would be protected against having any claims of the Government against the contractor arising independently of the contract set off against payments due it under the assignment, including any claims of the Government against the contractor arising from renegotiation, fines, penalties (except penalties assessed against the assignor for failure to perform the contract) or taxes, social security contributions, or the withholding or nonwithholding of taxes or social security contributions, whether arising from or independently of the assigned contract.63 It should be noted that the immunity from recapture which this statute affords lending institutions exists whether or not a "no setoff" clause is incorporated in the Navy contract. Insertion of a "no setoff" clause in the contract is necessary however, to clothe the lending institution with the additional protection permitted, but not created, by the statute against reduction or setoff for any liability of the contractor to the Government arising independently of the contract. The protection thus afforded assignee banks and lending institutions does not prevent the Government from enforcing the liability of the assignor by other means.64 The amendment of the Assignment of Claims Act in May 1951 was successful in removing the impediment to the participation of banks and other lending institutions in the financing of Navy contractors, and once again the assignment of claims both with and without a government guarantee resumed its key role in the defense contract financing program.

$4.39. Guaranteed Loans: Description 

Guaranteed loans, usually called "V-loans," 65 are essentially the same as other loans made by financing institutions without guarantee, except that under a standard form of guarantee agreement the Navy or other guaranteeing agency is obligated on demand of the lender to purchase a stated percentage of the loan and to share losses in the amount of the guaranteed percentage. Guaranteed loans afford an especially convenient medium for financing the borrower who holds subcontracts or numerous prime contracts or prime contracts with more than one contracting agency. 

Funds are disbursed and collected by the lending institution, and its personnel administer the loan. It is the policy of the guaranteeing agencies to limit borrowings under V-loans made primarily for working capital purposes, in accordance with an asset formula, to amounts which do not exceed specified percentages of the borrower's investment in defense production contracts. Within the limitations provided by this formula, the maximum amount of guaranteed credit and the maturity date of guaranteed loans or credits are tailored to the borrower's financing requirements for defense production contracts on hand at the time of application for guarantee. Security for V-loans usually takes the form of an assignment of claims under the contract or contracts being financed, but other collateral security, such as mortgages on fixed assets or liens on inventories, and special security devices, such as endorsements, guarantees, and subordinations of other indebtedness, are required as necessary for the protection of the Government. $ 4.40. Such applications are processed through the Federal Reserve Bank and are submitted, together with credit reports and recommendations, to the Office of the Comptroller of the Navy in Washington. Upon approval of the application by the Comptroller's Office, the Federal Reserve Bank issues the guarantee to the financial institution making the loan. Before such approval is granted by the Comptroller's Office, however, the Bureau or Office of the Navy interested in the procurement supported by the financing must find, through a certificate of eligibility, that the materials and services involved are essential to the national defense, and that, except in the case of small business, they cannot be procured readily from an alternative source without prejudice to the national defense. In this way, the financing is tied to the need for the procurement. $4.41. 

Involvement of Public Funds The Government's guarantee of loans to finance defense contracts or subcontracts is significantly different from the guarantee covering the financing of veterans' housing, in so far as the involvement of public funds is concerned. Specifically, the V-loan guarantee provides for a sharing of losses on a percentage participation basis under the loan, whereas the veterans' mortgage loan guarantee is applied to the whole loss up to the amount guaranteed. To the extent of the guaranteed percentage, then, the V-loan guaranteeing agency shares any loss incurred under the loan with the private lending institution. In order to encourage the lending institution to accept as great an exposure as possible, the Government charges a fee for its guarantee which varies with the percentage guaranteed. This fee is also designed to compensate the Government for the risk it assumes in making the guarantee. It is the policy of the three military departments as guaranteeing agencies to limit 100 percent guarantees to the greatest extent compatible with the requirements of the national defense. In other words, applications for 100 percent guarantees will be approved only in cases where the Navy determines that the circumstances are exceptional, that the operations of the borrower are vital to the national defense, and that no other suitable means of financing is available." 

The Navy, as guaranteeing agency, is also obligated to purchase, upon the demand of the lender, a part of the loan equal to the guaranteed percentage. Until such a purchase is executed or a loss is shared, no government funds are directly involved in the guaranteed loan program. In a sense, the Government becomes a potential participant in a loan upon the issu-

$ 4.42. Progress Payments: Description 

Progress payments are made as work progresses under a contract, on the basis of costs that have been incurred, percentage of completion accomplished, or on reaching a particular stage of completion of the work under the contract.69 Such payments are usually made without an interest charge. Permanent statutory authority for this method of financing permits the Navy to make progress payments under contracts in amounts not to exceed the value of the work done, when provision for such payments is specifically called for by the contract.70 Although this authority contemplates a lien on the things contracted for accruing to the United States on account of the payments so made, the Navy now customarily takes title to the inventories, work in process, special tooling, and other things acquired under the contract by way of securing the Government's interest. Progress payments are normally employed to supplement the working funds available to Navy contractors of all sizes. 

Accordingly, where such payments are based on costs, it is the policy of the Navy, in the case of new procurement effected on or after September 1, 1957, to limit them to 85 percent of direct labor and material costs, or 70 percent of the total costs, of the work done under the undelivered portion of the contract, except in unusual cases." And where progress payments are based on percentage or stage of completion, the maximum

For reasons that will be apparent, progress payments are especially helpful in production contracts that involve a long "lead time" or preparatory period between the beginning of work and the first delivery. 

Such contracts often require substantial predelivery expenditures that would tie up considerable amounts of the contractor's working capital and, but for Navy assistance in the form of progress payments, substantially impede performance under the contract. Progress payments based on percentage or stage of completion are confined to contracts for construction,73 shipbuilding, and ship conversion, alteration and repair. 74 

Where based on costs, they are most frequently made in such long "lead time" contracts as contracts for aircraft, engines, or complex items of electrical or electronic equipment.75 $ 4.43. Procedure

When progress payments based on costs are requested by contractors who hold production contracts involving a "lead time" of six months or more and who are known by the Navy to be reliable, competent, and capable of satisfactory performance, to have an adequate accounting system and controls, and to be in satisfactory financial condition, the request may be allowed up to but not exceeding the percentage limitations established by administrative regulation.76 In such a case, progress payments are regarded as reasonably necessary, and the contractor will not be required. to submit projections of cash receipts and expenditures or otherwise demonstrate actual need for progress payments. To this extent, for this class of contracts, the general preference for private financing, including guaranteed loans, does not apply, especially in the case of small business.77 

If the contract is formally advertised, the invitation for bids will contain the applicable progress payments clause and require the bidder who desires progress payments to make written request therefor in his bid, whenever the contracting officer considers that the "lead time" will exceed six months or that progress payments will be useful or necessary to avoid a substantial impact on a contractor's working funds. $ 4.44. Advance Payments: Description 

Advance payments are in the nature of loans made to a prime contractor by the Navy prior to, in anticipation of, and for the purpose of facilitating, complete performance under a contract or contracts. They are authorized by statute in the case of both negotiated and formally advertised contracts. Consideration for advance payments is obtained in the form of an interest charge of 5 percent per annum on the amount of the advance that is outstanding. In this respect advance payments are distinguishable from progress payments, since progress payments are usually not supported by an interest charge. Accordingly, there must be some other consideration moving to the Government for amending a contract to provide for the payment of progress payments where no interest is charged, whereas a contract may be amended to provide for advance payments with no consideration other than the interest charge. 

Also, advance payments are designed to be liquidated from payments due to the contractor incident to the performance of contracts, but they are not measured by performance as progress payments are.

ADVANCE PAYMENTS: PROCEDURE 

$ 4.45

EN As a general rule advance payments are used sparingly and are not authorized unless no other means of adequate financing is available to the contractor. The amount of the authorization, which normally does not exceed the contractor's interim cash needs as determined by the timing of the Government's reimbursement under the contract, is predicated upon maximum use of the contractor's own working capital. Exceptions to this general rule are made in nonprofit contracts with nonprofit educational or research institutions for experimental, research and development work, and contracts for the management and operation of government-owned plants.82 Advance payments are considered especially useful and appropriate in the following situations: contracts for acquisition of facilities at cost for government ownership; contracts so highly classified that the Navy considers it undesirable to permit the assignment of moneys due under the contract; essential contracts of weak or overextended contractors where performance may be fostered and the risk of financial loss to the Government minimized by the very close control by Navy personnel of funds and performance that is afforded by the advance payment procedure; and contracts for the financing of which a financing institution will not assume a reasonable portion of the risks under a guaranteed loan. In the case of contracts with small business concerns, advance payment financing is frequently more beneficial to the interests of the Government and more suitable to the financial condition of the contractor than other methods of contract financing. $4.45. Procedure 

In a typical case, a Navy contractor will require financial assistance in the form of advance payments only after all other methods of financing have been tried without success. It should be noted that advance payments can be made only to prime contractors, since a direct contractual relationship is necessary to secure the repayment of the advance. The application for advance payments is made to the contracting officer by the contractor, together with the reports, schedules, and statements required by applicable regulation.83 The application may be made either incident to a bid or proposal or after award of a contract, if the contractor is otherwise qualified. After review by the contracting officer, the contractor's application is forwarded to the Office of the Comptroller of the Navy with all the relevant information and documents.84 If the application is approved, the Comptroller's Office prepares the necessary advance payment clause, following the approved contract provisions in the regulation. This clause requires the contractor to establish a special

bank account in which the advance is deposited, as well as other payments under the contract as they become due. Withdrawal of funds from this account is controlled by an agent of the Navy who must countersign all checks to insure the application of funds to the performance of the contract. Once the advance payment is made into this special account, the 

Government's security for repayment of the loan takes the form of lien or title with respect to the funds in the special account as well as to the material and work in process under the contract for which these funds are used. Additional security may be provided for as necessary in individual cases, and the Government's interest is further protected by requiring the contractor to make certain representations and covenants relating to its fiscal structure and future actions which might affect it. 

These representations and covenants are similar to those usually required in private loan agreements. In order to assure the flow of repayments into the special account, the contractor is prohibited from making any assignment of the contract.

V. COLLECTION OF DEBTS A. THE PRIORITY OF THE UNITED STATES AS CREDITOR $ 4.46. The Statutory Priority of the United States: Purpose 

An important function that grows out of the Navy's procurement program is the collection of debts due the Government. The prosecution and settlement of such claims entails all the enforcement remedies available to the Government, including administrative setoff, assertion of priorities in bankruptcy or receivership, litigation, and compromise. The position of the United States as creditor has been governed for more than 150 years by a statute that provides for the prior satisfaction of claims of the United States against an insolvent debtor.86 As the Supreme Court said, in an early decision involving this statute The right of priority of payment of debts due to the government is a prerogative of the crown well known to the common law. It is founded not so much upon any personal advantage to the sovereign as upon motives of public policy, in order to secure an adequate revenue to sustain the public burdens, and discharge the public debts. 

The claim of the United States, however, does not stand upon any sovereign prerogative, but is exclusively founded upon the actual 86 "Whenever any person indebted to the United States is insolvent . the debts due to the United States should be first satisfied; and the priority established shall extend as well to cases in which a debtor, not having sufficient property to pay all his debts, makes a voluntary assignment thereof, or in which the estate and effects of an absconding, .. concealed, or absent debtor are attached by process of law, as to cases in which an act of bankruptcy is committed." REV.

STAT. § 3466 (1875), 31 U.S.C. § 191 

(1952). For a full discussion of the questions presented by this section, see A. B. 

Holman, The United States-Creditor, 9 

FED. B.J. 261 (1948), and the authorities collected therein. 214

APPLICATION OF PRIORITY STATUTE TO DEBTS OF U.S. $ 4.48 

provisions of their own statutes. The same policy which governed in the case of the royal prerogative may be clearly traced in these statutes, and as that policy has mainly a reference to the public good, there is no reason for giving to them a strict and narrow interpretation. Like all other statutes of this nature, they ought to receive a fair and reasonable interpretation, according to the just import of their terms.87

The liberal construction of the priority statute just noted is intended to serve its purpose of protecting the public revenue. This point is illustrated by a case involving a claim brought by the NLRB against a bankrupt based on a back pay order issued as a result of certain unfair labor practices of the bankrupt. Since the claim was asserted by the United 

States for the benefit of private parties, the victims of the unfair labor practices, it bore no relation to the function of protecting the public revenue and therefore it was held to be outside the scope of the priority rule." 

§ 4.47. Construction 

The priority given to the United States by the priority statute is absolute, not conditional; once it attaches it is final and conclusive and not subject to defeasance. Furthermore, the only exception to the priority accorded to the claims of the United States by this statute are those created by express statutory language or the plainest inconsistency. And in any case, a person who contests the "absolute" priority of the United States under this statute must sustain the burden of proving an exception in his case.⁹1 

§ 4.48. Application of the Priority Statute to Debts of the United States 

A question that often arises in cases involving the priority statute concerns the phrases "indebted to the United States" and "the debts due to the United States," and particularly the meaning of the term "United States." There has been some controversy, for example, over the application of the priority statute to claims that originate in the operations of government corporations and other quasi-independent government instrumentalities. If the government corporation is a distinct legal entity separate from that of the United States, the priority statute has been held to be inapplicable.92 Conversely, if the instrumentality has no distinct legal entity, and the claim which it asserts represents a debt of the United

Under this view, when funds of a government corporation or instrumentality are government funds and the losses government losses, the pecuniary loss test is satisfied and the priority statute should be applied. This construction is in accord with the purpose of the priority statute described in § 4.46 above. Under the guaranteed loan program in effect during World War II, the Government's priority was even extended to the exposure of private banks by means of the exercise by the Government of its option to purchase the loan whenever bankruptcy or insolvency of the borrower threatened. The take-over agreement, of course, provided for a pro rata distribution of collections. While never contested in an appellate court, the principle was frequently approved by allowance of such claims in federal district courts. $ 4.49. Insolvency of the Debtor

Since the priority statute is limited in its application to claims held by the United States against an insolvent debtor, another problem presented by the statute concerns the meaning of the word "insolvent." By a rather artificial construction the Supreme Court has limited the meaning of this word to the examples stated in the latter part of the statute.95 Within the limitations of this rule, the United States will be given priority as creditor whenever the debtor is divested of his property by a voluntary assignment for the benefit of creditors, whenever there is a legal insolvency such as a liquidating receivership under state law or an equity receivership in a federal court, and finally whenever the debtor commits an act of bankruptcy, whether or not it results in a petition, adjudication, or liquidation. The Priority Statute and the Bankruptcy Act 

One of the situations in which the claims of creditors against a debtor become matured and have to be asserted for participation in the distribution of a debtor's assets is the voluntary or involuntary resort by the latter to the provisions of the Bankruptcy Act. Section 64 (a) of the act ⁹ provides generally for the types of debts which are to have priority and be paid in full before dividends are paid to general unsecured creditors: (1) administration expenses, (2) wages up to $600 per claimant, earned within three months before the commencement of the bankruptcy proceedings, (3) special costs incurred by a creditor in setting aside the bankrupt's discharge, (4) federal, state, and local taxes owed by the bankrupt, and (5) "debts owing to any person, including the United States, who by the laws of the United States is entitled to priority. . . ." 

The most important aspect of this section is that it places certain classes of claims ahead of the general priority accorded to the United States by the priority statute." However, section 64(a)(5) preserves the priority over general unsecured creditors granted the United States by the priority statute. $ 4.51. 

Specific Proceedings Under the Bankruptcy Act 

The application of the priority statute, therefore, is determined in each type of bankruptcy proceeding by whether section 64 is applicable. In several types of bankruptcy proceedings there are provisions in the Bankruptcy Act to the effect that the order of priority established by section 64 is to be followed.' $ 4.52. The Priority Statute and Liens of Other Claimants 

Another problem presented by the priority statute concerns its operation with relation to liens asserted by other claimants against the debtor of the United States.4 The priority of the United States extends only to the property of the debtor at the time of his insolvency, which would, of course, exclude specific property of which he has been divested prior to that time by a bona fide conveyance to third persons, by a mortgage to secure a debt, or by levy of execution. Also, it would probably exclude property of which the debtor has been effectively divested by operation of law through a specific and perfected lien, although this question has never been decided." $ 4.53. 

Conveyances, Mortages and Attachments

The Supreme Court has held that the priority statute does not create a lien in favor of the United States; accordingly, a bona fide transfer of property by a debtor to third persons in the ordinary course of business while he is still solvent will not thereby be overreached. $ 4.54 the debtor's property, the Supreme Court has also held that a mortgage or an attachment prior to insolvency might postpone the Government's priority. The decision in the mortgage case was based on the view that a mortgage has the effect of a conveyance, divesting the debtor of his title and leaving nothing but an equity to which the preference of the United States could attach. In a jurisdiction which adopts the lien theory of mortgages, therefore, a different result might well be reached. Indeed, in a case decided in 1941, the Supreme Court in passing questioned the "current vitality" of the rule in favor of mortgages.⁹ 

$ 4.54. Inchoate Liens 

It is clear that inchoate liens, which do not effect divestment of specific property of the debtor until they are perfected by appropriate legal action, stand behind a claim of the United States asserted in proceedings where the priority statute is applicable. For example, in an early case the 

Supreme Court held that the United States was entitled to priority of payment over a judgment creditor on the ground that the judgment gave him merely a general lien on the debtor's property which, whatever its dignity, must yield to the preference of the United States created by the broad language of the priority statute.10 Presumably the result would have been different had execution of the judgment proceeded far enough to take the property out of the possession of the debtor. Again, in a case involving a lien for state unemployment compensation which attached to all the personal property of a debtor devoted to or used in his business, including after-acquired property, the Supreme Court ruled that the lien was not so specific and perfected as to overcome the statutory priority of the United States, even though notice of lien had been filed and recorded and a receiver appointed, and under applicable state law nothing further remained to be done to perfect the lien." The Court went on to say that "The long-established rule requires that the lien must be definite, and not merely ascertainable in the future by taking further steps, in at least three respects as of the crucial time. These are: (1) the identity of the lienor... (2) the amount of the lien... and (3) the property to which it attached." 12 Although the first two conditions were satisfied in this case, the Court reasoned that the lien was not perfected since it did not attach to specific property of the debtor but rather to personal property devoted

$ 4.55. Characterization of Liens a Matter of Federal Law 

In a case that involved the priority of the United States over a landlord's lien and a municipal tax lien, both of which were created by Virginia law, the Supreme Court held that the liens asserted by the landlord and the municipality were not sufficiently specific and perfected, on the date of the debtor's voluntary assignment, to affect the priority of the United States in spite of a determination by the Virginia courts to the contrary.13 After examining the action taken by the lien claimants, the 

Court stated that "it is a matter of federal law as to whether a lien created by state statute is sufficiently specific and perfected to raise questions as to the applicability of the priority given the claims of the United States by an Act of Congress. A state court's characterization of a lien as specific and perfected, however conclusive as a matter of state law, cannot operate by itself to impair or supersede a long-standing Congressional declaration of priority." 14 Finally, describing these liens as a warning of more perfect liens to come, the Court suggested that possibly an actual distraint, accompanied by transfer of title or possession, might serve to perfect the claimed liens. $ 4.56. 

Summary 

The long line of decisions of the Supreme Court involving the priority statute indicates that the Court generally looks with suspicion upon lien holders who have neglected to assert their rights until after the debtor has become insolvent. Conversely, it has recognized the superior rights of those who, before the insolvency of the debtor occurs, have taken affirmative action to protect their interests. In the present state of the law, it would appear that little less than complete divestment of a debtor's title to or possession of specific property, prior to the crucial time at which the priority of the United States attaches, would be effective to defeat a claim of the United States." 15

B. PROCEDURES FOR THE COLLECTION OF DEBTS 

$4.57. Administrative Procedures Within the Navy

The indebtedness of a contractor to the Navy may arise in a variety of ways. It may stem, for example, from a direct loan, an erroneous overpayment, a retroactive price reduction pursuant to the terms of the contract, or an obligation to pay rent. Or, when a contractor fails without excusable cause to complete his contract and the contract is then terminated for default, the Navy may seek the recovery of any excess costs that may be involved in repurchasing against the account of the defaulting contractor. Again, when a contractor commits a breach of contract, there may well be recoverable damages. In each of these situations the initial responsibility for the collection of the debt rests with the contracting officer (or disbursing officer in the case of an erroneous overpayment), who makes a formal demand upon the contractor for cash payment of the indebtedness within 30 days from the date of demand." 

If within this 30-day period the contractor shows that immediate repayment would impair his ability to continue operations or perform defense contracts or subcontracts, and if orderly collection within 90 days can be effected, the contracting officer may agree to a payment plan with the contractor that would defer ultimate collection for a period up to 90 days after the date of demand. If the contractor seeks a stretch-out of more than 90 days, however, the plan must be approved by the Navy Comptroller. Any deferred payment plan must be expressed in a written agreement that will protect the interests of the Government. Usually, such agreements provide for acceleration of the maturity of the indebtedness in the event of default or commission of an act of bankruptcy by the contractor. If payments are to be made beyond the initial 90-day period, the agreement must impose a 5 percent interest charge on such payments, commencing on the 91st day. $ 4.58. Setoff

During the 30-day period after the initial demand is made on the contractor or while a deferred payment plan is under consideration, the contracting officer may direct the disbursing officer to withhold payments otherwise due the contractor under Navy contracts. This action is fully sanctioned by law, which has always recognized a creditor's "justified refusal to pay what he owes until he is paid what is due him." 18 If within 

30 days after the date of the initial demand the debt has not been satisfied or a deferred payment plan has not been agreed upon, the contracting officer must report the indebtedness to the Office of the Navy Comptroller. 

16 The recovery of excess costs is discussed in § 9.28 infra. 

17 The formal instructions governing the Navy's administrative procedures for the collection of debts are set forth in 

SecNav Inst. 7810.4 (Mar. 17, 1955). 

18 United States v. Munsey Trust Co., 332 U.S. 234, 240 (1947). 221

$4.59

From this moment collection of the debt becomes the responsibility of that Office. The Navy Comptroller may set off moneys owing by the 

Navy to a contractor against the contractor's indebtedness to the Navy, even though wholly different contracts are involved. "It would be folly," the Supreme Court has said, "to require the Government to pay under the one contract what it must eventually recover for a breach of the other." " 

The Comptroller General has also had frequent occasion to recognize the right of the United States to resort to setoff.20 If there are no moneys owing a contractor, or if they are insufficient to liquidate the contractor's indebtedness, the Navy Comptroller will report the debt to the Navy Regional Accounts Office, Washington, D. C., which in turn reports the debt to the Chief of Finance, Department of the Army, who maintains a government-wide list of contractors indebted to the United States. This list, called the Consolidated Hold-Up List, enables the Navy to have moneys owing a contractor by another government agency applied against the contractor's indebtedness under Navy contracts. The Consolidated 

Hold-Up List is published quarterly, with interim supplements. All revisions to it for debts arising under Navy contracts are reported by the Navy Regional Accounts Office, Washington. When all attempts to liquidate a contractor's indebtedness through setoff or agreement prove unavailing, the Navy Comptroller refers the matter to the General 

Accounting Office.

C. COLLECTION OF DEBTS UNDER THE BANKRUPTCY ACT 

$ 4.60. In General

Insolvency statutes present a special problem for the collection of debts. 

In simplest terms, an insolvency statute may be characterized as one that seeks the orderly administration and liquidation of a debtor's estate, provides for a ratable distribution of the debtor's assets to his creditors, and discharges a debtor from his debts to the extent that his assets are insufficient to meet them-with or without the assent of the debtor and his creditors. At the present time the only insolvency statute in force is the 

Bankruptcy Act. The Supreme Court has ruled that "the enforcement of state insolvency systems, whether held to be in pursuance of statutory provisions or otherwise, would necessarily conflict with the National purpose to have uniform laws on the subject of bankruptcies throughout the United States," and for this reason, it has held state insolvency statutes invalid.26 The Bankruptcy Act, of course, is remedial in nature; it is designed both to relieve the insolvent debtor from the onus of his debts and to assist creditors in the administration and liquidation of the debtor's assets. In order to deal comprehensively with the debtor and his creditors, the Bankruptcy Act has become long, detailed, and complex; therefore, it requires careful study when proceedings under it are instituted by or against a Navy contractor. The sections that follow briefly discuss the act's pertinence to Navy contract law: first, ordinary

Foster, The General Accounting Office and Government Claims. 16 J.D.C. BAR 

Ass'n. 193, 275, 321, (1949). 

25 Exec. Order No. 6166 § 5 (1933), note foll. 5 U.S.C. §§ 124-132 (1952). See 

7 COMP. GEN. 193, 194 (1927). 

26 International Shoe Co. v. Pinkus, 278, U.S. 261, 268 (1929). Proceedings under the Bankruptcy Act, however, should be carefully distinguished from the composition of debts at common law and the assignment of a debtor's assets for the benefit of creditors, whether at common law or pursuant to state statute. 

While the composition and the assignment for the benefit of creditors, like bankruptcy proceedings, seek an orderly payment of debts, both require the assent of a debtor and his creditors; neither can alter the rights of nonassenting creditors. Because of this voluntary feature, neither is repugnant to the 

Bankruptcy Act. Johnson v. Star, 287 

U.S. 527 (1933). And, unlike bankruptcy proceedings, neither presents the 

Navy with special procedures for the collection of debts.

§ 4.61. Executory Contracts of the Navy 

Uncompleted contracts present the thorniest problem in bankruptcy proceedings. Under section 70 (a) of the Bankruptcy Act,28 the trustee in bankruptcy is vested with the bankrupt's title to almost all of the bankrupt's property as of the time at which the petition in bankruptcy is filed. The major exceptions to this rule are executory contracts, under which performance has not been completed, and leases. Under section 

70 (b),29 the trustee must assume or reject such contracts within 60 days after the debtor's adjudication as a bankrupt. This 60-day period is designed to afford the trustee ample time to appraise what is usually a chaotic state of affairs and determine intelligently which course is in the best interest of the bankrupt's estate. However, the court may extend or reduce this period upon a showing of cause. It is important to note that only after the trustee elects to assume an executory contract does title in that contract vest in the trustee.30 Assumption can be made only by the trustee at his discretion; thereafter, notification of the assumption must be made to the other party to the contract, although no particular form of notice is required. If the trustee remains silent during the prescribed period, his silence will be deemed a rejection.³¹

Usually, the intervention of bankruptcy is preceded by a failure on the part of the contractor to make satisfactory progress in the performance of his Navy contract or to meet his delivery date. This failure, of course, makes the contract subject to termination for default. The subsequent institution of bankruptcy proceedings by or against the contractor will not of itself deprive the Government of its right to terminate for default, although this right may be considered to have been waived if the contracting officer neglects to take appropriate and timely action.32 A special rule would seem to prevail, however, where the contractor is not in default of contract performance at the time of his adjudication as a bankrupt, but subsequently contract performance is halted while the trustee determines whether assumption or rejection is in the best interest of the estate.

EXECUTORY CONTRACTS OF THE NAVY 

$4.61 

While this work stoppage may constitute a failure to make satisfactory progress or may lead to a failure to meet an established delivery date, it should not confer upon the Government the right to terminate for default. 

According to one legal authority, an "important effect of assumption is to purge any anticipatory breach of contract based on the fact of bankruptcy itself." 33 It is consonant with this principle that the right accorded the trustee by section 70(b) to assume an executory contract shall be paramount, unless the terms of the executory contract expressly provide that bankruptcy shall give the Government the option to terminate the contract for default. In order to minimize the effect of this rule, the 

Government may, of course, move the court to reduce the 60-day period for assumption or rejection. Its only other remedy before the expiration of the assumption period would be to terminate the executory contract for the convenience of the Government. If the trustee elects to assume an executory contract, a default occurring after the institution of bankruptcy proceedings and prior to assumption, as well as an anticipatory breach, would appear to be purged. 

After assumption, the trustee has two possible courses of action. First, he may continue the bankrupt's plant operations for purposes of completing the contract. As the successor in interest to the original contractor by operation of law, the substitution of the trustee for the original contractor does not run counter to the statute prohibiting the assignment of government contracts.34 Since the trustee has elected to assume an executory contract, all claims by the Navy arising out of the trustee's performance after assumption are chargeable against the bankrupt's estate as administrative expenses. They are, therefore, first priority claims in the priority scheme set forth in section 64(a) of the Bankruptcy Act.35 

The second course open to the trustee is to assign the contract to a third person. Section 70(b) of the act authorizes such assignments to be made with court approval. To grant the other party to an executory contract protection against the substitution of an undesirable or irresponsible assignee, the section provides for notice and an opportunity for the other party to be heard. Section 70(b) is also noteworthy in expressly relieving the bankrupt's estate from liability for any breach of contract occurring after such an assignment. This second course of action raises a vital question in the case of government contracts—whether an assignment of a contract under section 70 (b) of the Bankruptcy Act is rendered invalid by the statute prohibiting the assignment of government contracts. 

Although this question has not been decided, it would seem that the

statutory prohibition against assignments should not be controlling in the bankruptcy context, since the protection of the interests of the Government intended by that prohibition " is fully provided for by section 70(b). Furthermore, the opposite result would tend to interfere with the purpose of the Bankruptcy Act, which should be given a broad construction in view of its remedial character.38 

If the trustee rejects an executory contract, there is usually no possibility of obtaining continued performance. The trustee is obviously unwilling to perform; and as for the bankrupt contractor, he is in no position to proceed with performance himself. While title to the executory contract will have remained with the bankrupt in this event, title to the bankrupt's operating assets and inventory will have passed to the trustee. A rejection of an executory contract by the trustee constitutes a breach of the contract as of the date of the filing of the petition in bankruptcy," and may give rise to a claim against the estate of the bankrupt contractor. $4.62. Unsecured Claims

As far as unsecured claims in bankruptcy arising under Navy contracts are concerned, the proof of claim in the form required by section 57(a) of the Bankruptcy Act,40 is filed by the local United States Attorney. 

This, however, is only the culmination of a process which begins with the contracting officer. The contracting officer first prepares a detailed report on the claim and forwards it to the Navy Comptroller. The Navy Comptroller then sends the report to the General Accounting Office, where a proof of claim is prepared and sent to the Department of Justice; the latter in its turn instructs the local United States Attorney to file the claim. 

A vital point here is that the Bankruptcy Act limits the time for filing claims by providing that all claims, in order to be allowed, must be filed with the court within six months after the first date set for the first meeting of creditors.41 In preparing his report, the contracting officer should bear in mind that the review of his report by the several offices concerned, as well as the preparation of the actual proof of claim, by the General
