Secured Claims 

The proof of claims procedure described in the preceeding section is intended only for unsecured claims. If a secured creditor files a proof of claim pursuant to section 57 (a) of the Bankruptcy Act, he may be deemed to have waived his security in order to participate in the general assets of the bankrupt's estate.45 A creditor must therefore choose whether or not to avail himself of his security. In cases where the legal validity of the security is doubtful, it may be the better course for the Navy to appear as an unsecured creditor. If, on the other hand, the value of the 

Navy's security is insufficient to meet its claim, a proof of claim pursuant to section 57 (a) may and should be filed for the unsecured balance. The proof of claim should, of course, make it clear that the Government is not waiving its security where that is the Government's intent. The procedure for foreclosing a security interest in property of the bankrupt will depend upon possession of the property at the time of the filing of the petition in bankruptcy. The general rule is that the bankruptcy court acquires jurisdiction over all property in the possession of a bankrupt at the time of the filing of the petition.47 If the secured property was within the possession of the bankrupt and came within the jurisdiction of the bankruptcy court, an intervening petition must be filed in the bankruptcy proceedings. Otherwise, the ordinary legal remedies for foreclosure of a security interest in property will prevail.

$4.64. Government-Owned Property in the Possession of a Bankrupt 

The proof of an unsecured claim and the intervening petition to reach secured assets deal only with money claims against the bankrupt, and they should therefore be carefully distinguished from a claim to specific property based upon the Government's assertion of title. All property within the possession of the bankrupt at the time of the filing of the petition in bankruptcy falls within the jurisdiction of the bankruptcy court.49 If the Government has a valid claim of title to any such property, it may petition the bankruptcy court and obtain reclamation.50 In such a situation, the contracting officer should report the matter to counsel for his procuring activity, who will see that the Department of Justice is requested to file the necessary petition. It is worthy of mention here that the Government's petition for reclamation in bankruptcy proceedings is not subject to counterclaim because of the doctrine of sovereign immunity. 

In the words of one court "A claim of title made by the Government in court is not a concession that its title may be subjected to demands or liens without congressional consent." 51 In the case of its money claims, however, a trustee in bankruptcy may counterclaim by way of recoupment so long as the counterclaim arises out of the same transaction that gave rise to the principal claim. The theory behind this rule is that the Government, in asserting its money claim, has consented as a matter of equity to the counterclaim. The trustee's recovery is limited to the amount of the 

Government's claim since the Government may not be considered to have consented to a counterclaim that results in an affirmative judgment against it.52 $4.65. Corporate Reorganizations and Arrangements 

Except for the chapters bearing upon ordinary bankruptcy, the only chapters of the Bankruptcy Act that impinge with frequency upon Navy procurement are Chapters X and XI. These chapters deal, respectively, with corporate reorganizations and arrangements. While ordinary bank-

CORPORATE REORGANIZATIONS AND ARRANGEMENTS 

$ 4.65 ruptcy seeks the liquidation and distribution of the bankrupt's assets to his creditors, Chapters X and XI seek the resuscitation of the debtor as a going concern. Speaking very broadly, Chapter X is employed by the corporation with numerous stockholders and bondholders among the general public, particularly if there is to be a revamping of the internal corporate structure; Chapter XI, by the smaller corporation or other business organization where little or no public interest is involved. 

As in the case of ordinary bankruptcy, the thorniest problem raised by Chapters X and XI is that of the assumption or rejection of an executory contract.53 Under Chapters X and XI, the decision to assume or reject an executory contract is made, not by the trustee, receiver, or debtor in possession, though his recommendation is important, but by the judge or court in his or its discretion.54 This decision is made in the light of what is deemed to be in the consequent advantage of the debtor's estate. 

In the case of Chapter X, "contracts in the public authority" may not be rejected.55 The term "contracts in the public authority" has not been judicially defined, but this exception seems to have been designed to cover contracts with a public agency where a public interest is involved, such as contracts to provide utility services or other essential public facilities. 

It is most probable that Navy supply contracts are not "contracts in the public authority" within the meaning of Chapter X.56 

There is no prescribed period within which an executory contract must be assumed or rejected under Chapters X and XI. The settled rule is that the trustee, receiver, or debtor in possession shall recommend a course of action to the court within a reasonable time after approval of the petition for reorganization or arrangement. Alternatively, a period

A final word should be added on what may be termed extrajudicial reorganization, that is, a reorganization conducted with the general consent of the creditors and stockholders of the debtor corporation, but without resort to the courts. While atypical, this procedure was sponsored by the Navy, in collaboration with the Air Force, in the case of an important airframe manufacturer whose sustained production during the period of reorganization was essential to the national defense. NEED FOR TERMINATION PROCEDURES 

$5.3 

$ 5.1. Introduction: Meaning of Termination for Convenience 

This chapter deals with the termination of contracts for the "convenience" of the Government. Such terminations occur when the contracting officer determines that, for reasons other than the default of the contractor, it is in the best interest of the Government to discontinue all or some of the remaining work under an uncompleted government contract. "Default" terminations, which result from the contractor's failure, actual or anticipated, to perform the contract, are discussed in Chapter 9. The term "termination" frequently is used herein to refer both to the act of terminating contracts for the convenience of the Government and to the settlement of contractor's claims resulting from such terminations. $ 5.2. 

Reasons for Termination for Convenience 

The rapid development of new weapons and fluctuating world conditions necessitate constant revisions in military procurement. Combat experience and fleet trials often reveal deficiencies in equipment or materials then in production. And for a variety of other reasons goods or services required at the time they were ordered may become excess to the Government's requirements before the contract is completed. An important device in maintaining flexibility is the adjustment of military procurement through the termination of contracts. The Government can avoid unnecessary expense and waste of materials, facilities and manpower by stopping performance under a contract when such performance is no longer desired. $ 5.3. 

Need for Termination Procedures 

A contractor whose contract is terminated for the convenience of the Government must of course be compensated fairly for the work which he has performed and for the preparations he has made for the work which is not to be performed. Often such terminations leave the contractor in possession of excess inventory, such as raw materials, work in process and finished parts, which he cannot profitably use in his other business. Contractors and subcontractors frequently have tied up their money and credit in engineering expenses, work in process and inventories for the terminated contract. Delays in the payment of termination claims might be fatal if contractors were forced to resort to the courts or to the Comptroller General for payment of their claims. Mass terminations occurring after a war or during a severe cutback in defense preparations could seriously affect the national economy if there were no expeditious method of paying the contractors and subcontractors. On the other hand, the Government may be exposed to liability for common-law damages for breach of contract, including anticipatory profits, unless the Government's right to terminate for its convenience is reserved in the contract. 

To meet these problems the Armed Services have devised a comprehensive 235

$ 5.

plan, including a termination clause and implementing regulations, for (i) the termination of work no longer desired, (ii) the processing and settlement of termination claims of both prime contractors and subcontractors, (iii) making partial payments to provide interim financing pending final settlement, and (iv) the disposition of termination inventory. $ 5.4. 

Complete and Partial Terminations 

The termination of a contract for the convenience of the Government may be either partial or complete. A contract is completely terminated when the Government directs complete cessation of all work remaining to be performed. In other words, complete termination is the cancellation of all supplies or services or all of the remaining supplies or services ordered or called for under the contract. Even though a contractor has made delivery under a contract, the termination is complete where he is directed to stop all further work on the supplies or services ordered. 

Partial termination is termination of a portion of the uncompleted work under a contract. It is a reduction or cancellation of part of the items still to be delivered under the contract. That part of the work not completed at the time of termination and which the contractor must continue to perform is referred to as the continued portion of the contract. 

That portion of the contract relating to work or articles completed and accepted prior to the effective date of the termination is the completed portion of the contract. The terminated portion of the contract is that portion which is not to be performed because of the termination. 

I. LEGAL PRINCIPLES 

$5.5. Authority To Terminate for the Convenience of the Government 

The authority to enter into a government contract includes authority to terminate it when to do so would be in the public interest and to make a binding agreement with the contractor in full and final settlement of his termination claim.' While Congress has the power to enact legislation providing for the termination of government contracts,2 Government departments have the authority to terminate their contracts without any specific statutory authority and without a provision in the contract reserving the right to terminate.3 The determination as to whether the public interest requires such termination is a matter for administrative decision by the contracting agency, and not the Comptroller General or the courts. $5.6. Damages for Breach of Contract 

While contracting agencies have the authority to terminate their contracts, the exercise of such authority where the contractor is not at fault consitutes a breach of contract as between the Government and the contractor⚫ unless the right to terminate is provided by statute or is reserved in the contract. When contracting with private parties, the Government has rights and liabilities similar to those of individuals who are parties to such instruments. The Supreme Court has long recognized the right of a government contractor to recover common-law damages when the Government breaches the contract by putting it to an end where the contractor is not at fault. In such cases the primary measure of damages is the amount of the contractor's loss, which may consist of (i) what the contractor already has expended towards performance, less the value of materials on hand, and (ii) the prospective or anticipated profits that he would have realized by performing the whole contract.10 $ 5.7.

Contractor's Expenditures 

The most obvious element of common-law damages are the costs, not in excess of the contract price, which the contractor has reasonably incurred prior to termination in performing the contract. From such expenses are deducted any installments of the contract price already paid and the value of any materials on hand that would have been consumed in completing the contract." However, if it is proved that full performance would have resulted in a net loss to the contractor, the amount of such loss also is deducted from the costs incurred by the contractor.12 In actions for breach of contract, the burden of showing that costs incurred by the

Anticipatory Profits for Breach of Contract The case of United States v. Speed 14 involved a Civil War contract under which the contractor was to slaughter and pack 50,000 hogs to be furnished by the Government. The Government furnished only 17,132 hogs so that the contractor was unable to perform the services contracted for on the remainder. As the measure of the contractor's damages resulting from the Government's failure to furnish the additional hogs, the Supreme Court allowed the difference between the cost of doing the work and what claimants were to receive for it, making reasonable deduction for the less time engaged, and for release from the care, trouble, risk, and responsibility attending full execution of the contract. 

Subsequently, in establishing the contractor's loss as the primary measure of damages for a breach putting an end to the contract, the Supreme Court pointed out that the rule of damages applied in the Speed case was circumscribed by the particular facts of that case and that the contractor cannot always recover anticipatory profits.15 For example, the cost of doing the work might equal or exceed the contract price; or the profits may be too remote and speculative and therefore incapable of that clear and direct proof which the law requires. Anticipatory profits will be denied if the contractor was not ready or did not have the capacity to perform the terminated contract.16 In such a case it would appear that the termination was not the direct cause of the contractor's failure to earn profits." The possibility that the contractor might have secured from the Government extensions of time or concessions in the number of items to be delivered will not justify awarding him unearned profits." 

The contractor must show by "clear and direct proof" that he would have been free to make the anticipated profit which he claims as damages.¹

$ 5.11. Effect of Termination Clauses 

Clauses in government contracts reserving to the Government the right to terminate for convenience are valid and will be upheld by the courts.38 

Terminations under such clauses, like terminations authorized by statute, are the exercise of a lawful right and do not constitute a breach of contract.39 Termination clauses can of course be used in the absence of termination statutes and can specifically exclude anticipatory profits. 

However, in the absence of specific provisions allowing or disallowing anticipatory profits, the courts have denied them where the termination clause provided for other compensation. In one case the Supreme Court decided that under a cost-plus-a-fixed-fee contract for the production of motors, cancelled on thirty days' notice pursuant to a termination clause which provided that a fixed fee would be paid for each completed motor, no fixed fee or profit was allowable on uncompleted motors.40 In another case, where the termination clause provided for payment of certain items, other than prospective profits, such profits were denied." As the court put it, “if that item of profits is recoverable, it is difficult to see what benefit accrues from the stipulated right of termination, the plaintiff having been made whole as to all other items." 42 In a third case, a concurring opinion construed a provision of the contract calling for "equitable adjustment" in the price on account of an increase or decrease of the performance required of the contractor, as prohibiting the recovery of prospective profits on items not delivered as a result of a decrease in the quantity ordered.43

It is well settled that a termination clause may provide a formula for the contracting officer to follow in making a determination as to the amount due the contractor in the absence of an agreement between the parties on the amount due. A determination made in accordance with such formula is binding on both parties, unless it is fraudulent, capricious

45 The practice of terminating contracts for the convenience of the Government and including provisions for such termination in the contracts is not of recent origin. The duty of the Secretary of the Navy, by the Act of April 30, 1798, creating the Navy Department, extends *** to 'the procurement of naval stores, and materials, and the construction, armament, equipment and employment of vessels of war, as well as all other matters connected with the naval establishment of the United States.' *** 

That legislation existing, the discharge of the duty devolving upon the Secretary necessarily requires him to enter into numerous contracts for the public service; and the power to suspend work contracted for, whether in the construction, armament or equipment of vessels of war, when from any cause the public interest requires such suspension, must necessarily rest with him. As, in making the original contracts, he must agree upon the compensation to be made for their entire performance, it would seem that when those contracts are suspended by him, he must be equally authorized to agree upon the compensation for their partial performance. Contracts for the armament and equipment of vessels of war may, and generally do, require numerous modifications in the progress of the work, where that work requires years for its completion. With the improvements constantly made in shipbuilding and steam machinery and in arms, some parts originally contracted for may have to be abandoned, and other parts substituted; and it would be of serious detriment to the public service if the power of the head of the Navy Department did not extend to providing for all such possible contingencies by modification or suspension of the contracts, and settlement with the contractors. $ 5.14. World War I Terminations 

Early upon America's entry into the First World War, legislation was enacted which enabled the Navy Department to handle the termination of its World War I contracts. The Urgent Deficiency Appropriation 

Act of 1917 53 empowered the President "to modify, suspend, cancel or requisition any existing or future contract for the building, production or purchase of ships" or material related thereto; provided that on cancellation the Government should make "just compensation to be determined... by the President." Contractors dissatisfied with a determination were to be paid 75 percent thereof, and could sue for the balance claimed. The President's authority under this statute was delegated to the Navy Department and to the United States Shipping Board. In settling contracts cancelled under that act the Navy Department paid the contractor for such items as raw and partly finished materials, purchased parts, special tooling, special facilities, work in process, overhead, depreciation, subcontract settlements, and profit on work done. Upon payment for such items the Government took title to the materials, tools, or facilities paid for, but in some cases permitted the contractor to retain the items paid for by appropriate credit for market or salvage values. 

The courts denied recovery of anticipated profits as part of "just compensation" under the act and held the act to be binding on contracts entered into before its passage as well as those entered into thereafter.54 $5.15. 

The Dent Act 

The War Department did not receive statutory authority for the settlement of terminated World War I contracts until after the war was over. 

The need to speed up procurement during the war had led to relaxation

DISARMAMENT TERMINATIONS 

$5.16 of procurement regulations. There were a great many "informal" contracts which were not evidenced in writing 55 or were not signed by a contracting officer. On November 25, 1918, the Comptroller of the Treasury ruled that settlements of contracts so made would be invalid.56 The decision admitted the liability of the United States, on a quantum meruit basis, for the fair value of articles delivered and accepted, but did not recognize liability for the value of incomplete work, material on hand, and expenses incurred in the absence of a legally executed contract. This situation resulted in the passage of the Dent Act early in 1919.57 

The Dent Act authorized the Secretary of War to adjust, pay, or discharge, upon a fair and equitable basis, any agreement, express or implied, that had been entered into in good faith during the war and prior to November 12, 1918. The payment of prospective or anticipatory profits was specifically prohibited, and June 30, 1919, was fixed as the time limit for filing of claims. The act gave the Court of Claims jurisdiction to award fair and just compensation where the contractor had not accepted the settlement offer made by the Secretary of War or where the Secretary of War refused or failed to make a satisfactory offer. To protect subcontractors, prime contractors were required to present satisfactory evidence of having paid their subcontractors or of the consent of the subcontractors to look only to the prime contractor for compensation. 

In the event of failure of the prime contractor to present such evidence, the Secretary of War was authorized to pay the subcontractor directly. 

In case of insolvency of the prime contractor, the subcontractor was given a lien, on funds due the prime contractor, superior to that of general creditors.

The prohibition in the act against the payment of anticipatory profits was upheld by the Court of Claims.58 $5.16. Disarmament Terminations

The International Arms Conference of 1922 resulted in agreement to discontinue or limit construction of vessels of war. By the act 59 which gave effect to our obligations under the treaty limiting naval armament, the President was authorized to discontinue the construction of certain warships. The act included express authority to cancel or modify any contract entered into involving the construction or equipping of such vessels and to make settlements upon such fair and equitable basis as the President might determine. $5.17. World War II Terminations 

Events leading up to the United States' entry into World War II placed emphasis on the need for a complete termination program. By the time of Pearl Harbor this country already was engaged in a tremendous defense procurement program. Shifting scenes of the war and the intensive application of scientific weapons caused corresponding changes in procurement planning, necessitating cancellation of contracts. A termination clause was needed which would define the rights of the Govern ment and the contractor on termination. Title II of the First War 

Powers Act, 1941,62 enacted shortly after the nation's entry into the war, conferred sweeping contracting authority upon the President. It empowered the President to authorize agencies connected with the prosecution of the war to enter into contracts and into amendments or modifications of contracts without regard to laws relating to the making, performance or modification of contracts, whenever he deemed that such action would facilitate the prosecution of the war. By Executive Order 

9001,63 this authority was delegated to the War Department, Navy Department and Maritime Commission and they were specifically authorized to modify and amend contracts without consideration and, by agreement, to modify or amend or settle claims under contracts. 

Following a determination by the Under Secretary of War that negotiated settlements upon termination would facilitate the prosecution of the war effort, a termination article for fixed-price supply contracts in use by the War Department since September 1941 was modified in 1942 to add a provision calling for negotiated settlements. This article became the basis for the War Department's termination procedure."

§ 5.18. - Joint Contract Termination Board In November 1943 the Director of War Mobilization established a Joint Contract Termination Board. In January 1944 the Board pro mulgated a uniform termination article for use by all procurement agencies in lump-sum supply contracts and directed its use to the fullest extent practicable including its insertion in existing contracts. At the same time the Board promulgated a uniform "Statement of Principles for 

Determination of Costs under Termination of Government Fixed-Price 

Supply Contracts."67 It also recommended the use of a subcontract termination article. These measures constituted an interim termination program worked out within the framework of existing law. Under this program contracts were terminated, termination claims settled, termination inventory disposed of under price policies established by the 

Surplus War Property Administration, and interim financing provided by means of partial payments. This termination system operated for approximately one year. It was replaced by the program based upon the Contract Settlement Act of 1944. 

$ 5.19.

Contract Settlement Act of 1944 

The Contract Settlement Act of 1944 69 became effective in July of that year. The objectives of the act were to facilitate maximum war production and to expedite reconversion to civilian production as war conditions permitted; to provide for speedy and equitable final settlements with both prime contractors and subcontractors; to assure uniformity

$5.19

of policies and procedures in the termination and settlement of contracts; to provide for adequate interim financing; to facilitate efficient use of materials, manpower and facilities for war and civilian purposes by providing prime contractors and subcontractors with advance notice of termination whenever practicable; to assure expeditious removal from contractors' plants of termination inventory which was not retained or sold; and to use all practicable methods compatible with these objectives to prevent improper payment and to detect and prosecute fraud. 

The act established the Office of Contract Settlement, presided over by a Director of Contract Settlement, to supervise the operation of the program and with authority to set up a board to hear appeals in disputes over claims for fair compensation. Fair compensation, in order to be uniform, had to accord with that provided for by the uniform termination article, regardless of whether or not the contract contained such article. Settlements were to be negotiated to the maximum extent feasible but, in the absence of agreement, contracting agencies were to determine the amount due. The elements of fair compensation were set forth in some detail and consisted of items of cost and profit delineated in the uniform termination article and in the statement of cost principles previously established by the Joint Contract Termination Board. Under certain conditions war contractors, including subcontractors, were to receive interest upon their claims. In addition to being eligible for partial or advance payments and guaranteed loans, to the same extent as prime contractors, a subcontractor was given the protection of direct settlement of his claim by the Government where he could demonstrate necessity therefor and, under certain circumstances, to direct payment where the prime contractor was insolvent, even though the prime contractor may already have been paid the sum due. Government officers and employees were specifically permitted to assist contractors in the preparation of their claims. The Comptroller General's function was confined to determining after final settlement (i) whether payments were being made in accordance with the settlement agreements, and (ii) whether or not settlements had been induced by fraud. He was permitted to investigate settlements made by the various agencies for the purpose of reporting to Congress on whether the contracting agencies were following the settlement procedures of the act.

The Appeal Board of the Office of Contract Settlement, established in 1945, operated as an independent quasi-judicial agency. It had jurisdiction of appeals from decisions of contracting agencies on claims arising out of contract terminations and claims based on defective, informal or quasi contracts. The Board also had jurisdiction like that of an arbitrator to decide disputes under terminated subcontracts if the subcontractor and upper-tier contractor agreed to submit the dispute to the Board; but this part of the Board's jurisdiction was infrequently 248

OTHER WARTIME LEGISLATION 

$ 5.21 exercised. Contractors could sue directly in the courts without first taking an appeal to the Board. A contractor dissatisfied with the 

Board's decision could appeal to the courts, but the Board's decision was final and conclusive on the Government. Decisions of the Board established precedents on important legal and accounting principles which were applied by the contracting agencies to the settlement of numerous similar claims. Due to the similarity of current termination clauses and regulations to those involved in appeals to the Board, its decisions still serve as helpful guides in current termination problems. 

The Board concluded its operations in January 1953.7⁰ 

$ 5.20.

Joint Termination Regulation 

In November 1944 the War and Navy Departments adopted the Joint Termination Regulation which is usually referred to as the "JTR." The 

JTR set forth detailed procedures and methods for carrying out the objectives of the Contract Settlement Act and implemented the regulations of the Director of Contract Settlements. The JTR was based primarily upon Army Procurement Regulation No. 15 which had been used as a basis for Army termination settlements prior to the adoption of the Contract Settlement Act. It recognized certain fundamental differences between the organization and structure of the two Departments, and where different procedures were to be followed by each Department they were spelled out in the JTR. 

$ 5.21. Other Legislation

Two other statutes affecting terminations were enacted in 1944. The 

War Mobilization and Reconversion Act of 1944" required contracting agencies to terminate prime contracts for war production whenever in their opinion performance was no longer needed for the prosecution of the war, unless the Office of War Mobilization and Reconversion decided the continuation of some or all of the contract would benefit the Government or was necessary to avoid substantial physical injury to plants or property. That act also required that curtailment of war production or terminations of war contracts be synchronized and integrated with the expansion, resumption or initiation of production for other war purposes and of production for non-war use to the extent compatible with the prosecution of the war. $ 5.22. Post-War Procedures and Developments Unlike other World War II legislation, the Contract Settlement Act of 1944 did not contain a provision specifying the date of its expiration. 

However, it applies only to "war contracts" and to "war contractors" as those terms are defined in that act. During the war and up until 

May 19, 1948, most supplies and services had been procured under the authority of Title II of the First War Powers Act.73 

With the enactment of a permanent peace-time procurement statute, the Armed Services Procurement Act of 1947,74 which became effective May 19, 1948, the Armed Services took the position that the Contract Settlement Act would not apply to the settlement of any contracts entered into under the new procurement statute because such contracts could not be considered "war contracts." Accordingly, although World War II was not officially ended by Presidential Proclamation until April 30, 1952,75 the Contract Settlement Act was not applied or used as authority for the termination or settlement of contracts entered into after May 

19, 1948.76

Following the adoption of the Armed Services Procurement Act of 1947, the Armed Services began working on a new uniform contract termination and settlement program without the benefit of the authority of the Contract Settlement Act and the First War Powers Act. Mean while each Service was left to its own devices with respect to the termination of contracts entered into after May 19, 1948. The policies and procedures of the Contract Settlement Act were followed in large measure. 

Interim Navy regulations made the JTR applicable to contracts made under the Armed Services Procurement Act, except to the extent that the JTR depended upon the Contract Settlement Act.

While the new termination regulations were being prepared for adoption as part of the Armed Services Procurement Regulation, the Surplus Property Act of 1944 was replaced by the Federal Property and Administrative Services Act of 1949.78 Also, the outbreak of hostilities in Korea in June 1950 resulted in the reactivation of Title II of the First War

CURRENT TERMINATION PROCEDURES A. REGULATIONS, CLAUSES AND RESPONSIBILITIES GENERALLY 

$ 5.23. Controlling Regulations

In terminating contracts for the convenience of the Government and in the settlement of contracts so terminated, the Departments of the Army, Navy and Air Force currently are governed by Section VIII of the Armed Services Procurement Regulation (hereinafter called ASPR 

Section VIII) which was first promulgated in January 1952.83 ASPR 

Section VIII provides uniform clauses, policies, methods, procedures, and forms for the termination and settlement of contracts, including the disposition of property incident to termination. It follows to a great extent policies and procedures of the Joint Termination Regulation.84 

Detailed termination procedures and methods, which vary among the three military departments primarily because of differences in their organizational structure, are provided separately by regulations of each department. The Navy Contract Termination Handbook," while not a regulation, is an excellent working manual for personnel engaged in the administration of terminations. It furnishes interpretations of various provisions, supplies background information regarding the intent behind the established termination policies, and provides "know how” and examples for the proper application of the regulations and the administration of terminations. 

§ 5.28. Termination Clauses Generally 

ASPR Section VIII provides several termination clauses for use in various types of procurement contracts. The two most important of these clauses are those (i) for commercial fixed-price contracts in excess of $1,000 for supplies or experimental, developmental, or research work, and (ii) for commercial cost-type contracts for supplies or experimental, developmental or research work.94 These are the principal types of contracts issued by the Navy Department. Other ASPR Section VIII 

termination clauses for special type contracts are discussed at the end of this Chapter. They include optional short-form clauses, and clauses for fixed-price construction contracts and for research and development contracts with non-profit institutions. In general, the ASPR termination clauses give the Government the right to terminate the contract, in whole or in part; state the contractor's rights and obligations after termination; and provide for a negotiated settlement of the contractor's claim. 

If the parties fail to agree on the amount to be paid the contractor, the contracting officer must make a unilateral determination of the amount due, which decision can be appealed to the Armed Services Board of 

Contract Appeals. Where no ASPR Section VIII clause is prescribed, as in the case of letter contracts, time and material contracts, personal service contracts, or facilities contracts, the procuring activity may use its own clause provided it is not inconsistent with the ASPR.95

94 The latter clause for cost-type contracts also provides for default termination, whereas a separate "Default" clause is provided in fixed-price supply contracts.

 $ 5.29. Effectuation of Regulations by Termination Clauses 

Since no statute makes the termination regulations in ASPR Section VIII apply to contracts which do not expressly incorporate them by reference or otherwise, the basic rights of the Government and the contractor upon termination must be found in the terms of the contract itself. The whole termination system established by ASPR Section VIII depends on the use in contracts of termination clauses provided in it or similar clauses. Indeed, the main function of ASPR Section VIII is to explain the termination clauses and to furnish guidance and directions to the contracting officer and his representatives in taking action under the termination clause. Some provisions of ASPR Section VIII may be incorporated by reference into the termination clause and thus have the same binding effect as any other part of the contract. However, to permit some flexibility in operations and modification of the regulations without a corresponding amendment of existing contracts, ASPR Section VIII provisions are incorporated by reference in the termination clauses only to a very limited extent. Instead, the regulations are made effective in the following manner. Most of the contractor's obligations upon termination are required by the termination clause to be performed as directed by, or subject to the approval of, the contracting officer. 

Thus, although the contract does not expressly require the contractor to observe the detailed procedures of ASPR Section VIII and implementing regulations, the contracting officer (who is controlled by them) in giving directions, or as a condition to granting approval, can require the contractor to follow the prescribed procedures. Also, the contractor must agree to the ASPR Section VIII policies, procedures and cost principles applied by the contracting officer, if a unilateral determination of his claim by the contracting officer (as provided for in the termination. clause) is to be avoided.% $5.30. Responsibilities for Termination Within the Navy 

When describing or requiring action to be taken on behalf of the Government, ASPR Section VIII and the termination clauses generally refer to the "contracting officer." Each Navy purchasing bureau or office will have one or more contracting officers authorized to act in termination matters. The contracting officer is responsible, among other things, for issuing the notice of termination, negotiating the final settlement with prime contractors and approving final settlement of subcontractor claims. 

The term "contracting officer" is defined in ASPR Section VIII and in most Navy contracts to permit the delegation of many termination functions and responsibilities to authorized representatives of the con-

B. PRELIMINARY TERMINATION PROCEDURES 

$ 5.31. Notice of Termination

The ASPR Section VIII termination clauses provide that the termination shall be effected by a written notice of termination. Customarily the notice is first sent in telegraphic form and then confirmed by letter. 

The notice must state (i) that the contract is being terminated for the convenience of the Government under the termination clause, (ii) the effective date of termination,³ (iii) the extent of termination and, in case of partial termination, the portion of the contract to be continued, and (iv) any special instructions. Stating the nature of the termination is particularly important in the case of cost-plus-fixed-fee contracts, where the termination clause provides for both default and convenience terminations. In determining the date and extent of termination it may be desirable under some circumstances to permit the contractor to complete some items in process that are no longer desired or needed for military purposes. For example, certain items nearing completion might be completed and be commercially valuable with a small amount of additional work, whereas in their uncompleted state they would only have scrap value. Special instructions include such things as directions concerning items of inventory which the Government may wish to acquire and directions for the disposition of special tooling. For example, if the contractor has bought critical materials for the contract and the Navy wants

VIII. 

$5.32. Obligations of the Contractor: Stop Work 

The obligations of the contractor after receipt of the termination notice are set forth in the termination clause. The primary duties of the contractor upon receipt of the notice are to (i) stop work at the time and to the extent directed, (ii) terminate all outstanding subcontracts and purchase orders to the extent that they relate to the terminated portion of the contract, and (iii) refrain from placing further orders and subcontracts except as may be necessary to complete any continued portion of the work. Usually the notice will direct the contractor to stop work immediately. If the contractor continues the work he does so at his own risk and for his own account. But if it is impossible, despite all reasonable efforts of the contractor, to discontinue certain costs and expenses immediately after termination, such costs and expenses may be included in the settlement. The period necessary for the contractor to stop work and terminate subcontracts and orders will vary with the nature of the terminated work, the volume of work at the time of termination, and the complexity of his business. In order to prevent stoppage of work on subcontracts and orders which relate to both terminated and continued work, the contractor may have to screen outstanding subcontracts, purchase orders, bills of material and continuing work requirements before issuing termination notices. The test as to whether the contractor discharged his obligation in this respect essentially is whether he acted prudently and reasonably under all the circumstances. While his compensation is not measured by common-law damages, there being no breach, the situation is somewhat analogous to the common-law obligation to minimize damages.

If the termination is partial, the contractor is required to perform the continued portion of the contract. Where the contractor has placed different orders for items common to both the terminated and continued portion of the contract and the price of items for the latter is higher, it may be advantageous to arrange with the contractor to terminate the order placed at the higher price, instead of the order applicable to the terminated portion of the contract. $ 5.33. -Termination Inventory

The contractor's obligations with respect to termination inventory are threefold: (1) he must to the extent, if any, directed by the contracting officer transfer title and deliver to the Government any termination in- 256

FOLLOW-UP BY THE INSPECTOR 

$5.36 ventory and any other property or information which would have been furnished to the Government if the contract had been completed; (2) he must take such action as may be necessary, or as the contracting officer may direct, for the protection and preservation of the inventory; (3) he must use his best efforts to sell any or all of the termination inventory, in the manner, at the times, to the extent, and at the price directed or authorized by the contracting officer. The contractor may not be required to extend credit to purchasers and may himself purchase termination inventory with the approval of the contracting officer's representative.7 

§ 5.34. -Subcontracts, Claims and Assignments 

The contractor is obligated to settle all outstanding claims and liabilities arising out of the terminated subcontracts or purchase orders unless otherwise directed by the contracting officer. To the extent required by the contracting officer, such settlements must be approved or ratified by the contracting officer or his representative. If the contracting officer so directs, the contractor must assign to the Government, to the extent directed, all of the contractor's right, title and interest under terminated subcontracts and orders, in which event the Government may, in its discretion, settle or pay claims arising out of the termination of such subcontracts or orders." $ 5.35. Submit Termination Claim

If the contractor desires to submit a termination claim, he is required to do so promptly, but in no event later than one year from the effective date of termination, unless the time is extended in writing by the contracting officer.10 

$5.36. Follow-up by the Inspector

Immediately after the notice of termination is issued, the cognizant inspector will contact the contractor, visit the plant, and endeavor to see that the contractor discharges his obligations under the termination clause and that the Government's interests are protected. The inspector discusses the termination with the contractor, checks the status of work and inventories, inspects completed items, encourages the diversion of termination inventory to other continuing or projected work, arranges for disposition of termination inventory, and arranges for the submission of contractor and subcontractor settlement proposals. $ 5.37. Termination Inventory Schedules 

All termination inventory for which the contractor claims reimbursement in a termination settlement must be listed by him on inventory schedules." In addition to supporting the contractor's charges for cost of inventory, the schedules are designed to permit Navy identification, screening, evaluation and disposal of termination inventory which the contractor does not retain at cost or return to his suppliers. Inventory schedules for contracts must not include common items which the contractor can, without loss to him, reasonably use on other work, unless the Government has required delivery of such items or unless the items are government-furnished property.12 Title to termination inventory is tendered to the Government when the schedule is submitted, unless the Government already has title, and the contractor warrants the inventory listed to be clear of all liens and encumberances.13 The inventory schedules must be reviewed and the termination inventory verified by the inspector to the extent practicable.14 The inspector checks the physical count and condition of inventories, substantiates that the items and quantities listed are allocable to the terminated contract, and checks the accuracy of the description and classification of the items. Inventory schedules covering all or a substantial portion of the inventory may be submitted prior to the submission of the settlement proposal. Generally, the contractor may, prior to disposition of the inventory, withdraw and retain at cost contractor-acquired items listed on the schedules. However, if the items have been submitted for screening 15 or if the Government has required delivery of the item, withdrawal is permitted only with prior approval of the appropriate government representative.16

Frequently it is necessary to clear a plant or production area of termination inventory so the contractor can get started with other work. Storage at the Expense and Risk of the Government 

The termination clauses for fixed-price and cost-type commercial contracts include a provision for plant clearance. At any time after the expiration of the plant clearance period the contractor may request the Government to remove the inventory or enter into a storage agreement covering it. The Government is obligated to comply with the contractor's request within 15 days.20 Storage agreements usually provide for storage by the contractor at a negotiated price. If the Government fails to remove the items or enter a storage agreement, the contractor may arrange for their storage and hold the Government liable for its failure to remove them. 

$5.40. Preparation of Settlement Proposals 

The termination clauses require the contractor to submit his termination claim in the form and with the certification prescribed by the contracting officer. The contractor prepares and submits his claims on forms called "settlement proposals." Settlement Proposals for Fixed-Price Contracts 

Normally a settlement proposal should cover all elements of the contractor's claim, including his own costs and settlement with subcontractors.26 Actual, standard, or average costs may be used in preparing settlement proposals if they are in accordance with generally recognized accounting principles consistently followed by the contractor." If such costs are not available, costs may be estimated by a reasonable method approved by the contracting officer. The Government does not require a contractor to maintain unduly elaborate cost accounting systems for fixed-price contracts merely because they may be terminated.20 

The two bases upon which a prime contractor may prepare his settlement proposal are the inventory basis and the total-cost basis. The use of any other basis of settlement, such as percentage of physical completion, would require the approval of the Secretary of Navy or his duly designated representative.29 $ 5.42.

Inventory Basis 

Use of the inventory basis for settlement proposals is generally preferred by the Government.30 Under the inventory basis the contractor lists only his costs relating and allocable to the terminated portion of the contract. Charges for the inventories are itemized according to their classification-i.e. raw materials, purchased parts, finished components, and work in process-at the purchase price or manufacturing cost. To this amount are added other applicable costs, such as preparatory costs, and allocable general and administrative expenses. To this total of the above items the contractor adds the profit " he claims on work done, costs of settlements with subcontractors, settlement expenses, and the price of

Under the total-cost basis where complete termination occurs, all costs incurred to the effective date of termination are summarized and an allowance for profit or an adjustment for loss, if any, is made.35 In the case of a partial termination, all costs incurred under the contract will be summarized including those incurred after termination on the continued portion of the contract.36 Payments made by the Government for completed units are then deducted. § 5.47. 

- Partial Payments 

Partial payments are payments made to a contractor on account of his termination claim in advance of final settlement, but without prejudice to the amount of the final settlement. ASPR Section VIII provides that, if the contract authorizes partial payments, the contracting officer may in his discretion make partial payments, upon written application therefor, subject to the terms of the contract.4% ASPR Section VIII termination clauses provide that the Government may from time to time make partial payments and payments on account against costs incurred by the contractor, subject to the following conditions: (1) the payments may be made under such terms and conditions as the Government may prescribe and only when in the opinion of the contracting officer the aggregate of such payments is within the total amount which will be due the contractor; (2) if the total of such payments exceeds the amount finally agreed or determined to be due, the excess shall be payable to the Government on demand with 6 percent interest from the date the excess payment was made to the contractor. However, interest is not payable on any excess payments which are attributable to the retention or disposition of termination inventory until 10 days after the date of such retention or disposition.47

C. TERMINATION SETTLEMENTS 

$5.49. Introduction

The final phase in the settlement of a terminated prime contract is the negotiation of a settlement agreement with the contractor and the execu tion of a settlement agreement. The ASPR Section VIII termination clauses provide that the contractor and the contracting officer may agree upon the whole or any part of the amount to be paid the contractor by reason of the termination, which amount may include a reasonable allowance for profit on work done.57 If the parties fail to agree, the contracting officer makes a unilateral determination of the amount to be paid the contractor as explained in section 5.59. But negotiation is the preferred and the usual method of settlement. Negotiations generally take place after the disposal of termination inventory, the settlement and approval of subcontract claims, and the collection of all information necessary for evaluation of the contractor's claim. 

$5.50. Adjustment of Price or Fee for Continued Work 

In addition to providing for compensation on account of the termi nated portion of the contract, the ASPR Section VIII termination clauses for fixed-price contracts provide that in the case of partial terminations, the contractor may request an equitable adjustment of the contract price of the continued portion of the contract, and that such equitable adjustment as the parties may agree upon shall be made in the contract price.58 The request for adjustment must be filed prior to the settlement of the terminated portion of the contract.59 The purpose of the equitable adjustment is to compensate the contractor for any increase in the cost of performing the continued portion of the contract resulting from the partial termination. For example, a decrease in the volume of production might increase the unit cost of the items still to be produced and delivered. The "continued portion of the contract" is defined in 

ASPR Section VIII to mean that portion of the contract not already completed and accepted at the date of termination and which the contractor must continue to perform.60 Under this definition the contractor is not entitled to an equitable adjustment in the price of articles delivered and accepted prior to the date of termination. Termination clauses in use prior to the adoption of ASPR Section VIII, providing for an equi-

Section VIII clauses), the contractor was entitled to price adjustment as of right, and not merely dependent upon the grace of the contracting officer as to whether he should receive it.

The termination clause for cost-plus-fixed-fee contracts provides for an equitable adjustment of the fee which is payable on continued work in case the contract is partially terminated.62 Adjustment of the fixed fee is subject to the statutory ceilings discussed in section 5.54. Adjustment of the price or fee applicable to the continued portion of a contract generally is negotiated separately from the settlement of the contractor's claim relating to the terminated portion of the contract. While such "equitable adjustments" stem from partial terminations, they are not referred to as termination "settlements." $ 5.51. Negotiated Settlements

The purpose of a negotiated settlement is to achieve mutual agreement of the parties on an amount which will fairly and equitably compensate the contractor for work done and preparations made for the terminated portion of the contract, including a reasonable profit or fee. Fair compensation is inherently a matter of sound business judgment and is not always capable of exact determination. Cost and accounting data may provide guides but are not rigid measures of fair compensation. The parties may agree on a total amount without agreeing on the particular elements entering into the total. In appropriate cases costs may be estimated, differences compromised, and doubtful questions settled by agreement. $ 5.52. · Contractor's Costs

The contractor's reasonable and necessary costs and expenses, which are allocable to the terminated work, usually constitute the principal element of the termination settlement. Fixed-price contracts ordinarily do not specify rules or principles for arriving at the contractor's costs that are to be considered in negotiating a settlement with the contractor. 

However, ASPR Section VIII provides a set of cost principles to be used as a guide for that purpose.63 However, in settlements by determination, where the parties have failed to agree, the use of such cost principles is mandatory to the extent the contract incorporates them by ref-

PROFIT ON FIXED-PRICE CONTRACTS 

$ 5.53 erence of otherwise.64 If a fixed-price contract does contain a special provision stating that a particular cost will or will not be considered, then the contract provision controls. The settlement of cost-type contracts is somewhat simplified by the fact that the contractor has been reimbursed on a cost basis to begin with. In negotiating settlements of cost-type contracts the provisions of the "Allowable Costs" clause in the contract govern which costs are properly allocable and reimbursable. The cost principles in ASPR Section XV are incorporated in most cost-type contracts by reference.65 $ 5.53. Profit on Fixed-Price Contracts

The ASPR Section VIII fixed-price contract clauses provide for a reasonable allowance for profit on work done." This includes preparations made and work done for the terminated portion of the contract. 

There are various methods for arriving at a reasonable profit. ASPR 

Section VIII suggests several criteria for consideration in arriving at a fair profit." Among the criteria which may be used is the rate of profit which was originally negotiated when the contract was entered into. A separate rate of profit can be applied against the different items of the claim, depending upon whether they represent a large or small portion of the work done. For example, a lower rate can be applied to unfabricated materials and a higher rate to materials on which work was performed. 

The contracting officer should consider the efficiency and extent of the work performed by the contractor, the difficulty of the job, the extent of risk assumed by the contractor, and any other factors that fair and equitable dealing may require. 

The amount of profit in a negotiated settlement of fixed-price contracts is not limited by ASPR Section VIII or the termination clauses therein. 

It may be less or more than the rate originally negotiated. However, it should be borne in mind that the contractor's risk, one of the elements which affected the contemplated profit when the contract was negotiated, has been largely eliminated by termination. ASPR Section VIII specifically prohibits (i) profits on the contractor's settlement expenses, (ii) profits measured by the amount of a contractor's settlement with his subcontractors, (iii) profits on interest on borrowings allowed as a cost, and (iv) the application in negotiated settlements of the profit formula prescribed in the termination clause for settlements by determination.68

 $ 5.54. -Fee on Cost-Type Contracts 

The policy on allowance of profits on fixed-price contracts applies to the allowance of a fee in the settlement of terminated cost-plus-fixed-fee contracts. That is, the fee is for work done and preparations made for the terminated portion of the contract. The fee allowed generally is related to the percentage of completion of the contract." Under the 

ASPR termination clause this criterion is mandatory in the case of settlements by determination,70 and it often is the only practical means of negotiating a settlement of the fee. The ratio of costs incurred to the total estimated costs of performing the contract is only one factor in computing the percentage of completion of the contract. The extent and difficulty of the work done are also primary factors."¹ 

By statute 72 the amount of fixed fee that may be allowed in procurements under cost-plus-fixed-fee contracts must not exceed 10 percent of the estimated cost of the contract, except that up to 15 percent of the estimated cost is permitted for experimental, developmental or research work, and not more than 6 percent of the estimated cost may be allowed for the fee in contracts for architectural or engineering services on public works or utility projects. These statutory ceilings (based on the cost estimate made at the time the contract was entered into) apply to the settlement of fees under terminated cost-type contracts. Terminations normally result in a reduction of the amount of fixed fee, which was established within the statutory ceiling to begin with. However, the statutory ceilings are mentioned here to bring out that there is a statutory limitation on the overall amount of the adjustment of fixed fees for both the terminated and the continued portions of the contract, even in negotiated settlements.73 $ 5.55. Loss Contracts

Where the entire cost of performing a contract to completion would exceed the contract price, the contract is referred to as a "loss contract.”

The termination for convenience of a loss contract reduces the amount of the contractor's potential loss. The ASPR Section VIII termination clauses for fixed-price contracts provide that in case of settlements by unilateral determination, no profit shall be allowed if it appears that the contractor would have sustained a loss on the entire contract had it been completed, and an appropriate adjustment shall be made reducing the amount of the settlement to reflect the indicated rate of loss.74 ASPR

$ 5.56 settlement is by negotiation or by unilateral determination, and provides formulae for reducing the amount of the settlement to reflect the amount of loss. In the case of settlement or determinations on a total-cost basis, the amount of the settlement or determination that represents the contractor's costs exclusive of settlement expenses is reduced by multiplying that amount by the ratio of (i) the total contract price to (ii) that amount plus the estimated cost to complete the entire contract. For example, if the contract price was $10,000, and the agreed costs incurred prior to termination were $5,000, and it is estimated that the additional cost of completing the entire contract would have been $7,000 had it not been terminated (so that the contractor would have lost $2,000 had the contract been completed), the contractor would be allowed $4,166.67 in the settlement for the costs incurred prior to termination, arrived at as follows: 

$5,000 × $10,000 $5,000+$7,000 =$4,166.67

In the case of settlements on an inventory basis, the amount of the settlement, exclusive of settlement expenses and the price of acceptable completed end items, similarly is reduced by multiplying that amount by the ratio of (i) the total contract price, to (ii) the total costs incurred prior to termination plus the estimated costs to complete the entire contract.76 $5.56.

Amount Due the Contractor 

The total amount payable to the contractor in settlement of his claim, before deduction of disposal credits and exclusive of his settlement of expenses, should never exceed the contract price less payments otherwise made or to be made. To the amounts allowed the contractor as his costs and profit or fee are added his settlement expenses and the amount of settlements with subcontractors. In the settlement of fixed-price contracts on the inventory basis the contract price of undelivered acceptable finished products (less any savings in freight, packing, etc.) is added separately." From the total of these items is deducted (i) the price of any termination inventory acquired by the contractor and the proceeds of material sold by him and not paid to the Government, and (ii) the amount of any unliquidated advance, progress, partial, or other payments previously made to the contractor, and (iii) the amount of any claim which the Government has against the contractor in connection with the contract. These deductions are provided for in the termination clauses." Claims of the Government arising independently of the contract are not deducted in the settlement agreement but, subject to the applicability of the no setoff provisions of the Assignment of Claims

79 Act," may be set off against the amount due under the agreement when the settlement voucher is presented to the disbursing officer for payment. $ 5.57. Review of the Settlement

Proposed termination settlements in "amounts" of $25,000 or more are subject to review and approval of one or more settlement review boards before they are ratified or approved by the contracting officer or his representative. In determining the "amount" of a proposed settlement for the purpose of ascertaining whether it is subject to review, credits to the Government for retention or other disposal of inventory by the contractor and for advance or partial payments are not deducted from the gross claim, but amounts payable for completed work at the contract price and for subcontract settlements are deducted." 

There are two types of settlement review boards in the Navy-those established at the bureau (procuring activity) level and those in the field offices. Prime contractors' settlements in the amount of $25,000 or more are subject to approval by a board at the bureau level. Subcontractor settlements for $25,000 or more are subject to approval by a field office (inspector's) settlement review board and if they amount to $500,000 or more they also are subject to approval by the review board at the bureau level before they are binding on the Government. If no settlement review board has been established for the appropriate field office then settlements which such board would have reviewed are referred to the bureau board. Each board must have at least three members. No person may serve as a member of a review board in reviewing a settlement in which he has participated. Where board review of a proposed settlement is not mandatory, a review may be requested by the head of the procuring activity, the contracting officer or, in the case of subcontracts, the inspector. Failure of the board to act on a settlement within 30 days, after submission to it of all the information it requires, operates as an approval by it."2 In general, approval or disapproval of settlements by the review board is final, subject to the contractor's right to appeal from the contracting officer's decision made in accordance with the board's findings. A board can of course reconsider its decision disapproving a proposed settlement and may require the submission of additional information.

The contractor is further entitled to his reasonable expenses incident to settlements with the Government and with subcontractors and to the reasonable costs of protecting or disposing of property allocable to the contract. As noted in section 5.55, if a loss contract is indicated no profit is allowed and the settlement amount is reduced to reflect the indicated rate of loss. The amounts paid cannot exceed the total contract price reduced by the amount of payments otherwise made and by the contract price of work not terminated. Further reductions may be made for lost or damaged property. The determination of costs is governed by the 

ASPR Section VIII cost principles. 

The termination clause for cost-type contracts contains somewhat similar provisions for determining costs and the fee due," but the cost principles of ASPR XV are applicable. Under the termination clauses of both fixed-price and cost-type contracts, the contractor has a right to appeal under the "Disputes" clause 2 of the contract from the determination made by the contracting officer unless he failed to submit his claim within the required time (one year, unless extended) and did not request an extension of time in which to file. 

D. SUBCONTRACT SETTLEMENTS $ 5.60. Relationship of the Government to Subcontractors 

There being no privity of contract between the Government and subcontractors, a subcontractor has no contractual rights directly against the Government upon termination of the prime contract. His rights are against the prime contractor or upper-tier subcontractor who placed the subcontract with him. Prime contractors and subcontractors are responsible for settling the termination claims of their immediate subcontractors. However, the termination clauses for prime contracts reserve to the Government the right to approve or ratify settlements with subcontractors. A suggested termination clause for fixed-price subcontracts, which will make subcontract terminations fit in with government termination procedures, is set forth in ASPR Section VIII.93 The failure of the prime contractor to include a termination clause in a subcontract will not affect the Government's right under the prime contract termination clause to require the termination of subcontracts.94 Accordingly, for their own protection, prime contractors and higher-tier subcontractors should include termination clauses in their subcontracts. The Government will not reimburse the prime for subcontractor's consequential damages or loss of anticipatory profits unless the subcontractor has obtained

$5.61. Approval of Subcontract Settlements 

In reviewing and approving subcontract settlements, the Government applies the same general policies and principles as are applied to the settlement of prime contracts. The final approval of proposed subcontract settlements is generally the responsibility of the inspector cognizant of the prime contractor. However, for specific contracts only, authority to approve settlements between subcontractors may be delegated to inspectors of immediate lower-tier subcontractors and, in turn, redelegated to inspectors of lower-tier subcontractors. Prime contractors may be, and generally are, authorized by contracting officers to settle claims of their immediate subcontractors in amounts not exceeding $10,000 without approval or ratification by the Government (i.e. in such cases the Government foregoes its right under the contract to approve or ratify settlements with subcontractors).% When a contractor having been granted this authority is also a subcontractor he may use it in the settlement of immediate lower-tier subcontracts." Otherwise, proposed settlements between subcontractors are submitted up the contractual chain until they come to the prime contractor or to a higher-tier subcontractor whose inspector has been authorized to approve them. Subcontract claims for more than $25,000 must have settlement review board approval as explained in section 5.57.

E. DISPOSITION OF TERMINATION INVENTORY § 5.63. Retention by the Contractor of Contractor-Acquired Property 

The contractor may retain at cost items of termination inventory other than government-furnished property, unless he is directed by the contracting officer to transfer such items to the Government.' The cost of such items is not included in the settlement, except that, if the property is to be used in other operations, reasonable handling and transportation charges may be included. Likewise, the contractor may return such items to his suppliers and include in his settlement proposal the supplier's normal restocking charge or 15 percent of the cost, whichever is less.³ 

Contractors are encouraged to retain or return to suppliers property acquired by them for the performance of the contract, and, as noted in section 5.37, generally they may withdraw such property from the inventory schedules and their settlement claims before the property is disposed of. 

$ 5.64. Screening of Termination Inventory 

Prior to disposal outside of the Government, certain kinds of property, not retained or returned to the supplier by the contractor, must be "screened" for items which can be used by the Navy or other government agencies. Screening of certain items is required by Department of Defense regulations issued by agreement with the Administrator of General Services. Navy directives require screening of additional items. Regulations on screening are subject to frequent revisions as conditions change. 

Except for certain kinds of production equipment, inventory classified as scrap, salvage, perishable or dangerous to public health or safety generally need not be screened. Other property listed on the termination schedules consists of two general classes: (1) that which need be screened by the purchasing bureau only, and (2) that which must also be screened by the Armed Forces Supply Support Center. In addition, special screening is accorded narcotics, intangible property, strategic and critical materials, and materials useful for the production of fissionable materials. Generally, the cost principles of ASPR Section XV will be applied, but as a rule no profit or fee is allowed and only direct costs are reimbursed where the facilities are to be furnished to the contractor. Ordinarily overhead is allocated to the supply contracts for which the facilities are furnished. Where the supply contracts are terminated the contractor then has no vehicle for recovering of overhead.

Renegotiation and Taxes $6.1. Introduction 

In 1935, in a letter to the Nye Committee investigating profiteering during the first World War, Bernard Baruch wrote:

Much as it may be decried, the cold fact remains that ours is an economy motivated by profits. A certain return on money is necessary to make our industrial system work. Much was said at the hearing about this being a new war psychology. Our whole industrial system is a complex massive machine built and geared to run on investment and profit. There is no proof that it will run on psychology and there is much that it will not. Certainly we should not select an hour when the enemy is at the gates to find out whether it will or not. . . . Money will not invest and run the extreme risks of war production for a fraction of 3 percent.' 

While "the problem of war profits is not new," as Mr. Justice Black has said,2 preventing the businessman from building "his greatness upon 

1 Baruch letter of April 12, 1935, to Nye 

Committee, reproduced in S. REP. No. 

944, Pt. 2, 74th Cong., 1st Sess. 11 at Note

Prior to the Present War, 10 Law & CON-

INTRODUCTION 

$ 6.1 his country's ruin" by reaping excessive profits in wartime is very difficult if excessive costs and inefficient production-the ditch on the other side of the road-are to be avoided. In short, how to steer the middle course of reasonable costs and reasonable profits on defense production within the framework of a profit-incentive economy has vexed the nation in every war of its history and continues as a major problem during the present seemingly endless period of "cold war" with its unprecedented high level of defense expenditures necessary to the nation's survival. 

Most every means have been attempted to limit war profits. Price fixing and price controls have failed because of the insuperable difficulties of enforcement and of setting separate prices for high and low cost producers to avoid exorbitant profits to the latter; profits fixed as percentages of cost have failed as they afford every incentive to increase costs; excess-profits taxation, essentially a revenue measure, has failed to accord sufficient incentive to low-cost production; and the necessity for government seizure of a recalcitrant industry perhaps evidences the greatest failure of all—the failure of private enterprise to respond to a national emergency. All of these methods, however, have correctly presupposed the inadequacy of contract pricing alone—whether by bargaining or by competition-to secure defense goods and services at reasonable costs and profits.

In the search for a more effective device to supplement contract pricing in holding contract prices and profits down during World War II, contract renegotiation evolved. As the term itself suggests, contract renegotiation began as an attempt to determine the actual costs and profits on each completed war contract and to recapture that portion of the profits found to be "excessive." From vague standards and rudimentary procedure renegotiation has become a sophisticated and, on the whole, well-administered process of an overall annual review of defense contractors' and subcontractors' renegotiable income for the preceding year to arrive at an informed judgment, through the application of objective criteria, of the extent to which that income reflects excessive profits and to recover such excessive profits. It is the principal concern

It is much to be lamented that each state long ere this has not hunted them down as the pests of society, and the greatest Enemys we have to the happiness of
