$ 6.

of this chapter to show, in a general way, how this process works, how it came about, and how it has evolved to maturity. 

That contract pricing cannot unaided do the job of assuring reasonable prices and hence reasonable profits for defense contracts is aptly illustrated in a study made by the staff of the Joint Committee on Internal 

Revenue Taxation: 

The renegotiation statute in the present law assumes that contract pricing alone, however careful, is not adequate to assure procurement at reasonable profit. There are two reasons for this assumption. 

The first is that the contractor's entire operation, rather than merely the separate contracts, must be examined. A reasonable price for article A may be $100 if this is the only article produced in a plant. 

If, later, a contract is placed for article B in the same plant it may develop that only very little extra labor, materials and management time are required, indicating a possible price for B of $50. Although not all of the plant overhead should be carried by article A, the appropriate allocation may be a very difficult question. The renegotiation process does not attempt to recalculate the price of each contract, of which there may have been hundreds, but seeks to determine whether or not the total receipts and total profits were reasonable for the services performed.

The second reason is that the extreme contingencies involved in continual changes in design call for a look at the whole operation of a contractor, after the contingencies have materialized. With respect to these contingencies renegotiation attempts the very difficult task of evaluating the resulting profit in terms of what the contractor did to make the contingencies come out as they did. High quality performance should justify higher profits than routine performance.4 

To this may be added the importance of renegotiation upon subcontractor pricing and profits which, for the most part, are otherwise beyond effective restraint so far as pricing of government contracts is concerned. 

Renegotiation has operated on a vast scale. During World War II government contracts and related subcontracts aggregating over 220 billion dollars were found to have excessive profits of over 11 billion dollars. Tax credits reduced the Government's net recovery to almost 

5 billion dollars.5 Moreover, during the War, in the face of renegotiation voluntary price refunds and reductions by both prime contractors and subcontractors saved many billions more; and it is probably fair to say that "the greatest contribution of wartime renegotiation lay in the fact that its existence contributed substantially to a desire on the part of contractors to price more closely than they would otherwise have done...." During the same period the administration of renegotiation cost about 41 million dollars. Under the Renegotiation Acts of

RENEGOTIATION IS NOT EXCESS-PROFITS TAXATION 

$6.3 

1948 and 1951 renegotiation recoveries and voluntary refunds through June 1958, after allowance for tax credits, have totalled approximately 539 million dollars on renegotiable sales of almost $200 billion. Given such an impact on the prices and profits of defense contractors and subcontractors, renegotiation has become a major factor in the pricing of defense procurement; and so long as renegotiation is administered promptly and with fairness and competence, one may anticipate its continuation as long as billions of dollars are expended annually for defense procurement.

I. WHAT IS RENEGOTIATION $ 6.2. Definition of Renegotiation 

Renegotiation is a process that embodies three basic steps: (1) the annual review by an independent government agency, the Renegotiation Board, of amounts received or accrued during its fiscal year by a contractor or subcontractor under certain contracts with specified government departments, or under related subcontracts; (2) the determination by the Renegotiation Board of whether profits on the amounts so received or accrued during the fiscal year are "excessive"; and (3) the entry into an agreement between a contractor or subcontractor and the Renegotiation Board for the return to the Government of such excessive profits, or, failing such agreement, the issuance by the Renegotiation Board of an order reflecting its determination of excessive profits. $6.3 

Renegotiation Is Not Excess-Profits Taxation 

Because renegotiation is designed to eliminate excessive profits it is sometimes confused with excess-profits taxes. But renegotiation differs from excess-profits taxes in several respects. In the first place, renegotiation does not apply to all of the income of a government contractor or subcontractor but only to income received under certain specified contracts with the Government or under related subcontracts. Excess-profits taxes, on the other hand, have been applicable, with certain exceptions, to all income of business firms regardless of the source of such income. 

Secondly, excess-profits taxes have treated each recipient of income on an equal basis and have been concerned solely in recapturing from such recipient amounts in excess of a stated fixed-percentage of his income. 

The renegotiation statutes, including the 1951 Act, on the other hand, set forth several factors to be applied in arriving at the amount of excessive profits, if any, the determination of that amount being essentially discretionary. The factors to be considered contemplate the application 

• Hearing Before the House Committee on Ways and Means on Extension of the 

Renegotiation Act, 85th Cong., 2d Sess. 

23 (1958); RENEGOTIATION BOARD SEC- OND ANNUAL REPORT 11 (1957); H.R. 

REP. No. 2549, 84th Cong., 2d Sess. 69 (1956). 285

$6.4

of judgment and seek to reward with a fair and just profit contractors who have dealt directly or indirectly with the Government. 

Finally, and most important, excess-profits taxes have been essentially revenue measures while the purpose of renegotiation is to eliminate excessive profits from contracts and subcontracts as an essential part of the larger process of effecting defense procurement at reasonable prices that is, at reasonable costs and profits." 

Nevertheless, from an individual contractor's point of view, renegotiation appears to be a 100 percent tax on that portion of his defense profits deemed "excessive." 

$ 6.4.

Renegotiation Is Not Price Redetermination 

The first renegotiation statute, enacted in 1942, spoke of renegotiation as the "refixing by the Secretary of the Department of the contract price." 10 This suggests a process very similar to that of price redetermination; and in the early days of renegotiation the two were very similar. 

But as renegotiation evolved during World War II, it became markedly different from price redetermination. Renegotiation essentially is not a matter of contractual agreement. Price redetermination, on the other hand, takes place only when the parties have agreed in advance that there will be a redetermination of the contract price and then only in accordance with the procedure theretofore agreed upon by the parties. 

Furthermore, redetermination provisions in contracts frequently contemplate that the contract prices may be increased or decreased upon redetermination. Renegotiation, on the other hand, is a one-way street in that it eliminates excessive profits on defense business. 

Another important distinction between the two processes is that the standards employed in price redetermination differ from those employed in renegotiation. The object of redetermination is to arrive at a fair and reasonable contract price by negotiations conducted after significant costs of contract performance have been experienced for procurements in which many unpredictable cost factors preclude an agreement on such a price at the outset of the contract. The emphasis in renegotiation is not on setting a fair or reasonable individual contract price midway in the performance of a single contract. On the contrary, the emphasis is on the elimination, in the light of hindsight, of unconscionable or "excessive" profits from a contractor's or subcontractor's total defense business. Redetermination is conducted on an individual contract basis, while renegotiation is generally conducted with respect to each fiscal year of a contractor or subcontractor on an overall renegotiable contract basis. The consequence of the overall approach is that no consideration

Renegotiation Is Not Compulsory Repricing of Individual Con tracts

Renegotiation also bears a superficial resemblance to compulsory repricing of contracts. However, compulsory repricing of individual contracts is quite a different process from either renegotiation or price redetermination. During World War II, Title VIII of the Revenue 

Act of 1943 12 provided that the Secretary of the Navy (or the Secretary of War), whenever he deemed that the price of required supplies or services was "unreasonable or unfair," "by order may fix the price" payable for furnishing such supplies or services. The failure of the contractor or supplier to furnish the article or services at such fair and reasonable prices rendered his plant subject to seizure in accordance with section 9 of the Selective Training and Service Act of 1940.13 Compul sory repricing resembles renegotiation only in that the power of the Government, under the repricing statute, may be exercised unilaterally. In substantially every other respect repricing is more like redetermination.

II. EVOLUTION OF RENEGOTIATION $6.6 Civil War Profiteering and Corruption; Ineffective Control of Profits 

During Spanish-American War

Profiteering has occurred in every war of this nation's history.14 During the Civil War fraud and corruption flourished in military procurement, as did unconscionable profits.15 Much of the procurement was in the hands of commission agents; 16 for example, the Secretary of the 

Navy appointed his brother-in-law agent to purchase ships for the Navy at a 22 percent commission when the going rate in Boston, at least, for ship-purchasing agents of private principals was one percent on purchases over $20,000.17 Congress did nothing to regulate profiteering, but did enact statutes relating to bribery and corruption in government contracting, some of which survive.18

ATTEMPTS TO PREVENT EXCESSIVE PROFITS: WORLD WAR I 

$ 6.7

In 1897, the year before the Spanish-American War, the Congress learned that the Navy had been paying between $574 and $671 per ton for armor for the new battle fleet, the construction of which had begun over a decade earlier. Believing such prices unreasonable, Congress enacted a series of laws limiting the price to $300 a ton,19 raising it to $400 a ton with the outbreak of the war and the refusal of armor manufacturers to sell at this price,20 but then in the following year lowering it again to $300.21 Finally, in 1901, after it had become obvious that armor manufacturers would not sell to the Navy at such prices, Congress abandoned the attempt and authorized the Secretary to purchase armor "at a price which in his judgment is reasonable and equitable." 22 

Such were the congressional efforts, albeit in price-fixing form, to control profits during the Spanish-American War. 

$ 6.7. Attempts To Prevent Excessive Profits During World War I 

When the United States declared war on the Central Powers in 1917, it found itself again unprepared to control either the prices or profits of wartime procurement. As the war progressed three principal devices came into use to control the prices and profits of war goods and services. 

These were cost-plus contracts, price fixing and control, and excess-profits taxes.

Competitive bidding and the lump-sum contract early proved to be not suitable to wartime procurement as labor and material costs skyrocketed with inflation and untried manufacturers turned to war production. 

Those who bid fixed prices included exorbitant contingencies, and other contractors refused fixed-price contracts.23 So the cost-type contract came into use early in the war in an attempt to avoid contingencies and to limit expenditures to actual costs. Initially, it took the form of the cost-plus-a-percentage-of-cost contract, and for a time its use supplanted all other forms of contracting for the larger military purchases.24 

That the cost-plus-a-percentage-of-cost contract achieved little in reducing procurement costs and profits and indeed afforded every incentive to increase costs to increase profits-was well recognized in 1918 by Charles Evans Hughes in his report to the Attorney General on the aircraft industry when he stated "contracts of this sort lead to waste, foster abuses, and impose an almost intolerable burden of cost accounting, in itself a hindrance to rapid production.” 25 To avoid the profit-incentive

Only corporate profits in excess of pre-war income were taxed; and corporations with small pre-war income were assured of at least a 10 percent return.31 

Profits resulting from inflation were not reached by excess-profits taxes, and according to Bernard Baruch this increased inflation.32

 $ 6.9. World War II and the Renegotiation Acts of 1942 and 1943 

With the tremendous expansion of war production following the attack on Pearl Harbor in December 1941,42 the regulation of exorbitant war profits received much congressional scrutiny.43 The advent of a virtually complete sellers' market and the mass production of wholly new and different types of military items foreclosed competitive bidding and militated against the possibility of close pricing in the negotiation of contracts. Further impetus to congressional action to limit profits was given by a Supreme Court decision in February 1942 that refused to invalidate certain World War I government contracts on the alleged ground that the profits made on them were unconscionable, the Court noting that "if the Executive is in need of additional laws by which to protect the nation against war profiteering, the Constitution has given to Congress, not to this Court, the power to make them." 44 

During the early part of 1942 Congress considered various measures to control wartime profits. The Smith-Vinson Bill,45 introduced in 

March 1942, provided that the profits of naval contractors in excess of 6 percent of the total cost of performing the contracts be paid to the Secretary of the Navy. Being essentially an extension of the Vinson- 

Trammell approach, the Navy vigorously opposed it and it died in committee.46 A somewhat similar measure was proposed a month later by Representative Case of South Dakota as an amendment to the Sixth 

Supplemental National Defense Appropriation bill, providing that no part of the appropriation should be available for final payments to war contractors who failed to file cost statements and that war contractors repay all profits in excess of 6 percent.47 This amendment passed the

The Renegotiation Act of 1942 initially applied to contracts of the War and Navy Departments and Maritime Commission.54 Such contracts of more than $100,000 and subcontracts thereunder in excess of $100,000 were required to include a clause providing for "renegotiation" -which the statute defined as "the refixing by the Secretary of the Department of the contract price" 55—of the contract price at a time when the profits can be determined with reasonable certainty and for the repayment or retention of "any amount of the contract price which is found as the result of such renegotiation to represent excessive profits.' 99 56 

The term "excessive profits" was not defined. The statute further "authorized and directed" the Secretary, "whenever in his opinion excessive profits have been realized, or are likely to be realized, from any contract" with his Department "or from any subcontract thereunder" "to require the contractor or subcontractor to renegotiate the contract price" and to recover "excessive profits" paid as determined by such renegotiation, such power to apply to all contracts heretofore or hereafter made whether or not they include a renegotiation clause, other than contracts under which final payment had been made prior to April 28, 1942.57 In addition, broad powers were given the Services to examine contractors' records and to compel cost statements.58 The statute provided for the delegation of the Secretary's powers in accordance with regulations prescribed by the President.59 The statute by its terms was to "remain in force during the continuance of the present war and for three years after the termination of the war." 60 No mention was made of judicial review on behalf of aggrieved contractors or subcontractors. 

It will thus be observed that as finally enacted the concept of "renegotiation" was significantly different from that proposed by the Services. 

In the first place, the statutory concept of renegotiation encompassed the recapture of excessive profits on completed contracts, so long as they had not been completed prior to the date of the act. The Services' proposal would have limited renegotiation to contracts under which final payment had not been made. Secondly, under the statute the definition of renegotiation as "the refixing by the Secretary of the Department of the contract-price" meant that the Government could unilaterally determine excessive profits, whereas under the Services' proposal renegotiation looked to bilateral agreement. Under the statute the inclusion of a renegotiation clause was mandatory for contracts and subcontracts over $100,000; the Services had proposed discretionary use of such a clause.

Lastly, the statute provided that renegotiation might occur at any time until three years after the war, whether or not the affected contracts included a renegotiation clause, while under the Services' proposal any renegotiation had to be conducted during the life of the contract. All this is not to suggest that statutory renegotiation, as it first emerged in April 1942, was essentially concerned with recapture of profits and not with the repricing of uncompleted contracts. Actually, it was concerned with both, although the administration of the law gradually tended to emphasize profit recapture or the "discretionary excess profits tax of 

100%," as some called it.61 

61 "The full significance of the changes that Congress had made in the procurement agencies' proposal soon became ap parent. Up until April, 1942, the renegotiation of contract prices was an integral part of the procurement process.

Whether or not renegotiation was conducted under a so-called 'renegotiation' clause, the objective was the same-the adjustment of the contract price to a figure which would have been regarded as reasonable at the time of the original negotiation, had the facts been available to the parties. Furthermore, such a negotiation was in every instance undertaken during the lifetime of the contract at a time when the incentives of a fixedprice method of contracting could still have sufficient scope within which to operate. It is true that under the 'renegotiation' clause, price adjustments might be retroactive to the beginning of the contract. In almost no case, however, was recapture of profits the primary result, although in some cases payments for units thereafter delivered might be greatly reduced as a result of excessive payments previously made. "Renegotiation as conducted under the statute, on the other hand, took on a different aspect. This was principally due to the fact that renegotiation was applicable to all contracts and subcontracts and could be required after the contract affected had been completed. As generally construed by contractors and their counsel, the statute rendered contractors liable, until three years after the war, to be called upon to refund such part of any profits earned by them on their war contracts or subcontracts as the head of the procuring agency or his delegates might see fit to require, and this liability would continue until any contract subject to renegotiation had been finally dealt with. This situation presented a serious dilemma.

The natural hesitancy of contractors to make contracts which would subject them to a liability undetermined in amount and indefinite in duration threatened to impede the procurement program. Since it was obviously impossible to examine and renegotiate individually the prices of all contracts and subcontracts subject to the statute within any reasonable period, some other means for disposing of this potential liability with reasonable promptness had to be found. "To avoid this impasse, there was developed the method of 'overall' renegotiation. Under this procedure the contractor's profits on its entire war business for a specified fiscal period were examined in order to reach an agreement for eliminating excessive profits on the contracts as a group, and an agreement made covering the period involved. In addition to giving contractors clearance with reasonable promptness, this method had several other important advantages. 

By dealing with all contracts together, cost accounting and the allocation of costs were reduced to a minimum, and time was saved for both contractors and the Government. Furthermore, this method permitted contractors to offset losses on any war contracts against profits from other war contracts during the same period. "By its very nature, however, overall renegotiation tended more and more to ward recapture of past profits rather than refixing of prices for future periods. 

Since it was based on the fiscal year of the contractor it was more convenient to postpone renegotiation until the usual financial statements for the period had 295

$ 6.9

As originally enacted in April 1942, the Renegotiation Act did not, on its face, contain a provision for overall renegotiation of a contractor's renegotiable contracts as a group. However, it was soon recognized that it would be administratively impractical, as well as unfair to contractors in certain instances, to renegotiate contracts and subcontracts on an individual basis. Specific authority for overall renegotiation was granted by the Revenue Act of 1942.62 While this change together with others that clarified the Secretary's power to compel the repayment of excessive profits unilaterally determined,63 tended to emphasize the recapture of past profits rather than refixing prices for future periods, other amendments made by the Revenue Act of 1942 afforded opportunity for a shift of emphasis to prospective pricing as incentives for efficient production and cost control.64 Thus the Secretary concerned was given discretionary power to exempt from renegotiation any contract or subcontract under which "the profits can be established with reasonable certainty when the contract price is established." 65 Another discretionary power was that been prepared. In addition, because of the difficulty of forecasting profits before the end of the fiscal period, contractors preferred to postpone a settlement until their profits were known. For the same reason, government officials, especially in the beginning, hesitated to give a clearance to the contractor for a future period on the basis of predictions. Administered in this way, the law was in effect a tax of 100% on all profits from war business, which the procuring agencies regarded as excessive, and was wholly different from the procedure for revising contract prices after part performance, which had inspired the statutory scheme. 

In fact, when contracting officers desired to provide for such individual price revision, they asked permission to use the old form of contract renegotiation clause, in addition to the statutory provision.

Thus, many contracts now exhibit the paradox of two renegotiation clauses substantially similar in wording, but wholly different in their practical operation. 

This curious practice illustrates dramatically the extent to which statutory renegotiation on an overall basis had departed from the actual adjustment of contract prices, and indicates that renegotiation under Section 403 as practiced during the early months of its operation, was merely a discretionary excess profits tax of 100%." Other changes to the Renegotiation Act of 1942 made by the Revenue Act of 1942 may be briefly noted. Contracts of the Treasury Department were made subject to renegotiation.69 The term "excessive profits" was "defined" as "any amount of a contract or subcontract price which is found as a result of renegotiation to represent excessive profits." 70 

The term "subcontract" was defined to mean "any purchase order or agreement to perform all or any part of the work, or to make or furnish any article required for the performance of another contract or subcontract."" Constitutionality of Wartime Renegotiation: Lichter v. United States 

In Lichter v. United States,82 decided on June 14, 1948, the Supreme

Court upheld the constitutionality of the 1942 and 1943 Acts in all important respects both as to contracts entered into prior to the effective dates of the acts as well as subsequently thereto. The constitutional justification for renegotiation was found in Article I, Section 8, of the Constitution which gives Congress the power "To raise and support 

Armies, ...; to provide and maintain a Navy; . . . And To make all

Laws which shall be necessary and proper for carrying into Execution the foregoing Powers. . . ." If Congress could conscript men then, a fortiori, the Court reasoned, it could conscript property.83 That the Renegotia-

All these cases had commenced as suits by the Government to recover excessive profits on certain subcontracts under which final payment had not been made as of April 28, 1942, the date of enactment of the Renegotiation Act of 1942. All the defendants were the subcontractors involved, and none of the subcontracts in question contained renegotiation clauses. Moreover, none of the subcontractors had availed themselves of the remedy of a de novo proceeding in the Tax Court afforded by the 1943 Act and made retroactive to the 1942 Act. $6.10

tion Acts of 1942 and 1943 were "necessary and proper" to the power of Congress to raise and support armies and to provide and maintain a Navy was evidenced by the fact that an unprecedented productive effort was required of industry and by the necessity that such productive effort be secured without subjecting the Government to exorbitant costs.84 

Congress might, if it chose, have mobilized all industry on a totalitarian basis. This plan Congress rejected in favor of renegotiation which, the Court stated, "appears in its true light as the very symbol of a free people united in reaching unequalled productive capacity and yet retaining the maximum of undivided freedom consistent with a general mobilization of effort." 85 Since experience showed that contracts at fixed initial prices provided the best incentive to production, and since accurate advance estimates of cost were frequently impossible, renegotiation was an eminently satisfactory solution of the problem of excessive profits confronting Congress. Cost-plus-fixed-fee contracts, escalator clauses in contracts, and excess-profits taxes, could only partially solve the problem.

Those contesting the constitutionality of the Renegotiation Acts argued, however, that even assuming Congress' authority to eliminate excessive profits from war contracts, Congress could delegate such authority to the Secretaries of the Departments or to an independent administrative agency such as the War Contracts Price Adjustment Board only if it adequately defined the applicable legislative policy and standards. The 

Court disposed of this contention by pointing out that it was always difficult to define precisely the nature of the standards which Congress must specify in granting administrative authority and that, in time of crisis, the Constitution could not be construed to hinder rather than help the people in defending their national security. In any event, the standards contained in the 1943 Act were held to be sufficiently precise since renegotiation had been conducted in accordance with the same standards administratively for some time prior to the enactment of the 1943 Act in February 1944. Congress, therefore, had knowledge of these standards at the time it enacted the 1943 Act and was presumably satisfied that they carried out Congress' intention. The 1942 Act which defined “excessive profits" as "any amount of a contract or subcontract price which is found as a result of renegotiation to represent excessive profits" obviously contained somewhat less definite standards. The Court was satisfied, however, that when the term "excessive profits" was read in the light of the conditions to which it was applied, it was sufficiently mean- 

84 Id. at 757-65. 

85 Id. at 766. 300

CONSTITUTIONALITY OF WARTIME RENEGOTIATION 

$ 6.10 ingful to provide adequate guides to the renegotiation agencies in the elimination of excessive profits.86

The final argument made against the constitutionality of the Renegotiation Acts was that "due process" was not accorded contractors under the rather informal renegotiation procedure which has been heretofore described. Any defects in this respect that may have existed in the 1942 

Act, as originally drafted, were corrected by the 1943 Act which provided for a hearing de novo before the Tax Court of the United States to all contractors who were aggrieved by determinations of excessive profits made under the 1942 Act, as well as under the 1943 Act. The aforementioned de novo hearing afforded an aggrieved contractor all the elements of "due process" accorded a taxpayer who has been aggrieved by a decision of the Commissioner of Internal Revenue, including the right to cross-examine witnesses and the making of a record. It is elementary that the demands of due process do not require a hearing at the initial stage or at any particular point in an administrative proceeding, so long as the requisite hearing is held before the final order becomes effective.87 

At the time of this writing there has been no constitutional test of the 1948 or 1951 Renegotiation Acts. It is probable that renegotiation of most contracts would be upheld as against constitutional objections since the Supreme Court is not likely to be persuaded that its reasoning in the Lichter case was not applicable to periods when this country is engaged in a "cold war." 88 Furthermore, most prime contracts and many subcontracts have contained the requisite renegotiation article, and there would thus be a contractual as well as a statutory basis for enforcing the Government's right to renegotiate them.89

United States, 276 U.S. 394, 409. Standards prescribed by Congress are to be read in the light of the conditions to which they are to be applied. "They derive much meaningful content from the purpose of the Act, its factual background and the statutory context in which they appear.' Ameri can Power & Light Co. v. S.E.C., 329

 $6.11. The Renegotiation Act of 1948 

World War II renegotiation terminated with respect to profits attributable to contract performance subsequent to December 31, 1945. This coupled with repeal of the excess-profits tax the same day left the Vinson- Trammell Act, limited as that was to contracts for ships and aircraft, as the only statutory control of excessive profits for post-war procurement."1

But victory in World War II did not secure peace, and a new era of cold war began. By 1948, defense procurement had resumed on a large scale, and on May 21st of that year, Congress, in connection with the authorization of a 70-group air force, enacted the Renegotiation Act of 1948.92 In all essential respects, the 1948 Act adopted procedures previously employed under the 1942 and 1943 Acts. The 1948 Act, however, was applicable only to contracts and subcontracts in excess of $1,000 that obligated appropriations or were entered into under contract authori zations made by the Supplemental National Defense Appropriation Act, 1948 93-primarily contracts for the procurement of aircraft and related facilities and equipment. 

About a month later, Congress authorized the Secretary of Defense to extend the Renegotiation Act of 1948 to any contract of the military departments "for the procurement of ships, aircraft, aircraft parts, and the construction of facilities or installations outside the continental United States" "which obligates any funds made available for obligation in the fiscal year 1949." 94 On June 30, 1948, the Secretary of Defense directed the inclusion of a clause incorporating the Renegotiation Act of 

1948 in all Navy and Air Force contracts for aircraft and aircraft parts.95

Subsequent appropriation acts made the Renegotiation Act of 1948 applicable to all negotiated Department of Defense contracts in excess of $1,000 entered into during the fiscal years 1950 % and 1951.97 

Under the 1948 Act the question arose as to whether aircraft contractors were intended to be subject to both renegotiation and the profit limitation provisions of the Vinson-Trammell Act. To an extent, Congress clarified this in 1949 by providing that the Vinson-Trammell Act "shall not apply to any contract or subcontract which is subject to the Renego-

$6.12. The Renegotiation Act of 1951 

The outbreak of the Korean War in June 1950 signalled a revival of defense procurement that approached the magnitude of World War II procurement. In September of that year wage and price controls and materials priorities and allocations were authorized by the Defense Production Act of 1950. Three months later the President declared a national emergency; 2 and in January 1951 an excess-profits tax was enacted. With renegotiation under existing law applicable only to negotiated contracts made prior to July 1, 1951, Congress on March 23, 1951, enacted the Renegotiation Act of 1951.4 Applicable, at first, to receipts and accruals attributable to contract performance between January 1, 1951 and December 31, 1953, the law has been extended four times, and it currently applies to contract performance prior to July 1, 1959. Again, the profit limitation provisions of the Vinson-Trammell Act and the Merchant Marine Act of 1936 have been suspended for the duration of renegotiation. The scope of the 1951 Act, its coverage and relationship to and departure from earlier renegotiation statutes, and the administrative procedure of renegotiation are the subject matter of the remaining sections of this chapter.

III. ADMINISTRATION OF RENEGOTIATION 

$6.14. The Renegotiation Board and Its Predecessors 

Prior to 1951, renegotiation was administered by boards established in the government departments whose contracts were subject to renegotiation. Under the 1942 Act, the War and Navy Departments each established a Price Adjustment Board to administer renegotiation; " however, the 1943 Act replaced these separate boards with an overall War Contracts Price Adjustment Board.12 This Board was composed of members appointed by the various government agencies whose contracts were subject to renegotiation, and usually the members of the wartime Board were also the heads of their departmental renegotiation boards.

THE RENEGOTIATION BOARD AND ITS PREDECESSORS 

$ 6.14 

The Renegotiation Act of 1948 placed all power of administration in the Secretary of Defense, with power of delegation. To a Military Re negotiation Policy and Review Board authority was given to make regu lations after approval by the Secretary of Defense, to exempt contracts from renegotiation by classes or types, to audit the books and records of contractors and subcontractors subject to the act, and to review determinations made by subordinate boards established in each military department.13 To these subordinate boards-jointly known as the Armed Services Renegotiation Board and made up of a separate division for each Department-power was given to conduct renegotiation and to make determinations of excessive profits, subject to review by the Military 

Renegotiation Policy and Review Board.14 Authority to exempt con tracts on an individual basis was delegated to the Secretaries of the Military departments.15 Thus under the 1948 Act the administration of renegotiation closely paralleled its World War II counterpart: there was a so-called top board that made policies and reviewed the actions of the lower boards; the latter, in turn, conducted the bulk of the day-to-day operations of renegotiation. 

We have seen that the Renegotiation Act of 1943 divorced renegotiation from the repricing of contracts and made it into the recapture of excessive profits on completed contracts.16 But even with this separation, renegotiation was for the most part administered by the contracting departments and to an extent was part of the procurement process in that cost statements submitted by contractors for renegotiation purposes were ordinarily available to contracting officers as an aid to pricing new contracts and repricing contracts already made. The Renegotiation Act of 

1951 effected a complete separation of the renegotiation from the procurement process. For by that act a Renegotiation Board was created "as an independent establishment in the executive branch of the Government," to consist of five members appointed by the President, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate." The role of the military departments in the selection of the members of the Board is one of making recommendations to the President.18 Like other officials of the Executive

Branch, the members of the Board have no fixed term of office; they serve at the President's pleasure.

The separation of renegotiation from procurement by the 1951 Act was further emphasized by the limitations on the Renegotiation Board's powers to delegate certain of its functions to procurement officials of the military departments." But this separation does not preclude access

$6.15. The Board's Power To Delegate Certain of Its Functions 

Under the Renegotiation Act of 1943, the War Contracts Price Adjustment Board had an unlimited power of delegation of its functions and duties to the Secretaries of War and the Navy with full powers of redelegation within their departments.21 A comparable power of delegation was given to the Secretary of Defense under the Renegotiation Act of 1948. But under the 1951 Act, to maintain a buffer between procurement and renegotiation, the Renegotiation Board may not delegate or authorize the redelegation of any of its functions to any person (other than the Secretary of a Department) "engaged on behalf of any Department in the making of contracts for the procurement of supplies or services, or in the supervision of such activity." 22 Subject to this limitation and to others prohibiting the delegation of the rule-making power and of the power to grant permissive exemptions, the Renegotiation Board is authorized to delegate its functions to any agency of the Government.23 $ 6.16.

Renegotiation Proceedings

The procedure for renegotiation contemplated by the 1951 Act is substantially similar to that provided for in previous renegotiation statutes and the regulations promulgated thereunder. 

The first step looking toward the renegotiation proceeding proper is taken by the contractor, who is required to file a financial statement with the Board within five months after the close of any fiscal year in which he has renegotiable contracts or subcontracts.32 The Board must formally commence the renegotiation proceeding by the sending of a notice by registered mail to that effect within a year after the contractor has filed his statement.33 This is accomplished by the Regional Board to which the case has been assigned. 

Meetings are thereafter held with the contractor, in the course of which information concerning his operations is elicited and during which the contractor is given an opportunity to demonstrate why he has not realized excessive profits, or, if he concedes that he has realized some, the extent, in his opinion, to which he has done so. These meetings are not hearings in the sense that a record is made or that rules of evidence and of procedure commonly followed in judicial and quasi-judicial pro-

If it is determined that excessive profits have been realized and the contractor is agreeable to the determination, he is requested to enter into an agreement whereby he agrees to refund to the Government the amount of excessive profits so determined, less the tax credit to which he is entitled under the provisions of section 1481 of the Internal Revenue Code of 1954. If the contractor is not in agreement with the determination, he has the right to appeal to the Renegotiation Board, which reviews the case and makes its own determination, or advises the contractor that it has decided not to review the case. In the event that either the Regional Board or the 

Board itself makes a determination to which the contractor will not assent, an order embodying such determination is issued.35

IV. RENEGOTIATION UNDER THE RENEGOTIATION ACT OF 1951 A. CONTRACTS SUBJECT TO RENEGOTIATION $6.20. Renegotiation Clause Included in Certain Contracts; Effect of In clusion or Omission of Clause

As with its predecessors, the Renegotiation Act of 1951 directs the insertion in contracts and subcontracts subject to renegotiation of a clause by which the contractor or subcontractor, as the case may be, agrees to (i) the elimination of excessive profits through renegotiation, (ii) the withholding or repayment of excessive profits, (iii) the relief of contractors of liability to subcontractors for amounts due the subcontractor withheld by the Government on account of the subcontractor's renegotiation indebtedness, and (iv) the insertion of comparable provisions in lower-tier subcontracts.38 Insertion of the clause is not required in the case of contracts or subcontracts covered by a mandatory exemption under section 106(a) of the act,39 and the Renegotiation Board has directed that the clause be omitted from contracts and subcontracts covered by permissive exemptions from renegotiation.40 But the insertion of such a clause does not bind a contractor or subcontractor to renegotiation if the contract or subcontract is not otherwise subject to it. The act itself is explicit on this point.41 Conversely, if the transaction is subject to renegotiation, the omission of the required clause likewise does not affect the outcome.42 Accordingly, the Renegotiation Board must determine for itself in each renegotiation proceeding whether a given contract dicial review than could be had under the 1943 Act. Interestingly enough, the 

1951 Act returns essentially to the 1943 Act scheme of finality of Tax Court excessive profit determinations. Whether this reversal will lead the courts to accord wider scope to the finality provisions concerning Tax Court renegotiation orders under the 1951 Act than was done under the 1943 Act remains to be seen.

As under the 1943 Act, renegotiation ordinarily relates to the aggregate receipts and accruals during a contractor's fiscal year attributable to his renegotiable contracts and subcontracts; 50 but if that aggregate does not exceed the applicable statutory minimum amount subject to renegotiation, to that extent there may be no renegotiation of amounts received or accrued during that fiscal year.51 For example, under the present statutory floor of $1,000,000, a 2.5 million dollar contract for military items may contemplate installment deliveries over a thirtymonth period, thus covering three fiscal years of the contractor. If the contractor's receipts and acruals under that contract during each of those years are less than $1,000,000, and there are no other receipts or accruals for each of those years attributable to renegotiable contracts or subcontracts performed by him, the amounts received under that contract would not be subject to renegotiation notwithstanding that the contract price exceeded $1,000,000.

One or two examples may indicate the broad scope of renegotiation at the subcontract level: A sells steel to B which B incorporates in a battery it sells to C who includes the battery in an engine it sells to D who in turn sells an airplane with that engine to the Navy. Each of these transactions is subject to renegotiation, and it is immaterial whether or not they antedate the related government contract or the subcontractor had knowledge of the government contract. Such a literal application of the act is, of course, impossible and could not be expected; however, it serves to depict the amorphous bog of uncertainty encountered when you try to determine whether this sale or that sale might be renegotiable." 62 Perhaps it is not surprising that business firms often have not regarded their transactions as government subcontracts and occasionally have contested the renegotiation of them on the ground that they only remotely related to renegotiable government contracts.63 $ 6.23. Brokers and Manufacturers' Agents 

The third class of subcontracts to which the Renegotiation Act of 1951 applies are contracts by renegotiable prime contractors or subcontractors with brokers or manufacturers' agents under which the amounts payable to the broker or agent are contingent upon the procurement of a renegotiable prime or subcontract or are determined by reference to the amount of such renegotiable prime or subcontracts, or under which any "part of the services performed or to be performed consists of the soliciting, attempting to procure, or procuring" a renegotiable contract or subcontract.70 Contracts found by the Board to involve the employeremployee relationship are excepted," but contracts with "bona fide established commercial or selling agencies maintained by the contractor for the purpose of securing business" are subject to renegotiation.72 Thus by reaching the solicitation of subcontracts and by discarding the exception for established agencies maintained by a contractor to obtain business, it will be observed that the Renegotiation Act of 1951 goes considerably further toward imposing government regulation of contingent fees incident to government procurement 73 than do the procurement statutes and regulations by themselves.74 But renegotiation of these contingent-fee contracts is subject to a $25,000 floor,75 and in some cases they may be exempted altogether from renegotiation because of receipts or accruals from exempt prime or subcontracts.76

In the face of complaints by industry and the unworkable burden on the Board, Congress in 1956 substantially modified the exemption and the procedure for claiming it. While the stock test was retained for standard commercial articles, the alternative commercial-use test was replaced by a "catalog test" under which an article qualified if sold "in accordance with a price schedule regularly maintained by the contractor or subcontractor." For articles "identical in every material respect with a standard commercial article" the commercial-use test gave way to the test of "a price which is reasonably comparable with the price of such standard commercial article" sold by the party claiming exemption." at pp. 4 and 5: "The operation of the above stock or catalog tests may be illustrated by the following example: Assume that a company manufactures and stocks or catalogs typewriters of various models which it sells under renegotiable contracts as well as to other purchasers. 

If at least 35 percent of the aggregate dollar amount of sales of a particular model in the fiscal year under review and the immediately preceding fiscal year is made on nonrenegotiable orders, such item will qualify under the stock or catalog test, and the sales of typewriters of that model under renegotiable contracts during the year under review are excluded from renegotiable sales without the necessity of filing an application for exemption and obtaining the approval of the Board. "In the case of similar articles that differ only by a measurable characteristic, it is still possible under the substantial identity test that all such articles will be exempt as standard commercial articles if only one of them is a standard commercial article. 

Thus, if a contractor sells 50 percent of his output of 3-inch pipe and 50 percent of his output of 1-inch pipe under nonrenegotiable contracts, he may be able to obtain the standard commercial article exemption for his output of 2-inch pipe which may be sold exclusively under renegotiable contracts. 

It will be necessary, however, to file an application with the Board and establish that the 2-inch pipe is of the same kind and content as the other pipe sizes; that the price of the 2-inch pipe is reasonably comparable with the other prices; and that 35 percent of the combined sales of the three categories of pipe are nonrenegotiable. "In some cases the above changes in present law will tighten the standard commercial article exemption. For example: Assume a contractor's total sales in a given fiscal year and the preceding fiscal year of an article which is stocked are $10 million of which 3,400,000 is sold under nonrenegotiable contracts. Under present law he could obtain an exemption if the Board made a finding that 'the competitive conditions are such as will reasonably prevent excessive profits.' 

Under the bill the article would not qualify under either the stock or catalog tests because the contractor did not sell 35 percent to purchasers other than under renegotiable contracts. He may qualify nevertheless by filing an application with the Board if the article is substantially identical with another article which he manufactures 318

Contracts That Do Not Have a Direct and Immediate Connec tion With the National Defense 

The Renegotiation Act of 1951 exempts "any contract which the Board determines does not have a direct and immediate connection with the national defense," the Board's determination in this respect to be final and conclusive and not reviewable by the Tax Court or any other agency or court. This exemption appears for the first time with the 1951 Act; it had no counterpart in the 1943 Act. While provision is made for the exemption of individual contracts and subcontracts by application to the Board through the government procurement agency concerned, the exemption in the main has been applied through the designation of classes and types of contracts the Board has determined not to have a direct and immediate connection with the national defense. Some sixteen such class determinations have been made, covering such procurements as building maintenance and repair contracts, maintenance dredging contracts, contracts for items purchased for resale to government personnel and their dependents, contracts for laundry and garbage disposal services, and contracts for materials or services used in the manufacture of synthetic rubber for sale to private persons for nondefense uses. In addition, certain contracts of particular government agencies have been brought under this exemption;10 and recognition is given to the possibility of exempting emergency procurements made in consequence of and which does qualify as a standard commercial article if by combining the total sales of both articles in the year under review he can show that of this total at least 35 percent represents sales that are not covered by renegotiable contracts. If he did not manufacture another article qualified as a standard commercial article then he could under no circumstances obtain an exemption for his renegotiable sales of the article, although he might obtain the exemption under present law."

Contracts With Other Governmental Agencies 

The Renegotiation Act of 1951 exempts "any contract by a Department with any Territory, possession, or State, or any agency or political subdivision thereof, or with any foreign government or agency thereof." 15 

Under the 1943 Act the exemption covered the foregoing and contracts with "any other department, bureau, agency, or governmental corporation of the United States" as well." But it is difficult to conceive of the federal government subjecting its own internal transactions to renegotiation, and so that much of the 1943 Act exemption was eliminated." 

The Renegotiation Board Regulations interpret "political subdivision” of a state to include municipal corporations, "whether acting in a proprietary or governmental capacity." $6.29.

Agricultural commodities covered include commodities resulting from soil cultivation, tree saps, gums and resins, animals and fish, and the produce of live animals such as wool, eggs, milk, and cream.20 To meet the statutory test of exemption, the agricultural commodity must be sold, under the contract or subcontract in question, "in its raw or natural state, or if the commodity is not customarily sold or has not an established market in its raw or natural state, in the first form or state, beyond the raw or natural state, in which it is customarily sold or in which it has an established market." 21 The raw materials exemption goes one stage beyond the "established market" test for agricultural commodities and covers "any contract for the product of a mine, oil or gas well, or other mineral or natural deposit, or timber, which has not been processed, refined, or treated beyond the first form or state suitable for industrial use." 22 Thus, for example, cotton in its baled and ginned form would qualify for exemption as an agricultural commodity "in the first form or state, beyond the raw or natural state, in which it is customarily sold or in which it has an established market," while cloth made from such baled cotton would not; on the other hand, both iron ore and pig iron-the latter one step beyond iron ore—would qualify under the raw materials exemption since pig iron is not "beyond the first form or state suitable for industrial use." 23

Contracts and Subcontracts With Tax-Exempt Organizations 

The 1943 Act exempted from renegotiation "any contract or subcontract with an organization exempt from taxation under section 101 (b) of the Internal Revenue Code." 34 The 1951 Act continues this exemption with the important difference that the exemption does not apply to the extent that receipts and accruals of tax-exempt charitable institutions are taxable as "unrelated business taxable income" under section 511 of the Internal Revenue Code of 1954.35 Thus if an educational institution performs defense work which is not substantially related to the educational purposes of the institution, the receipts and accruals attributable to that defense work will be subject to renegotiation in the event they are subject to federal income taxation.

SUBCONTRACTS UNDER EXEMPT CONTRACTS AND SUBCONTRACTS § 6.33. Subcontracts Under Exempt Contracts and Subcontracts 

The Renegotiation Act of 1943 exempted from renegotiation "any subcontract, directly or indirectly under a contract or subcontract" covered by a mandatory exemption.43 This residual exemption for subcontracts was continued by the 1951 Act.44 With the addition of the standardcommercial article exemption in 1954,45 the residual subcontract exemption was amended to exclude subcontracts "directly or indirectly under" exempted contracts or subcontracts for standard commercial articles to avoid exempting all subcontracts under exempt contracts for such articles, thus frustrating the legislative purpose to deny the exemption if the Board found that competitive conditions were inadequate to prevent excessive profits.4% In 1956 the residual subcontract exemption was further limited and made inapplicable to subcontracts made after June 30, 1956, "directly or indirectly" under exempt contracts with other governmental agencies or under contracts or subcontracts with tax-exempt organizations, thus closing inadvertent loopholes that had afforded undue advantage to commercial enterprises supplying materials or services to tax-exempt institutions.49 47

 § 6.34. Partial Mandatory Exemption of Contracts and Subcontracts for New Durable Productive Equipment 

The 1951 Act for the first time accorded a partial exemption from renegotiation of sales of new machinery, tools and other production equipment with an average useful life of over five years to contractors and subcontractors for use in the performance of renegotiable contracts and subcontracts.51 The objective was to subject to renegotiation only that portion of those sales that corresponded to the period of time the machinery would be used on defense work and to exempt from renegotiation the remainder of the sales receipts allocable to the use of the machinery on ordinary commercial production. The 1943 Act did not explicitly deal with this matter, and the regulations under that act allocated receipts from such sales on the basis of the use of the machinery as between renegotiable and nonrenegotiable production.52 Under the 1948 

Act's broad permissive exemption authority such sales were made substantially exempt from renegotiation.53

The 1951 Act proceeds upon the assumption that for the first five years of its service life, a production machine originally acquired for defense production will be devoted entirely to that purpose and that for the remainder of its life it will be used for ordinary commercial work."4 

Accordingly, the 1951 Act makes subject to renegotiation that portion of the sales price of the machine attributable to an arbitrarily fixed five-year period of its use for defense production.55 The renegotiable amount is the product of the sales price multiplied by the ratio between five years and the average useful life of the machine.56 For example, if a machine has a useful life of fifteen years, one-third of the proceeds from its sale will be subject to renegotiation and two-thirds exempt. The average useful life of the machine is determined according to Bulletin F of the Bureau of Internal Revenue (1942 Edition), or it is estimated by the Renegotiation Board in cases not covered by Bulletin F.57 

The exemption originally excluded sales of production equipment to the Government,58 but in the face of substantial government stockpiling 

51 Section 106(c), 65 Stat. 18, 50

U.S.C. Subcontracts as to Which It Is Not Administratively Feasible To Segregate Profits 

The 1951 Act continues the permissive exemption in the 1943 Act for "any subcontract or group of subcontracts not otherwise exempt from the provisions of this section, if in the opinion of the Board, it is not administratively feasible in the case of such subcontract or in the case of such group of subcontracts to determine and segregate the profits attributable to activities not subject to renegotiation." 95 Under the 1943 

Act, this exemption was applied primarily to subcontracts "directly or indirectly" under exempt construction contracts % and to subcontracts with public utilities. By contrast, under the 1951 Act this permissive exemption has been applied only to materials purchased by subcontractors for stock-known as the "stock-item" exemption." This stock-item exemption will be briefly considered in the next section. $6.41.

Stock-Item Exemption 

The 1951 Act did not, as has been pointed out in section 6.26 above, until 1954 provide for the specific exemption of standard commercial articles in contrast to the provision of the 1943 Act for the permissive exemption of such articles. On the other hand, to attempt, particularly at the multi-tier subcontract level, the segregation of profits attributable to renegotiable and nonrenegotiable sales of standard commercial articles would have proved to be a vast and fruitless undertaking. Accordingly, and following a precedent established under the 1948 Act," the Renegotiation Board has exempted "all subcontracts subject to the act which are for materials (including maintenance, repair and operating supplies) customarily purchased for stock in the normal course of the purchaser's business, except when such materials are specially purchased for use in performing one or more prime contracts or higher tier subcontracts subject to the act." 1 Articles are considered to be "specially purchased" and hence not within the "stock-item" exemption if (i) the specifications of the article are adapted to renegotiable business only; (ii) the article was earmarked for the performance of renegotiable contracts or subcontracts; (iii) the purchaser of the article represented to the supplier that the article was required to perform renegotiable contracts

There is obviously overlapping between the present mandatory exemption for standard commercial articles and the stock-item exemption so far as subcontractors are concerned. Perhaps the fundamental distinction between them is that the availability of the stock-item exemption depends upon the behavior of the subcontractor's purchaser, factors that are largely beyond the subcontractor-seller's control; on the other hand, a subcontractor's claim to the standard commercial article exemption turns primarily on whether or not at least 35 percent of his annual sales of the article are nonrenegotiable. It is apparent that both exemptions apply equally to many cases, and to an extent sales of articles not meeting the 35 percent nonrenegotiable test will come under the stock-item exemption. 

$ 6.42. - Subcontracts Related to Exempt Contracts and Subcontracts 

Paralleling the mandatory exemption for subcontracts under mandatorily exempt contracts and subcontracts, the Renegotiation Board has exempted "all subcontracts related to" contracts and subcontracts covered by permissive exemptions,5 except (i) those related to exempt contracts and subcontracts to be performed abroad and (ii) "when the Board, in exempting prime contracts or subcontracts, determines that the exemption will not extend to some or all of the subcontracts related to such prime contracts or subcontracts." 6

For most subcontractors, especially lower-tier subcontractors, segregating receipts and accruals as between renegotiable and nonrenegotiable sales to arrive at the aggregate of renegotiable receipts or accruals may prove very difficult. While placing this burden upon the subcontractor concerned," the regulations do not require subcontractors to inquire of their customers of the end uses to which their products or services have been put in the case of customers whose purchases from the subcontrac tor aggregated less than $2,500 for the fiscal year or of customers whose business "is such that it would be unreasonable to expect them to be engaged in supplying materials to the Department directly or under subcontracts." 17

Where the aggregate of the renegotiable receipts or accruals exceeds the applicable statutory floor, all of such receipts or accruals, and not just the amount in excess of the statutory floor, are subject to renegotiation. However, the amount of excessive profits that may be determined by renegotiation may not be greater than the excess of the aggregate renegotiable receipts or accruals over the applicable statutory floor.19 

§ 6.44. Costs Allocable to and Allowable Against Renegotiable Business 

Whether or not a contractor or subcontractor has excessive profits on his renegotiable business for a given fiscal year requires first that the costs of performing renegotiable contracts and subcontracts be segregated from other costs paid or incurred in that year. The 1951 Act defines profits on renegotiable contracts and subcontracts as the "excess of the amount received or accrued under such contracts and subcontracts over the costs paid or incurred with respect thereto and determined to be allocable thereto." 20 The test of allowability of costs of renegotiable business is, 16 RBR §§ 1456.2, 1456.3 (Oct. 17, 1956). 

The Renegotiation Board's regulations suggest various tests for subcontractors to employ in ascertaining their renegotiable receipts and accruals. One is a sales-ratio test by which the subcontractor applies to his sales to a particular customer the ratio of that customer's renegotiable sales of the end product embodying or utilizing the subcontractor's product or service to the customer's total sales of such product. If the subcontractor has numerous customers in the same industry for a single product, a representative sampling of such customers is suggested to arrive at the renegotiable sales ratio. Other tests suggested are whether the subcontract contains a renegotiation clause or indicates a defense priority rating or shipment to a military activity or performance to military specifications, although admittedly none of these indicia is controlling. The regulations also permit other methods for subcontractors to segregate renegotiable from nonrenegotiable receipts so long as the Board is satisfied that the method selected "affords the best basis for reasonably precise determination." $ 6.44 ." 22 generally speaking, whether the item claimed is allowable as an exclusion or deduction for income tax purposes under Chapter 1 of the Internal Revenue Code of 1954.21 Costs are allocated to renegotiable business in accordance with "the contractor's established cost accounting method if that method reflects recognized accounting principles and practices;" but if the contractor's method of cost accounting does not properly allocate costs between renegotiable and nonrenegotiable business, the Board may impose a particular method subject to review by the Tax Court.23 

Ordinarily the method of accounting employed by the contractor or subcontractor in treating income and costs during a given fiscal year for income tax purposes is to be followed for renegotiation purposes for that same year, and the regulations permit the use of other accounting methods only under limited circumstances.24 

In deciding whether costs allocable to renegotiable business would be allowable as an income-tax deduction or exclusion, the Board gives "due consideration" to published rulings of the Bureau of Internal Revenue, but deductions or exclusions allowed or disallowed by revenue agents are "not regarded as conclusive." 25 Similarly, the regulations are explicit that the allowance or disallowance of costs under the provisions of government cost-type contracts or under procurement regulations "are not controlling with respect to recognition of such costs for renegotiation purposes if such cost is a proper Federal income tax deduction." 26

While interest on borrowed capital will only be allowed to the extent permitted as an income tax deduction, allocation of this expense may be denied if the contractor or subcontractor's current funds or marketable securities are "obviously in excess of the reasonable working capital needs of its business" or if the contractor or subcontractor has "a significant amount of assets not directly related to" its renegotiable business.34

Renegotiation and Taxes
