$7.24. Ship-Repair Contracts $7.25. Civil Construction Contracts $7.26. Architectural and Engineering Services Contracts $7.27. Utility Contracts $7.1. Introduction 

The enormous scale, complexity and novelty of Navy procurement during and since World War II greatly stimulated the development of new types of contracts having greater flexibility than the standard fixed-price contract but without the vice of the cost-plus-a-percentage-of-cost contract. The success of that effort is indicated in some measure by the variety of contracts described in this chapter. Yet it would be easy, by thinking too much in terms of the number of new types of contracts developed, to 

*Prepared by Albert H. Stein, Deputy General Counsel, Department of the Navy. 

345

$ 7.

exaggerate the success achieved. The truth is that the perfect type of government procurement contract has not yet been drafted. Each of the types discussed in this chapter has its own weakness, and the more clearly this is recognized, the less is the danger. It can be stated with assurance, however, that real progress has been made during and since the war years in the development of types of contracts which more nearly meet the needs of naval procurement. However, for the most part, flexibility in fashioning types of government procurement contracts is limited to situations where the procurement is not required by law to be entered into by means of formal advertising.

While the availability of more suitable types of contracts greatly enhances the possibility of negotiating a successful contract, ultimate success depends more upon the skill with which the contract is negotiated than upon the particular type of contract employed. For this reason, it is deceptive to think of new types of contracts, however ingenious, as assuring good contracts. New types of contracts represent only more suitable forms with which the negotiator may work; they are not a substitute for good negotiation. The successful negotiation of contracts also is dependent upon the closest cooperation between counsel and negotiator: first, to develop and draft good types of contracts; second, to select the right type of contract for a specific procurement; and third, to make the best use of the type of contract selected.

The term "type of contract" is commonly used with several different connotations. It is used in one sense to distinguish significantly different compensation arrangements. In this sense fixed-price contracts, cost-plusfixed-fee contracts, and time and material contracts are examples of different types of contracts. In another sense the term "type of contract" is used, irrespective of the compensation arrangement, to indicate differences in the form and structure of the contract. In this sense letters of intent to contract, purchase orders, and open-end contracts represent different types of contracts. Finally, the term "type of contract" is used to indicate the end purpose for which the contract is intended, regardless of the compensation arrangement or the form and structure of the contract. In this sense research contracts, supply contracts, construction contracts, and ship repair contracts constitute different types of contracts. 

While it is convenient to think and write of types of contracts in the several senses described above, it must be emphasized that these are not mutually exclusive categories and that every contract represents the synthesis of form, compensation arrangement and end purpose (e.g., an openend contract for ship repair on a fixed-price basis, or a letter of intent for construction of an ammunition depot on a cost-plus-fixed-fee basis). It is impossible in the amount of space allotted for this purpose to describe all of the types of contracts used by the Navy or to describe any single type of contract in a really comprehensive manner. Certainly no such attempt 346

FIRM FIXED-PRICE CONTRACTS 

$ 7.3 is made in this chapter. Here is simply a brief summary of some of the more common types of contracts—the possible combinations and variations of which may truly be said to be limited only by the imagination and by express statutory limitations.'

I. COMPENSATION ARRANGEMENTS 

$7.2. In General

Prior to 1940 there was little variety of compensation arrangements in Navy contracts. Procurement was normally accomplished by competitive processes. The Navy paid on a fixed-price basis for what it bought. The tremendous increase both in the magnitude and in the complexity of naval procurement, which began in 1940, coupled with the corresponding increase in the authority of the Navy Department to negotiate contracts, necessitated, and at the same time made possible, the use of different types of compensation arrangements. In this part, we shall consider the principal types of compensation arrangements old and new-used during the war and presently being used in Navy contracts. 

$7.3. Firm Fixed-Price Contracts 

The basic type of contract for the procurement of naval supplies is the firm fixed-price or lump-sum type of contract. When procurement is accomplished by means of formal advertising, this type of contract must generally be employed.2 When procurement is by negotiation, a wide variety of types of contracts is available for selection; however, even in the case of procurement by negotiation, the Armed Services Procurement Regulation specifies that "the firm fixed-price contract shall be used unless . . . another type of contract is more appropriate. "3 The firm fixed-price contract, as the name implies, represents an agreement by the contractor to furnish designated supplies or services at a specified price which is not subject to adjustment in the light of performance costs. In its basic form the firm fixed-price contract carries the greatest risk and offers the greatest possibility of profit or loss of any type of contract, since the contractor cannot collect more than the agreed fixed price but is entitled to receive the full amount of the fixed price, and no more, regardless of the actual cost of performing the contract. 

This type of contract is preferred whenever a sound estimate of the cost Thus, in connection with negotiated procurement, the Secretary of each military department is authorized, subject to certain explicit exceptions, to "make any kind of contract that he considers will promote the best interests of the United 

States." 10 U.S.C. § 2306(a) (1958) 

(formerly 4(a) of the Armed Services • • 

Procurement Act of 1947, 62 Stat. 23 

(1948)). 

2 This is because under compensation arrangements that are more or less based on cost reimbursement it is generally impossible to say who is the low bidder within the meaning of 10 U.S.C. § 2305 (c) 

(1958). 

3 ASPR 3-403 (July 15, 1958). 

347

$ 7.4

of performing a contract can be made at the time of negotiation. Since it is fundamentally a simple exchange of a specified sum of money for a specified item, it is also the easiest and least costly of all types of contracts to administer.

Because the firm fixed-price contract provides for the future delivery of supplies or services at a price agreed upon at the time the contract is negotiated, contractors frequently seek to protect themselves against contingencies by including allowances therefor in their fixed-price quotations. 

However, the negotiator may find that it is better business for the Government to assume the risk of specified contingencies than to include an allowance for such contingencies in the price, which the contractor will retain whether or not the contingency in fact materializes. Indeed, ASPR 3-403.1 (c) provides that the firm fixed-price contract shall not be used when contingencies in the proposed contract price are considered unreasonable. Hence, contracts may provide for payments by the Government over and above the fixed price upon the happening of a specified contingency (such as the imposition of additional taxes, or an increase in the cost of labor or material). Such contingency provisions are frequently balanced by provisions for reducing the price in the event that the happening of the contingency reduces the cost of performing the contract (as in the case of a reduction in taxes or a decrease in the cost of labor or material). Such provisions, commonly called "escalation" clauses, are described in more detail in Chapter 9.5 From this point, the "fixed-price contract" loses its character as an unequivocal undertaking by the contractor to deliver at a firm price. $7.4.

Maximum Fixed-Price Contracts 

It sometimes happens either that the lowest fixed price obtainable by the Government is greater than the negotiator is willing unequivocally to obligate the Government to pay, or that a reasonably accurate estimate of the cost of performing the work cannot be made prior to performance of part of the work under the contract. Yet the parties may wish to retain the benefits of the fixed-price type of contract. To meet this situation, the "maximum fixed-price" or "fixed-price with redetermination downward" type of contract has been developed. In this type of contract, the parties agree upon an initial fixed price which represents only the maximum price which the Government may be required to pay for the supplies or services to be furnished. Whatever the contractor's costs may be, the Government will not pay more than the specified maximum fixed price; however, if the contractor's cost experience, ordinarily based upon partial performance of the contract, indicates that the maximum price is too high, the Government is entitled to a price reduction. 

4 July 15, 1958. 

5 See 89.42 infra. See also ASPR 

3-403.2 (July 15, 1958). 348

MAXIMUM FIXED-PRICE CONTRACTS 

$7.4

This type of contract provides that at a specified point after commencement of the work (which may be after completion of a specified percentage of the work, or of a specified number of units, or at a specified date) the parties will redetermine the contract price on the basis of actual costs incurred and estimated costs to be incurred under the contract. There are two schools of thought as to when price redetermination should take place, one group contending that it should be deferred as long as possible in order to give the Government the maximum benefit of the contractor's actual cost experience, and another group contending that the redetermination should take place rather promptly in order that the contractor will not in effect be guaranteed its costs (within the maximum) and thus be able to proceed with little risk and an assured profit. In general, the latter view has prevailed in the Navy Department. In this connection, the Armed Services Procurement Regulation provides: "Generally, the time designated as the cut off point for price redetermination purposes should be the earliest practicable and generally should not exceed 20 percent of deliveries, 20 percent of shop completion, or 40 percent of cost of performance on a cost incurred basis, as compared with the initial estimates."6

The basis upon which the redetermination is conducted will depend, of course, upon the exact terms of the redetermination clause employed." 

In general, the contractor is required, after the redetermination point has been reached, to submit to the contracting officer a breakdown of costs incurred and an estimate of costs expected to be incurred in the performance of the contract, using for this purpose a prescribed Department of Defense form. On the basis of such information and any other relevant information which the contracting officer may request, or which may otherwise be available to him, the contract price or prices, as the case may be, are redetermined by agreement of the contracting officer and the contractor, it being the intent of this type of contract that the redetermined prices will be fair and reasonable under all the circumstances to the contractor and to the Government. In the negotiation of such fair and reasonable redetermined prices, the contracting officer may take into account, as factors in determining a reasonable profit allowance, any unwarranted delay on the part of the contractor in submitting its breakdown of costs and estimate of costs at the time required, as well as the efficiency, economy and ingenuity with which the contractor has performed the contract to the redetermination point. It is particularly important in this type of contract that the contractor's skill and economy of performance 6 ASPR 3-403.3 (ii) (c) (1) (April 4, 1955). 

7 See ASPR 3–403.3(ii) (April 4, 1955) for approved types of price redetermination clauses. 

8 DD Form 784 (Cost Analysis For 

Contract Price Redetermination) is prescribed by ASPR 16-207 (June 11, 1958). 349

$ 7.4

be accorded full consideraion in determining the ultimate allowance for profit in order thereby to provide an incentive to the contractor to reduce the cost of performance. Such redetermined prices may apply to supplies delivered and to be delivered, but the redetermined price or prices, as the case may be, cannot in any event exceed the maximum unit price or the maximum total contract price set forth in the contract. The redetermined prices and the manner of making necessary adjustments with respect to payments previously made by the Government are thereupon set forth in an amendment, which is signed by the contracting officer and the contractor. In the event the parties are unable mutually to agree upon the redetermined prices, such failure is deemed to be a dispute concerning a question of fact and is decided by the contracting officer subject to appeal by the contractor to the Secretary of the Navy in accordance with the standard provisions in Navy contracts governing the settlement of disputes.

In order to insure against the possibility of substantially over-paying the contract price prior to redetermination, all price-redetermination (and fixed-price incentive) type contracts are required to contain a clause which provides that any payments for items delivered or for services performed and accepted by the Government in excess of the total amount of costs allocable to such items or services and an assigned interim profit to such items or services shall be refunded at the end of each quarterly period.' 

Prior to the requirement for the insertion of this clause, it had been the practice of the Government to withhold a specified percentage of the amounts otherwise payable by it to the contractor under the contract, or suspend payments after a specified percentage of the total contract price had been paid to the contractor. These withholding and refunding provisions are not wholly inconsistent with each other and price redetermination clauses may still provide for a percentage to be withheld from payments otherwise due, each based upon the contracting officer's estimate of the reduction which would occur upon redetermination of the contract price. Where payments are so withheld, the amount of refunds at the end of quarterly periods is decreased. Basically, the purpose of the refund provision is to limit the amount of outstanding progress payments to an amount not in excess of costs allocable to work done plus the assigned interim profit on such work. The application of a limitation based on costs and allocated profit avoids any hardships which may arise where a delay in price redetermination occurs through no fault of the contractor. The limitation of payments to costs and an allocated profit should not result in retarding the redetermination of prices which should occur within a reasonable time following the dates specified during which costs breakdowns are required to be submitted by the contractor. 

9 See generally, NPD 7-016 (May 27, 1957). 350

MAXIMUM FIXED-PRICE CONTRACTS 

$7.4

Once the concept of a redeterminable fixed price is grasped, the possibility of numerous variations in the form and procedure of redetermination is evident. For example, the contract may provide for redetermination of the unit prices only, or of the total contract price. This distinction may be extremely important since if only the unit prices are to be redetermined, each unit price must be within the maximum unit price; whereas if the total contract price is to be redetermined, it is sufficient if the total redetermined contract price is within the maximum total contract price. It has already been noted that the time of redetermination may vary, depending upon the circumstances. Likewise, the number of redeterminations may vary. The contract may provide for redetermination to take place only at a specified time, or it may provide for redetermination to take place upon the demand of one or both of the parties. During World War II, considerable use was made of a type of redetermination clause which provided for periodic price redetermination with the redetermined prices to apply only to future deliveries. Strictly speaking, these provisions should not be considered in the general class of redetermination provisions since, in effect, they involve the negotiation of new contracts for future deliveries. 

Provisions of this type proved useful during the war when it was desired to contract with a particular supplier for deliveries over an extended period so as to tie up its production and get its commitment for deliveries even though the contractor refused to give a firm price for the full term of the contract. In addition to the advantages stated above, and the further obvious one of avoiding the unnecessary drafting of new contracts, the use of prospective redetermination provisions (rather than contracting for shorter periods) permits any failure of the parties to agree upon a price for the future deliveries to be treated as a dispute upon which the Secretary of the Navy or his duly authorized representative may make a final and conclusive decision.

One of the more troublesome problems concerning price redetermination is the correlation between price redetermination and statutory renegotiation. Unless a special reserve is set up in renegotiation for this purpose, the objection to having the price redetermined after the contract has been renegotiated is obvious. On the other hand, redetermination and renegotiation are inherently independent one of the other in that redetermination is concerned with the fairness of a particular contract price while renegotiation is concerned with the fairness of the contractor's overall profits on renegotiable business. While various approaches to this problem were followed during the war, the most satisfactory approach, and the one being followed at the present time, is to allow the contractor to set up a reserve in the renegotiation proceedings to cover the possibility of downward price redetermination.10 This method of treatment is not only 

10 Regulations issued by the Renegotiation Board under the Renegotiation Act of 1951, as amended, so provide. 

RBR 1457.5(d)(ii) (June 30, 1958). 503533 0-59-25 351

$ 7.5

easier of administration, but permits price redetermination under procurement contracts to operate independently of the impact of renegotiation, and thus leaves the procurement function unaffected. This approach is recognized in current redeterminable price contracts by an express provision to the effect that any redetermination of the contract prices pursuant to the redetermination provisions thereof is without prejudice to the rights of the Government under any statute or order now in effect. 

$7.5. Flexible Fixed-Price Contracts 

It has been seen that the "maximum fixed-price contract" assures the Government that it will not be required to pay more than the maximum price agreed upon at the time the contract is negotiated, but at the same time permits that price to be reduced if it should appear, in the light of actual experience up to the repricing date, that the maximum price is too high. Occasionally, however, the undertaking may be so amorphous, or the parties may be so uncertain as to what the cost of performance will be, that the contractor is not willing to obligate itself to perform the contract within a maximum price. If the general fixed-price type of contract is still preferred, the answer may be to use a type of contract in which the specified fixed price is subject to redetermination at a specified point, either upward or downward, as may be appropriate in the light of the contractor's actual experience to the repricing date. A price ceiling is established which the contract price may not in any event exceed. This type of contract is frequently referred to as a "flexible-fixed-price" or "fixed price with upward or downward redetermination" type of contract.

This is not a preferred type of contract, and its use in the Navy Department is restricted.10a

From the working standpoint, the "flexible fixed-price contract" operates very much like the "maximum fixed-price contract," with the important exception that the redetermined price may be greater than the original price specified in the contract. 

$7.6. Fixed-Price Incentive Contracts 

From the standpoint of the Government, the worst type of contract is the type of contract (like the cost-plus-a-percentage-of-cost contract) under which the allowance for profit is increased as the cost of performance increases. Obviously, this type of contract serves as an incentive to contractors to increase the cost of performing the contract in order to secure a larger allowance for profit. Conversely, the best form of contract would seem to be one which gives the contractor the greatest incentive to reduce costs. Of course, the firm fixed-price contract gives the contractor such an incentive, but the Government does not share in the resulting saving of cost. The maximum price contract theoretically 

10a NPD 7-107.4 (June 6, 1958). supra. 352

FIXED-PRICE INCENTIVE CONTRACTS 

$ 7.6 1 1 provides some incentive to reduce costs, since the negotiator may recognize economy of performance by allowing a greater sum for profit in the redetermined price; however, many contractors feel that by reducing the base against which profit is customarily measured, the overall profit allowed may be reduced, and so the incentive (if any) to reduce costs in this type of contract is slight. To meet the need for a type of contract which would provide a realistic incentive to save cost, the "fixed-price incentive contract" was devised."

The fixed-price incentive contract requires, first, that a realistic estimate be made of the cost of performing the contract. To this amount (usually called "the firm target cost") a reasonable allowance for profit (the target profit) is added. The sum of these amounts constitutes the "base" or "target" price, in other words the price which the Navy estimates would be fair and reasonable. A ceiling price which the final contract cannot exceed is next determined. If the final cost of performing the contract is exactly equal to the estimated target cost, the contractor receives the target profit. If the final cost is less than the target cost, the contractor shares the cost saving on the basis of previously negotiated percentages; the contractor thereby benefits by receiving a larger profit, while the Government benefits by being required to pay a lower total contract price. If the final cost of performing the contract is greater than the target cost, the contractor's profit is reduced by the previously negotiated percentage. If the final cost is equal to the ceiling price, the contractor makes no profit; and if it exceeds the ceiling price the contractor is required to absorb the excess at its own expense. Obviously, care must be exercised to keep the ceiling price as low as possible if the Government is to enjoy the advantages inherent in the incentive contract. For this reason, the incentive contract should be used only where there is sufficient previous cost experience to make it possible to determine a realistic base or target price. 

Under an alternate form of this type of contract, there are negotiated at the outset an initial price and a production point, generally prior to initial delivery or shop completion of the first item, at which time a firm target cost, target profit and a final profit-and-price formula and price ceiling will be negotiated.

Final costs under the fixed-price incentive contract are determined by negotiation and agreement between the contractor and the contracting officer after completion of all work under the contract. Since final costs are determined by negotiation and are not subject to audit and review, the contractor is assured of the finality of the cost determination; and since final costs are negotiated after completion of all work under the contract, the contractor is protected against unknown costs for which

When the final contract price is determined, the amount thereof is evidenced by a supplemental memorandum of agreement or amendment signed by the contractor and the contracting officer. Failure of the parties to agree upon the final redetermined price is treated as a disputed question of fact and handled in accordance with the standard disputes procedure. 

Pending determination of the final contract price, payments are made by the Government to the contractor on the basis of a specified billing price. Provision is usually made in the contract for adjusting the billing price for payment purposes, if it should appear that actual costs will be substantially greater or less than the billing price. In order to avoid the possibility of a contractor receiving amounts in excess of the final contract price as a result of billing prices being set too high, there is currently a requirement that payments made for deliveries prior to the establishment of the final contract price shall not exceed actual costs incurred plus the target profit applicable to such costs.12

The way the fixed-price incentive contract operates is illustrated by the following case: The Bureau of Ships desires to contract for the construction of 67 Tank Landing Ships. There has been sufficient previous experience to permit close estimating. There are sufficient units involved in the proposed procurement to permit the contractor to achieve all possible economies. On the basis of previous experience, it is estimated that each LST will cost $1,200,000. However, the contractor is apprehensive of possible unknown costs and insists upon many contingency allowances, which bring its estimate of costs for a fixed-price contract to $1,350,000 per vessel. Under these circumstances, the parties decide to use an incentive-type contract. The contractor's contingency-inflated estimate of $1,350,000 becomes the maximum price per vessel which the Government will be required to pay. A profit formula is negotiated under which the contractor is entitled to retain as profit 52 percent of any amount up to the first $50,000 by which the final cost is less than the maximum price; 

48 percent of the second $50,000 of saving; 32 percent of the third $50,- 

000; and 20 percent of any additional saving. 

What this arrangement means to the contractor and the Government is shown in the accompanying table. 

It will be recalled from the above example that the Bureau of Ships estimated on the basis of previous experience that each LST would cost $1,200,000. The profit formula was devised so that, if this estimate was exactly correct, the contractor would earn $66,000 per vessel, or 5.5 percent of cost.

In point of fact, this contract turned out as follows: 

The contractor completed the contract at an average cost per vessel of $1,054,089.48, which is $295,910.52 per vessel less than the maximum price

It will be observed that the contractor earned $95,182.10 per vessel upon an average cost per vessel of $1,054,089.48, or approximately 9 percent of cost. This may seem like a rather handsome profit, considering that the 

Government assumed most but not all of the risk. However, note that the Government, which would have paid $1,266,000 per vessel on a straight fixed-price contract, paid only $1,149,271.58 per vessel under the incentive-type contract, representing a saving to the Government of over $116,000 per vessel. This illustrates how the incentive-type contract sets the profit motive to work for the Government, since the more the contractor earns the more the Government saves.

It has been stated above that, in order to receive the full benefit of the incentive-type contract, the ceiling price must be negotiated with care.

A study of the above case will demonstrate why this is so. However, it should be noted that a mistake in estimating is less costly to the Government under the incentive-type contract where the Government participates in the saving than it would be under the straight fixed-price contract where the contractor pockets the entire saving. 

It should be emphasized that the example provided above represents only one of a great number of possible uses of the incentive-type contract. In this case, because the negotiator considered the estimates to be "tight," the contractor was permitted to share heavily in the first saving of cost. If the negotiator had considered the estimates to be high, he might have counterweighted the arrangement by loading the profit at the bottom of the formula so that the contractor's share of the cost saving would be relatively low at the beginning and would not reach its peak until substantial savings had been achieved. 

One point to watch carefully in the incentive-type contract is the way change orders are handled. Since the cost of performing changes will be included in the contractor's total cost, it is necessary in computing the allowance for profit to adjust the contractor's costs downward to compensate for changes involving increased cost and to adjust the contractor's costs upward to compensate for changes involving decreased cost. In other words, if the Navy Department authorizes a change, the effect of which is to increase the cost of performing the contract, the contractor should not be penalized by permitting the increased costs 356

COST-PLUS-FIXED-FEE CONTRACTS 

$7.7 1 1 attributable to such change to wipe out savings of costs in which the contractor would otherwise share. Conversely, if the Navy Department by change order decreases the amount of work to be performed by the contractor, the estimated cost of performing the deleted work should be added to the contractor's actual allowable cost in order to prevent the contractor from receiving a profit for savings of costs which are attributable to a decrease in the amount of work to be performed rather than to any economy on the part of the contractor. 

There are two points of view with respect to escalation under an incentive-type contract. During the war, some negotiators preferred to treat possible increases in labor or material costs like any other contingency and to include an allowance therefor in the maximum price. 

Other negotiators preferred to disregard it completely in negotiating the maximum price, but to make the maximum price subject to adjustment upward or downward in the event of an increase or decrease in the cost of labor or material under the contract. This is a choice which should be made in the light of the facts and circumstances existing at the time of the negotiation. 

By virtue of 10 U.S.C. § 2306 (c), incentive contracts, whether of the fixed-price or incentive-fee type, are authorized only if the Secretary of the Department concerned or a duly authorized contracting officer determines "that such a contract is likely to be less costly to the United States than any other kind of contract or that it is impracticable to obtain property or services of the kind or quality required except under such a contract.” 13 

$7.7. Cost-Plus-Fixed-Fee Contracts 

The most severely criticized type of contract used by the Navy Department is the cost-reimbursement type of contract (i.e., one under which the Government agrees to reimburse the contractor for the allowable cost of performing the contract, usually with some allowance for profit). 

During World War I, extensive use was made of the cost-plus-a-percentage-of-cost contract, under which the contractor received payment from the Government of the cost of performing the contract plus a specified percentage of such costs as an allowance for profit. Thus, if the specified percentage was 10 percent, the contractor received ten cents in fee for each one dollar of reimbursable costs which it incurred. The encouragement which this type of contract offered to contractors to be wasteful, inefficient and extravagant is too obvious to require elaboration. 

It is sufficient to note that the use of the cost-plus-a-percentage-of-cost type of contract by the Navy Department has been prohibited since 1940 and that this prohibition was repeated in section 4 of the Armed Services ment Act of 1947, 62 Stat. 23 (1948). 

13 10 U.S.C. § 2306 (c) (1958), formerly 84(b) of the Armed Services Procure- 

357

$7.7

Procurement Act of 1947.14 In furtherance of this policy, the Armed 

Services Procurement Regulation specifies that all contracts on other than a firm fixed-price basis shall by an appropriate clause prohibit cost-plus-a-percentage-of-cost subcontracts.15 

Following the President's declaration of a limited national emergency by Executive Order 8248 of September 8, 1939, and the subsequent entry of the United States into the war, the Navy was faced with procurement problems which virtually dictated the use of some type of cost-reimbursement contract. In many cases it was necessary to get the work started before precise specifications could be issued or before the full scope of the work had been determined. In other cases the contractor was called upon to produce items which it had never produced before and with respect to which it had no cost experience, or to undertake projects of such magnitude that even a small percentage of error in estimating for a fixed price might mean financial ruin for the contractor. To meet these problems, the Navy Department used the cost-plus-fixed-fee contract. 

Under the cost-plus-fixed-fee type of contract, the contractor is reimbursed for the "true" or "allowable" cost of performing the contract and receives, in addition, a fixed fee for its services. Since June 1940, the maximum amount which the Navy can pay as fee under a cost-plus-fixedfee contract has been limited by statute or executive order. The Act of June 28, 1940,16 limited the fee payable under cost-plus-fixed-fee contracts entered into by the Navy under the authority of the act to 7 percent of the estimated cost of the work as determined by the Secretary of the Navy. Executive Order No. 9001 (December 27, 1941), which authorized the Navy Department to perform the functions and exer cise the powers described in Title II of the First War Powers Act, 1941, expressly preserved the existing statutory limitations on fee and provided further that, in the absence of a statutory limitation, the fixed fee to be paid to the contractor under any cost-plus-fixed-fee contract entered into by the Navy under the authority of that order should not exceed 7 percent of the estimated cost of the contract (exclusive of the fee as determined by the Secretary of the Navy). The Armed 

Services Procurement Act of 1947 increased the maximum permissible fee under a cost-plus-fixed-fee contract entered into pursuant to that act to 10 percent of the estimated cost of the contract, exclusive of fee, as determined by the agency head at the time of entering into such contract. 

This act further authorizes payment (1) of a fee not in excess of 15 percent of such estimated cost in any such contract for experimental, developmental or research work, and (2) of a fee, inclusive of the contractor's costs, and not in excess of 6 percent of the estimated cost of the project (exclusive of fees) as determined by the agency head at

(1958). 

15 ASPR 3-401 (Sept. 18, 1958).

$7.7 the time of entering into the contract, in contracts for architectural or engineering services relating to any public works or utilities project." 

It should be noted that these percentages represent the maximum fees which the Navy can pay under cost-plus-fixed-fee contracts. The policy of the Navy Department has been to keep fees well below these respective maxima.

All Navy cost-reimbursement-type contracts provide for the determination and acceptance of costs by the Contract Audit Division of the Comptroller of the Navy, usually in accordance with a statement of cost principles which is specifically designated in the contract. Prior to April 

1942, the reimbursability of costs under Navy cost-type contracts was determined in accordance with Treasury Decision No. 5000, which had originally been issued by the Treasury Department with the approval of the War and Navy Departments as a basis for determining costs for purposes of the profit limitation provisions of the Vinson-Trammell Act.18 

In April 1942, the War and Navy Departments jointly issued a new set of cost determination principles, entitled "Explanation of Principles for 

Determination of Costs under Government Contracts, War Department- 

Navy Department," more commonly called the "Green Book." In addition, a somewhat different set of principles known as the "Blue Book" was developed for use in connection with non-profit contracts with educational institutions, which do not generally follow commercial accounting practices. Thereafter, Navy cost-type contracts provided for the determination and acceptance of costs in substantial accordance with the principles enumerated in the "Green Book." In 1949, these principles were revised in the light of World War II experience and were in corporated in Section XV of the Armed Services Procurement Regula tion. This section is now used as the basis for determining costs under all cost-reimbursement contracts and establishes separate cost principles applicable to supply and research contracts with commercial organizations, research contracts with non-profit institutions, and construction contracts.

Because the cost-plus-fixed-fee contract obligates the Government to reimburse the contractor for the allowable cost of performing the contract without regard to the estimated cost, it has been the general practice in the Navy Department, in order to avoid over-obligating appropriations, to specify a maximum amount beyond which the Government will not be obligated to reimburse the contractor. The maximum may be more or less than, or equal to, the estimated cost. The contractor does not guarantee to complete the contract within the limitations of the maximum, and is excused from further performance when the maximum has been reached unless the contracting officer increases the maximum. 

17 Now codified as 10 U.S.C. § 2306(d) 

(1958). 

18 See § 6.8 supra for a discussion of the Vinson-Trammell Act. 

359

$7.7

The cost-plus-fixed-fee contract avoids the vice of the cost-plus-a-percentage-of-cost contract in that the contractor does not benefit by increasing the cost of performing the contract. Irrespective of whether its actual costs are greater or less than the estimated cost, the contractor receives the predetermined fixed fee, unless the scope of work has been increased or decreased, in which event the estimated cost and fixed fee are appropriately increased or decreased. 

On the other hand, the cost-plus-fixed-fee contract offers no encouragement to a contractor to reduce its costs. There has been widespread feeling that since the Government is paying the bill, many contractors are indifferent about effecting economies. The feeling against cost-plus-fixed fee contracts grew so intense during the latter part of World War II that legislation was introduced in Congress on several occasions to prohibit the use of this type of contract. No such legislation has been enacted, and the cost-plus-fixed-fee contract is recognized by the Armed Services Procurement Act as a proper and available type of contract. 

While the Navy Department considers that circumstances sometimes necessitate the use of the cost-plus-fixed-fee contract and has opposed its proscription for that reason, it has made every effort to minimize its use. Today, this type of contract is used primarily for experimental, research or developmental work where firm estimates cannot be made. 

The objections to the cost-plus-fixed-fee contract, and the policy of the Navy Department to prefer fixed-price types of contracts, are summarized in a directive by the Secretary of the Navy, dated March 20, 1943, as follows:

Experience with the various methods of paying compensation to Navy contractors has established that some method of fixed price compensation is always more satisfactory than provision for compensation on a cost basis or a cost-plus-a-fixed-fee basis. The fixed price method of compensation has advantages which make it more satisfactory than either of the other two methods of compensation (hereafter collectively referred to as the 'cost' method of compensation), even in those cases where the contractor lacks production experience or where other factors require some degree of flexibility in the arrangement for compensation. Contracts providing for compensation on a cost basis present the following problems, among others: control by the Navy Department of the contractor's costs is difficult; the contractor has little or no incentive to reduce costs; the inevitable uncertainties in cost determination give rise to timeconsuming controversies which may delay production; the supply of competent accountants available to the Navy is inadequate; and 

Navy disbursing officers lack assurance that payments by them are definitive and not subject to subsequent question. The Secretary of the Navy hereby finds with respect to contracts other than construction contracts that in general the compensation arrangement which fixes firm prices effective over a relatively short term, is more satisfactory than a cost method of compensation, and is in general 360

COST-SHARING CONTRACTS 

$7.9 practicable in those circumstances under which a cost method of compensation has heretofore been adopted in Navy contracts. 

It should be noted that the objections to the cost-plus-fixed-fee type of contract are not entirely one-sided. In a number of respects, this type of contract is not attractive to the contractor. The fact that the Government is directly reimbursing costs frequently necessitates governmental inspection and control to an extent which many contractors consider burdensome. For example, every subcontract or purchase order directly entered into by a contractor under a cost-plus-fixed-fee vessel construction contract with the Bureau of Ships is subject to the approval of that Bureau. Furthermore, the contractor has no assurance that all of the costs which it actually incurs or claims to be allocable to the performance of the contract will be reimbursed, since only those costs which are accepted in accordance with the applicable set of cost principles set forth in Section XV of the Armed Services Procurement Regulation (which the contract incorporates by reference) are reimbursed. During World 

War II, approximately 12 percent of the costs claimed for reimbursement under cost-type contracts was disallowed. In 1956 the disallowance rate was approximately 15 percent. Such disallowed costs must be absorbed by the contractor. Lastly, there is no finality of payment under a cost-type contract; and the General Accounting Office may disallow costs years after they have been accepted and paid by the Navy Department. 

$7.8 Cost-Without-Fee Contracts 

The cost contract is the same type contract as the cost-plus-fixed-fee contract except that no fee whatever is paid to the contractor. It is used principally, but not exclusively, with educational or other non-profit institutions. 

$7.9. Cost-Sharing Contracts 

A little-used type of contract, but one which may be worthy of further consideration, is the cost-sharing type of contract. This type of contract recognizes that the contractor sometimes benefits substantially (apart from profit) by the performance of a government contract. This is particularly true in the field of research and development where the results of the research and development performed under a government contract may have profitable commercial application. Where the prospect of commercial application can be foreseen at the time of entering into the contract, the Navy Department has occasionally negotiated contracts which provide that the Government will reimburse the contractor for only a specified percentage of its costs. The unreimbursed percentage represents the contractor's contribution to what is in effect a joint enterprise. 361

$ 7.

As in the case with the incentive-type contract, the cost (or costsharing type of contract) and the cost-plus-fixed-fee type of contract may be used only after the Secretary of a military department or his duly authorized contracting officer determines "that such a contract is likely to be less costly to the United States than any other kind of contract, or that it is impracticable to obtain property or services of the kind or quality required except under such a contract.” 19 

$7.10. Cost-Plus-Fixed-Fee-Incentive-Type Contracts 

It has been emphasized repeatedly that one of the major faults of the cost-plus-fixed-fee contract is that it provides no incentive to the contractor to reduce the cost of performing the contract. To meet this criticism, the Navy devised a type of cost-plus-fixed-fee contract which assured the contractor only a relatively modest fixed fee but which permitted the fixed fee to be increased to a specified limit if the contractor performed the contract for less than the estimated cost. 

This type of contract has been used almost exclusively in connection with the construction of vessels; however, it is adaptable to other types of procurement as well. Under this type of contract, the Government and the contractor agree at the time of negotiation of the contract upon the estimated cost of performance. The fixed fee is thereupon determined, as in the case of the ordinary cost-plus-fixed-fee contract, in relation to the estimated cost. The contract provides, however, that if the allowable cost of performing the contract is less than the estimated cost, the contractor will be entitled to a bonus for saving of cost equal to a specified percentage of the total costs saved, subject to the limitation that the amount of the bonus cannot exceed an agreed maximum. 

Since the bonus in effect constitutes additional fee, the bonus provision must be arranged at the outset so that the total combined fixed fee and maximum bonus for saving of cost do not exceed the applicable statutory limit.

Like the fixed-price incentive-type contract, the cost-plus-fixed-feeincentive-type contract is susceptible of many variations. In the case of unavoidable procurement from a high-cost producer, the Navy Department may base the fixed fee upon comparative estimated costs, even though the comparative cost is less than the probable cost to the contractor of performing the contract. In this manner, a high-cost contractor is not permitted to benefit fee-wise by reason of its higher costs. However, since it is anticipated that the actual allowable cost of performing the contract will exceed the estimated cost, the Department, in order to give the contractor an incentive to reduce its costs, may increase the estimated cost for purposes of computing the bonus for saving of cost. Thus, if a 

19 10 U.S.C. § 2306 (c) (1958). 

362

CONTRACTS WITH NEGOTIATED OVERHEAD RATE 

$7.11 contractor reasonably estimated the cost of performing a given contract to be $1,000,000, although the same article was being procured from other contractors at an estimated cost of $900,000, the Department might establish the estimated cost in the case of this contract at $900,000 for purposes of computing the fixed fee but add $100,000 to the estimated cost for purposes of computing the bonus for saving of cost. 

Because increases and decreases in labor and material costs are largely beyond the control of the contractor, the estimated cost under the costplus-fixed-fee incentive-type contract has generally been made subject to adjustment by reason of increases or decreases of this type. The estimated cost is also adjusted for change orders. However, the cost of any correction, replacement or segregation of defective material or workmanship, being within the control of the contractor, is generally included in allowable cost, even though the correction or replacement may be effected by the Navy Department. 

$ 7.11. Cost-Plus-Fixed-Fee Contracts With Negotiated Overhead Rate 

This type of contract is somewhat of a hybrid, combining features of the cost-plus-fixed-fee and fixed-price type of contracts. It resembles a straight cost-plus-fixed-fee contract in its negotiation in that the parties agree upon the estimated cost of performance and the fixed fee to be paid to the contractor. However, instead of providing, as in the usual costplus-fixed-fee contract, that the Government will pay the contractor the allowable cost of performing the contract, it provides only that the Government will pay the contractor the allowable cost of specified categories of direct costs plus an allowance for overhead computed on the basis of a fixed rate, which is arrived at by negotiation rather than by audit. This rate may be applied to direct labor hours, direct labor dollars, or any other mutually agreeable base. 

Until 1956 it was the general practice in this type of contract to provide for periodic prospective adjustment of the overhead rate. The most common arrangement was to provide for semi-annual adjustment of the rate; however, the rate could be made firm for longer or shorter periods if the parties desired. Failure of the parties to agree upon the rate for the succeeding period was treated as a disputed question of fact to be resolved under the disputes clause. 

The Comptroller General in 1956 expressed the opinion that the use of predetermined fixed overhead rates in cost-reimbursement type contracts violates the prohibition against the cost-plus-a-percentage-of-cost system of contracting and has requested that the use of such predetermined fixed overhead rates be discontinued in future cost-reimbursement type contracts and in connection with the modification of overhead rates stipulated in existing cost-reimbursement type contracts.20 While the Navy 

20 35 COMP. GEN. 434 (1956); see 35 

COMP. GEN. 63 (1955). 363

$7.12

does not share the Comptroller General's view that the predetermined overhead rate, as previously employed in Navy contracts, violates the prohibition against cost-plus-a-percentage-of-cost systems of contracting, it has agreed as a matter of policy to discontinue use of the predetermined overhead rate.

A fuller discussion of the Comptroller General's decision and the views of the Navy on this subject, together with an outline of the manner in which the military departments have modified this form of contract to accommodate the Comptroller General's views," is set forth in Chapter 8.22 What is said there with respect to cost-type research and development contracts would apply in this respect equally to other cost types of contracts. 

$7.12. Time and Material Contracts 

All of the types of contracts described thus far in this chapter depend, within varying degrees of tolerance, upon a reasonable estimate of the cost of performing the contract being made prior to entering into the contract. However, there are occasions, particularly during time of war, when the cost of performing the contract cannot be estimated in advance with reasonable accuracy or when there is not sufficient time for careful estimating. The time and material contract (commonly called "T and 

M" contract) may be the only workable type of contract under these circumstances.

Under this type of contract, the contractor is compensated for materials at cost and for labor, overhead and profit on the basis of a negotiated fixed rate. The rate may be applied to whatever period of time the parties consider convenient and appropriate for the purpose (e.g., hours, days, weeks, months, etc.). The rate may be firm for the life of the contract or it may be subject to prospective adjustment at stated intervals. 

This is a dangerous type of contract. Although it provides for payment of a fixed price per applicable unit of time, it is evident that, unless the rate is insufficient to cover the contractor's costs, the total amount of profit under the contract is increased proportionately as the number of hours are increased. For this reason ASPR 3-405.1 (a) provides that this type of contract may be used only after the contracting officer determines "that no other type of contract will suitably serve.' 

Because the time and material contract has been intimately associated in the Navy Department with the performance of ship repair work (although it has also been used under numerous other circumstances), the details of this type of contract will be elaborated during the discussion of ship repair contracts later in this chapter.

LETTER CONTRACTS 

$ 7.14 1 $7.13. In General

II. FORM 

We are concerned in this Part II with the form of the contract only to the extent that the form of the contract itself is a procurement tool. 

We are not concerned here with the format or appearance of the contract. For this reason we shall not consider the ordinary definitive contract, except as its form may appear from the discussion later in this chapter of types of contracts from the standpoint of their end purpose. 

Each of the forms discussed in this Part represents a short-cut-a means of getting the work under way sooner than would be possible under the ordinary definitive contract. Because these are short-cuts, they must be handled with care.

In the discussion which immediately follows, we shall describe each form and shall endeavor to point out its principal advantages and disadvantages. 

$7.14. Letter Contracts 

In its generic and descriptive sense, the term "letter contract" refers to any contract in the form of a letter. For example, on small repair or construction jobs, the contractor may submit a letter offer embodying all the proposed terms of a contract, and this letter, with the contracting officer's acceptance, is the only document executed. Occasionally, after long negotiations or exchange of correspondence, the Government summarizes the complete contract terms agreed upon in a letter offer to the contractor, and this letter, when accepted, becomes a preliminary contract which is to be converted thereafter to a formal bilateral contract. 

In other cases, such as on large construction projects, a letter notice of award or acceptance is issued by a contracting officer in response to a competitive bid or a negotiated proposal setting forth all the terms of a proposed contract. The letter award or acceptance is to be followed by the appropriate standard form bilateral contract incorporating without substantive change all the contract terms previously agreed upon. 

The purpose of the preliminary letter is to get the work started immediately and avoid the delay of preparing bulky contracts including lengthy specifications and numerous drawings. It is, nevertheless, well-settled in such case that even though the formal bilateral contract contemplated by the parties is not executed, a final and binding contract enforceable against the contractor and the Government comes into being with the issuance of the letter notice of award or acceptance.23 In other words, the contract itself is final and not subject to change in substance. Only the form is preliminary and subject to change. 

23 United States v. Purcell Envelope 

Co., 249 U.S. 313 (1919). See also 26

COMP. GEN. 365 (1946). 

365

$ 7.14

For the most part, the term "letter contract" is used in military procurement as a term of art in the special sense of a binding contract document which is preliminary not only in form but to some degree in substance as well. Such documents were formerly called "letters of intent." As defined by ASPR 3-405.3 (a), "a letter contract is a written preliminary contractual instrument which authorizes immediate commencement of manufacture of supplies, or performance of services, including, but not limited to, preproduction planning and the procurement of necessary materials." 24 The discussion hereafter is directed to such letter contracts.

Often the contracting officer can be fairly confident on the basis of past relationships and preliminary negotiations that he will be able to agree upon satisfactory price and other terms with a contractor. For the moment this may not be possible, not because of price differences between the parties, but because the precise military requirements or specifications have not been settled, the item is novel, or the necessary cost data are not at hand. Nevertheless, the general scope and nature of the work may be sufficiently known so that much can be accomplished immediately by way of production planning, engineering, plant rearrangement, special tooling, and ordering of materials and equipment. 

In such circumstances, a letter contract is a useful device to accelerate procurement. However, its disadvantages are such that it should be used only under the compulsion of military necessity. 

In essence, a letter contract of this kind signifies the intention of the Navy to enter into a formal contract and the contractor's undertaking to commence performance of the work immediately in exchange for the Navy's undertaking to reimburse the contractor for all interim costs in the event of failure to agree upon the terms of a final contract. In the interest of narrowing the area of future negotiation and possible disagreement, the letter contract should include as many definitive contract provisions as can be agreed upon, particularly with regard to the compensation arrangements, such as whether a cost- or fixed-price type of definitive contract is contemplated. 

Since a letter contract is a true contract,25 it must comply with all applicable statutory requirements such as those for bonds, determinations and clauses.26 It also generally covers such matters as the prompt negotiation and execution of a definitive contract, the submission by the contractor of firm quotations or estimates with appropriate supporting cost data, the fixed time limit for executing the definitive contract subject to extension by the contracting officer or by mutual agreement, and the maximum amount of liability of the Government prior to execution of a

It will be apparent to any lawyer that a letter contract is not a satisfactory contractual document. Once the commitment is made and time and money invested, the Government is in a poor bargaining position in future negotiations with the contractor since it can seldom do better by terminating the letter contract and placing the work elsewhere. For this reason, ASPR 3-405.3 authorizes letter contracts only when "the interests of national defense demand that the contractor be given a binding commitment so that work can be commenced immediately" and "negotiation of a definitive contract in sufficient time to meet the procurement need is not possible," 30 and only after a determination that "no other type of contract is suitable." 31 The expressed policy under the regulation is to limit the Government's maximum liability to 50 percent of the total estimated cost of the procurement and to require execution of a definitive

The Comptroller General has criticized letter contract procedures as "more in the nature of settlement of the contractors' claims than the negotiation of contracts," in a case where the time and liability limitations were repeatedly exceeded and extended and definitive contracts were not executed until substantial completion of the work.33 Under such circumstances he also rejected the view that a ceiling on expenditures and audit controls on costs placed an arrangement in the letter contract for a fee or profit on a percentage basis outside the scope of the statutory prohibition against the cost-plus-a-percentage-of-cost system of contracting. 

Since the only certain obligation under a letter contract preliminary to a fixed-price contract is to reimburse the contractor for its interim costs, there is some difference of opinion as to whether the letter contract should be regarded as a fixed-price or a cost-type contract. The question is of considerable practical importance since, in the latter case, the procurement would have to start off with burdensome cost controls and special record keeping and audit requirements and these would become unnecessary and wasteful when the definitive fixed-price contract was executed. Navy practice is to treat the procurement as fixed-price from its inception, with the provision for cost-reimbursement operative, as with other fixed-price contracts, only in the event of termination. This is sound as a practical matter since almost all letter contracts are ultimately converted. 

$7.15. Purchase Orders 

The purchase order is another form of contract designed to simplify and expedite procurements not in excess of $2,500 of standard commercial supplies and services. Addressed to a selected supplier and signed only by the contracting officer, the purchase order by its terms does not require or contemplate the supplier's promissory acceptance, but it does request the supplier's acceptance by its performance of the act specified in the order. As a legal concept, the purchase order is designed for use as an offer by the Government of a unilateral contract-in short, the Government's promise for the supplier's act. 

Prior to January 1, 1957, two forms of purchase orders for purchases not in excess of $1,000 were used within the Department of Defense, namely DD Form 702 (Order for Purchase of Supplies or Services) and DD Form 738 (Order and Voucher for Purchase of Supplies or 

Services). These forms, when used as purchase orders, did not differ materially from one another. However, the forms differed in that DD

On December 27, 1941, the President of the United States, by Executive Order No. 9001, delegated to the Navy Department the authority conferred upon him by the First War Powers Act, 1941, to enter into contracts (expressly including purchase orders) without regard to the provisions of law relating to the making of contracts. On December 28, 1941, this authority was extended by the Secretary of the Navy to the contracting officers of the Navy Department with the restriction that all contracts in excess of $500 should be reduced to writing and signed by the contracting parties. However, the advantages and convenience of the purchase order for wartime procurement soon became so evident that the Secretary on August 19, 1942, increased the monetary limitation upon the use of purchase orders to $5,000. On September 4, 1943, the monetary limit was again increased, this time to $100,000, but with the important restriction that the purchase order device could be used for the purchase of materials or services, the price of which is in excess of $5,000 but under $100,000, only if the purchase order was based upon an established price list or was preceded by a written or oral quotation of prices. The use of purchase orders was prohibited in any one of the following cases: 

1. If all deliveries were not to be completed within 120 days from the date of the purchase order; 

2. If the purchase transaction was classified as secret or confidential; 

3. If the Government was furnishing any material or equipment to the supplier; 

4. If any changes in specifications were anticipated; 

5. If the work to be performed was of a developmental or experimental nature; or 

6. If the contracting officer deemed the circumstances to be such as to make it desirable to bind the supplier to a contract. 

With the return to peacetime procurement practices and the enactment of the Armed Services Procurement Act of 1947, purchase orders became limited primarily to procurements of not over $1,000.44 However, following the declaration of a national emergency by the President on December 16, 1950, and the consequent determinations by the Secretaries of the military departments to negotiate certain purchases and contracts purзuant to section 2(c) (1) of the Armed Services Procurement Act of 1947,45 the monetary limitation upon the use of purchase orders was increased to $5,000. Effective September 15, 1956, this limitation was again reduced to $2,500 in conjunction with the curtailment of the general availability of section 2(c) (1) as negotiation authority for the duration of the national emergency declared by the President on December 16, 1950.46

But continued reliance on the negotiation authority of exception (1) to support the across-the-board use of purchase orders between $1,000 and $2,500 was obviated by legislation enacted August 28, 1958, that increased the open market purchase authority of the military departments to $2,500.47 As a practical matter, the purchase order method of procurement-that is, the Government's offer of a unilateral contract-is now for the most part limited to transactions not over $2,500 in consequence of the requirement of section 1311 of the Supplemental Appropriation Act, 1955, for a binding agreement as a condition precedent to the obligation of funds by contract for substantially all procurements in excess of that amount.48

The main legal objection to the use of purchase orders is the uncertainty as to when the parties are bound to its performance. When the purchase order has been preceded by a written or oral quotation of prices, or is based upon an established price list, it may be contended that the purchase order represents the Government's acceptance of the contractor's offer and that a bilateral contract is created by the issuance of the purchase order. This theory explains the wartime requirement, noted above, that purchase orders could be used in transactions involving more than $5,000 only if the issuance of the purchase order had been preceded by a written or oral quotation of prices or if the purchase order was based upon an established price list. However, since the purchase order almost always contains terms and conditions which vary from those specified in the contractor's quotation, the purchase order may very well be regarded as a counteroffer by the Government.49 If the purchase order is construed to be an offer by the Government looking to performance by the offeree as acceptance, i.e., an offer of a unilateral contract, it would not seem to make any difference whether or not the purchase order was based upon a prior quotation or an established price list, since, on this theory, it is the performance of the offeree, not his promise, for which the Government is bargaining. This statement must, however, be weighed in the light of the clear preference shown by the courts for construing an offer as contemplating a bilateral rather than a unilateral contract.50 

Considering the purchase order as an offer by the Government of a unilateral contract, it would seem to follow, at least in theory, that the Government is free to revoke its offer at any time prior to completion of performance by the offeree, and that the offeree has no obligation to the negotiation of purchases and contracts between $1,000 and $5,000 was withdrawn. Effective September 15, 1956, this authority was restored with respect to purchases and contracts between $1,000 and $2,500.

However, because of the manifest hardship of permitting the offeror to revoke his offer after the offeree has commenced performance, most courts, in the few cases in point, have held the offeror to be bound, although it is not always clear on what theory.51 The corresponding injustice of holding the offeror to be bound while the offeree is not has not so often been considered.

Assuming that the Government may be bound by the purchase order at some time prior to completion of performance by the offeree, there is the difficult question of determining when it becomes bound. The weight of modern authority (most of the cases are in state courts) indicates that the offeree may bind the Government by tendering a portion of the articles called for by the purchase order. This view is adopted and com mented upon by the Restatement of Contracts as follows: 

§ 45. REVOCATION OF OFFER FOR UNILATERAL CONTRACT; EFFECT OF PART PERFORMANCE OR TENDER. 

If an offer for a unilateral contract is made, and part of the consideration requested in the offer is given or tendered by the offeree in response thereto, the offeror is bound by a contract, the duty of immediate performance of which is conditional on the full consideration being given or tendered within the time stated in the offer, or, if no time is stated therein, within a reasonable time. Comment: a. What is tendered must be part of the actual performance requested in order to preclude revocation under this Section. Beginning preparations though they may be essential to carrying out the contract or to accepting the offer, is not enough. b. Tender, however, is sufficient. Though not the equivalent of performance, nevertheless it is obviously unjust to allow so late withdrawal. There can be no actionable duty on the part of the offeror until he has received all that he demanded, or until the condition is excused by his own prevention of performance by refusing a tender; but he may become bound at an earlier day. The main offer includes as a subsidiary promise, necessarily implied, that if part of the requested performance is given, the offeror will not revoke his offer, and that if tender is made it will be accepted. Part performance or tender may thus furnish consideration for the subsidiary promises. Moreover, merely acting in justifiable reliance on an offer may in some cases serve as sufficient reason for making a promise binding (see § 90). c. As to the difficulty of determining whether an offer proposes a unilateral or a bilateral contract, and the presumption in favor of the latter interpretation (see § 31 and Comment thereon). 

51 For an interesting discussion of this problem, with citations, see 1 WILLISTON,

CONTRACTS §§ 60, 60A (3d ed. 1957); 

McGovney, Irrevocable Offers, 27 HARV. 

L. REV. 644, 654-63 (1914). 373

$ 7.16

While it appears that part performance by the offeree would bind the Government to a contract so that the Government could not thereafter revoke its offer or change the order without the consent of the offeree, it is doubtful that the offeree is bound to fulfill the purchase order.52 However, if the offeree does not complete performance, it probably is not entitled to payment under the contract, its remedy, if any, for partial performance being in the nature of quantum meruit. 

The foregoing discussion will explain the reasons for the statement made earlier in this chapter that purchase orders should not be used if the circumstances are such that the contracting officer deems it desirable to bind the supplier to a contract. Where the Government is purchasing "off-the-shelf" articles for early delivery, little difficulty will ordinarily result from the use of a purchase order. But where the desired articles must be "made-to-order" or where other complexities in the procurement make it desirable to have an enforceable agreement between the parties, the purchase order should not be used. 

$7.16. Open-End Contracts: In General 

Another convenient device for shortcutting procurement is the "openend" type of contract (sometimes referred to as the "master" or “indefinite quantity" or "requirements" type of contract). This type of contract represents an agreement between the contractor and the Government concerning the terms and conditions under which the contractor will perform orders (sometimes called "task orders" or "job orders") subsequently to be issued by the Government and may or may not obligate the contractor to furnish any specific quantity of the desired supplies or services without its further consent. The open-end contract usually includes all applicable contract provisions except price, quantity, and time and place of delivery (although even the price may be specified). 

It is used to avoid the necessity of preparing and executing a series of similar contracts, and occasionally it is used as a means of decentralizing procurement. If the contractor is bound without its further consent to perform orders placed by the Government under the contract, there is the further benefit to the Government of establishing an assured source of supply and (under unusual circumstances) a firm price with respect

Wayne Corrugated Paper Co., 278 Fed. 

483 (7th Cir. 1921), the court held that an offer to purchase a large quantity of tape to be delivered weekly had been accepted by the offeree by making a number of weekly shipments and that the buyer could sue the seller for damages for failure to complete the weekly deliveries of the total amount of tape specified in the order. See also Plumb v. Campbell, 129 

Ill. 101, 107, 18 N.E. 790, 792 (1888), where the court suggested that the appellant (the offeror) could be bound in three ways: "First, by appellee engaging within a reasonable time to perform the contract on his part; second, by beginning such performance in a way which should bind him to complete it, and third, by actual performance." 374

MASTER TYPE CONTRACTS 

$7.17 to future procurements. For the sake of convenience and for want of better terms, open-end contracts under which the Government is not obligated to order any minimum amount of supplies or services are hereinafter referred to in this chapter as "master type contracts," while open-end contracts under which the Government is committed to order at least a specified minimum amount of supplies or services, or to order all its requirements for designated supplies or services for a specified period, are hereinafter referred to as "indefinite quantity" type contracts and as "requirements" type contracts, respectively. However, the reader is cautioned that these terms are not always used outside of this chapter with this distinction in mind. $7.17.

Master Type Contracts 

Master type contracts may range from the extreme, on the one hand, of requiring the contractor's acceptance in writing of each order issued by the Government to the extreme, on the other hand, of requiring the contractor to perform all orders placed by the Government under the contract, usually within a specified period of time. A common middleground approach is for the contract to provide that the contractor shall perform all orders properly placed thereunder unless it affirmatively rejects such orders within a specified period of time. The significant point to note under this type of contract is that the Government is not bound to issue any orders or to accept any of the supplies or services described in the master contract, except in accordance with orders issued by it. 

Since the Government may, at its discretion, refrain from placing any orders under the master type contract, and since the quantity of supplies or services which may be ordered and the prices to be paid are usually left open, the agreement may be objected to on the ground either that there is no consideration for the Government's promise or that the agreement is too indefinite to be enforced. Professor Williston states that "A promise to buy such a quantity of goods as the buyer may thereafter order, or to take goods in such quantities 'as may be desired,' or as the buyer 'may want' is not sufficient consideration since the buyer may refrain from buying at his option and do so without incurring legal detriment himself or benefit the other party." 53 The weight of authority is clearly in accord.54 However, it does not necessarily follow that the master type contract is unenforceable for this reason, since other consideration may be present or the need for consideration may be obviated by statute, seal or otherwise. Nor is the indefiniteness of the agreement necessarily fatal, since a means is provided for making both the quantity and the price definite. 

53 1 WILLISTON, CONTRACTS § 104 (3d ed. 

1957); accord, RESTATEMENT, CONTRACTS 

878 (1932). But see Great Northern

Railroad v. Witham, [1873] L.R. 9 C.P. 

16. 

54 For a collection of cases, see 1 WIL 

LISTON, CONTRACTS § 104 nn. 12, 13 (3d ed. 1957). 375

$ 7.17

It is difficult to generalize concerning the legal effect of the master type contract since this type of contract takes many different forms, each of which may produce a somewhat different legal result. Where the contractor's acceptance of the order is required, it seems probable that the order represents an offer by the Government and that no enforceable contract exists unless the contractor accepts the offer (order). However, in many cases the master type contract may properly be construed as a continuing offer by the contractor which the Government may accept from time to time by placing orders for specific quantities." 55

Since the master type contract does not bind the Government contractually, it follows that for appropriation purposes that the placing of each order under the contract (or the acceptance of the order by the contractor if the contract so provides) is an obligating event and must be supported by an appropriation or fund then current.5% Likewise, the placing of each order under such contracts must be supported by negotiation authority in the usual case where the order has not been entered into by means of formal advertising." If job orders or task orders are to be compensated on a cost or incentive basis, this too requires separate justification.58

The operation of the master type contract in a typical situation is illustrated by the following case: The Navy from time to time requires the repair of navigational equipment. Each repair job may be relatively small, but the aggregate of anticipated repairs is substantial. 

The contracting officer decides to use a master type contract. The contract provides that the contractor will repair such navigational equipment for the Government as the contracting officer may from time to time order under the master type contract, up to a maximum amount specified in the contract. Because the contractor cannot predict its future work load at the time the contracting officer may issue an order, the contractor reserves the right to reject any such order; however, the contract provides that unless the contractor rejects such order in writing within ten days from receipt of such order, its acceptance thereof shall be conclusively presumed. The contract provides further that all orders thereunder shall (i) refer to the master contract; (ii) contain a description of the services to be performed; (iii) state the price for such services if the price has been agreed upon by the contractor and the contracting officer prior to issuance of the order; and (iv) set forth the appropriation to which the order is chargeable. If no price has been agreed upon prior to the issuance of the order, the contractor is required, unless it intends to reject the order, to submit to the contracting officer, promptly
