Thereupon, the price for such services is determined by mutual agreement between the contractor and the contracting officer and is evidenced by a supplement to the job order signed by the parties. In the event of failure of the parties to agree on the price, the contract provides that the price will be determined in accordance with the provisions of the contract relating to disputes. The contractor is expressly enjoined from proceeding with the performance of any order until the price therefor has been determined, except that in cases where the contracting officer considers the circumstances so to require, he may direct the contractor to proceed with the performance of the order pending the determination of the price, and in such event the contractor is obligated to proceed forthwith with performance of the order. 

$ 7.18. - Indefinite Quantity Contracts 

The indefinite quantity open-end contract is similar to the master openend contract, except that it specifies a minimum and a maximum quantity of supplies or services to be purchased or sold. While the minimum is usually relatively small, it is no doubt enough to constitute sufficient consideration for the contractor's cross-promise.59 The specification of minimum and maximum quantities to be furnished under the contract also avoids the indefiniteness .which makes enforcement and proof of damages under the master type contract so difficult. However, the indefinite quantity contract is enforceable against a contractor only to the extent of its defaults in orders placed. For appropriation purposes, the indefinite quantity type contract is considered to obligate funds current as of the time each order is placed thereunder. Further, the procurement method by which the indefinite quantity contract was placed-whether by advertised competitive bidding or by the proper exercise of negotiation authority-applies to each order placed under the contract which the contractor is bound to accept, thereby obviating the necessity for justifying the method of procurement each time such an order is placed. $7.19.

The requirements type of open-end contract is similar to the indefinite quantity open-end contract except that it obligates the Government to

While Navy use of the requirements type contract is minimal, it is widely employed by the Federal Supply Service of the General Services Administration in the procurement of standard commercial supplies and services for all federal agencies and ordinarily for their mandatory use.62 Under this type of contract the purchaser's promise to take from the seller all of a particular item of supply or service which the purchaser needs or requires during a certain period is sufficient consideration for the seller's promise.63 $ 7.20. Basic Agreements

We have seen that one major purpose of the open-end form of contract is to facilitate the placing of multiple contracts with a single supplier for essentially similar supplies or services. A variation on this form of procurement simplification is known as the "basic agreement." But unlike the open-end form of contract, a basic agreement, standing alone, is never a contract since its scope is limited to a written understanding, negotiated between a military department and a particular supplier, as to what contract clauses or general provisions will be applicable to certain types of negotiated contracts as thereafter may be made between any procuring activity of the military department and that supplier during the term of the basic agreement. In short, the basic agreement is a useful way for negotiated contracts to incorporate standard clauses and general provisions by reference on a departmental-wide basis, and for a Department to negotiate and agree upon special clauses which will be applicable to certain types of negotiated contracts thereafter made by any procuring activity of the negotiating Department with a particular contractor.64 In the Navy, the use of basic agreements is authorized when multiple Navy procuring activities customarily have a number of negotiated fixed-price supply contracts with the same supplier, each with substantially similar general provisions and contract clauses.65 But

III. END PURPOSE 

$7.21. In General

It will be recalled that the third category into which we somewhat arbitrarily divided types of contracts at the beginning of this chapter covered differences in types arising out of differences in end purpose. 

It is proposed to treat this last group by selecting a few representative end products and discussing the contracts under which they are procured, principally from the standpoint of content, with emphasis where it is pertinent or particularly interesting on the historical development and principal problems of such contracts. To some extent, this part will overlap the treatment in Chapter 9 of specific types of contract clauses. 

However, the disadvantage of some slight repetition seems to the writer to be overweighed by the advantage of considering at least a few representative contracts as cohesive instruments instead of as mere collections of clauses. 

$7.22. Supply Contracts 

The Navy buys most supplies in definite quantities to established specifications and at fixed prices. The type of contract representing this synthesis of compensation, form and end product is known as the "fixedprice supply contract." It is ordinarily entered into by means of formal advertising in accordance with procedure described in Chapter 2. The essence of such a contract is the "General Provisions" (often called the "boilerplate") and the "Schedule." The General Provisions, for the most part, consist of clauses required by statute or regulation to be included in procurement contracts. The Schedule, on the other hand, represents the "tailor-made" elements of the deal that are the substance of what and on what terms the parties are buying and selling, namely, the description of the supplies and their quantity; the specifications for the manufacture of the supplies-either set forth at length or incorporated by reference; the time and place for the delivery of the supplies; the point of final inspection and acceptance of the supplies; and, of course, the contract price to be paid upon delivery and acceptance of the supplies. 

The problem of inconsistency between the Schedule and the General Provisions is obviated by a provision in the contract that, in the event of such a conflict, the Schedule shall prevail. 379

$ 7.22

*******sa.m 

Briefly summarized, the fixed-price supply contract provides that the contractor shall furnish and deliver the supplies and perform the services set forth in the Schedule for the prices stated therein. The Government reserves the right, within the general scope of the contract, to make changes in (i) the drawings, designs or specifications, (ii) the method of shipment or packing, and (iii) the place of delivery. If any such change affects the cost of, or the time required for, performance of the contract, an equitable adjustment may be made in the contract price or delivery schedule, or both. Payments are made by the Government, upon submission of properly certified invoices or vouchers, of the contract prices for supplies delivered and accepted; however, unless otherwise specified, payments are made on partial deliveries accepted by the Government when the amount due on such deliveries so warrants or, if the contractor so requests, whenever such payments would equal or exceed $1,000 or 50 percent of the total amount of the contract. The contract may provide, in addition, for payments from time to time on the basis of progress in the completion of the contract as certified by the naval inspector. All articles, materials and workmanship are expressly made subject to inspection and test by the Government during manufacture and at all other times and places, to the extent practicable. In case any article is defective in material or workmanship, the Government may reject such article or require its correction, or may require delivery of such articles at a reduced price which is equitable under the circumstances. Final inspection and acceptance are usually made at the point of delivery, but acceptance is not conclusive in respect of latent defects or fraud and does not otherwise restrict the Government's rights under any applicable guaranty. The contractor is expressly made responsible for the contract articles until they are delivered at the specified delivery point, and the contractor bears all risk on rejected articles after notice of rejection. Where final inspection is at the point of origin but delivery by the contractor is at some other point, the contractor's responsibility continues until delivery is accomplished. 

The contract provides for marking of shipments in accordance with prescribed Navy procedure and contains the customary provisions regarding assignment of claims, wages and hours of contractor employees, nondiscrimination in employment, convict labor, gratuities, examination of records, officials not to benefit, contingent fees, and disputes. 

If the Government is required to furnish any material or equipment to the contractor for the performance of the contract, the contract provides for the delivery of such material or equipment. The Government is expressly absolved of liability to the contractor for damages or loss of profit by reason of any delay in delivery or failure to deliver any or all of the government-furnished material, except that in case of such delay or failure, upon the request of the contractor, the contracting officer may 380 429

LEADING YARD ARRANGEMENTS 

$ 7.23 extend the time for the completion of performance and an equitable adjustment will be made in the contract price. If the contract is classified as "Top Secret," "Secret," or "Confidential," it will include the standard military security requirements clause relating to the safeguarding of classified information. Provisions relating to taxes, renegotiation, patents, termination for convenience and for default, foreign purchases, priorities and allocations, utilization of small business concerns in subcontracting, and liquidated damages are also included in the General Provisions to the extent required by applicable statutes, regulations and directives.

Where general guaranty provisions are deemed desirable by the contracting officer, the contract will ordinarily provide for a guaranty by the contractor that, at the time of delivery, the contract articles will be free from defects in material and workmanship and will conform to the requirements of the contract. Performance guarantees or other special guaranty provisions are seldom used.

The standard provisions of the fixed-price supply contract have been drafted in the light of the combined experience of the military departments in order to eliminate differences in treatment which are not justified by problems peculiar to a particular procuring activity or to a particular procurement. ASPR 1-10966 reflects the policy of the military departments not to permit deviations from these provisions merely because they are requested by individual suppliers. To do so would manifestly result in unequal treatment of contractors and would greatly increase the administrative burdens of the Department of the Navy.

For this reason, deviations from the uniform General Provisions to meet problems peculiar to a particular procuring activity or to a particular procurement may not be made except with the approval of the Chief of 

Naval Material. 

$7.23. Leading Yard Arrangements

Although not really a different type of contract, the leading yard arrangement represents a sufficiently novel and important variation of the supply type contract employed for the procurement of vessel construction to warrant separate mention. This arrangement is used in connection with multiple vessel construction programs under which a number of different shipbuilders are constructing the same type vessel at the same time. Under these circumstances, the Navy designates one of the private shipbuilders as the "leading yard," and the contract with that shipbuilder provides that the contractor will furnish to each of the yards constructing the same type vessel, usually called "following yards," a complete set of working plans together with such engineering services 

66 March 5, 1956. 381

$ 7.24

as may be required by the following yards or as may be specified in the contract between the Government and the leading yard. 

The contract may also designate the leading yard as the central procurement agency for materials, supplies and equipment, specified in the contracts to be centrally procured, to be used by the following yards in the construction of the vessels. As central procurement agent for the shipbuilders, the contractor places purchase orders for such materials, supplies and equipment in the name and for the account of the respective following yards, which assume all responsibilities with respect to payment. During World War II, when the central procurement arrangement was extensively used, it was necessary for the Navy Department to guarantee payment to vendors, in the event the following yard failed to make payment, in order to induce vendors to extend credit to yards to whom they may not otherwise have been willing to give credit. After 

World War II, however, and even during the Korean conflict, the Government did not guarantee payments to vendors. 

If one of the following yards is a naval shipyard, the leading yard does not procure for the naval shipyard; however, the contract with the leading yard ordinarily provides that the leading yard will furnish the naval shipyard with copies of the procurement documents used in procuring materials for the private yards. This gives the naval shipyard the advantage of the procurement work done by the leading yard even though the leading yard has no responsibility to place any actual orders for the Navy yard. To assist the Navy yards, the leading yard invites bids on quantities which include amounts needed by the Department for the vessels being built by the naval shipyard. In this way, better prices and delivery dates are obtained. The Navy Department, however, is responsible for the entire procurement including placing of orders, inspection, acceptance, and payment for all such items and the expediting thereof. 

$7.24. Ship-Repair Contracts 

No type of naval procurement presents a more difficult contracting problem than the procurement of ship-repair services in time of war or emergency. The overriding importance of getting repairs under way before accurate estimates can be prepared, and frequently before the full scope of the work has been determined, virtually precludes the successful use of the fixed-price or cost-plus-fixed-fee types of contracts for such services. It was suggested in § 7.12 that the time and material contract is the only type of contract which has been found to meet the essential requirements of these problems-however imperfectly. 

Under the impetus of the preparedness program of 1940, an open-end contract for ship repair was developed by the Navy, which provided for payment for each hour of work on a vessel at a specified hourly rate, 382

SHIP-REPAIR CONTRACTS 

$ 7.24 inclusive of labor, overhead and profit; for direct material at cost plus 10 percent; and for material from stock at cost plus 10 to 25 percent, as approved by the naval inspector, for warehousing and handling. The hourly rate was computed with respect to each of the various classifications of labor; in one instance, the schedule included 255 separate labor classifications. There was also included a schedule of drydocking and hourly rental rates for tools (even the use of scaffolding planks and paint brushes was billed at hourly rates). The rates were generally those developed by the ship repair industry during NRA days and were based on overhead rates in effect during a period when the average ship repair yard had a relatively small volume of work, hence a high ratio of overhead to labor. The contract required that an estimate of the cost of performing each job be included in the related job order, the sum of the estimates applicable to any vessel becoming the ceiling beyond which the Government would not be obligated to reimburse the contractor. 

Largely because of the distorted overhead rates, this type of contract in practice produced excessive profits and was generally unsatisfactory in operation. To meet this problem, the contract was revised in 1941 to provide for quarterly prospective adjustment of the billing rates, upward or downward. In order to avoid the necessity of adjusting each individual hourly rate in each contract each quarter, a system of discounts was devised. The discount was negotiated on the basis of the contractor's actual experience for the preceding quarter and was always applied prospectively only. Following negotiation of the discount, the contract was amended to establish the new rate for the succeeding quarter. 

The use of many different hourly rates for various classifications resulted in a tremendous volume of detailed work in computing and auditing billings. A survey made at the time of various ship repair yards to determine the average prime labor cost per hour disclosed that the variations between yards and between ships of various sizes were insignificant. 

A composite billing rate was therefore adopted for all labor, the cost of dry docking and use of tools being allocated to overhead which was applied to each hour of labor billed. This change greatly simplified the administration of the contract.

During this period, the War Shipping Administration had been using the Navy form of time and material ship-repair contract with the important exception that it did not provide a ceiling on the cost of each job order. The Comptroller General objected that the War Shipping 

Administration form of contract violated the statutory prohibition against the cost-plus-percentage-of-cost system of contracting and advised War Shipping Administration to revise this form of contract to remove such objection.67 In his letter to the Chairman of the Maritime 

67 Comp. Gen. Dec. A-51647, Aug. 28, 1942 (unpubl.). 503533 0-59—27 383

$ 7.24

Commission, the Comptroller General expressly called attention to the procedure followed by the Navy, referring with approval to the proviso that the estimated cost represented the maximum amount which the Government was required to pay for the work. The War Shipping Administration, however, took the position that it was impossible to estimate the cost of work in advance and that the ceiling was, therefore, unrealistic. The efforts of the War Shipping Administration to develop and draft a new type of ship-repair contract eventually involved the Army and Navy, and the project became a joint enterprise. Out of this joint effort came the Master Time and Material Ship Repair Contract. 

The Master Time and Material Ship Repair Contract was placed in use by the War Department, the Navy Department, and the War Shipping Administration on July 1, 1943, and replaced other forms of shiprepair and alteration contracts in use in the several agencies prior to such date. The contract followed the general structure of the master type open-end contract and provided for the issuance of job orders from time to time by the naval inspector. The contract continued by its terms, subject to the availability of appropriations, for the period of World War II and for six months thereafter, unless sooner terminated. 

There was no provision in the Master Time and Material Ship Repair 

Contract for estimates on job orders or a ceiling on the total amount to be paid by the Government. Instead, the contract provided that the contracting officer might require the contractor after the end of each calendar quarter or any shorter fiscal period, or after completion and billing for all work on an individual vessel, to negotiate the price to be paid for work billed during such quarter or shorter time or on such vessel. If within 30 days after commencing such negotiations the parties were unable to agree upon the price, the contract provided for submission of the question to the Secretary of the Navy (or Secretary of War or War Shipping Administrator, as appropriate).

Under the Master Time and Material Ship Repair Contract, payments were made to the contractor for work done under job orders on the basis of a single composite hourly billing rate for labor, which was arrived at by dividing labor cost plus overhead for the previous quarter by the number of payable hours (pay of employees converted to hours at their respective straight-time rates of pay) of labor, and adding to the quotient so obtained an allowance for profit on labor, overhead and material. In addition to the amount computed by application of the billing rate, the contractor was (i) reimbursed, without further profit, for the cost of direct materials, for payments under approved subcontracts and for payments to third persons for the use of temporary facilities, tools and equipment and services hired for the performance of any part of the work with the approval of and at the rate approved by the naval inspector, and (ii) compensated for dry dock, marine railway, floating 384

SHIP-REPAIR CONTRACTS 

$ 7.24 derrick- and tug boat services furnished to the vessel at rates approved by the naval cost inspector. 

Within 45 days after the end of each calendar quarter during the life of the contract, the contractor was required to submit a comprehensive report to the contracting officer with respect to its operating experience and costs during the preceding quarter. On the basis of such reports and any other available information, the parties agreed to negotiate in good faith to determine a revised billing rate, such revised rate to be effective from a date not earlier than the end of the preceding quarter. 

If the parties failed to agree within 75 days after the end of the preceding quarter, the revised rate for the applicable quarter was determined by the appropriate Secretary or Administrator after consideration of the recommendation of a board composed of representatives of the three interested government activities. 

The original Master Time and Material Ship Repair Contract con tained a "recapture clause" pursuant to which the contracting officer could require the contractor to repay any profits earned under the contract during the preceding year which were deemed by the contracting officer to be excessive, provided that the contractor could not be required to repay an amount which would reduce its profit to less than 10 percent of its cost. Thus, if the contractor earned in excess of 10 percent of allowable costs for any one year, it was required to refund the excess; but if the contract yielded less than 10 percent, no adjustment was made to cover the deficit. This provision was revised in 1945 to permit the 

Government to recapture (1) profits in excess of 7 percent of the first $4,000,000 and 62 percent of the balance of costs, if the total of costs under the contract during the related year aggregated less than $25,000,000 and (2) all profits in excess of 62 percent of costs, if the total of all costs under the contract during the related year, including the first $4,000,000 of cost, aggregated more than $25,000,000. 

It will be seen from the foregoing that great strides were made between 1940 and 1943 in the development of a type of ship repair contract which would permit repair work to be performed with the expedition required in time of war and with a minimum of administrative burden, and at the same time would protect the Government against exorbitant prices. 

To a reasonable degree, each of these objectives was attained. The 

Navy was less successful in its efforts to provide an inducement to ship repair contractors to reduce their costs. It must be recognized that the Master Time and Material Ship Repair Contract did not provide any compensation incentive to contractors to cut costs.68 To the con-

In the early 1950's, it was considered desirable that a uniform Master Fixed-Price Ship Repair Contract be developed for use by the military departments. As a result, the military departments adopted a new standardized form of Master Contract for Repair and Alteration of 

Vessels (DD Form 731), and its use was prescribed by ASPR 16-503 

commencing in November 1953. A Job Order Form (DD Form 731-1), by its terms subject to the provisions of the master contract, was also issued for use in conjunction with the master contract. This contract and the job order form are used for both advertised and negotiated procurements.

As in the case of the 1945 fixed-price contract form, an effort was made in the ASPR fixed-price ship repair contract to meet the problem of urgent work and the problem of unknown work. The master contract provides, concerning urgent work, that the contractor shall perform work on a vessel, within its capabilities, on the basis of a written order issued by the contracting officer whenever the contracting officer determines that a vessel, its cargo or stores would be endangered by delay or that military necessity requires immediate performance of work on a vessel, and that the price of the work shall be mutually agreed upon as soon as practicable after the job order is issued. With respect to unknown work, the contract provides that, if the nature of any repairs is such that their extent and probable cost are not readily ascertainable, an agreed price job order may be issued for the work necessary to determine the nature and extent of repairs; then, upon the determination of the nature and extent of repairs, the contractor shall perform such work as may be determined by the contracting officer necessary to accomplish the repairs specified in a job order, the price for such work to be mutually agreed upon. In either instance, if the contractor and the contracting officer are unable to agree on the price of the work, the disputed question of price constitutes a dispute and is treated in accordance with the procedure stated in the "Disputes" clause of the contract. 

$7.25. Civil Construction Contracts 

The construction, alteration, restoration, and repair of real property constituting the naval shore establishment are accomplished under civil construction contracts. Construction contracts encompass such diverse projects as buildings, roads, airfields, piers, docks, ship channels and berths, dry docks, graving docks, ammunition dumps, railroads, cranes, power, gas, telephone and other utility lines, and water and sewage treatment systems. For particular purposes, the term "construction con- 387

$7.25

tract" may have a special meaning. For example, under the Davis- 

Bacon Act 69 prescribing minimum wages, the term applies to "painting and decorating" as well as to construction, alteration, and repair work. 

Civil construction for the Navy Department may be undertaken on either a cost-plus-fixed-fee or a fixed-price basis. In the latter event, the fixed price generally represents a lump sum which the contractor receives for the complete job; but frequently, particularly in the case of dredging, excavation and road projects, where neither the total amount of work nor the amount of the different classes of work making up the total can be accurately estimated, the contract will provide for payment on a "unit price basis" under which the contractor is paid a stated amount per cubic yard, or other measure, for each class of work specified. Occasionally, a construction contract combines "lump sum" and "unit price" features, either by providing a lump sum for a part of the work and unit prices for the balance or by providing for adjustment of the overall lump sum on a unit price basis in the event of variations between the contract estimates for specified classes of work and the actual quantities of such classes of work. More rarely "lump sum" contracts incorporate elements of the "time and material contract," as in the case of a contract under which the contractor receives, in addition to a lump sum for building construction, an hourly rate for furnishing expert supervision of equipment installation. 

10 U.S.C. § 2304 does not authorize the negotiation of contracts for the construction or repair of buildings, roads, sidewalks, sewers, mains, or similar items unless the contract is to be performed outside the continental United States or unless the contract is negotiated pursuant to exceptions (1) (national emergency), (2) (public exigency), (3) (under not more than $2,500), (10) (competition impracticable), (11) (experimental, developmental and research work), (12) (classified projects), or (15) (negotiation after advertising) to the requirement of the Armed Services Procurement Act for procurement by formal advertising.70 In addition, current Military Construction Authorization Acts" require competition so far as practicable and consistent with the national security and the Armed Services Procurement Act. Except for contracts not in excess of $2,500, the authority to negotiate construction contracts is seldom in fact utilized under current conditions. The rare exceptions arise in cases of sudden damage or other public exigency where the need for repair does not allow time for advertising; in the case of overseas work where there is a lack of reliable cost experience; and in cases of rehabilitation and repair projects where the scope of the work cannot be determined in advance of performance. CIVIL CONSTRUCTION CONTRACTS 

$7.25 and the Executive Branch have long decried the use of costly cost-plusfixed-fee contracts in the military construction program. Generally speaking, there is little or no justification for the use of such contracts except in highly technical construction or in the construction of facilities in isolated and previously unknown areas. 972 Although the Armed Services Procurement Act permits the payment under a cost-plus-a-fixed-fee contract (other than for research and development work, or for architectural or engineering services for a public work or utility) of a fee not in excess of 10 percent of the estimated cost of performance of the contract 73 and although ASPR 3-404.3 (c) generally limits the fee to 7 percent of such estimated cost,74 it is Navy practice to limit fees on construction contracts to a substantially smaller percentage.

The problem of defining and determining reimbursable costs under cost-plus-fixed-fee construction contracts differs from that under supply contracts in that practically all of the work, except the furnishing of equipment and materials by suppliers, is performed on the site by a labor, supervisory, and administrative organization specifically mobilized for the purpose. Such costs are inherently segregated, and no problem of apportionment exists. The only indirect expenses of the contractor are those for operating and maintaining its permanent "central office" organization and these are small enough to be absorbed as part of the contractor's fee. ASPR 15-404 (b) accordingly expressly disallows reimbursement of "central office expenses of the contractor, such as supplies, equipment, rent, or any other expenses incident to its maintenance and operation except to the extent authorized by the contracting officer." 75 

In this way, the difficult problems of allocating overhead, inventory and general costs incident to cost-reimbursement supply contracts are avoided on construction contracts.

Examples of items of allowable costs for cost-reimbursement type construction contracts are listed in ASPR 15-403. They include such items peculiar to construction as camp operation, temporary use of land and structures, restoration and clean-up of site and facilities, structures and facilities of a temporary nature, and on-site recreation activities. In order to maintain close control over reimbursable costs under such contracts, provision is ordinarily made for the prior written approval of the contracting officer for all subcontracts, all purchases in excess of $500, and certain equipment rentals from third parties. 

A contractor is not expected to make a profit on cost-reimbursement type construction contracts except out of the fixed fee. Accordingly, the contract provides for the determination of rental reimbursement for

No standard form of contract is prescribed for cost-reimbursement construction contracts. $ 7.25 tracts the possibility that conditions may differ from those described in the specifications or that unknown conditions may be discovered during the performance of the work. It is apparent that a contractor who has bid on the reasonable assumption that only dirt was to be excavated may be financially ruined if it is required to remove rock at the same price. If the risk of changed or unknown conditions is forced upon the contractor, the contractor may be expected to protect itself by adding large contingencies to its fixed-price quotations. For this reason, it is considered better business for the Government to assume the risk. This is accomplished by the Changed Conditions clause which provides for an equitable adjustment in the contract price or completion date where the contractor promptly and before the conditions are disturbed notifies the contracting officer in writing of "(1) subsurface or latent physical conditions at the site differing materially from those indicated in this contract, or (2) unknown physical conditions at the site, of an unusual nature, differing materially from those ordinarily encountered and generally recognized as inhering in work of the character provided for in this contract." In the latest revision of this clause, the word "physical" was added to make it clear that the clause applies only to changed material conditions and does not include changes in prices, delays in delivery of materials, or alterations in use of the site, as some contractors had previously claimed.83 In the light of bidding instructions requiring the contractor to visit the site of the work, the provision regarding unknown conditions is generally interpreted so as to charge the contractor with notice of anything he should have discovered by reasonable investigation. 

Finally, the requirement that the contracting officer be notified before existing physical conditions are disturbed is intended to give the contracting officer an opportunity to verify the alleged changed condition and to make such changes in the project as he may deem advisable. 

Construction and supply contracts also differ in their use of payment and performance bonds. While their use is discretionary in connection with supply contracts and with cost-reimbursement type construction contracts,84 they are required by the Miller Act for all fixed-price construction contracts over $2,000 in amount.85 The payment bond is intended to give contractors, employers and material men the same security that they ordinarily have under state mechanic's lien laws, but which, because of the Government's constitutional immunity, they do not have on Federal property or work.86 The penal sums for payment bonds run from 50 percent of the contract price for contracts under $1,000,000 and 40 per-

$ 7.26. Architectural and Engineering Services Contracts 

This type of contract is used to procure the services of civil and marine architects and engineers, as the case may be, (i) for the production of construction designs, plans, drawings, and specifications, such services being referred to as "architectural-engineering services," and (ii) for miscellaneous engineering services such as topographic surveys, soil testing, construction supervision, and preparation of "as built" drawings or models, the latter type of services being referred to as "engineering services." The terms "architectural-engineering services" and "engineering services" are used hereafter in this section as words of art in accordance with the foregoing definitions. 

Express authority for the procurement of "architectural-engineering services" is contained in section 3 of the Act of April 25, 1939,88 (hereinafter called "the 1939 Act"), while authority for the procurement of "engineering services" is provided by section 15 of the Act of August 2, 1946.89 

Under the 1939 Act, outside architectural services may be procured only "whenever the Secretary of the Navy believes that the existing facilities of the Department of the Navy are inadequate and he considers... [such procurement] advantageous to national defense." 90 Whether these requirements are present in any individual procurement depends upon the nature, location, urgency and magnitude of the project, and the current volume of work by naval personnel. In general, outside architects-engineers are retained in the majority of large projects involving the construction, alteration and repair of naval facilities. During World 

War II and the Korean Emergency, outside naval architectural-engineering services were frequently procured by separate direct contract in con-

At the present time, direct contracts for this purpose are still sometimes used; however, it is the more common practice to provide in vessel contracts for such services to be furnished by the shipbuilder, or its approved design agent, incident to the construction of the vessel. 

The 1939 Act provides further that "the fee for any service under this Section may not exceed 6 percent of the estimated cost, as determined by the Secretary, of the project to which the fee applies." " This ambiguous language immediately posed the question whether the fee subject to the 6 percent limitation included or excluded the architectengineer's costs. The Department of the Army, operating under a similar statute, took the position that the statute required only that the architect-engineer's fee, exclusive of his costs, be within 6 percent of the estimated cost of the project. However, the Comptroller General rejected this interpretation, holding, with a few minor exceptions (e.g. reimbursement for authorized travel), that the total of all payments made to the architect-engineer could not exceed 6 percent of the estimated cost of the project." The Comptroller General's view was followed by § 4(b) of the Armed Services Procurement Act which, as now codified in 10 U.S.C. § 2306 (d),94 provides that "The fee for performing a costplus-a-fixed-fee contract for achitectural or engineering services for a public work or utility plus the cost of those services to the contractor may not be more than 6 percent of the estimated cost of that work or project, not including fees." Hence, it is now clear that the gross payments to the architect-engineer, whether on a lump-sum or a cost-plusfixed-fee basis, may not exceed 6 percent of the estimated project cost, exclusive of the fixed fee if the project is performed on a cost-plus-afixed-fee basis. In applying these statutes, a sharp distinction must therefore be drawn between the word "fee" and the words "fixed fee," as used in contracts for achitectural-engineering services, and also between the term "contract cost" and the term "project cost." 

The Comptroller General has construed the 6 percent limitation of the 1939 Act as applicable only to architectural-engineering services and not to engineering services, and has permitted the gross fee in a contract for combined architectural-engineering and engineering services to exceed 6 percent where that part of the fee which is based upon the architectural-engineering services was affirmatively shown to be less than 6 percent.95 This construction was based upon the fact that the 1939 Act referred only to the "production and delivery of designs, plans, drawings, and specifications." In this connection, it is pertinent to note that, even in the absence of specific statutory authority, the Comptroller General has recognized an "implied powers" rule of government administration under which engineering services essential to the accomplishment of an authorized project may be procured out of funds appropriated for the project, provided that such services are not in the nature of personal services for which civil service personnel under the Classification Act are available. 

In distinguishing between personal and nonpersonal services, the Comptroller General has considered the following factors: (1) the degree of direct government supervision, (2) the furnishing of equipment and supplies, (3) the furnishing of office or working space, (4) the use of special knowledge or equipment, (5) the temporary character of services which no government employee is qualified or available to perform, (6) whether the fee or contract price is based upon the results to be accomplished rather than the time actually worked, and (7) whether the amount paid as compensation covers not only the contractor's time but the use of his facilities, office staff, equipment, etc.'

$7.27. Utility Contracts 

Utility contracts are used for the procurement of various services such as electricity, gas, water, sewage disposal, and steam necessary to operate the Naval Shore Establishment. In rare cases, services may be available from several suppliers and may, therefore, be procured by formal advertising. Ordinarily, however, the supplier of a utility is the sole source of such services in a particular area, and, in such a case, the procurement of utility services would be negotiated pursuant to 10 U.S.C. § 2304 (a) (10).³

Utility rates and other conditions of services are generally governed by public regulation. Services to the Government in areas under State jurisdiction are generally subject to the same regulatory control as service to private consumers. Even in the absence of regulated rates, the 

Government is protected against unjust discrimination by common-law rule in the case of private utility companies, and by statutory and administrative restrictions in case of local municipalities.5 

Because of the many differences in local Navy needs, public regulations, and other conditions of services, several procedures have been evolved to permit procurement of utilities in the simplest and most efficient way adequate for the purpose. When the rates are regulated by a public body, or when the annual amount involved does not exceed the open market limitation within the fiscal year, services may be procured without a formal contract. In such cases, a simple letter or memorandum of request will suffice, and the obligation against appropriations is considered to accrue as the service is rendered. 

These informal procedures are generally helpful and adequate for a large number of small routine transactions. Frequently, however, a contract will be more advantageous to the Government even though the service is a regulated one.

If a utility company is in a position to serve a number of activities, "area service" contracts may be entered into. This may be done by the 

Navy when only Navy activities are concerned, or by the General Services Administration when other federal agencies are involved. Each Navy activity may then fulfill its individual requirements by placing an order under such "area service" contract in the same manner as orders are placed under GSA Federal Supply Schedule Contracts or other "openend" contracts. A standard form (DD Form 1155) must be used for such order except when a special form is prescribed by the contract itself." 

For small individual contracts requiring no special facilities, a stand ard Short Form Utility Service Contract (DD Form 671) is prescribed for use. This is a one-page form which, in essence, merely designates the point, classification, and scheduled rate of service and includes, in addition to the necessary contract "boilerplate," provision for automatic escalation of the rate in accordance with any change approved by regu latory commission.

For large contracts, the Navy uses a Long Form Utility Service Contract (NavDocks 504) which has been coordinated with the Army and Air Force. In addition to "boilerplate," this form provides for detailed service specifications, "most favored" consumer treatment, and extensive clauses dealing with rate changes, service facilities, technical provisions, and connection charges. This form merely furnishes a guide or starting point for negotiation of the special provisions. They may be changed in the course of negotiation to meet local needs and conditions, regulatory requirements, or company demands. Sometimes a special contract must be tailor-made for the transaction, as in the case of contracts providing for connection of private and Navy utility plants and lines and interchange of service, or for bilateral standby emergency service, or for wheeling or transportation of service from a distant government source connected by company lines with the Navy activity. 

Utility services are usually chargeable against annual maintenance appropriations which ordinarily cannot be obligated beyond the current fiscal year. However, in order to avoid the burden of affirmative renewals from year to year, utility contracts usually provide for the furnishing of service "until further notice" or "until terminated at the option of the Government." This is done on the basis of a ruling by the Comptroller General that such contracts do not impose an obligation upon the Government until the services are actually used and therefore do not obligate the Government beyond the current fiscal year.10 Utility contracts accordingly may run on indefinitely, and provision is therefore made for changes in regulated rates or rates of "most favored" consumers.

In special cases, the Navy is authorized, to enter into a firm commitment for a term up to ten years." This may be done where lower rates, larger discounts, or more favorable conditions of service are obtained, where connection or special facility charges are eliminated or reduced, or where the utility refuses to render service except under a firm long term contract. 

If utility service requirements are large, and if extensive connecting lines or other facilities are needed to furnish the desired service, the supplier may require the payment of a connection charge unless otherwise assured of continued use of service over a period long enough to amortize the company's investment. The connection charge is paid by the Government after completion of the installation. In consideration of such payment, the Government is usually granted a "rate concession" in the form of a credit of a specified percentage or fixed amount on each monthly bill until the total connection charge has been credited. The connection charge is, in effect, a guarantee that the Government will purchase sufficient service to reimburse the supplier for the expense of providing the service. Title to the facilities for which a connection charge is paid ordinarily remains in the supplier which is in the best position to maintain and assume responsibility therefor. Nevertheless, the connection charge is considered a proper service charge and, on this basis, is approved by the Comptroller General.¹2 

Because of the monopoly position occupied by the utility supplier, it is in a strong bargaining position in negotiating with the Government. While this circumstance is tempered somewhat by the fact that rates and some of the other terms of service are generally set by public regulation, it tends to make it difficult to compose differences when they do arise, as sometimes happens when the Navy seeks to include standard provisions such as the nondiscrimination clause.

Disclosure by Inspection or Analysis of Related Product Secrecy in Fact $8.1. Introduction: A Forward Look 

Outstanding manifestations of what research and development means to our national defense are all around us. On January 17, 1955, when the submarine NAUTILUS cast off at Groton, Connecticut, and signalled "Underway on nuclear power," the operational use of atomic power for ship propulsion had become a reality. The numerous records which the 

NAUTILUS and later nuclear-powered submarines have set since then are just some of the events which give convincing proof that we are in the midst of an era of unprecedented change in our naval power. 

In May 1955, the NAUTILUS completed a fully-submerged 1,300 mile voyage from New London, Connecticut, to San Juan, Puerto Rico. In 

August 1956, the prototype reactor of the NAUTILUS completed a sustained 66-day-and-night full power run. In January 1957, this submarine completed its second year of operation on the original charge of uranium fuel; and it was not until March 1957 that it was refueled for the first time after 62,562 miles of operation.

Before the close of 1958, the NAUTILUS not only had more than doubled the above mileage but had completed its most significant voyage. Commencing at 2 a.m. on July 23, 1958, the NAUTILUS headed north from 401

Pearl Harbor and travelled submerged 2,900 miles through the narrow Bering Strait between Alaska and Soviet Siberia. Off the coast, at 

Point Barrow, Alaska, the NAUTILUS surfaced for a brief navigational check and to overcome the combination of difficulties encountered in the heavily ridged ice above and the shallow water below the vessel, as it made its way through the Chukchi Sea. After twenty-four hours of discouraging effort, the NAUTILUS located a tongue of the Deep Barrow 

Submarine Canyon, previously discovered by icebreakers. Armed with the knowledge that this would lead to the even deeper Arctic Ocean, her captain, Cdr. Anderson, ordered the dive which enabled the NAUTILUS to complete a further 2,114-mile history-making voyage under the Polar Ice Cap, charting the course of a new Trans-Arctic seaway. It passed under the North Pole, at 11: 15 p.m. (E.D.T.), on August 3, 1958. After thus joining the company of earlier polar explorers like Perry, Byrd, and Floyd Bennett, it emerged from under the ice and surfaced some 36 hours later in the Greenland Sea, between Greenland and Spitsbergen. 

In the process of completing history's first transpolar voyage, the world's first atomic submarine managed to change fiction to reality barely a century after Jules Verne's NAUTILUS was taken under the Antarctic ice by Captain Nemo.

A few days after completion of this epic voyage,' the Navy's third nuclear submarine, SKATE, entered beneath the Polar Ice Cap from the Atlantic side. During 10 days of under-ice studies, it surfaced nine times in open leads to gather information about weather and ice, once within 40 miles of the North Pole. It twice reached the Pole and made a complete circle around it, thereby going "around the world" in less than 50 minutes. The NAUTILUS and SKATE both sounded the Arctic depths, sometimes finding variances of as much as a mile between estimated and actual depths, the NAUTILUS alone compiling over 11,000 soundings. Both also measured salinity, temperatures, and ice thicknesses. Although the mass of data has yet to be evaluated, enough is now known to establish that both the volume of ice present in the region and the ruggedness of its under surface are much greater than anyone had previously suspected.2

On October 6, 1958, the Navy's second nuclear-powered submarine, the SEA WOLF, Surfaced in the Atlantic after being submerged continuously on a voyage from New London, Connecticut, for 60 consecutive days. 

This doubled the submersion record of the NAUTILUS of 30 days, which previously had been surpassed only by the 31-day record of the SKATE.

INTRODUCTION 

$ 8.1 ing apace. And the Navy has under construction a nuclear-powered guided missile cruiser as well as an 85,000-ton attack aircraft carrier of the Forrestal class. Also, nuclear-powered frigates armed with guided missiles are now planned to take their places with the fleet, thereby reviving in modernized form the class of vessels between the destroyer and the cruiser.

The Polaris fleet ballistic missile is fast approaching the point where, with the aid of launching devices to be placed on nuclear-powered submarines and on surface vessels, it can provide a most versatile means of delivering payloads of tremendous striking power without diminishing the quality of mobility which has always been the hallmark of naval power.

Confident predictions are also made that the day of nuclear-powered aircraft is approaching. On this subject, Research Reviews, published by the Navy's Office of Naval Research, has this to say: 

The airplane when it flies will be capable of a range limited only by crew endurance. It will completely destroy the distance barrier. There appears to be no ... limitation which will prevent the ultimate achievement of speeds now anticipated for large chemical powered aircraft. 3 In the fall and winter of 1957-58, with the vast potentialities of the Atomic Age only partially tapped, the world suddenly found itself plunged with shocking suddenness into the Space Age. On October 4, 1957, while sixty-four nations were engaged in a cooperative venture to study the earth, its crust, and the space around it, under the designation "The International Geophysical Year," a new word “sputnik" ³ became emblazoned in our memories, as well as in our language, almost from the moment that Russian scientists crossed the threshold of space with their man-made earth satellite. The impact of that event was followed in less than a month by Sputnik II. Fortunately, however, before 

1958 had grown very old, three satellites launched by the United States. were also put in orbit around the earth. The smallest in size, but by no means the least of these, is the first test satellite of Project Vanguard sponsored by the Navy's Office of Naval Research. With its unique solar batteries deriving power from the sun for its radio transmitter, which will be transmitting space data to generations yet unborn, Vanguard I has achieved an orbit which, predictions indicate, will permit it to remain in space indefinitely. Also, the elaborate minitrack system set up under Project Vanguard locates radio signals from the various satellites in orbit around the earth and, by this means, acquires much helpful data relative to the space around us. 

3 From "sputnik zemli," Russian for "satellite of the earth." 403

$ 8.

There will undoubtedly be a number of additional man-made satellites completing their orbits around the earth in periods of time ranging from one-and-a-half to two-and-a-half hours. Much speculation and, undoubtedly, much sound prediction, are made of "man-made satellites" orbiting around the moon or the sun, "space platforms," "space ships," "trips to the moon," "trips to Mars," and "trips to other far-distant planets." Before these and similar predictions can become realities, solutions must be found for many problems, such as "environmental problems,” “landing problems," "return take-off problems," and "reentry problems." While the possibility of these predictions becoming realities may now seem fantastic, no prudent person can say with confidence that they are any more remote than was once said of the prediction that the earth is round.

These numerous recent achievements of research and development, as well as the goals which have been set for the years immediately ahead, are but the most recent steps in man's climb to expand the frontiers of knowledge-and thus to master his environment. 

No one seriously doubts that the goals which already have been achieved will be multiplied many times over as the years go by. In making any evaluation of what the future holds, a look at the past can provide a helpful guide. An attempt is made in the next section to provide such a guide. 

$ 8.2. Historical Background 

Research and development are not new to the Navy; nevertheless, the vast sums that are today made available for these purposes would have staggered the imagination of Navy pioneers. 

As long ago as 1813, Secretary of the Navy William Jones took a great interest in technical problems. He approved Uriah Brown's submarine, and gave Robert Fulton financial assistance in the development of a torpedo, a bulletproof boat, and the steam frigate DEMOLOGOS. In 

1830, the Depot of Charts and Instruments was established in the Department to carry on observations in astronomy, magnetism, and meteorology. In 1838, the Navy sent out its first exploring expedition, under 

Lt. Charles Wilkes. In 1840, a joint board of Army and Navy officers was appointed to supervise the experiments of Edwin A. and John C. 

Stevens in developing laminated armor. In 1841, Congress appropriated $50,000 for testing improvements in naval ordnance.

In 1842, Congress appropriated $15,000 for continuing Col. Samuel 

Colt's experiments on an electrically-detonated torpedo. With this, Colt succeeded in destroying a schooner five miles away and a 300-ton brig in 

New York Harbor. 

404

HISTORICAL BACKGROUND 

$ 8.2 

In 1879, the Navy allocated $2,000 for experiments to determine the velocity of light. With the funds so provided, Master A. A. Michelson, USN, completed development of his phototachometer, conducted measurements from Fort Whipple (now Fort Myer, Virginia) to the Naval Observatory and to the foot of the Washington Monument and determined the velocity of light to an accuracy of 1 part in 10,000. From this noteworthy beginning, Michelson went on to become the first American Nobel 

Prize winner in physics. 

In the '80's and '90's, under a series of contracts placed with industrial concerns, the Navy was instrumental in developing a domestic steel armor and heavy ordnance industry, thus freeing the nation from its dependence on foreign sources for these supplies. Under these contracts, the Creusot method of manufacturing steel plate was developed, the Harveyized steel plate introduced, and other substantial improvements in the processing of armor plate were brought about. 

In 1885, Secretary of the Navy William C. Whitney made this significant statement:

A naval vessel at the present moment is a product of science. Taking the world over, it will be found that each part of her her armor, her armament, her power, her form, and the distribution of her parts or characteristics-each of these features of the completed vessel is absorbing from year to year the exclusive study of a class of scientific men. And as men of science throughout the world are continually stimulated to new discoveries and inventions, no vessel that can be built can be considered a finality in any particular. 

The problem of keeping pace with the march of improvement in these lines of industry is one of incalculable difficulty; and yet unless the Government is prepared to avail itself promptly of all the improvements that are made in the construction and equipment of its ships its expenditures are largely useless. 

It is of little service to a nation to have any navy at all unless it is a fair expression of the highest scientific resources of its day. The destructive power of the modern implements has become so great as to dominate in actual warfare. The bravest and best commander is helpless without them.

For the construction and maintenance of such a navy we have made but little provision.* 

Except for the last sentence, Secretary Whitney's statement is as true in 1958 as it was in 1885. The Navy today is very much alive to the necessity of scientific research and development. The President's budget for the fiscal year 1960 allocates over 970 million dollars for these and related purposes within the Navy.5

The Role of the Lawyer 

Since most research and development work is done under contract, the Navy lawyer must be thoroughly familiar not only with the laws pertaining to government contracts generally, but also with those having special application to research and development contracts. Perhaps the biggest challenge confronting the lawyer in connection with research and development contracts is the fact that each day brings new problems which have to be decided on their own facts with little in the way of guidance from the realm of precedent. Here the challenge frequently calls for all of the skill and ingenuity that the resourceful lawyer can commandnot only in draftsmanship alone but also in the broader fields of counselling, negotiation, and conciliation. 

This chapter will consider some of the problems of concern to the lawyer in the research and development field. First, we shall look at the Navy's authority to conduct research and development by contract and by other means, and then, in order, Department of Defense and Navy organization for conducting research and development, types and methods of contracting, contract clauses and related considerations, and finally some special problems involving property and facilities, insurance and indemnity, and patents, copyrights, and data. 

I. AUTHORITY TO CONDUCT RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT BY CONTRACT AND OTHERWISE A. SUBSTANTIVE AUTHORITY $ 8.4. Prior to World War II 

Prior to World War II, authority to conduct naval research and development was implied from the general procurement authority of the Navy and its Bureaus," and from the purposes set forth in the annual appropriation acts. Reliance was also placed on the general rule that an appropriation to accomplish a specific purpose is available for all expenditures which fiscal year, the President proposes that funds aggregating $187,920,000 for test and evaluation activities formerly carried on under various other Navy appropriations now be included with funds formerly carried under the head "Research and Development," and that the designation of that head be changed to 

"Research, Development, Test, and Eval uation, Navy." Development of this phase of the Navy budget is discussed under § 8.19 infra. Compare, also, the proposed rearrangement of all appropriations for the Department of Defense in terms of major purposes rather than of organizational units. The broad cate gories are: (1) military personnel; (2) operation and maintenance; (3) procurement; and (4) research, development, test, and evaluation. See Budget Message of the President, for the fiscal year ending June 30, 1960, wherein he states, at page M32: "This rearrangement will permit consideration of the Department of Defense Budget on a more uniform and more clearly understandable basis.

Gradually, however, the appropriation acts began to carry language specifying research, experimental, or developmental work as one of the objects for which funds were being appropriated. However, appropriation language of this character raised the question of whether it carried with it implied authority to contract for research and development or whether such authority was restricted to carrying on such work in government facilities. 

Substantive authority, of a sort, for research and development was afforded by section 10 (k) of the Aircraft Procurement Act of 1926 which authorized the purchase of designs, aircraft, aircraft parts, and aeronautical accessories, necessary for experimental purposes in the development of the best kinds of these items for the Army or Navy. Similarly, the statute establishing the Ship Model Basin, authorized the Bureau of 

Ships to "conduct at the David W. Taylor Model Basin... investigations to determine the most suitable shapes and forms for United States vessels and aircraft and investigation of other problems of their design." 10

But generally speaking, prior to World War II, authority for research and development contracting was scattered, haphazard, and vague. 

$ 8.5. During World War II Title II of the First War Powers Act was originally enacted on Decem ber 18, 1941. It provided that the President could "authorize any department or agency of the Government exercising functions in connection with the prosecution of the war effort, in accordance with regulations prescribed by the President . . ., to enter into contracts . . . without regard to the provision of law relating to the making of contracts whenever he deems that such action would facilitate the prosecution of the war." 11

$ 8.7. Project Orders and Economy Act Orders 

Project orders 30 are described in § 4.24 supra. Navy research and development projects are considered proper purposes for the issuance of project orders. However, maintenance and operation of research and development facilities, such as laboratories or test stations, are not proper purposes.

The activity receiving the project order must be in a position to handle the work itself or perform a substantial portion of it. Hence, the making of subcontracts under a project order which equal or are almost equal to the total amount thereof is prohibited. These restrictions serve to prevent the abuse of the project order as a device for "banking" appropriations in order to make them available for obligation for a longer period than intended under the law.

Although project orders are to all intents and purposes like contracts, it is not customary to issue long and complicated contractual instruments since the parties are, in fact, governmental activities. The order is usually a short document describing the work in summary fashion. 

Economy Act" orders are described in § 4.25 supra. Their similarity and dissimilarity to project orders are explained fully in that section. 

They are available for research and development work. A typical example would be the issuance of an Economy Act order by the Office of Naval Research on the National Bureau of Standards to perform in its own laboratories, or to have performed through one of its established contractors, an experimental or test phase of an overall research and development contract being conducted by the Office of Naval Research.

Another example would be an order placed by the Bureau of Ships on the Atomic Energy Commission for reactor components in connection with a nuclear-powered vessel to be developed by that Bureau. 

The placing of such an order would put the Atomic Energy Commission in a position to fill the order by placing a contract with the same contractors that are then engaged in developing a land-based reactor for the Atomic Energy Commission as part of its overall program of fostering the exploitation of industrial and other uses of atomic energy. 

In this way, the Bureau of Ships would be able to take advantage of the most recent developments in the field and, at the same time, probably save considerable time and money in proceeding with its own program. Of course, Bureau of Ships funds would be made available to the Atomic Energy Commission to pay for the components. 

§ 8.8. Authority To Make Grants for the Support of Research 

The Act of September 6, 1958,32 conferred on the military departments authority to make grants to nonprofit institutions of higher education or to other nonprofit institutions whose primary purpose is the conduct of scientific research. This authority is subject to three conditions.

First, the purpose of the grant must be for the support of basic scientific research conducted by a nonprofit institution of one of the two types described above. 

Second, there must be a determination by the department making the grant that it is in furtherance of the objectives of that department. 

Third, each department making such grants shall make an annual report to the appropriate committees of both Houses of Congress, 32 72 Stat. 1793, 42 U.S.C. § 1891 

(1958). This act applies to all agencies of the Government that have authority "to enter into contracts for basic scientific research at nonprofit institutions of higher education, or at nonprofit organizations whose primary purpose is the conduct of scientific research." Compare § 8.47 and especially, § 8.47, n. 15 infra for related authority provided by this act to dispose of equipment acquired with funds from "contracts," as well as under grants (to the extent authorized), for basic or "applied" scientific research. 

In this latter connection, it is noted that no authority is provided by this act (and, hence, none is available to the military departments) to make grants for "applied" scientific research. 

It is further noted that the term "grant-in-aid" is not used in connection with the authority provided by the Act of September 6, 1958. Although this term is sometimes used in connection with authority similar to that provided by this act, it is considered more appropriate to confine the term to various forms of intergovernmental aid, for example, those from the federal government to the states or from the states to municipal or other local governments. 

See ANDERSON, THE NATION AND THE STATES, RIVALS OR PARTNERS? 176, and Chap. 11, Grants-In-Aid and Centraliza tion of Government (1955). In connection with the first of these conditions, it is significant to note that the request from the Director of the National Science Foundation to Congress for enactment of the above legislation was accompanied by an explanation of the proposed bill which included the following definition of basic research: 

Basic research is that type of research which is directed toward the increase of knowledge in science. It is research where the primary aim of the investigator is a fuller knowledge or understanding of the subject under study, rather than a practical application thereof.34 

Although the exact pattern of implementation of this authority in the Department of Defense is not presently known, it is considered that, where grants are made, they will be accompanied by a document to be signed by the parties setting forth a number of provisions similar to those contained in fixed-price contracts for basic research. It would seem to be particularly appropriate to include provisions which would assure the Government of an irrevocable royalty-free, nonexclusive license under any patents issued on inventions first conceived or reduced to practice during the performance of work supported by the grant and, also, similar rights with respect to copyrighted materials first produced under like circumstances. Also, it is considered that provision should be made for return of the funds granted, as appropriate, where the grantee is unable to utilize them for the purposes intended.

There are differences, however, between a grant and a research contract which appear to be of some significance. 

First, it will be possible to pay out some or all of the funds in advance of the completion of any of the research and without obtaining the necessary approvals and satisfying the other statutory requirements in connection with advance payments under contracts.35 

Of course, this would not preclude the making of grants in installments as the work progresses where that course is considered desirable. 

Second, to the extent accounting and auditing requirements are used, they will be as agreed to by the parties and will not be mandatorily imposed.36

Third, where desirable and otherwise appropriate, modifications in the original terms of the grant may be made without the need to satisfy the requirements of legal consideration. 

It appears that use of the grant should most appropriately be confined to those cases where the Government desires to stimulate and support

Although there is widespread recognition of the desirability of supporting basic research 37 at educational and other nonprofit institutions, the extent to which this will be accomplished in the military departments by grant rather than by contract remains somewhat speculative. For one thing, the new authority was not accompanied by additional funds. Hence, for the present at least, funds used for grants must come out of appropriations made to cover research contracts. Also, the contract instrument is considered to be necessary in those cases where the research is directed toward the solution of a specific problem since this would require a narrowing of the scope of the inquiry in a manner considered to be incompatible with the making of a grant. Similarly, the contract form would be needed where the department desired to maintain a fairly close rein on the conduct of the research, in which case provisions should be included for on-the-site observance of the course of the work, regular periodic reports on the progress of the research, and such guidance by the department's scientific officer, as may be appropriate.38 This type of fairly close administrative control is considered to be out of keeping with the making of a grant.

All in all, therefore, it would seem that the decision as to whether to make a grant or a research contract will be one which rests in the exercise of sound discretion by the supporting department in determining which

B. CONTRACTING PROCEDURES: AUTHORITY TO NEGOTIATE 

$8.9. In General

By their very nature, research and development are unique and, generally, contracts for such work cannot be placed through formal advertising. Frequently, there is only one source of supply-the particular institution or organization which has the specialized facilities and the expert personnel to conduct the work desired. When there is more than one source, it is usually important to be free to select the one best qualified. 

Even if this were not the case, it is generally impossible to formulate precise specifications upon which prospective contractors could bid against each other. In placing certain development contracts, however, it may be possible to draft performance specifications which afford a basis for procurement by formal advertising. 

Prior to World War II, the Navy had no express statutory authority to negotiate research and development contracts. Such contracts could be negotiated upon a showing that procurement by formal advertising under section 3709 of the Revised Statutes was impracticable." During World 

War II, express authority to negotiate research and development contracts was provided by Title II of the First War Powers Act,40 and Executive 

Order 9001 41 thereunder.

The inherent difficulties in obtaining research and development by formal advertising were fully recognized in passing the Act of August 1, 1946, and the Armed Services Procurement Act. Both statutes authorize the negotiation of contracts for research or development. 

39 The Army had an exception from the general requirements for formal advertising under the Act of March 2, 1901, 31 Stat. 905, by the terms of which purchases by the Army were not required to be made by formal advertising in cases "where it is impracticable to secure competition." Further, in construing Rev. 

Stat. § 3709, the courts, the Attorney

General, and the Comptroller General have consistently ruled that competitive bidding was not required thereunder in circumstances which make it impracti cable to secure competition.  $ 8.10. Act of August 1, 1946 

In connection with the broad grant of authority to enter into contracts for research, as discussed in § 8.6 above, section 6 of the Act of August 1, 1946,42 further provided that such contracts could be entered into without regard to the statutory requirements for formal advertising, and without performance or other bonds.

As pointed out in § 8.6, this statute is still in effect. Prior to the reenactment and codification, in 1956, of both this statute and the Armed Services Procurement Act,44 it may have been debatable whether the specific provisions of section 6 of the Act of August 1, 1946, which permit negotiation, as distinguished from formal advertising, were superseded by the subsequently enacted provisions of the Armed Services Procurement Act covering the same subject. Grounds for this debate have now been eliminated by such reenactment and codification.45 As a practical matter, however, the Navy has consistently complied with all the requirements of the Armed Services Procurement Act; and the Armed Services 

Procurement Regulation so provides. 

$8.11. Armed Services Procurement Act 

Seventeen exceptions to the general rule that contracts will be placed by formal advertising, which are discussed in detail in Chapter 3, are set forth in 10 U.S.C. § 2304 (a) (formerly section 2(c) of the Armed Services 

Procurement Act of 1947). Of these exceptions permitting the negotia tion of contracts, two in particular affect research and development procurements. One is contained in 10 U.S.C. § 2304(a) (5) (formerly section 

2(c) (5) of the Armed Services Procurement Act of 1947) which authorizes negotiation of contracts for any service to be rendered by any university, college, or other educational institution. The committee reports indicated that this would include research. Accordingly, the Armed Serv. ices Procurement Regulation 46 states that this exception is available for contracts for experimental, developmental, or research work (including services, tests, and reports, necessary or incidental thereto) to be conducted by any university, college, or other educational institution, and reports furnished in connection therewith. Since educational institutions com.. prise about 80 percent of all contractors for research, and a high percentage of contractors for development, this exception is available in a large proportion of cases.

The principal negotiation exception is provided by 10 U.S.C. 

§ 2304 (a) (11) (formerly section 2(c) (11) of the Armed Services Pro curement Act of 1947) which authorizes negotiation if the Secretary

In the case of contracts of not more than $25,000, the chief officer or official of the agency responsible for procurement may make such determination.

The Armed Services Procurement Regulation lists detailed illustra tions of types of cases in which exception (11) is available.48 It provides that it shall not be available for quantity production unless such quantity production is necessary for complete and adequate experiment, development, research, or test. 

Several questions have arisen under this exception. (1) Is it available for a development contract which calls for the ultimate delivery of experimental or test models or prototypes? The answer is "yes," provided the number of models or prototypes is "reasonable." Such a contract is not one for quantity production. (2) Is it available for the purchase of any supplies for research, as an extreme example, brooms for the Naval Research Laboratory? 

A literal reading of the statute and regulation would say "yes."

Administratively, such a reductio ad absurdum has been avoided by limiting the exception to cases where the equipment is of a specialized and technical nature and is not available off the shelf, but must be specially manufactured for the purpose. (3) Is it available for the purchase of equipment to be tested, as distinguished from testing equipment? As an example, the Marine

Corps desired to purchase for evaluation two units for distilling fresh water from sea water, made by a particular manufacturer. These units were available commercially from this manufacturer. It was decided that this purchase should not be made under exception (11), but under exception (10) (competition impracticable).49 The rationale was that exception (11) was intended primarily to cover research and development, and incidentally specialized equipment necessary to facilitate such work. It should not be extended to cover cases not within the spirit of this, even though within the letter of the law. 50
