On the relationship between exception (5) and exception (11), under the statute the following is significant:

First, only contracts with educational institutions can be placed under exception (5);

Second, any research or development contract, whether with an educational institution or an industrial concern, can be placed under exception (11); and

Third, a formal Determination and Findings is required under exception (11) but not under exception (5). 

As a practical matter, therefore, from the time of passage of the Armed Services Procurement Act, exception (11) has not been used in the Navy where exception (5) was available. By amendment to the Armed Services Procurement Regulation, this has been the uniform procedure required in all of the military departments since 1956.51 

A third exception which permits the negotiation of research and development contracts is afforded by 10 U.S.C. § 2304 (a) (16) (formerly section 2(c) (16) of the Armed Services Procurement Act of 1947). In fact, this exception (16) authorizes contracts, whether or not for research or development work, to be negotiated if the Secretary determines that "the interest of national defense in maintaining active engineering, research, and development, would . . . be subserved." The negotiation authority of exception (16) is thus supplementary to that afforded by exceptions (5) and (11) and may be used where the placement of contracts with selected contractors is made primarily for the purpose of keeping their organizations actively engaged in research and development work to avoid the dissipation of critical scientific and engineering skills needed for national defense.

Two further exceptions are available for the negotiation of research and development contracts as well as other contracts. § 8.12. - Determinations and Findings 

Before a contract for research or development work can be placed under exception (11) with an organization other than an educational institution, there must be a Determination and Findings under 10 U.S.C. 

§ 2304 (a) (11) (formerly section 2(c) (11) of the Armed Services Pro curement Act of 1947) that the proposed contract is for research or developmental work. In imposing this requirement, it is apparent that

Accordingly, the approval of counsel is required when exception (1) is used in the same manner as when exception (11) is used.

The practical effect of the above requirements is to place before the Navy lawyer a difficult problem of draftsmanship regardless of the exception used. Having satisfied himself that the project is in fact for research or development, he must now draw findings which will support such a determination without being a mere statement that "research is research."

A suggested solution follows. The findings are broken down into four parts.

First, a brief statement of what the contract is for. This statement should be clear and concise, should avoid jargon, and should be intelligible to a non-scientific reader and at the same time scientifically accurate. It should, of course, avoid stating that the contract is for research, which is after all the ultimate conclusion to be drawn.

Second, a more detailed statement of facts which will support the conclusion that the work is in fact research or development. This may take a wide variety of forms, such as: the existing state of the art, indicating that further progress is not possible without theoretical analysis, studies, or experimentation; the nature of the studies to be undertaken; the possible or probable methods of solution; and the like. For this, the lawyer's ingenuity and resourcefulness are the only guide; arbitrary formulas should be avoided. Again, this statement should be clear, concise, and intelligible to the lay reader. 

A common error to avoid is the assignment of reasons why the project is desirable from a technical or operational standpoint. This may be presumed as a matter of sound contracting policy. In any event, that, where exception (6), based on 10 

U.S.C. § 2304 (a) (6), formerly § 2(c) (6) of the Armed Services Procurement Act of 1947, which relates to property and services "to be procured and used" outside of the United States, is available, it must be used in lieu of any authority which would otherwise be available. See

ASPR 3-211.3, 3-203.3 and 3-205.3 (Nov. 

3, 1958). The order of precedence also requires that, where the amount involved does not exceed $2,500, exception (3), based on 10 U.S.C. § 2304 (a)(3), formerly § 2(c) (3) of said act, shall be used except where exception (6) is authorized. 

57 NPD 3-201.5 (April 11, 1958). 

420

$ 8.it forms no part of the required determination, which is merely that the proposed project is in fact research, developmental, or experimental work, as the case may be. 

Third, a statement that the contract does not call for quantity production.

Fourth, a statement that definite drawings and specifications cannot be drawn, but only the ultimate objectives and general scope of the work outlined. 

Naturally, this general scheme may have to be varied to fit particular cases. For contracts involving the purchase of equipment or supplies for research, a somewhat different presentation is required. 

The following Determinations and Findings, adapted from actual cases, will illustrate the above points. The first is for a research contract, the second a development contract, and the third a contract for the purchase of supplies and equipment for experimentation and test. 

EXAMPLE 1. RESEARCH WORK 

Findings 1. The proposed contract provides for research and study toward determining the feasibility of a hydrofoil-supported amphibian tracked vehicle. 

2. With the advent of atomic weapons, wide dispersal of ships and other large targets has become mandatory. Because of the requirement for such dispersal as well as an increase in ship-to-shore distances, the present-day landing craft and landing vehicle is obsolescent. To meet this change in tactics, there is a need for a fast amphibious landing vehicle for transporting troops and supplies from the ship to shore and to inland points. Should this study prove the feasibility of a hydrofoil amphibious tracked vehicle, it will provide the military departments with the necessary information for the design and construction of a vehicle with approximately eight times the speed of present LVT's. 

3. The proposed contract does not call for quantity production of any article. 

4. It is impossible to describe in precise detail or by definite drawings and specifications the nature of the work to be done under the proposed contract; only the ultimate objective and the general scope of the work can be outlined. Determination The proposed contract is for research work.

EXAMPLE 2. DEVELOPMENT WORK 

Findings 1. The proposed contract calls for the design, development, construction, and testing of photo-rectification equipment. This equip- 421

§ 8. 

ment is intended to rectify and ratio print oblique aerial photographs into the equivalent vertical view for use in producing topographic maps and mosaics in the field and aboard ship. 

2. In connection with the making of topographic maps and mosaics, there is a need for compact, light-weight photo-rectifying equipment, capable of simple operation and suitable for use in the field and aboard ship. Equipment presently available lacks the desired design characteristics. It is considered expedient and desirable, therefore, to conduct the necessary studies, experimentation, engineering, design, and construction work, to produce and test prototypes of the desired equipment, as a preliminary to the actual production thereof. 

3. The proposed contract does not call for quantity production of any article. 

4. It is impossible to describe in precise detail or by definite drawings and specifications the nature of the work to be done under the proposed contract; only the ultimate objectives and the general scope of the work can be outlined. Determination The proposed contract is for developmental work.

EXAMPLE 3. SUPPLIES FOR RESEARCH OR DEVELOPMENT 

Findings 1. The proposed contract provides for the making and furnishing of fourteen (14) electronic ray tracers to be used for research and development in undersea warfare. 

2. In the field of undersea warfare research and development relating to detection of and development of countermeasures for enemy antisubmarine devices, it is important to be able to isolate and describe sound fields emanating from undersea point sources. This is a complex problem affected by the sound velocity structure in the medium, the depth of the water, the structure of the bottom and sub-bottom, the depth and power of the projector, and other factors. 

A useful approximation to the sound field in deep water is provided by the ray theory wherein the density of the rays at any point is taken as proportional to the acoustic intensity. The computation and display of the ray field by manual methods is tedious and time consuming. The electronic ray tracer, while subject to some inherent approximations, has been developed to perform this operation with such speed and to such a degree of accuracy as to be useful for scientific research and development as well as naval operational purposes. 

3. The proposed contract calls for only such quantity of equipment as is necessary for research and development. 422

B. DEPARTMENT OF THE NAVY 

$8.16. The Office of Naval Research and the Bureaus 

As mentioned in § 8.6, the Act of August 1, 1946, established the 

Office of Naval Research in the Office of the Secretary of the Navy. As a result of this act, as implemented by Secretarial directives of August 21, 1946, and October 29, 1946, the Navy established a general policy, subject to a number of variations and qualifications, that basic research would be handled by the Office of Naval Research, development by the bureaus, and applied research by all of these. The effect of these directives was to make the Office of Naval Research the principal contracting agency of the Navy for research projects and, until 1954, to leave the bureaus free to contract for their own development projects. 

In 1954, the Navy began an era of marked changes in its administrative organization for research and development. The changes which have been made stem principally from recommendations made after a study of the organization of the Department of the Navy by a committee headed by Hon. Thomas S. Gates, Jr., then Under Secretary of the 

Navy. They are all in the direction of more formal integration and coordination of research and development. 

From the standpoint of the Office of Naval Research, the most important and far-reaching recommendation of the Gates Committee was that the Chief of Naval Research be given responsibility for coordi- 

61 Section 8(b) of the Department of

Defense Reorganization Act of 1958, 72 Stat. 519, 10 U.S.C. § 5034 (1958), re duced the number of Assistant Secretaries of the Navy from four to three.

$8.16

nating the developmental phases of research and development. This recommendation was implemented by the Secretary of the Navy on June 24, 1954.62 For the first time, a central point was established for coordinating the many development programs being carried on by the technical bureaus. However, coordination through the means of a central focal point does not necessarily imply control. The bureaus continue to be responsible for preparing and carrying out their portions of the program in support of their weapons' areas. The Office of Naval 

Research continues to conduct supporting research necessary to provide new knowledge which is essential to the growth of these programs. The general objective of the Office of Naval Research in carrying out coordination of development is not to control or to "master mind," but to work together with the different bureaus, their laboratories, and contractors. Coordination of development is handled by a new group which reports to the Chief of Naval Research. There is no single system which can effect coordination of military development in the many ways in which it must be coordinated. Development must be coordinated "horizontally," that is, in terms of equipments which perform the same function, to take advantage of all technical advances and to eliminate unwarranted duplication. It must also be coordinated "vertically", that is, in terms of the tactical, or warfare, situation to see that related equipments are compatible and that they mesh together without gaps. 

In the coordination of research which the Office of Naval Research has been effecting for some years, emphasis has been placed on improvement of the flow of information among persons actually performing research. Occasionally, that Office has taken steps to sharpen a program and to accelerate the flow of results into the applied and developmental areas. In some cases, this has been done by an overall study of a technical field to determine the current state of progress, and by pointing out potential lines for military application. This kind of coordination not only will be continued, but also will be added to, as methods are worked out for coordination of development programs. The administrative structure is being established in the Office of Naval Research to do the planning and work out procedures. The Research Group within that Office has responsibilities for coordination of all naval research, and the position of Deputy Science Director for Research Coordination has been established to serve as the focal point for policy direction of research coordination activities. Research coordinators have been designated for the various technical fields.

Also important in the Navy's organization for research and development is the Naval Research Advisory Committee.63 It is appointed by the Secretary of the Navy and consists of not more than 15 persons from civilian life who are pre-eminent in the fields of science, research, and development work, with at least one member from the field of medicine. III. TYPES AND METHODS OF CONTRACTING FOR RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT 

$ 8.20. In General

A. TYPE BY METHOD OF COMPENSATION 

In general, research and development contracts are either of the costreimbursement type or the fixed-price type, the two principal types of contracts used for other kinds of procurement. Both of these broad types of contracts have variations which, because of their use in different kinds of procurement, are discussed more fully in Chapter 7; 6 and, accordingly, only a brief outline of their salient features will be covered in this chapter. 66 It should be noted at the outset, however, that the question of a satisfactory type of contract for research and development is still a matter open to experimentation. Hard and fast lines between fixed-price and costreimbursement contracts have shown a tendency to disappear. Concepts are fluid and solutions are varied. The Navy lawyer must keep an open mind on all this and resist the inclination to freeze contract forms into rigid, unyielding patterns. 

$ 8.21. Cost-Reimbursement Type 

The three types of cost-reimbursement contracts most frequently used for research and development contracting are the cost-plus-a-fixed-fee contract, the cost contract, and the cost-sharing contract. One of these types of contracts will usually be found to be the most satisfactory for research and development work. With commercial research and development organizations, the cost-plus-a-fixed-fee contract is most frequently used. However, the majority of research contracts and not a few development contracts are placed with universities and other nonprofit educational institutions. Since these institutions are not in business for profit, the 

Navy's policy with them has been to place its research and development head "Research," requesting $61,000,000 on the limited basis applicable in prior years (THE BUDGET OF THE UNITED STATES GOVERNMENT FOR THE FISCAL YEAR ENDING JUNE 30, 1955, pp. 534 to 

536) with the appropriation as actually made under the head "Research and Development" for $419,874,900, 68 Stat. 345 (1955). 

65 See § 8.2, n. 5 supra as to the proposed designation of this appropriation for fiscal 1960. 

66 See also ASPR Section III, Part 4. 

428

DETERMINATION AND FINDINGS 

$ 8.22 contracts on a cost-without-fee basis. This policy has gained widespread acceptance.

Cost-sharing contracts are used in certain cases where joint sponsorship of a research project by the Government and the contractor will result in benefit to the contractor, which the contractor is willing to accept in lieu of full monetary reimbursement. Cost sharing in research and development contracts has taken a variety of forms, for example: 

An agreement not to claim reimbursement for the compensation of certain of the scientists working on the project; 

Acceptance of a lower rate of overhead than would be permissible on the basis of actual costs; 

An agreement to erect certain facilities or acquire certain equipment without cost to the Government; or 

An agreement to prorate all allowable costs, a stated percentage to be charged to the Government, the balance to be absorbed by the contractor.

Whatever the method of cost sharing, it is important that the basis and mechanics should be clearly set forth in the contract. $ 8.22. Determination and Findings 

The Armed Services Procurement Act provides that a cost-reimbursement type contract may be used only after a determination that such method of contracting is likely to be less costly than other methods, or that it is impracticable to secure supplies or services of the kind or quality required without the use of such type of contract.67 If a fee is involved, the determination must state the amount of the estimated cost, the amount of the fee, and the percentage relationship of the two. Such determination may be made by the contracting officer when supported by written findings made by him.68

Here is a typical example of such a Determination and Findings supporting the use of a cost-plus-a-fixed-fee contract for research: 

Determination and Findings 

Upon the basis of the following findings and determination which I hereby make as a Contracting Officer pursuant to the provisions of 10 

U.S.Č. § 2310 and authority delegated under 10 U.S.C. § 2311, the proposed contract may be entered into on a cost-plus-a-fixed-fee basis, pursuant to the authority of 10 U.S.C. § 2306 (c), for research and development work on reflex klystron tubes with the XYZ Research Company.

3. The exact nature and extent of the work covered by the proposed contract, and the precise method of performing that work, cannot be established in advance, but must be freely subject to improvisation and change as the work progresses. 

4. The costs of performing the work under the proposed contract cannot be estimated with reasonable accuracy so as to permit the undertaking of such work for a fixed price. Determination 1. It is impracticable to secure services of the kind or quality required without the use of the proposed type of contract. 

2. The estimated cost of the proposed contract, exclusive of the fee, is $100,000. $8.23. Firm Fixed-Price Type

A fixed-price contract is something of an anomaly in the case of research. It is often difficult to describe the work in a manner which will afford an adequate basis for pricing. For the same reason, it may be difficult to be certain when performance is complete. 

Nevertheless, the fixed-price type contract has been and is used for research. It has these two principal advantages. 

From the contractor's standpoint, the fact that he does not have to keep detailed cost records and submit to periodic audits reduces the contractor's costs and eases the administrative burden. 

From the Government's standpoint, the elimination of the necessity for detailed audits is a similar boon to the Government. Moreover, the Government knows exactly what the work is going to cost, and the risk of any loss has been assumed by the contractor. 

The fixed-price type contract has proved particularly suitable in the case of small research contracts, up to about $25,000. In many of these cases, it is possible to make a fairly close estimate of costs so as to arrive at a fair price; and the amounts involved do not justify the additional expense of keeping detailed accounting records. There is no reason, in principle, why even larger contracts could not be handled this way. Despite the emphasis which the Armed Services Procurement Act and the Armed Services Procurement Regulation place upon the general desirability of fixed-price contracts," there has not up to the present been any consistent 

69 See § 8.22, n. 67 supra and ASPR 

3-402 (Sept. 18, 1958). 430

FORM OF CONTRACT 

$ 8.25 tendency toward widespread use of this method of contracting for research and development. Although from time to time emphasis has been placed on the use of such contracts, more frequently this has not been the case. 

However, it is definitely an area where the final word has not yet been spoken and it will be interesting to watch future developments. 

§ 8.24. Fixed Price With Redetermination 

Fixed-price contracts which provide for redetermination of the price initially negotiated by calling for its subsequent negotiated adjustment, in whole or in part, are sometimes used in research and development contracts.

This type of contract may be appropriate in order to shift some but not all risks from the contractor to the Government so as to eliminate or minimize contingencies in the contract price. Should the contingencies occur, the initial price may be redetermined correspondingly. If costs are in excess of the initial price, the contractor can be made whole to the extent permitted by the contract; conversely, if costs are less than anticipated, the Government gets the benefit. 

The use of a clause providing for redetermination after completion of the contract should be carefully restricted. The use of such a clause is intended only where, but for special or unusual circumstances, a costreimbursement type contract would normally be used. Such a clause should not be used unless the amount involved is relatively small or the time of performance is relatively short and then only after the initial price negotiated is as fair and reasonable as the circumstances permit. 

The Navy has used this type clause in a very few isolated instances and then only in research contracts negotiated on a no-profit basis where the clause provided for downward redetermination only with a view to assuring the elimination of profit.

One danger of using a redetermination clause, in the case of research and development, is that it may amount to little more than a cost-reimbursement type contract in disguise.

Properly used, however, the fixed-price contract with provision for redetermination may be the answer in some types of research and development contracts.

B. FORM OF CONTRACT 

$8.25. In General

This subpart treats primarily the format of the contract, as distinguished from subpart A above, which discusses the type of contract. 

Over the years, a number of different methods of drawing research and development contracts have grown up. The methods now approved for use within the Navy fall generally into two categories: the separate contract, and the task-order type contract. 503533 0-59—30 431

$ 8.26

 $8.26. Separate Contract 

A separate and distinct contract is made for each task calling for research or development, or both, with a particular contractor. The contract describes the work to be done, obligates the necessary funds therefor, and is, in general, handled much as any other contract for supplies or services. Provision may be made, within the framework of this type of contract, for the issuance of "instructions" by the scientific or technical officer.70 

$ 8.27. Task-Order Contract 

Under this form, the contract consists of two parts: a basic agreement," which sets forth the general provisions, and one or more task orders. A "task order" is a document (issued under a basic agreement) which sets forth, either generally or specifically, the research or development work, or combined research and development work, to be undertaken under such task order, states the period of performance, and sets forth the total estimated cost and the fixed fee, if any, or, if appropriate, the contract price, for such work. Any number of task orders may be issued under a single basic agreement. The basic agreement is executed by both parties, but is not treated as obligating funds. Each task order requires acceptance by the contractor, and each is executed by both parties. Each task order is treated as a separate obligating document, and is in fact a separate contract which incorporates by reference the provisions of the basic agreement. In view of its bilateral nature, it is perhaps more accurately referred to as a task-order contract. 

The basic agreement may contain a general description of the work, with more specific work assignments set forth in each task order. Under this practice, the work under the various task orders will be in the same general area and will constitute different phases or segments of the one overall project. Alternatively, the basic agreement may merely provide for the conduct of research or development, generally, and reserve all specific work descriptions for the task orders. Under this latter practice, there is no requirement that the work involved in one task order be related to that involved in another. This practice has been followed for some time by the Office of Naval Research.

$8.28. Reason for the Influence

Prior to 1946,72 significant legal problems had to be solved in regard to financing long-term Navy research and development contracts out of

$ 8.29. The Controlling Statute and Its Interpretations 

74

Annual appropriations are intended primarily to meet the "current needs" of government agencies; and, accordingly, they are available for obligation only for the fiscal year for which the appropriation is made.75 

Theoretically, they should be fully expended each year. But the actual practice does not always coincide with the theory since frequently these contracts take several years to perform. Consequently, the law permits the use of appropriations beyond the expiration of the fiscal year for the fulfillment of contracts properly made within that year.76 As more able the Office of Naval Research to carry out its functions would, if obligated in the fiscal year for which appropriated, remain available for expenditure for four years following the expiration of such fiscal year. Section 3 of the Act of July 16, 1952, c. 882, 66 Stat. 

725 (reenacted and codified in 10 U.S.C. § 2352 (1958)), provided that contracts of the military departments for services and the use of facilities for research or development, or both, could be made for a term not to exceed five years and, also, could be extended for an additional period of five years, subject to the availability of appropriations therefor.

$ 8.29

fully covered in Chapter 4, the general rule, prior to 1956, was that all annual funds properly obligated remained available for expenditure in the original appropriation for two fiscal years after the year for which the appropriation was available for obligation." At the end of that period, the funds were said to lapse. However, under a law enacted in 

1956, the obligated balance in the appropriation still remaining unexpended is then transferred to successor appropriation accounts within the agency responsible for liquidating the obligation. In these accounts are merged all amounts similarly transferred from all appropriations for the same general purposes.78 Funds so transferred remain within the control of the contracting agency to liquidate obligations properly incurred.

The above general rule concerning "current needs" is simple enough to apply to a contract for the purchase and delivery of a six-ton truck, or 2,000 barrels of fuel oil. But what of a contract for services where the compensation is in proportion to the amount of work performed and such work is severable by fiscal years, such as an employment contract, a contract for maintenance and repair of aircraft, or the like? 

Here the Comptroller General has said that the "current need" is for services to be performed within the fiscal year and, therefore, that any such contract must not extend beyond the end of the fiscal year.79 

To this rule the Comptroller General has recognized a corollary: if the services are clearly defined in advance so as to constitute a specific entire job, not severable by fiscal years, and if this job is to be commenced in one fiscal year with performance extending into the next, the contract, even though only for services, may be placed for the entire period and financed entirely out of the appropriation current at the date of the contract. Thus, he has ruled that a contract for the cultivation of a specified number of acres of rubber plants at a definite price per acre, payable upon completion of the services, constituted one undertaking, which, although extending over a part of two fiscal years, was determinable both as to the services needed and the price to be paid at the time it was made. Accordingly, such a contract should not be placed on a fiscal year basis, and the entire amount thereof should be obligated against the appropriation current at the time it was made. 

When the research contract appeared on the scene, it had to be fitted into this conceptual framework. Evidently it was a service contract, as distinguished from a supply contract. But it was a good deal more

THE CONTROLLING STATUTE AND ITS INTERPRETATIONS 

$ 8.29 1 than an ordinary service contract, for the contractor undertook to do a specific job: to devote his resources of staff, laboratory, equipment, technical know-how, and professional skill to the solution of a given problem in a certain field of scientific research or development. And this takes time. If a contractor, whether a university or a commercial research organization, is to assemble a staff and guarantee employment to its members, if it is to build specialized laboratories and buy expensive equipment, and if the Government is to expect worthwhile results, the contractor must be given assurances of continuing government support.

Faced with this practical problem, the Government had no choice but to place its research and development contracts on a long-term basis. 

Justification could be found in the Comptroller General's decision in the rubber cultivation case, discussed above. Congress helped by providing, in the act establishing the Office of Naval Research, that funds appropriated to enable that Office to perform its functions would remain available for expenditure for four years following the year of appropriation and obligation. Such a provision was meaningless if research contracts had to be limited to a fiscal-year basis. 

Not all research contracts can, however, be fully assimilated to the concept of an "entire job" such as was present in the rubber cultivation case. Sometimes a project, though definable in terms of overall scope and area of investigation, is still too general to be called an "entire job," yet is such that the work must be continued over a period of years if valuable results are to be obtained. It may be desirable in such cases to finance the work on an installment basis, giving the Government an option to renew the work from time to time by making additional funds available out of their current appropriations. In an opinion given to the Secretary of the Navy in 1946, the Comptroller General approved the placing of a contract of this sort on an installment basis.82 The exact meaning and effect of this opinion are not certain, but it appears to provide authority for the installment type of research or development contract to be described more fully below. 

Finally, frank recognition had to be given to the fact that in many research contracts what the Government is actually buying is the research resources which the contractor has agreed to make available for a stated period of time. This has resulted in the evolution of the "term" basis for contracting under which the contractor agrees to conduct research in a given area for a stated time. This is sometimes conveniently 

81 See § 8.28, n. 72 supra. 

82 Comp. Gen. Dec. B-56712, April 9, 1946 (unpubl.). 435

$ 8.

referred to as buying a "package of time"-a cube whose three conventional dimensions may be conceptualized as follows: (1) Width scope or breadth of the work description; (2) Length=contract period; and (3) Height=level of contractor's agreed effort, including utilization of research personnel and facilities. This, also, will be discussed more fully below. 

The whole process has been one of gradual evolution and adaptation. 

This evolution is still in process, and it is difficult to lay down definite categories. In general, however, the following methods of financing research and development contracts are in current use within the Navy. $8.30. Fiscal-Year Basis

In a contract on the fiscal-year basis, the current appropriation is obligated for work to be performed during the fiscal year. Although this method may be used for any type of research or development contract, generally, it does not provide a desirable basis for financing such a contract. However, it must be used where the work consists essentially of personal services compensated for on a time basis and is severable by fiscal years. Again, where the contract calls for services on an indefinite quantity basis, as where the contractor agrees to furnish consulting services from time to time as ordered, the fiscal-year basis must be used. Any such fiscal-year contract may provide for renewal in subsequent fiscal years, subject to the availability of funds therefor, and provided this does not project the contract an unreasonable number of years into the future. $ 8.31. Entire Job

A research contract on the entire-job basis is, for appropriation purposes, treated like a supply contract. The appropriation current at the time the contract is made is obligated for the total estimated cost of the work. The period of performance may extend beyond the fiscal year as long as the appropriation rule of "current needs" is met. To justify this method of contracting, the following conditions must be satisfied: (1) The project must be clearly defined in advance, so that a definite goal or target is set up and a definite end product (even if only a report) is required; (2) More than personnel services must be involved, such as an agreement by the contractor to furnish his research facilities, plant, staff, know-how, or other resources; and (3) It must be possible to estimate the total cost of the work with reasonable accuracy.

Task orders issued under a task-order type contract may be handled on an entire-job basis, provided the above conditions are met with respect to each task order. That is, each task order may be regarded as obligating 436

TERM BASIS 

$8.33 the funds necessary for its completion, provided it is issued during the fiscal year when the funds are current, even though the work may carry over into subsequent fiscal years. 

§ 8.32. Installment Basis 

A contract on the installment basis is made for work over an extended period with an overall estimated cost agreed upon and stated therein. 

Only a certain portion of this overall cost is obligated at the outset. By subsequent amendments or modifications to the contract, whether in the same or later fiscal years, additional sums may be obligated (out of then current appropriations but not out of prior appropriations) for continuance or completion of the work. Funds thus obligated, whether by the initial contract or by amendments or modifications thereto, remain available for expenditure. This method is available only— (1) Where the contract is on a cost or cost-plus-a-fixed-fee basis and calls for the services and facilities of the contractor for research or development work as distinguished from a personal services or consultant type contract; (2) Where the contract is for a specific project, which can be defined in advance in terms of scope and area of investigation, problems to be solved, prototypes to be developed, or the like; (3) Where the research or development work is of such a nature as necessarily requires its continuance over a period of years if valuable results are to be obtained; (4) Where it is desired to insure the continued availability of the contractor for the projected research over an extended period if and when appropriations are available and it is desired that the projected research be continued; and (5) Where it is possible to estimate the overall cost with reasonable accuracy, so as to provide a basis for arriving at the overall fixed fee if a fee is to be paid. 

§ 8.33. Term Basis 

A contract for research or for research and development (but not development without research) may be placed on a term basis where— (1) It is not possible to assign a definite end product, other than a report of work done and results accomplished, or where it is not possible to describe the work involved with any degree of partic.. ularity; and (2) It is not possible to arrive at a reasonably accurate estimate of the cost of the project. 

In a contract placed on this basis, the contractor must agree to make available his facilities, material, and personnel, and to devote his best efforts for a stated period of time to the conduct of research or of research and development in a given area. The contract should specify generally the facilities, material, and personnel to be employed upon the work and, 437

$8.34

thus, set forth the three dimensions of the "package of time" referred to in § 8.29 above. On or before expiration of the period specified in the contract, the Government and the contractor may agree to continue the work for a longer period, either under a new contract, or an amendment to the old contract. This is accomplished simply by increasing the second dimension or "length" of the contract. Similarly, a new or amended contract may result from a change in either or both of the other dimensions of the original "package," namely in the "width" (scope of the work) or "height (level of the contractor's effort). Any such new contract, or amendment to an old contract, is new procurement and must charge then current appropriations. Funds thus obligated, whether by the initial contract or by an amendment, would remain available for expenditure. 

Accordingly, the term of the contract could continue for a corresponding period, even though this might extend the contract into a subsequent fiscal year or years.

The term basis should not be used: (1) Where the contract is one for purely personal services, consulting services, or the like, as distinguished from the conduct of research or research and development; or (2) Where either the entire-job basis or the installment basis is reasonably available for use.

Once an election has been made to use any one of the foregoing bases for obligating funds under a particular contract, discussed in this and the three preceding sections, such basis may not be subsequently changed and an alternative basis followed. 

IV. CONTRACT CLAUSES AND RELATED CONSIDERATIONS AFFECT- ING RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT PROCUREMENT 

$ 8.34. In General

Some attention should be given to special types of contract clauses which have to be used in research and development contracts,83 as well as to related matters for consideration in the making of such contracts. 

In the development of contract clauses for research and development contracts, the general pattern has been to follow the standard clauses for supply contracts, which are explained fully in Chapter 9, except where the subject matter requires different treatment. Some of these clauses can be omitted in research and development contracts, others require modification, and clauses other than those prescribed for supply contracts may be used; however, a complete explanation of these details is beyond the scope of this chapter. 

83 Coverage of the clauses to be used in fixed-price and cost-reimbursement type research and development contracts with the military departments is to be included in ASPR Section VII, Parts 3 

and 4, respectively. 438

DESCRIPTION OF WORK 

$ 8.35 

$8.35. Description of Work 

In one sense, this is the most important clause in the entire contract because it is the clause which sets forth what the contractor is expected to do. It is difficult to draw because of the indefinite nature of so many research projects. However, the lawyer should make an effort to describe the work with some degree of precision so that, not only will the parties have a reasonable understanding of what is expected, but the contract itself will not be rendered invalid for vagueness and indefiniteness. At the same time, a description which is too exact may tie the hands of the contractor, destroy his initiative, and discourage him from pursuing promising lines of inquiry. The contract draftsman should steer a middle course between these two extremes. In the case of a development contract, the problem is not too great: the desired end product can be described, engineering specifications attached, and the number of prototypes required stated.

In the case of basic or applied research a little more ingenuity is required. The lawyer should be careful not to accept as gospel any work description handed to him by a scientific or technical officer. He must insist on the parties saying exactly what they mean, and should abhor all fuzziness of thought and obscurity of expression. If the business arrangement cannot be expressed in clear, workmanlike language, it is probable that there is no real "meeting of the minds" necessary to bind the parties to a contract, but only a vague "understanding." In such a case, the lawyer must step in, find out what the parties really mean, and then formulate it for them. If he finds, as he may, that they do not know exactly what they mean themselves, he will have to enter the negotiations himself and help bring both sides to agreement. Given the basic material to work on, the lawyer does not have to be a scientist or engineer to draft an acceptable work description. A working knowledge of semantics and a judicious use of Webster and Fowler are the principal tools required.

Much of what has been said of the role of the Navy lawyer in regard to the making of contracts applies with equal force to the lawyer for the research and development contractor. 

The following work descriptions, adapted from Office of Naval Research contracts, are by no means perfect but they afford some idea of what should be covered by this clause. 

EXAMPLE 1. BASIC RESEARCH 

The Contractor shall furnish the necessary personnel and facilities for, and, in accordance with any instructions issued by the Scientific Officer or his authorized representative, shall conduct, theoretical 439

$ 8.35

research on the application of quantum and statistical mechanical methods to problems of atomic and molecular structure, molecular interactions, and chemical reaction rates.

EXAMPLE 2. APPLIED RESEARCH 

The Contractor shall supply the necessary personnel and facilities for, and, in accordance with any instructions issued by the Technical Officer or his authorized representative, shall conduct, research as set forth in subparagraphs (1) through (4) below. (1) The Contractor shall endeavor to ascertain, so far as practicable, the possibilities and limitations of— (a) superconducting methods for detecting small magnetic fields; and (b) detecting small changes in magnetic fields from the change in resistance of suitable metallic wires. 

(2) The Contractor shall conduct a search for new supercon ducting metals and alloys and make a study of their- (a) behavior under varying conditions of composition; (b) crystal structure; (c) magnetic environment; (d) current density; and (e) impulse frequency. (3) The Contractor shall endeavor to establish the necessary relationships leading to engineering design of instruments for the detection of radiation and magnetic fields using superconducting sensitive elements. (4) The Contractor shall conduct experiments to determine the relation between oscillating superconducting fields and electromagnetic radiation in the region of wave-lengths lying between about 0.1 and .0001 cm. in order- (a) to find out more about the mechanism of coupling between radiation and the electric fields within partially superconducing metals; and (b) to test the possibilities of using superconductors as generators and receivers of wave-lengths in the region below 0.1 cm.

In Example 3, the attached specifications covered 61 pages and included the following: a general description of the system; a breakdown of the system into component parts; nine pages of illustrations of the system;

Specification. 

The following factors common to all of the work descriptions should be noted: (1) The contractor agrees to furnish the necessary personnel and facilities for, as well as to conduct, the research or development specified. This is desirable because it shows that there is more involved in the contract than the mere performance of services. (2) The phrase "in accordance with any instructions issued by the Scientific Officer," or a similar phrase, is highly desirable. The purpose of this is to permit the scientific or technical officer to issue written or oral instructions to supplement the work description contained in the contract. This is intended to enable him to fill in details, to suggest possible lines of inquiry, and to disapprove lines of investigation which appear to be wasteful. Such instructions, however, must be within the scope of the work described in the contract. They cannot be used to make new assignments of work or to direct changes in the specifications. For new work a duly executed amendment is required; for a change in the specifications a change order may be used. In both cases, the contracting officer, and not the scientific officer, must sign for the Government. $ 8.36. Payment of the Contract Price or of Allowable Costs and Fee

In the case of fixed-price contracts, provisions for payment of the contract price follow a fairly consistent pattern. The clause recites the total compensation to be paid and makes provision for payment, usually in equal monthly or quarterly installments with the final payment to be made upon completion of the work. The payment of the fee in cost- 441

$8.36

reimbursement contracts is provided for in a similar manner. However, the following special problems do arise in both types of contracts. 

Fulfillment of the Contractual Commitment. Before final payment of the price or the fixed fee can be made, the Government has to be satisfied that the contractor has earned it, or in other words, has fully performed the work called for by the contract. Frequently, this cannot be made dependent upon the successful outcome of the project. Research and development by their very nature involve explorations into the unknown, the little known, and the untried. 

The possibility of a negative result is often present. It does not follow from this, however, that the contractor should be entitled to his price or fee merely upon the expiration of the stated time or upon expenditure of the total estimated cost.84 The important thing from the Government's standpoint is to measure the contractor's performance against the contractual commitment it made on entering into the contract.

The Extent of the Contractual Commitment. Where the possibility of a negative result is clearly contemplated, it is proper for the Government to permit the contract to provide that the contractor shall use its "best efforts" to accomplish the result being sought. 

Whether the contract calls for the contractor's "best efforts" or a more definitive obligation, it should always provide that the work performed will conform to high professional standards. Accordingly, in all cases before payment is made, the Government must be satisfied as a minimum that the work performed conforms to high professional standards, that the contractor has, in fact, exerted its "best efforts" to do the work required, and that the reports furnished (or in the case of a development contract, the models of prototypes delivered) are satisfactory. For this the contract administrator has to rely upon the judgment of the scientific or technical officer. 

The contract should, however, provide for acceptance of the work by the Government before final payment. It is desirable that it provide for a certificate by the scientific or technical officer that the work has been satisfactorily performed in accordance with the requirements of the contract.

In connection with the "best efforts" type of commitment in a costreimbursement type contract, a related point should be borne in mind. 

Cost-reimbursement type contracts, generally, contain a Limitation of Costs clause 85 in which the contractor agrees to use its best efforts to perform the work and all obligations called for by the contract within 84 For downward revision of fee on termination for default of cost-plus-a-fixedfee contracts, where the parties cannot agree on the amount of the fee to be paid in final settlement, see ¶ (e) (i) (D) of the Termination clause (ASPR 8-702, Sept. 2, 1958). For downward revision of fee on termination for convenience, see § 5.28 supra and other provisions of the 

Termination clause supra. However, as a practical matter, these termination remedies are rarely used, and appropriate reductions in the fee are usually agreed to without resort to either of these termination remedies. 

85 See ASPR 7-203.3 (May 14, 1958) for the clause prescribed in all costreimbursement type supply contracts. 

The forthcoming ASPR Section VII, Part 4, as approved for printing, contains a similar clause for use in costreimbursement type research and development contracts. See also § 9.35 infra. 442

PAYMENT OF THE CONTRACT PRICE 

$8.36 the estimated cost set forth in the contract. This estimated cost in effect imposes a contractual ceiling—

First, on the obligation of the contractor to continue performance unless the contracting officer notifies it that the estimated cost has been increased and provided the contractor can establish that it employed its best efforts to complete the work within the original estimated cost; and

Second, on the obligation of the Government to reimburse the contractor for incurred costs unless and until the contracting officer has revised the estimated cost and so notifies the contractor. 

It should be noted that this clause is designed to give the Government, unilaterally, an effective tool to prevent the over-expenditure of appropriated funds. The clause is used regardless of the nature of the contractual commitment for the work itself, which would be contained in a separate clause setting forth the description of the work." The 

Limitation of Cost clause is used both in cases where the commitment for the work itself is unequivocal and where the commitment is only to employ "best efforts" to complete the work. In other words, both types of commitments are conditioned upon the Government obligating any additional funds that may be necessary, by means of revising the estimated cost of performance. Where the necessary funds have been made available, the difference comes down to this- In the case of the unequivocal commitment, nothing short of completion of the task will satisfy the performance requirements and earn the full amount of the fee; but 

In the case of the "best efforts" commitment, performance requirements may be satisfied and the fee fully earned even though the task is not completed provided the contractor has in fact employed its "best efforts" to that end.

The matter is somewhat more complicated when the Government elects not to increase the cost limitation and the task is incomplete. Since the 

Limitation of Cost clause is silent on the matter of fee, it may be well to have the fee provisions specifically call for an equitable adjustment under such circumstances.87a

A further discussion of questions relating to fixed fees, generally, and also of their application to specific kinds of contracts appears in §§ 8.388.41 infra.

Matters requiring additional consideration in the case of cost-reimbursement contracts are the various types of costs which may not be allowable at all unless there is specific agreement to include them. These include, among others, such costs as- (1) Those incurred as an incident to the work covered by the contract but prior to its execution, in which case the agreement must include specific identification of the types of costs and the period involved; (2) Those of research programs of a general nature; (3) Insurance and liability to third persons; (4) Patents and royalty payments; and (5) Wages or salaries of partners or sole proprietors.

These and other costs which may require special consideration prior to entering into the contract are more fully covered in Section XV, Part 5, of the Armed Services Procurement Regulation. 

$ 8.37. Cost-Reimbursement Type Contracts: Overhead Rates 

In cost-reimbursement contracts, in lieu of reimbursement based on true costs, as referred to in the preceding section, compensation is frequently provided for through a method based on the negotiation of overhead rates to cover all indirect costs. Under this alternative method, since the contract will specifically provide that all costs not identified as direct costs are to be recovered as part of the overhead rate, it is necessary for the parties to come into agreement at the outset on a detailed listing to be included in the contract of all items to be treated as direct costs. In addition, it is customary to include in this listing an omnibus provision under which payment may be made of direct costs not listed, but not expressly excluded, if the contracting officer deter- Inines that they may properly be included in the cost of the work and are certified by him as properly payable. Some flexibility in the identification of direct costs is permitted in the standard contract clauses providing for overhead rates which, in connection with a contract amendment setting forth the final overhead rate negotiated for any period, permit the inclusion of changes in the previously agreed listing of direct costs.8 88

Under this overhead rate method, until recently, it was customary to provide for the payment of indirect costs by negotiating a predetermined fixed overhead rate, in the form of a percentage of direct labor costs or other agreed basis, applicable prospectively for an agreed period (usually 6 or 12 months) during contract performance. Generally, such rates were negotiated on the basis of an advisory audit for the period preceding the one to which the rates were to be made applicable and had been redetermined periodically on this basis throughout the life of the contract.

Although for a number of years the Comptroller General apparently had acquiesced in the use of such fixed overhead rates, in a 1956 decision to the Secretary of Defense he held that such method is in violation of the prohibition against the cost-plus-a-percentage-of-cost system of contracting and, hence, is illegal. Shortly before this decision, he had been sharply critical of predetermined fixed overhead rates in an audit report relating to procurement by the Department of the Army 90 and in a decision to the Secretary of Commerce." 89 As a result of this development, and pursuant to agreement with the Comptroller General, predetermined fixed overhead rates have not, except for a brief further period in the case of educational institutions, been used in contracts entered into after June 30, 1956. The law does not permit a distinction between nonprofit and commercial organizations with respect to the factors involved in the use of fixed overhead rates in contracts.

-Fixed-Fee Problems Generally In cost-reimbursement type contracts with commercial concerns, the matter of providing for and administering the payment of fee is frequently an extremely vexing problem. Fixed-fee problems relating to the nature and fulfillment of the contractual commitment have already been discussed in § 8.36 supra. Here are some further difficulties which the fixed fee presents. (1) The Government must protect itself against excessive charges by way of fee. Commercial concerns are of course in business for profit. The protection afforded by competitive bidding is absent in most research and development contracts. (2) Commercial concerns sometimes consider themselves entitled to a "fair profit" on all expenditures made by them. An attempt by the 

Government to accommodate this point of view fully would run afoul of the statutory prohibition against the cost-plus-a-percentage-of-cost

(4) For the same reason, it may be very difficult to say when new work is being required, over that initially contracted for, so as to justify payment of an additional fee. (5) If it becomes necessary to extend the time for performance of a research or development contract (and it often does), it is very difficult to determine whether an additional fee is warranted. 

For dealing with these difficult problems, only general guidelines can be suggested. Here, as elsewhere, the lawyer must exercise sound judgment. $ 8.39.

The estimated cost and fixed fee should be stated in the contract at the outset. Although the Armed Services Procurement Act allows a fee of 

15 percent of the estimated cost, the Armed Services Procurement Regulation has imposed a general administrative limitation of 10 percent." 

In practice, fees in the Navy are ordinarily well within this limitation. 

Once the fee has been agreed to, it may not thereafter be increased, even though the estimated cost is exceeded, unless the contract is changed or amended to provide for an increase in the extent of the work previously described or is otherwise changed or amended in a manner which substantially increases the contractor's cost of performance. To justify an increase in the fixed fee, such increase in work or in the cost of performance must result from either- 

(1) a supplementary contractual commitment (usually an amendment to the contract) providing for the procurement of new or additional research or development; or (2) a unilateral order, issued by the Government, and changing the specifications or some other element of the contract in a manner per-

Frequently, although not always, such changes or amendments involve an extension of the time of performance. Occasionally, extensions of the time for performance may be made which are unrelated to a change order or to an amendment providing for new or additional procurement.

In Installment Contracts 

When the installment type of contract is used, the fee, if any, is stated at the outset and may not be subsequently increased, even if the actual cost exceeds the original overall estimate. Again, as discussed in the preceding section, this fee is governed by the statutory limitation of 15 percent and the administrative limitation of 10 percent of the original overall estimated cost. The contract also includes appropriate provisions for payment of the fee. If desired, provision may be made for payment of the entire fixed fee if the contractor completes all the work originally contemplated, even though it accomplishes this in a shorter period of time or at a lower cost than originally estimated. However, the fixed fee should be revised downward if the parties decide not to continue the work to completion as originally contemplated. As we have already seen in connection with the discussion relative to fulfillment of the contractual commitment in § 8.36, the standard contract termination clause, discussed in Chapter 5, provides for a downward revision of the fixed fee when the contract is terminated by the Government. 

$ 8.41.

In Term Contracts 

In the term-type contract, the fee is based upon the expectation that the contractor will conduct research or research and development work of a certain kind for an agreed period of time. For each such period, the fee is governed by the statutory and administrative limitations discussed in the two preceding sections just as though each period were a separate contract, which in effect it is. Upon expiration of each agreed period, the full amount of the fee is payable to the contractor, provided: 

(1) The contractor certifies that he has used his best efforts to do all the work called for by the contract; (2) The Government, as represented by the contracting officer or scientific officer, certifies that the contractor has performed satisfactorily the work called for; and

ADVANCE PAYMENTS 

$ 8.42 (3) No circumstances have arisen which have prevented the contractor from performing the work in the manner and to the extent contemplated at the inception of the contract. 

If these conditions are not met, an equitable adjustment of the fee should be made, and the contract should so provide. If the fee is to be paid in installments, provision should be made for withholding a portion thereof so that any necessary equitable adjustment can be made at the end of the contract period.

At the end of the agreed period, the Government and the contractor may agree to extend the work for a further period, and may also agree upon an additional fee for such further period. However, during the agreed period, or such period as extended, the fee may not be increased, in the absence of an actual increase in the contractor's commitments, for example, by enlarging the other dimensions of the "package" referred to in § 8.29 and § 8.33, namely the "width" (scope of the work) or the "height" (level of the contractors' effort). In some cases, the contract provides that the Government has the right, when the contractor has failed to render the amount of effort originally contemplated within the period of performance, to require further performance by the contractor, without additional fee, for such additional period as would permit completion of the amount of effort originally contemplated. $ 8.42. Advance Payments

Many research contracts involve substantial expenditures of money. 

When the contractor is a university, this may require it to use its endowed funds until such time as it can obtain reimbursement. Where the contract is large and extends over a long period of time, this may mean that a substantial amount of the university's funds will be tied up for an indefinite period because, as fast as reimbursement is made for certain costs, the university has to incur new costs. Most universities feel that this is an improper use of endowed funds and, in any event, it involves a loss of interest for which they will receive no compensation. A large commercial loan is not ordinarily available to a university. Even if it were, the university would lose the interest on such loan because interest charges are not regarded as allowable costs. 1 One solution to this problem may be to provide in the contract for ad vance payments by the Government. Section 6 of the Act of August 1, 

1946, authorizes advance payments in the case of research contracts. 

Also, the Armed Services Procurement Act, as amended, authorizes the military departments to make advance payments under contracts in any amount not exceeding the contract price, provided they are made upon. adequate security, and provided the Secretary of the department con-

The whole matter of advance payments is discussed in Chapter 4,3 and no purpose would be served in going into it here in detail. However, these three points should be made. (1) Advance payments in connection with nonprofit contracts for research or development with nonprofit educational or research institutions are being made under the authority of the Armed Services Procurement Act; and, in connection with such contracts, an exception is made to the general requirement that contractors must pay interest on all such advances.4 (2) The contract, generally, provides that such payments are made to a controlled bank account on which, by virtue of the Armed Services Procurement Act, the Government is granted a lien paramount to all other liens. Simplified Voucher Procedures

The normal rules for the itemization, substantiation, and certification of contractors' vouchers under cost-reimbursement type contracts are unduly rigid when applied to educational institutions. University professors do not punch time clocks nor do they adhere to fixed time schedules. As is the case with most people engaged in creative activity, any attempt to police their time as though they were working on an assembly line not only would work to the disadvantage of the Government but would be foredoomed to failure. Fund accounting used by most universities is quite different from commercial type accounting. Furthermore, doing business under contract is the exception rather than the rule for many educational institutions. As a result, generally they are not as well prepared as commercial concerns to keep elaborate cost records and to submit detailed and fully itemized vouchers.

§ 8.44. New Features of Design 

For some time Navy research and development contracts have included a clause called "New Features of Design." It is expected that an adaptation of this clause will be included in the new Section VII, Part 4, of the Armed Services Procurement Regulation. The clause is designed to provide a means of controlling expenditures of government funds on work called for under a research and development contract when, prior to completion of the work under the contract, and whether or not in connection with performance of the contract itself, new and improved or alternative means of accomplishing the desired goal are developed by the contractor. The clause requires the contractor, to the extent not otherwise called for under the contract, to give the contracting officer notice of—

V. SOME SPECIAL PROBLEMS A. PROPERTY AND FACILITIES 

In research and development contracts with commercial organizations, the clauses relating to property furnished by the Government or acquired by the contractor at government expense are the same as those used in other Navy contracts. Somewhat different clauses are used in research and development contracts with educational or other nonprofit organizations where no profit or fee is contemplated. Some of the special problems presented in research and development contracts with respect to facilities and other property are discussed in this part. 

$8.46. Providing Facilities for Research and Development 

Generally speaking, there is no authority to acquire or construct facilities except as specifically authorized by Congress. Thus, the erection under a research contract of a laboratory or an observatory having general utility would not be permissible. However, even in the absence of specific statutory authority, the acquisition and installation of items such as specialized scientific equipment have been provided for as part of a research or development contract where such acquisition and installation are necessary for the effective prosecution of the work. This authority is said to be necessarily implied from the authority to place contracts for the conduct of research and development. Normally, such items of equip- 

9 See ASPR 13-505 and 13-506 (Dec. 

23, 1955). 452

DISPOSITION OF FACILITIES 

$ 8.47 ment are relatively small, but this is not always the case. For example, the Navy has had a number of contracts which provide for the design, development, and construction of particle accelerators (e.g., cyclotrons) and similar facilities for research in nuclear physics, as well as a number of contracts for wind tunnels for research in aerodynamics. In 1952, Congress made it unnecessary to rely solely on implied authority. In that year it granted specific statutory authority 10 for the construction or other acquisition by the contractor of research, developmental, or test facilities in cases where the Secretary of the military department concerned " determines them to be necessary for the performance of the research and development contract involved. In enacting this legislation, Congress guarded against abuse by not extending the authority to: (1) new construction or improvements having general utility; or (2) installation or construction of facilities on property not owned by the Government, which would not be readily removable or separable without unreasonable expense or unreasonable loss of value, unless the contract provides for (i) reimbursement to the Government of the fair value of the facilities on completion or termination of the contract, or within a reasonable time thereafter, (ii) an option in the Government to acquire the underlying land, or (iii) an alternate provision that the Secretary concerned 12 considers to be adequate to protect the Government's interest in such facilities. 

Where facilities or other property are acquired at the expense of the Government, the normal procedure is to provide that title thereto vest in the Government with a further provision for disposition at the end of the contract. This matter is treated in some detail in Chapters 9, 10, and 11. $ 8.47. Disposition of Facilities

Special problems arise where the contractor is contributing to the cost of performance. $ 8.47

Even in these cases where the Government bears the full cost involved, difficult problems arise. This is especially true where the contract calls for minor alterations (as distinguished from new construction) of the contractor's premises. An old form of Navy contract provided that as to such alterations the contractor could elect (i) to retain the benefit thereof, in which case it would pay the Government the fair value as determined by negotiation, or (ii) to have the premises restored to their prior condition, the cost of such restoration to be borne by the Government. This proved to be an unsatisfactory arrangement. The "fair value," after the contract was made, was usually claimed to be only a fraction of the original cost. On the other hand, the cost of restoration could actually exceed the cost of installation. Such a provision gives the contractor a superior bargaining position because, by threatening to demand restoration, it can keep the "fair value" of retaining the benefits down to a nominal figure. There is always the danger that it will insist on restoration. Contract clauses now in use provide that, in the absence of a special contract provision, the Government shall not be obligated to restore or rehabilitate, or to pay the costs of the restoration or rehabilitation of all or any portion of the contractor's premises which is affected by the removal of government facilities or other property.13 

Some university contractors have taken the position that building and equipment costs are essentially no different from any other costs of research, and that the Government should agree to assume them without demanding title to the property. The Act of July 16, 1952, makes it clear that such facilities and other property should be made available to the contractor only by means of a lease, a loan, or sale at fair value.14 

However, in connection with basic or applied research contracts which are otherwise authorized, the Government may now, under recent legislation 15 which is discussed in § 8.8 supra, vest title to equipment purchased with contract funds in certain educational and other nonprofit institutions performing such contracts. Under this new act, the Government has discretion to vest such title either without further obligation to the Government or on such terms or conditions as it deems appropriate. B. INSURANCE AND INDEMNITY 

Navy research and development contracts generally include the standard insurance and indemnification clauses which are explained in detail in Chapter 9. Some special problems have arisen, however, in connection with research and development contracts. 

The Insurance Liabilities to Third Persons clause 16 for cost-reimbursement type contracts provides that the contractor shall obtain workmen's compensation, employers' liability, and other public liability insurance as required by the Government. The Government agrees to pay its fair share of the cost of the premiums on such insurance and to assume any risks over and above the amount of the insurance which has been required or approved. This is perfectly acceptable in most cases. However, as discussed in succeeding sections, special problems do arise in certain cases.

§ 8.50. Indemnification Against Nuclear and Other Risks 

In some cases, where the risks have been considered extraordinary, insurance companies have refused to insure them except on an indemnity basis. During World War II, indemnity agreements with insurance companies were entered into in a number of cases by the Manhattan District. This was because the projects were secret and, therefore, inaccessible to insurance inspectors, as much as because of the hazardous nature of the work. The practice, however, has not generally been looked on with favor by the Government, particularly in peacetime. 

Another area in which insurance companies have been loath to assume risks and in which contractors have requested indemnification from the Government is in connection with experiments involving the artificial modification of weather. In such experiments, the possibility exists that an artificially induced rainfall or snowfall might cause widespread injury to crops or, if accompanied by lightning, might even cause death and serious personal injuries.

Insurance companies have been understandably hesitant, also, about entering into fields such as those involving research in nuclear physics or radioactivity or the development of nuclear power because of the general belief that these risks 18 are extremely hazardous and, particularly, because of the lack of reliable statistics upon which actuarial calculations could be based. When insurance companies have assumed risks of this character, as in the development of atomic submarines, they have been careful to limit the amount of insurance coverage and impose other restrictions. As experience has been gained in the practical applications of atomic energy, however, these limitations have become somewhat less restrictive. Although the nature of these risks is such that a single incident could cause loss and damage of catastrophic proportions, it now appears that the commercial insurance industry is prepared to assume a significant share of similar risks.19

Protection Against Atomic Hazards, INS.

The above insurance coverage has been made available in connection with the requirements of this act that licensees for nuclear reactors furnish "financial protection" as a condition precedent to receiving their licenses. "Financial protection" means "the ability to respond in damages for public liability" and to meet the costs of investigating and defending claims and settling suits for such damages. With respect to certain licensees, the law makes this requirement mandatory (§§ 103 and 104 of the act; and compare § 185 as to construction permits) and as to others merely permissive (§§ 53, 63, and 81 of the act). The Act of September 2, 1957, also permits the Atomic Energy Commission to indemnify its contractors under fixed-price as well as cost-reimbursement type contracts and under contracts and projects financed in whole or in part by the Commission. It also makes the requirement for furnishing "financial protection" merely permissive in the case of the Commission's contractors. The policy of the Commission has been not to require it to be furnished, in such cases, either in the form of insurance or otherwise.

There are a number of unique features in the above act which was passed in an effort to break down resistance which had built up to the commercial exploitation of atomic energy, largely as the result of the former provisions of the Atomic Energy Act, which required licensees to indemnify the Government. 

The Act of September 2, 1957, accord ingly, warrants careful reading in its entirety by anyone having occasion to deal with it. For example, the term "public liability," against which the Commission may extend indemnity is defined to include damage to "property" of the "persons indemnified" except property located at the reactor site and used in connection with the activity where the nuclear incident occurs. Also, the term "person indemnified" is defined to include not only the person with whom an indemnity agreement is executed but also "any other person who may be liable for public liability."

$8.51. Authority for Indemnification: Prior to 1952 

Prior to 1952 the authority of the Government to enter into contracts providing for government indemnification of a contractor for its liabilities to third parties and for loss of, or damage to, its property was not entirely clear. At that time it was necessary to rely on the legal theory that, where such an indemnity was regarded as a necessary incident to the placing of a particular research contract, the appropriation properly obligated under that contract could by implication be deemed to cover, within its limits,20 the cost of any such indemnity as well as any other expenses of completing the contract work. The application of this theory with respect to such indemnity was well recognized in connection with cost-reimbursement type contracts.21 However, since the costs of the Government's indemnity to a contractor for third-party liabilities and for loss of or damage to the contractor's property are pure contingencies, the theory was obviously of little value where a firm fixed-price contract was involved. However, it is considered permissible to combine in a single contract certain elements on a fixed-price basis and others on a cost-reimbursement basis; and in some cases such combinations have been employed for purposes of indemnifying contractors for work under what in other respects are fixed-price type contracts. 

During periods of emergency, it was considered that Title II of the First War Powers Act, 1941, as amended, provided statutory authority on the basis of which the Government could grant indemnification to contractors.22 But it is clear that Title II authority, as limited by 

Executive Order, did not permit the Government to indemnify a contractor or an insurance company in excess of the limits of the available appropriation.23 It is this limitation, as well as that mentioned above with respect to implied authority to indemnify, which has pointed up the need for additional legislation to cover the many cases which could result in liability, loss, or damage of great magnitude far exceeding the amount of funds available in the applicable appropriation.
