WALSH-HEALEY PUBLIC CONTRACTS ACT 

$ 9.7 

$ 9.7. Walsh-Healey Public Contracts Act 

The purpose of the Act of June 30, 1936,61 commonly called the "Walsh- Healey Public Contracts Act," is to require persons having supply contracts over $10,000 with the Government "to conform to certain labor conditions in the performance of the contracts and thus to eliminate the practice under which the Government is compelled to deal with sweat shops." 62 

In effect, this act extends to workers engaged in the performance of government supply contracts the same kind of protection afforded by the Eight-Hour Law of 1912 (discussed in § 9.4 supra) and the Davis- 

Bacon Act (discussed in § 9.5 supra) to laborers and mechanics engaged in government construction contracts. 

The Walsh-Healey Act provides that all government contracts "for the manufacture or furnishing of materials, supplies, articles, and equipment in any amount exceeding $10,000” shall contain certain representations and stipulations with respect to the performance of such contracts.63 

Said representations and stipulations are to the effect that (i) the contractor is the manufacturer of or a regular dealer in the items contracted for; (ii) the contractor will pay its employees not less than the minimum wages determined by the Secretary of Labor; (iii) no employee of the contractor will be permitted to work in excess of eight hours per day or forty hours per week; 64 (iv) the contractor will not employ males under sixteen or females under eighteen years of age; (v) no convict labor will be used; and (vi) no part of the work will be performed, nor will any of the items be manufactured or furnished, under working conditions which are unsanitary or hazardous or dangerous to the health and safety of employees. 

The act further provides that breach by the contractor of any of the above stipulations or representations gives the contracting agency the right to cancel the contract and repurchase the contract items from others, charging any additional costs to the original contractor; and in addition thereto, any breach renders the violating contractor liable to the Government for the amount of any underpayments to its employees and for an additional $10 per day, as liquidated damages, for each child worker or convict laborer knowingly employed on the contract.

In accordance with the requirements of Executive Order No. 325A, all government contracts involving the employment of labor must, unless otherwise authorized by law, contain a clause prohibiting the employment of any persons undergoing sentence of imprisonment at hard labor.76 

Excluded from this mandate would be any contract subject to the Walsh- Healey Public Contracts Act (because that act contains its own convict labor prohibition) and any contract for the purchase of supplies from 

Federal Prison Industries, Inc. (adverted to below). Also excluded are contracts which merely require the furnishing of finished articles. 

Such contracts do not necessarily involve the employment of labor since the contractor may secure the contract articles in the open market or from existing stocks." On the other hand, contracts for the construction of things, for articles requiring special fabrication, or for the furnishing of services do involve employment of labor and therefore are precluded by the executive order from being performed with prison labor, even if the contractor is a state instrumentality." 

In order to increase the opportunity of inmates of federal penal institutions to acquire skills in occupations which will provide them with a means of earning a livelihood upon release, the Act of May 27, 1930,79 has delimited the prohibition set forth above by directing that: 

The several Federal departments and agencies. . . shall pur- chase at not to exceed current market prices, such products of the industries authorized by this chapter as meet their requirements and may be available.

Federal Prison Industries, Inc., a government corporation created by 

Executive Order No. 6917, dated December 11, 1934, has the responsibility for determining the extent to which such industries are carried on in the federal prisons. Said corporation issues a "Schedule of Products" listing the commodities available for purchase by government agencies."

NONDISCRIMINATION IN EMPLOYMENT 

$ 9.9 $ 9.9. Nondiscrimination in Employment

Executive Order No. 8802 of June 25, 1941, as amended by Executive 

Order No. 9346 of May 27, 1943, provided in part as follows:

All contracting agencies of the Government of the United States shall include in all contracts hereafter negotiated or renegotiated by them a provision obligating the contractor not to discriminate against any employee or applicant for employment because of race, creed, color or national origin and requiring him to include a similar provision in all subcontracts.

The foregoing requirement for a nondiscrimination clause having at first been construed by the Comptroller General to be merely directive rather than mandatory," President Roosevelt, in a letter to Attorney General

Biddle dated November 5, 1943, emphatically reiterated the principle that discrimination by war industries against persons for any of the reasons named in the executive order was detrimental to the prosecution of the war and contrary to democratic processes; and the President made it clear that inclusion of a nondiscrimination provision in government contracts was mandatory. 

Although the above requirement had as its expressed purpose the maximum utilization of manpower for war production, and although the Committee on Fair Employment Practice (FEPC), to which enforcement of the provisions of the executive order had been entrusted, became inoperative July 1, 1946, as a result of the failure of the Congress to appropriate funds for its operation during the fiscal year 1947, nevertheless the executive orders on nondiscrimination are still in effect. Executive Order 

No. 10210 of February 2, 1951, implementing the First War Powers Act of 1941, as amended by the Act of January 12, 1951,82 expressly provides that "there shall be no discrimination in any act performed hereunder against any persons on the ground of race, creed, color or national origin, and all contracts hereunder shall contain a provision that the contractor and subcontractors thereunder shall not so discriminate." President Truman, by Executive Order No. 10308 of December 3, 1951, established a

Committee on Government Contract Compliance to determine whether compliance with the nondiscrimination provisions of contracts could be strengthened and improved. Subsequently, President Eisenhower, by 

Executive Order No. 10479 of August 13, 1953, replaced this Committee with a Government Contract Committee to improve and make more effective the nondiscrimination provisions of government contracts. 

By Executive Order No. 10577, dated September 3, 1954, President 

Eisenhower approved the following revised nondiscrimination clause recommended by the Government Contract Committee and set forth in 

ASPR 12-802 (May 14, 1958):

Buy American Act 87 The Act of March 3, 1933,86 usually called the "Buy American Act," requires that all articles, materials and supplies 7 acquired for public use within the United States, its territories or possessions must be of domestic origin (ie., mined or produced in the United States, or manufactured in the United States substantially all 88 from supplies mined, produced or manufactured in the United States) unless (i) they are for use abroad; or (ii) they, or the articles, materials or supplies from which they are manufactured, are not obtainable domestically in sufficient and reasonably available commercial quantities and of a satisfactory quality (this exception is interpreted as not permitting the purchase of supplies manufactured outside the United States from raw materials which are produced only abroad, if such supplies are manufactured in the United States in sufficient and reasonably available commercial quantities and of a satisfactory quality); 89 or (iii) the head of the department concerned determines that domestic purchase would be inconsistent with the public interest or would be at an unreasonable cost. In order to give it full effect, the aforesaid requirement of the Buy American Act is incorporated in every contract within the purview of that act. If the contractor fails to comply with such provision, it is not entitled to the stipulated contract price, and at best can then be paid only on a quantum valebat basis."1

It is the position of the military departments that in the case of manufactured products, the Buy American Act applies to the end product itself

This clause is no longer included in contracts in view of the repeal of section 12 of the Neutrality Act of 1939 by section 542 (a) of the Mutual 

Security Act of 1954. When used, the clause read as follows: 

If any of the supplies to be delivered under this contract are arms, ammunition, or implements of war, as listed in the current proclamation issued by the President pursuant to the Neutrality Act of 1939 (22 U.S. Code 452), the Contractor either (i) represents that it is properly registered under said Act and agrees to furnish satisfactory evidence thereof upon request, or (ii) represents that it is not subject to said Act and agrees to furnish satisfactory evidence thereof upon request.

Although the Mutual Security Act of 1954 continues the requirement for registration with the Department of State contained in section 12 of the Neutrality Act of 1939, it does not continue the prohibition in section 12 against the purchase by the Government of arms, ammunition or implements of war from any person who shall have failed so to register.10 

The above clause, having been promulgated in implementation of this prohibition, is no longer needed.

Renegotiation Act of 1951

With the advent of the Korean War and the extensive funds made available for national defense expenditures, the Renegotiation Act of 1951 24 was enacted to eliminate any excessive profits from government contracts. The act provides for the inapplicability of the Renegotiation 

Act of 1948,25 and other profit limitation statutes, under the conditions stated therein.

The Renegotiation Act of 1951 expired, in part, on December 31, 1954; but on August 3, 1955,26 it was extended to December 31, 1956, and on August 1, 1956, was further extended by section 2 of the Renegotiation Amendments Act of 1956 27 to receipts and accruals reasonably attributable to performance under contracts or subcontracts on or before December 31, 1958. Again, in September 1958, the act was extended an additional six months, that is through June 1959.28

Although section 104 of the Renegotiation Act of 1951 requires the inclusion of certain terms and conditions pertaining to the elimination of excessive profits in each contract made by the military departments and certain other government agencies, the act by its terms applies to the contract or subcontract even if such terms and conditions have not been inserted in the contract. The act also provides that any agreement of the contractor or subcontractor contained in the contract "Renegotiation" clause shall be binding only if the contract or subcontract actually is subject to the act.

In view of the above, and considering the possibility of future expiration and inapplicability of the Renegotiation Act of 1951 unless and until Congress extends the act or enacts different legislation on the subject, the "Renegotiation" clause, currently prescribed in ASPR 7-103.13 (March 17, 1958), provides that the contract is subject not only to the 1951 act, but also to any subsequent act providing for the renegotiation of contracts. It provides, however, that no renegotiation obligation is imposed with respect to the prime contract or subcontract which is not imposed by an act of Congress. By the terms of the clause the contract is deemed to contain all the provisions of section 104 of the Renegotiation Act of 1951 and of any other act providing for renegotiation of contracts, without any need for a subsequent contract amendment specifically incorporating its provisions. The prime contractor agrees to insert the provisions of the clause in all subcontracts as defined in section 103g of the act or any subsequent act of Congress providing for the renegotiation of contracts.

Inasmuch as the new self-effectuating and self-deleting "Renegotiation" clause is to be inserted in all contracts, there is no longer any need to determine in advance whether or not a particular proposed contract is or is not exempt from the act in order to determine whether or not to include or exclude the clause from a contract. 

A full discussion of renegotiation is contained in Chapter 6 supra. $9.15. Assignment of Claims

After a series of scandalous episodes and publicly debated abuses, it became apparent to Congress that legislation was necessary to protect the Government from the effects of assignments of claims against it. In 

1846, therefore, an act was passed 29 setting forth the conditions under which transfers and assignments might properly be made of any claim against the United States. This statute directed that any such transfer or assignment would be void unless made after the allowance of the claim, the ascertainment of the amount due, and the issuing of a warrant for its payment. In 1862 another act of Congress 30 declared that no contract or order, or any interest therein, might be transferred by a contractor, and that any attempt to do so would cause the annulment of the particular contract or order insofar as the United States was concerned. 

Taken together, these statutes were designed to prevent collusive and speculative bidding in government contracts, to prevent harassment by multiplying the number of persons with whom the Government had to

The act further provided, among other things: (1) that no claim shall be assigned if it arises under a contract which forbids such assignment; (2) that unless otherwise expressly permitted by a contract, any such assignment shall cover all amounts payable under the contract and not already paid, shall not be made to more than one party, and shall not be subject to further assignment (except that any such assignment may be made to one party as agent or trustee for two or more parties participating in the financing); (3) that in the event of any such assignment, the assignee shall file written notice of the assignment, together with a true copy of the instrument of assignment; and (4) that any contract entered into by the War Department or the Navy Department may provide that payments to an assignee of any claim arising under such contract shall not be subject to reduction or set-off for any indebtedness of the assignor to the United States arising independently of such contract. It has been general Navy practice not to prohibit an assignment of claims. 

However, the assignment does not permit the assignee to deal with the Government in place of the contractor in determining the amount of money due or to become due in connection with a particular claim. It merely entitles the assignee to receive the money.44 

In 1949 the Comptroller General held that in case of a price revision under a government contract, any amount above the contract price as revised might be withheld from payment to the assignee or recovered from the assignee if already paid.45 In the subsequent year he ruled that government claims against a contractor on account of unpaid social security contributions and withheld income taxes were claims which did not arise independently of the assigned contract; they could, accordingly, be set off by the Government against payments due the contractor under the contract.46 As a result of rulings of this type, banks refused to make loans to government contractors on the security of an assignment of claims because of their uncertainty as to whether there was any other indebtedness of the contractor to the Government. To remedy this situation, the Assignment of Claims Act was amended on May 15, 1951, to provide expressly that an assignee under the act shall have no liability to make restitution, refund or repayment to the United States of any amount received since July 1, 1950, on account of any liability of the assignor to the United States, whether arising from or independently of the contract. The 1951 amendment also authorized the Department of

The Act of May 15, 1951, provided further that the effect of such a "no set-off" clause would be to render payments to an assignee after May 15, 1951, of monies due or to become due under a contract not subject to set-off (i) for any liability of the contractor to the Government which arises independently of the contract, or (ii) for any liability of the contractor on account of renegotiation, fines, penalties (except penalties in accordance with or for failure to comply with the terms of the contract), or from taxes, social security contributions, or the withholding or nonwithholding of taxes or social security contributions, whether arising from or independently of the contract.

The present "Assignment of Claims" clause 48 provides that "payments to an assignee of any moneys due or to become due under this contract shall not, to the extent provided in said Act, as amended [the Assignment of Claims Act], be subject to reduction or set-off." A note following the clause indicates that this language has the effect prescribed for a "no set-off" clause by the Act of May 15, 1951. While this effect is sweeping, it should be noted that it does not rule out all set-offs. Thus, when a contract is terminated, the excess costs arising out of the reprocurement may be set off against monies due or to become due an assignee of the terminated contractor.49 A claim for excess costs is not deemed a claim arising independently of the contract.50 In addition, it has been held that the "no set-off" clause does not bar a set-off arising out of the Government's claims against the assignee. The clause only affects claims that could have been asserted against the contractor-assignor.51 Moreover, the "no set-off" clause does not bar a set-off against amounts due a contractor which exceed the amount of the contractor's indebtedness to the assignee.52

Although the risk of set-off has been eliminated, there still remains a possible deterrent to the granting of loans by banks and lending institutions. This deterrent will arise only when payment and performance bonds are required; 53 it stems from the claim of surety companies that their rights to monies due a contractor are superior to those of assignee banks. $9.16. Subcontracts Under Cost-Reimbursement Contracts 

10 U.S.C. § 2306 (e) (formerly section 4(b) of the Armed Services 

Procurement Act of 1947) requires that all cost and cost-plus-a-fixed-fee contracts must provide for advance notice by the prime contractor to the procuring agency of any subcontract on a cost-plus-a-fixed-fee basis and of any fixed-price subcontract or purchase order which exceeds in dollar amount either $25,000 or 5 percent of the total estimated cost of the prime contract. This requirement is incorporated into a standard contract clause providing for such advance notification, and at the same time providing that no subcontract shall be entered into on a cost-plus-a-percentage-of-cost basis (which is an overall prohibition imposed by 10 

U.S.C. § 2306 (a)). 

The required clause referred to above is uniform throughout the Department of Defers in the case of cost-reimbursement type supply contracts, being prescribed in ASPR 7-203.8 (July 15, 1958). This clause also requires the written consent of the contracting officer in the case of some or all of the subcontracts for which advance notification is required. 

It expressly provides, however, that any approval of the contracting officer of any of the provisions of the subcontract shall not be construed to constitute a determination of the allowability of any cost under the contract, unless such approval specifically so states. Paragraph (e) of the clause requires the contractor to notify the Government of any action or suit filed, or claim made, against the contractor by any subcontractor or vendor which, in the opinion of the contractor, may result in litigation related in any way to the contract under which the contractor may be entitled to reimbursement from the Government. 

Although no uniform subcontract clause has been promulgated with respect to cost-reimbursement type contracts for construction or research

Examination of Records 

To afford a means whereby Congress could be informed of any excessive or unreasonable payments to contractors holding negotiated contracts, and to serve as a deterrent to the making of contracts providing for unreasonable profits to government contractors,59 the Armed Services Procurement Act of 1947 was amended on October 31, 1951,60 to require all contracts negotiated under said act to include a clause to the effect that the Comptroller General of the United States or any of his duly authorized representatives shall until the expiration of three years after final payment have access to and the right to examine any directly pertinent books, documents, papers, and records of the contractor or any of his subcontractors engaged in the performance of and involving transactions related to such contracts or subcontracts. Prior to this amendment, this requirement applied only to action taken under the First War Powers Act.

The "Examination of Records" clause currently prescribed by ASPR 7-104.15 (Nov. 3, 1958) 61 differs from the one originally promulgated (which used virtually the statutory language) in that it expressly defines the term subcontracts as excluding (i) purchase orders not exceeding $1,000 and (ii) subcontracts or purchase orders for public utility services at rates established for uniform applicability to the general public.62 

The first exclusion extends to prime contractors the same kind of exception which had been extended to the Government with respect to its purchase orders through informal discussions with the General Accounting Office. The second exclusion is based upon the analogous exemption contained in section 106 (a) (4) of the Renegotiation Act of 1951.63 The current clause also differs from its original form in requiring subcontractors to retain their records only for three years following final payment under their subcontracts rather than for three years following final payment under the prime contract. This difference, first permitted only in experimental developmental and research contracts,64 was later extended to all negotiated contracts of the military departments.65 

In the case of cost-reimbursement type contracts, the "Examination of Records" clause discussed above is made a part of the "Records" clause discussed in § 9.36 of this chapter.

Gratuities Clause 

In 1951 the Senate Appropriations Committee became concerned by evidence that officials in the military departments who could influence the awarding of contracts had received various gratuities from contractors or agents of contractors seeking government business. In an effort to curb this practice the committee added a section to the Department of Defense Appropriation bill which ultimately was enacted as section 631 of Department of Defense Appropriation Act, 1952.66 This section, initially continued without substantial change in subsequent appropriation acts, was made permanent by section 719 of the Department of Defense Appropriation Act, 1955.67 It provides that no money appropriated to the 

Department of Defense is to be expended under any contract entered into after enactment of the section, except one for personal services, unless the contract provides that the Government may terminate the contract if the Secretary or his designee finds, after notice and hearing, that gratuities were offered or given by the contractor or his agent or representative to a government officer or employee with a view toward securing a contract. The statute speaks of gratuities "in the form of entertainment, gifts or otherwise." The section also requires that the contract provide for termination by the Government if gratuities were offered or given to secure favorable treatment as to awarding or amending the contract, or as to the making of any determinations relating to the performance of the contract. The existence of the facts on which the findings of the Secretary or his designee are made must be in issue and be susceptible to review in any competent court. Finally, the section requires that the contract provide that if the contract is terminated by the Government because of the offering or gift of gratuities, the Government may pursue the same remedies against the contractor as for breach of contract and will also be entitled to exemplary damages as a penalty against the contractor. 

The standard "Gratuities" clause, set forth in ASPR 7-104.16 (June 11, 1958), in addition to containing the requirements of the statute, specifically provides that the Government's rights and remedies provided in the clause are not exclusive, but are in addition to any other rights and remedies provided by law or under the contract.68 

The Armed Services Procurement Regulation, in Appendix D, sets forth the rules for notice and hearing required by the statute. The rules

$ 9.19 11 require at least ten days notice to be given of the hearing, alleging the circumstances of the offering of the gratuity in sufficient detail to indicate the issues involved in the hearing. The parties to the hearing are to be the Government and the contractor involved. The rules prohibit intervention in the hearing by any other person. Testimony may be received at the hearing which would be inadmissible under legal rules of evidence, but immaterial, irrelevant, or unduly repetitious evidence is to be excluded. 

Testimony is to be under oath, cross-examination is allowed, depositions may be taken and placed in evidence, oral argument may be allowed, and written findings and conclusions must be made with respect to all material issues. If made by a designee, the findings are to be forwarded to the 

Secretary with recommendations as to terminating the contract and the amount of exemplary damages, if any, to be imposed. 

A contractor guilty of offering a gratuity faces criminal prosecution under several sections of the Criminal Code: 18 U.S.C. § 201 (offering a gratuity), 18 U.S.C. § 371 (conspiring to defraud the United States), and 18 U.S.C. § 1001 (defrauding the United States). On the administrative level, the contractor may be debarred and suspended from the list of contractors eligible to bid for Department of Defense contracts. 

Such action is authorized by ASPR 1-604.1 (b) (Jan. 28, 1958).

II. OTHER CLAUSES OF GENERAL APPLICATION 

$9.19. Contractor's Undertaking; Order of Precedence

The clause setting forth the contractor's undertaking (ie., "The parties hereto agree that the Contractor shall furnish and deliver all the supplies and perform all the services set forth in the attached Schedule, for the consideration stated therein.") appears on the cover page of the Department of Defense Negotiated Contract Form (DD 351). In the case of advertised supply contracts, an equivalent undertaking is set forth in the 

Invitation and Bid (Standard Form 30). 

Prior to the issuance of Form DD 351, a "Scope of Contract" clause was set forth in the contract containing both the contractor's undertaking and the "Order of Precedence" clause (i.e., "The rights and obligations of the parties to this contract shall be subject to and governed by the Schedule and the General Provisions. To the extent of any inconsistency between the Schedule or the General Provisions, and any specifications or the other provisions which are made a part of this contract by reference, or otherwise, the Schedule and the General Provisions shall control. To the extent of any inconsistency between the Schedule and the General 

Provisions, the Schedule shall control."). The "Order of Precedence" clause now appears on the execution sheet of the Department of Defense Negotiated Contract Form (DD 351-2). In advertised supply contracts, the "Order of Precedence" clause (incorporating also the Terms and 531

$9.20

Conditions of the Invitations for Bids and placing precedence thereof after the Schedule but on a par with the General Provisions) is usually made a part of the General Provisions. Neither the clause covering the contractor's undertaking nor that covering the order of precedence ap pears on U.S. Standard Form 32. 

$9.20. Definitions

The first contract clause appearing in Section VII of the Armed Services Procurement Regulation (entitled "Contract Clauses"), and in U.S. 

Standard Form 32, is entitled "Definitions." It appears in ASPR 7-103.1 (March 17, 1958) and sets forth the contract definition of the terms "Secretary" (as meaning the Secretary, Under Secretary or any Assistant 

Secretary of the Department) and "his duly authorized representative" (as meaning any person or persons or board, other than the contracting officer, authorized to act for the Secretary), "contracting officer" (as meaning the person executing the contract on behalf of the Government and any other officer or civilian employee who is properly designated contracting officer, and as including the authorized representative of a contracting officer acting within the limits of his authority), and "subcontracts" (as including purchase orders under the contract). The regulation authorizes the inclusion in the contract of additional definitions not inconsistent therewith. $9.21. Changes

The necessity for incorporating design improvements in naval vessels while under construction became apparent as long ago as the Civil War, as evidenced by the numerous changes made in the ironclad ETLAH during its construction.69 The contractual arrangement then adopted as the most practicable for meeting this need was the reservation in a shipbuilding contract of a right in the Government to make unilateral changes in the plans and specifications at any time during the progress of the work.70 

Such a reservation has come to be referred to as the "Changes" clause. 

This type of clause has proved so valuable that it is presently standard 

69 See McCord v. United States, 9 Ct. 

Cl. 155 (1873), aff'd sub nom. Chouteau v. United States, 95 U.S. 61 (1877). 

70 Section 16 of the contract between 

McCord and the United States, entered into on July 9, 1863, provided: "It is further agreed, that the . . . [United

[McCord] ... they will pay for the same at fair and reasonable rates; and should said changes cause less work and expense... a corresponding reduction to be made from the contract price; and in each case the cost of the alteration to be determined when the changes are directed to be made."

CHANGES 

$ 9.21 2 3 "boilerplate,” not only in shipbuilding contracts, but also in almost every government contract.

The "Changes" clause for fixed-price type supply contracts is set forth in ASPR 7-103.2 (March 17, 1958); that for cost-reimbursement type supply contracts is set forth in ASPR 7-203.2 (May 14, 1958). These clauses require that the modification be made in writing (usually called a "change order") and that it be issued by the contracting officer. Provision is made in these clauses for modification in (i) drawings, designs or specifications only where the supplies are to be specially manufactured for the Government, (ii) the method of shipment or packing and in the place of delivery, and (iii) the amount of government-furnished property (in the case of cost-reimbursement type supply contracts). Where the right is to be reserved to make modification in other contract requirements, such as in the content of spare parts lists, it is usually done by means of a separate clause entitled "Additional Changes." Provision is also made in these clauses for the parties equitably to adjust the contract price (the estimated cost and fixed fee, if any, in the case of cost-reimbursement type supply contracts) and the time of performance to the extent that the change order has an effect in the performance of any part of the work under the contract, whether or not changed by the change order. In the case of cost-reimbursement type supply contracts, provision is also made for an equitable adjustment in such other provisions of the contract as may be affected by the change order. For fixed-price type supply contracts, the right is reserved to the contracting officer to prescribe the manner of disposition of property made obsolete or excess by the change order, where the cost of such property is included in the contractor's claim for equitable adjustment. The failure of the parties to agree to any adjustment becomes a dispute concerning a question of fact to be resolved in accordance with the "Disputes" clause (discussed in § 9.30 of this chapter). However, the contractor is required to proceed meanwhile with the contract as changed. 

Prior to its revision in October 1957,72 the equitable adjustment terms of the "Changes" clause for fixed-price type supply contracts provided that if any change order "causes an increase or decrease in the cost of, or time required for, performance of this contract, an equitable adjustment shall be made in the contract price or delivery schedule or both.” 73 Under this language the adjustment was limited to the actual or estimated cost (plus profit) of the contract work so changed and did not permit reimbursement for standby changes and consequential cost increases in the work not within the scope of the change order.74 But this technical in- 

71 This clause is also ¶2 of Standard 

Form 32 (Oct. 1957 ed.). 

72 See 12 of Standard Form 32 (Oct. 

1957 ed.). See also ASPR Revision No. 

28 of Jan. 28, 1958. 

73 ¶ 2 of Standard Form 32 (Nov. 1949 

ed.); ASPR 7-103.2 (Jan. 3, 1955). 

74 See United States v. Rice, 317 U.S. 61 (1942). 533

$ 9.21

terpretation caused hardship and was not uniformly administered. Accordingly, the clause has been revised to permit equitable adjustment in the contract price or performance time when the change order "causes an increase or decrease in the cost of, or time required for, the performance of any part of the work under this contract, whether changed or not changed by any such order." 75 A like revision has been made to the "Changes" clause for cost-reimbursement type supply contracts.76 However, these modifications should not be understood as sanctioning the repricing of an improvident contract.7

In order to assure that the change order is "priced out" prospectively and not after its completion, the "Changes" clauses require the contractor to submit its proposal for such pricing action within thirty days (unless a longer period is specified elsewhere in the contract). These clauses provide that late claims by the contractor for increase in the contract price (or fixed fee) or in the time for performance can be made only if such claims are made prior to final payment under the contract and the contracting officer decides that the facts justify his acting upon them. 

Any modification in the work that is unilateral in nature and properly the subject of a change order which necessitates an adjustment in price is chargeable or creditable, as the case may be, to the appropriation against which the contract was entered into, since the change order "relates back" to the date the contract was made.78 So too, in the case of additional work which nevertheless remains within the original scope of the contract, the increase in price may be charged to the original appropriation. However, if the modification calls for work not within the original scope of the contract, it must be charged to the appropriation current at the time of the agreement by the contractor' to undertake the new work.79

It is important to emphasize that the use of the change order must be limited to situations where unilateral directions are issued to the contractor calling for a modification of the work within the original scope of such work as expressed in the contract. If the direction issued to the contractor either materially alters the character or scope of the contract, or expands the contract to include additional work to any considerable degree, the modification in the contract ceases to be unilateral and becomes the subject for a bilateral amendment to which the contractor must agree. If forced to comply with a unilateral order for additional work, the contractor may recover damages from the Government for breach of

The Armed Services Procurement Regulation requires the inclusion in all fixed-price supply contracts of two one-sentence, self-explanatory clauses entitled, respectively, "Extras" and "Variation in Quantity."

The "Extras" clause 3 provides that "Except as otherwise provided in this contract, no payment for extras shall be made unless such extras and the price therefor have been authorized in writing by the Contracting Officer." Prior to the promulgation of the regulation, the use of this clause by the Navy was generally limited to construction contracts. 

The "Variation in Quantity" clause 4 provides that "No variation in the quantity of any item called for by this contract will be accepted unless such variation has been caused by conditions of loading, shipping, or packing, or allowances in manufacturing processes, and then only to the extent, if any, specified elsewhere in this contract." Whether there may be a variation in the quantity of supplies, and to what extent, is ultimately dependent upon the nature of the supplies involved. $9.23. Inspection

In order to assure strict conformity with contract specifications, it is important that, to the extent practicable, inspections and tests be conducted by the Government not only at the time of delivery or acceptance of the supplies being procured, but also at all times during their manufacture or construction. The prescribed "Inspection" clauses for fixed-price type supply contracts is set forth in ASPR 7-103.5 (May 14, 1958) and for cost-reimbursement type supply contracts in ASPR 7-203.5 (May 14, 1958).

These clauses include the customary requirements as to inspection which are to the effect that (i) the contractor and its subcontractors will furnish reasonable facilities for and assistance in inspection, (ii) the contractor will maintain its own technical inspection system in a manner acceptable to the Government, and (iii) rejected work will not be resubmitted without notice of its prior rejection. The "Inspection" clauses expressly reserve to the Government the right to require delivery, at an equitable reduction in price, or fixed fee, of supplies which it has a right to reject. 

In the case of the fixed-price contract "Inspection" clause, express provision is also made that final inspection and acceptance will not be conclusive as regards latent defects, fraud, or the Government's rights under any "Guaranty" clause.

For the purpose of carrying out the inspection requirements referred to above, the Department of the Navy, through its Office of Naval Material (Field Services Division), maintains throughout the country an extensive organization of technical inspectors, called Inspectors of Naval Material. The services of these Navy inspectors are available to all procuring activities of the Department. In addition, the technical bureaus maintain their own inspectors, who are specially trained in inspection problems peculiar to the particular bureau. Thus, Supervisors of 

Shipbuilding have the inspection responsibility with respect to vessel contracts awarded by the Bureau of Ships, as do Inspectors of Naval Machinery in the case of propulsion equipment contracts for such vessels. 

Bureau of Aeronautics Representatives have similar responsibility with respect to contracts placed by that Bureau, as do Naval Inspectors of Ordnance in the case of procurement of technical ordnance or ordnance equipment by the Bureau of Ordnance. These bureau inspectors, however, are an integral part of the "Material Inspection Service, U.S.N.," and are under the technical supervision of the Office of Naval Material. 

The policy of the Department of Defense as to inspection requirements, inter- and intradepartmental responsibility for inspection, subcontract inspection, and acceptance is set forth in Part 1 of Section XIV of the 

Armed Services Procurement Regulation.

It is long standing Navy policy to incorporate by reference in all fixedprice supply contracts its current edition of "General Specifications for the Inspection of Material." This incorporation by reference is generally effected by means of a separate clause captioned "General Specifications for the Inspection of Material." This specification is in the form of a

Responsibility for Supplies

Title to supplies contracted for on a fixed-price basis ordinarily passes to the Government upon delivery and acceptance of the supplies. Until then the contractor has complete responsibility with respect to such supplies absent a showing of damage to the supplies caused by the Government's negligence during the interval between delivery and acceptance or rejection. Following notice of rejection of delivered supplies the contractor has the risk of loss in the absence of gross negligence by government personnel in dealing with the supplies. This responsibility is set forth in a clause entitled "Responsibility for Supplies." "

Generally, the designated delivery point is the destination of the supplies with respect to shipments of less than carload or truckload lots (arbitrarily defined to be approximately 20,000 pounds) and f.o.b., carrier's equipment, wharf, or freight station (at the Government's option), at or near contractor's plant, where destinations are unknown at the time the contract is made, where the supplies are for ultimate delivery to destinations outside the continental United States, or where the bid price based upon delivery at contractor's plant in the case of carload or truckload lots is more advantageous to the Government." Title to, and responsibility for, supplies procured on a cost-reimbursement basis are discussed in § 9.37 of this chapter. 

It should be noted that in certain limited situations fixed-price contracts provide that title to supplies or work in process shall pass to the Government at a time earlier than the time of their delivery and acceptance. 

So shipbuilding contracts state that "title to the vessels under construction shall be in the Government and title to all materials and equipment acquired for each vessel shall vest in the Government upon delivery thereof

An earlier vesting of title may also be required where a contract provides for advance or progress payments. Here the vesting occurs at the time at which the payment is made. Additionally, the Government may always effect an earlier vesting of title under fixed-price contracts when there is a termination of the contract, whether for default or for the convenience of the Government. While the standard termination clauses prescribed by the Armed Services Procurement Regulation do not provide for an automatic, self-executing transfer of title upon termination, they do grant the Government the power to demand an immediate transfer of title, if it so wishes."1

A distinction must be made between the transfer of title provisions which deal with supplies furnished by the contractor and the retention of title provision which becomes necessary in the case of supplies or property furnished by the Government. The former have been the subject of this section; the latter is discussed in § 9.40 of this chapter. 

§ 9.25. Payments 

The basic undertaking of the Government is to pay the contractor for performing a contract. In the case of fixed-price supply contracts, this undertaking is to pay stipulated prices for supplies delivered and accepted or services performed and accepted; in cost-type contracts, the 

Government's obligation is to pay the contractor the "allowable costs" incurred by it in the performance of the contract and usually, in addition, a fixed fee for such performance. These undertakings are substantially different and require separate consideration. 

The "Payments" clause prescribed for fixed-price supply contracts, set forth in ASPR 7-103.7 (March 17, 1958) and in paragraph 7 of Standard Form 32 (Oct. 1957 ed.), provides that, upon the submission of proper invoices or vouchers, the contractor shall be paid the prices stipulated in the contract for supplies delivered and accepted, or services rendered, less such deductions as are specified. In order to permit payment for partial deliveries and at the same time prevent an influx of invoices for small sums, the aforesaid clause also provides that payment will be made on partial deliveries accepted by the Government whenever the amount due on such deliveries so warrants, or whenever such payments equal or exceed either $1,000 or 50 percent of the total contract price. 

90 For a discussion of the legal effect of this clause, see In re American Boiler 

Works, Inc., 220 F. 2d 319 (3d Cir. 1955). 

91 See, e.g., ASPR 8-701(b) (vi), 8707 (d) (Sept. 5, 1958). See also §§ 5.63, 5.64 supra. 538

PAYMENTS 

$ 9.25

However, contractors may be unwilling or unable to undertake, on the above payment basis, the furnishing of supplies involving extended periods of manufacture or considerable initial investment unless a portion of the contract price is paid in advance of delivery. To do this requires statutory authority in view of the general prohibition of section 3648 of the Revised Statutes against advance payments.92 But specific authority to make progress and advance payments does exist, and the circumstances and procedures concerning the making of such payments have been discussed in sections 4.42 through 4.45 of this book. 

Where fixed-price supply contracts not only involve the furnishing of designated supplies but also call for instruction books, plans, drawings, specifications, designs, patent rights, test after delivery, or other similar requirements, specified amounts are usually withheld from payments otherwise due the contractor until all the aforesaid requirements are met." The release of these sums is considered to be final payment inasmuch as no special final payment clause is usually provided in such contracts. However, in the case of vessel contracts, construction contracts, and the like, a separate final payment clause is included, usually conditioning such payment upon the release of the Government, its agents and employees from any and all liabilities arising under the contract. 

In cost-reimbursement type contracts the matter of "payments" in the case of supply contracts is usually dealt with in a clause entitled "Allowable Cost, Fixed Fee and Payment" (ASPR 7-203.4(a), June 11, 1958).

Moreover, in cost-reimbursement type contracts, the payments are largely determined by "allowable costs." Allowable costs are defined in the contract as comprising those costs incurred by the contractor in the performance of the contract and accepted by the Government, usually represented in the Navy by the Contract Audit Division of the Comptroller of the Navy (formerly the Cost Inspection Service of the Bureau of Supplies and Accounts), as properly chargeable to the contract in accordance with designated cost and accounting principles. Such principles, which are either set forth in the contract or incorporated therein by reference, are contained in Section XV of the Armed Services Procurement Regu lation, with separate consideration being given to costs under supply and research contracts with commercial organizations, costs under research contracts with educational institutions, and costs under construction contracts.

And in all cases of contracts for the performance of any service, or the delivery of articles of any description, for the use of the United States, payment shall not exceed the value of the service rendered, or of the articles delivered previously to such payment."

$9.25

Payments on account of allowable costs are made upon the submission by the contractor of invoices supported by a statement of costs claimed to be allowable. Such invoices are usually required to be submitted monthly, must be in such form and detail as the auditor may require, and must be certified by an official of the contractor who supervises accounting with respect to the contract. Inasmuch as all such costs are audited by the Department prior to final payment (often a lengthy process), provisional payment, to the extent of 80 percent of costs incurred, is made by the Government in advance of such audit, with appropriate adjustments thereafter.94 

The fixed fee (if any) under a cost-type contract is normally due and payable upon the satisfactory completion of the entire work.95 However, where performance may extend over a substantial period, installment payments are made on account of the fixed fee, based either on a percentage of completion of the work or on actual costs incurred. But, in either case, 15 percent of the total fixed fee, or $100,000, whichever is less, is generally withheld until final payment." In the case of cost without fee contracts, payments on account of allowable costs are withheld, after payment of 80 percent of the estimated cost of the contract, until a reserve of either 1 percent of the estimated cost or $100,000, whichever is less, is set aside; such reserve is paid at the time of final payment. 

All cost-reimbursement type contracts also provide, usually as part of the same "Allowable Cost, Fixed Fee and Payment" clause, that the contractor and each assignee under an assignment under the contract in effect at the time of final payment, shall execute, at the time of and as a condition precedent to final payment, a release discharging the Government, its officers, agents, and employees from all liabilities, obligations and claims arising out of the contract. $ 9.26. Additional Bond Security 

The Armed Services Procurement Regulation requires the inclusion in all fixed-price supply contracts, except purchase orders not exceeding $5,000, of a self-explanatory, one-sentence clause entitled "Additional Bond Security." This clause, set forth in ASPR 7-103.9 (par. 9 of 

Standard Form 32, Oct. 1957 ed.), provides that "If any surety upon any bond furnished in connection with this contract becomes unacceptable to the Government, or if any such surety fails to furnish reports as to financial condition from time to time as requested by the Government, the Contractor shall promptly furnish such additional security as may be required from time to time to protect the interests of the Government and of persons supplying labor or materials in the prosecution of the work contemplated by this contract." This clause is useful in any contract under which a bond is furnished. $ 9.27. Federal, State, and Local Taxes

Few problems of government contracting are more vexatious, both legally and economically, than the impact of state and local taxation upon government contractors. While the legal principle is fundamental that the United States is constitutionally immune from state and local taxation in the absence of congressional assent," the extent to which this immunity shelters government contractors is highly controverted, as recent Supreme Court decisions have shown.98 The distinction between constitutionally permissible state and local nondiscriminatory taxation that merely imposes additional economic burdens on the federal government " and constitutionally objectionable taxation that puts the legal incidence 

97 M'Culloch v. Maryland, 17 U.S. (4 

Wheat.) 316, 425-437 (1819). 

98 See, e.g., United States v. Detroit, 355 U.S. 466 (1958); Detroit v. Murray

Corporation of America, 355 U.S. 489 

(1958). In all these cases there were strong dissents, and in Murray the Court divided 5-4. For a discussion of state and local taxation of contractors' possessory interest in government facilities, see 88 10.47-10.50 infra. 

99 See cases cited in § 9.27, n. 98 supra;

Alabama v. King & Boozer, 314 U.S. 1 

(1941); James v. Dravo Contracting Co., 302 U.S. 134 (1937). 541

$ 9.27

of the exaction directly on the federal government, its property or its agents,' or that discriminates against the Government or its contractors,² is one that will long continue to confront courts and lawyers with great difficulties, particularly as the states and municipalities seek new sources of revenue. No less troublesome are the legal uncertainties of state taxation as a burden on interstate commerce in the context of the performance of government contracts in interstate commerce.3 

The constitutional uncertainty of a great range of state and local tax devices, present and future, as applied to government contractors obviously poses the likelihood of enormous contingency factors in the pricing of fixed-price type government contracts. Added to this is the uncertainty-particularly in procurements of long lead-time items of increases in the tax rates or the imposition of new taxes, and this too loads the tax-contingency factor in prices quoted on government work. 

The military departments have devised two tax clauses for fixed-price type contracts. The theory of the clauses, generally speaking, is to substitute a combination of price escalation and competitive pricing for price contingencies and to permit contract prices to be inclusive of all lawfully applicable taxes as of the contract date, except taxes from which the contracting parties, the transaction itself, or any property covered thereby are then exempt.

In pricing theory, if a firm fixed-price type government contract be silent about taxes, the risk of tax costs not included in the price would rest wholly with the contractor. By the same token, contingencies for taxes included in the contract price would represent gains to the contractor to the extent his liability for such taxes did not eventuate. To an extent, the device of awarding government contracts on the basis of price competition, particularly among bidders from different tax jurisdictions, minimizes the Government's risk of excessive tax contingencies in contract prices; but where the legal uncertainty of the applicability of state or local taxes to the contract or the risk of new or increased taxes is substantial, excessive tax contingencies are best avoided by the device of price escalation-the Government's promise to increase the contract price by the amount of the contractor's liability for tax costs properly excluded from the contract price.

The tax clauses currently in use by the military departments in fixedprice type contracts reflect these two approaches. The clause for formally advertised contracts and for other contracts where competition or bargaining eliminates contingencies for state and local taxes, ASPR 11–401.1 (Nov. 3, 1958), essentially is on the theory of firm fixed-price contracting so far as the contractor's liability for most state and local taxes is concerned. Upward escalation of the contract price for such taxes is limited to "those levied on or measured by the contract price or sales price of the services or completed supplies furnished under this contract." 5 By contrast, the tax clause for all other negotiated fixed-price type contracts, ASPR 11-401.2, essentially follows the escalation approach to avoid excessive price contingencies for state and local taxes and provides for price escalation for all types of state and local taxes except for real property taxes and a fairly narrow class of income and franchise taxes." 

But, under both ASPR tax clauses, before a contractor can qualify for escalation of the contract price for state and local taxes-to the extent each of the clauses permits such escalation as stated above-or for federal taxes and duties (the extent of escalation for federal taxes and duties will be summarized below), he must meet several other conditions. First, the contractor must show that he is required to pay such taxes or to bear the burden of them and that this liability (including any liability for interest or penalties) is not incurred through the contractor's fault or negligence or failure to follow the contracting officer's instructions.Ⓡ 

Next, the contractor must show that as of the "tax inclusive date," such taxes, by the terms of the tax clause, were not to be included in the contract price because they were taxes from which the Government, the contractor, or the transactions or property covered by the contract were then 5 ASPR 11-401.1(c)(4) (Nov. 3, 1958).

The "Default" clause for fixed-price type supply contracts, set forth in ASPR 8–707 (Sept. 5, 1958), deals exclusively with the defaulting contractor situation, whereas the "Termination" clause for cost-reimbursement type contracts set forth in ASPR 8-702 (Sept. 5, 1958) deals not only with termination for the contractor's default, but also with termination for the convenience of the Government. Both clauses permit the Government to terminate the contract for default when there is a failure or refusal of the contractor to deliver the required supplies or to perform the required services or otherwise to perform the contract (i.e., the usual breach of contract at common law), or when there is a failure of the contractor to make progress so as to endanger performance of the contract. The clauses expressly provide that before terminating the contract for default, the contractor shall be given an opportunity to cure any such default (except a failure to make timely delivery in the case of the "Default" clause) within a period of at least ten days after receipt of notice from the contracting officer specifying the default. Procedures applicable to terminating fixed-price supply contracts for default are set forth in ASPR 8–602 (Sept. 5, 1958).

The standard "Default" clause expressly requires termination thereunder to be effected "by written Notice of Default." $ 9.28 ment contract calls for "substantially different" rather than "similar" supplies or services,32 although the Government may still recover from a defaulting contractor whatever actual damages may be occasioned by the default.33 A different result obtains where identical supplies are not available; here purchase of the best available substitute, even though of a different kind or quality, will not relieve the contractor from its liability for excess costs.34 The contractor also remains liable when identical supplies are repurchased on terms different than those in the defaulted contract, provided the obligations reflected by the added terms are ascertainable in amount and, if they enhance the cost of reprocurement, are credited against the excess costs charged the contractor.35 It should be noted that the term "excess costs" is broader than the term "increase in contract price." It covers not only the increase in contract price existing at the time the replacement contract is entered into 36 (which would be the full extent of the damages recoverable at common law, assuming no unreasonable delay in the act of reprocuring), but also whatever actual damages might arise from delay in performance of the reprocurement contract. On the other hand, in computing total excess costs, the contractor is entitled to be credited for any savings effected by reletting the contract at prices lower than the defaulted contract.38 

In addition to imposing liability upon a contractor for excess costs, the "Default" clause expressly permits the contracting officer to direct the defaulted contractor to transfer title and deliver to the Government the property (including completed supplies) specifically produced or acquired in connection with the performance of the contract (or for the terminated portion of the contract, if the termination is not of the whole contract).39

"The "Default" clause expressly provides that, except for subcontractor defaults, the contractor shall not be liable for any excess costs if any failure to perform the contract arises out of causes beyond the control and without the fault or negligence of the contractor, such causes to include, but not to be restricted to, "acts of God or of the public enemy, acts of the Government in either its sovereign or contractual capacity, fires, floods, epidemics, quarantine restrictions, strikes,40 freight embargoes, and unusually severe weather." 41 With respect to subcontractor defaults, the prime contractor is relieved of liability for excess costs if the subcontractor's default is due to causes beyond the control and without the fault or negligence of both the prime and subcontractor "unless the supplies or services to be furnished by the subcontractor were obtainable from other sources in sufficient time to permit the Contractor to meet the required delivery schedule." 42 The propriety of a termination for default may be appealed to the Secretary of the Navy under the "Disputes" clause of the contract (discussed in § 9.30 of this chapter). TERMINATION FOR DEFAULT 

$ 9.28 upon for all other property transferred to the Government, but no more than this. If the termination for default is later determined to have been improper, the "Default" clause provides that the "Notice of Default" shall be deemed to have been issued pursuant to the "Termination for Convenience of the Government" clause of the contract (discussed in § 5.28 supra). Thenceforth, the latter clause governs the rights and obligations of the parties. In consequence, the contractor becomes entitled to payment for all costs incurred in connection with its performance of the contract and to reimbursement for its expenses in connection with the termination. Except in one very limited situation, this conversion from a termination for default to a convenience termination does not affect the Government's right to obtain a transfer of title to and delivery of the completed supplies and other property produced or acquired in connection with the performance of the contract. For like the "Default" clause, the "Termination for the Convenience of the Government" clause has a provision permitting the Government to demand such a transfer of title. The limited situation alluded to above is that in which the default has been caused by the act or failure to act of the Government. One federal court has held that in this set of circumstances the court will refuse to enforce the Government's right to obtain a transfer of title under the "Termination for the Convenience of the Government" clause because of the Government's inequitable conduct.43 The rule does not bar a contractor from assenting to a demand by the Government that title be transferred, and it will not be invoked if it will result in an unjust enrichment of the contractor. 

The "Termination" clause of cost-type supply contracts 44 contains no provision for an assessment of excess costs in the event of a termination for default. Instead, it provides for the same consequences as in the case of a termination for the convenience of the Government, with the following exceptions: (1) the costs of preparing the contractor's settlement proposal are not allowable and (2) the fixed fee, if any, is paid only with respect to supplies delivered and accepted. Such contracts are required to contain the "Excusable Delays" clause set forth in ASPR 7-203.11 (July 15, 1958). This clause provides that the contractor shall not be in default if the cause thereof is beyond its control and without its fault or negligence, listing substantially the same causes as in the case of "Default" clause; and it requires revision of the delivery schedule to the extent that these causes have contributed to delays. 

Finally, it should be kept in mind that the rights and liabilities of subcontractors are not affected by a termination for default. Termination is solely a matter between the prime contractor and the Government.

It sets forth the policies and methods to be followed in connection with the termination of contracts for the convenience of the Government; provisions as to the settlement of contracts so terminated, including disposition of property incident to termination; and approved clauses and forms for use in terminating contracts for the convenience of the Government and in the settlement of termination claims arising under such contracts. Detailed consideration of these matters may be found in Chapter 5, supra. $9.30. Disputes 46 The "Disputes" clause has been a feature of government contracts since approximately 1920. Its evolution, particularly under the stresses of the intensified procurement program of World War II, has been outlined in Chapter 1 above.45 In its present form the "Disputes" clause 4 requires that any dispute concerning a question of fact arising under a Navy contract be decided initially by a contracting officer. The contracting officer is required to reduce his decision to writing and to mail (by registered mail) or otherwise furnish a copy to the contractor. In the case of cost-reimbursement type supply contracts, ASPR 7-203.12 (Sept. 5, 1958), permits the "Disputes" clause to be modified to permit disputes concerning the allowability of costs to be decided initially by the activity performing the particular military department's audit functions, in lieu of the contracting officer. The Navy's audit functions are performed by the Contract Audit Division of the Office of the Comptroller. 

Under the "Disputes" clause an aggrieved contractor is entitled to appeal the decision of a contracting officer on any question of fact arising under the contract. The appeal must be mailed or otherwise furnished to the Secretary of the Navy within thirty days from the date of receipt by the contractor of the decision of the contracting officer.47 If the contractor fails to carry its appeal within thirty days, this decision becomes "final and conclusive," and judicial review of the decision will be denied.48

The thirty-day period may be extended if the request for an extension is made and granted before the period has lapsed.49 The mere making of a request for an extension, however, will not toll the running of the the head of the procuring activity whose contract is involved. DISPUTES 

$ 9.30 period; the contracting officer must assent to it.50 Once the thirty-day period has lapsed, no further time for appealing may be granted, for to do so would deprive the Government of the right vested in it by the "Disputes" clause that the contracting officer's decision shall become final and conclusive when no appeal is taken in the time allowed for appeal.51 

The "Disputes" clause has been liberally interpreted to afford the contractor's right of appeal every possible protection. Thus, it has been held that an appeal is timely so long as it is deposited in the mails within the thirty-day period, even though it is not received by the Secretary until after the expiration of this period.52 There has been equal liberality with regard to the proper form of an appeal. While contractors have on occasion been extremely lax in clearly designating an appeal as such, this has not defeated their appeal. It has been held that a writing need only show an intent to appeal to constitute a valid notice of appeal within the meaning of the "Disputes" clause.53 Moreover, this intent may be evidenced by testimony extrinsic to the letter of appeal.54 

A recurring problem is whether a particular letter appealed from by a contractor was intended to be a "decision" within the meaning of the "Disputes" article and hence appealable. Because of the ease with which a contracting officer may identify a decision as a decision, ambiguities have been resolved in favor of the contractor. Thus, an appeal has not been held untimely on the ground that an earlier letter, not the letter appealed from, constituted the contracting officer's decision, when the earlier letter had not been identified as a decision.55 On the other hand, appeals from improperly designated decisions have been sustained against the allegation that they were premature if the contractor "was reasonable in concluding that further efforts to obtain a responsive decision on its claim for an equitable adjustment would be of no avail.56 

After an appeal addressed to the Secretary of the Navy has been received, it is forwarded to the Navy Panel of the Armed Services Board of Contract Appeals. The Board is the present authorized representative of the Secretaries of the military departments for the hearing of such appeals, and it is empowered to hear and determine the appeal without either the personal consideration or concurrence of the Secretary.

The historical development of the Board, its organization, and its rules of procedure are discussed in Chapter 1 above.57 The reader need only be reminded here that the Board adjudicates disputed questions of fact de novo.

This permits the contractor to submit to the Board evidence not submitted to the contracting officer; it also permits the Board to hear the evidence upon which the contracting officer based his decision. In addition, the Board is empowered to reduce as well as enlarge the extent to which the contracting officer's decision is favorable to the contractor's claim. It may, therefore, review the decision of the contracting officer in its entirety though only a portion of the decison has been appealed from. 59

The "Disputes" clause provides that the decision of the Armed Services Board of Contract Appeals shall be "final and conclusive" "unless determined by a court of competent jurisdiction to have been fraudulent or capricious or arbitrary or so grossly erroneous as necessarily to imply bad faith, or not supported by substantial evidence." This language accurately reflects the Act of May 11, 1954,58 which Congress enacted to overcome the effect of the Supreme Court's decision in the Wunderlich case.5 

It is important to note that Congress limited the scope of judicial review to cases in which the power of decision has been abused. By this limitation Congress has implicitly recognized the desirability of attaching "finality" to administrative decisions on questions of fact. While the clause carefully preserves to a contractor the right to have its side of a dispute fully aired, and protects the contractor against any possible abuse, one of its primary purposes is to prevent the continual rehearing and relitigation of the same question of fact. This concept of "finality" is at the core of the "Disputes" clause and has found frequent expression in the decisions of the Board of Contract Appeals. An illustration is the 

Board's frequent holding that after the period for an appeal has passed, neither the request of a contractor that a decision be reconsidered nor actual reconsideration by a contracting officer of a previously decided question of fact can revive the right of appeal.60 

A discussion of the "Disputes" clause should emphasize that only certain types of disputes fall within its purview and may in consequence

be heard by the Armed Services Board of Contracts Appeals. The "Dis putes" clause was never intended to cover all disputes. When the clause speaks of disputes "arising under this contract," it thereby limits the jurisdiction which it confers on the Board." The Board, for example, may not hear appeals based upon representations which are made prior to the contract and which are in no way reflected in the contract itself. 

Disputes of this sort obviously do not arise under the contract. Similarly, the Board is not empowered to hear an appeal in which the contractor seeks to reform a contract, whatever the ground of reformation. A suit for reformation does not arise under the contract, but seeks rather to vary the contract.62 A corollary of this lack of jurisdiction to entertain suits for reformation is the Board's refusal to hear appeals which challenge the Department's denial of a request for relief under Title II of the First War Powers Act of 1941.63 The powers exercised under Title II are fre quently those of reformation (e.g., to amend a contract without consideration to the Government and to amend a contract in order to correct a mutual mistake) and do not raise issues of fact under the contract itself. 

In addition, of course, the First War Powers Act grants a contractor no contractual rights. 

The "Disputes" clause imposes a second limitation on the jurisdiction of the Board by confining it to "any dispute concerning a question of fact"; the Board must therefore dismiss for lack of jurisdiction disputes which present questions of law only.64 This limitation stems from the view that while an administrative agency is particularly expert in passing upon questions of fact arising under its contracts, questions of law are fully within the competence of the courts which Congress has created. 

This view was reflected in the Act of May 11, 1954, which provides that "no government contract shall contain a provision making final on a question of law the decision of any administrative official, representative or board." 65 It is recognized, of course, that many disputes raise issues which involve mixed questions of fact and law. When this situation presents itself, and it is not infrequent, the Board may in its discretion pass upon all questions of law necessary for a complete adjudication of

The provision limiting the Board's jurisdiction to questions of fact arising under the contract also forecloses the Board from entertaining appeals in which a contractor seeks unliquidated damages for breach of contract, whatever the source of the breach.68 The question of liability in an action for breach of contract is a legal one, and the rights of the parties are not determined by the contract. Although the Board may, insofar as the evidence permits, make findings of fact with regard to claims for unliquidated damages without expressing an opinion on the question of liability,70 it rarely does so. The making of such findings, of course, falls within the area of jurisdiction conferred on the Board by the "Disputes" clause. $ 9.31. Patents and Copyrights

$ 9.33. Guaranty

Early in World War II it was observed that prices quoted to the Navy for supplies often included large amounts to cover the contingent liabilities of contractors under "Guaranty" clauses in government supply contracts. This was particularly true where the terms of a guaranty were severe and the guaranty extended for periods in excess of six months after delivery. Consequently, as early as January 1943, the Secretary of the Navy directed that, unless prior approval was obtained from the Office of Naval Material, no "Guaranty" clause should provide for a guaranty period in excess of one year in any contract for supplies, ordnance, aircraft parts or accessories, or in any contract for the construction of naval vessels or ship propulsion machinery, or the repair or alteration of naval vessels. It was further directed, at that time, that no guaranty provision should be included in any Navy contract whenever inspection and acceptance tests would afford full protection to the Government in ascertaining conformance to specifications and the absence of any defects or deficiencies.

The standard "Guaranty" clause used for Navy fixed-price supply contracts provides that the contractor guarantees the supplies delivered under the contract to be free from any defects in material or workmanship and to conform to the requirements of the contract as of the time of their delivery. Notice of any such defects or non-conformance must be given the contractor by the Government within one year after delivery. 

The clause further provides that the Government may, at its election, require the contractor either to correct or replace the defective or nonconforming supplies or to repay to the Government an equitable portion of the contract price. If correction or replacement requires transportation of the supplies involved, shipping costs not exceeding usual charges from the delivery point to the contractor's plant and return are to be borne by the contractor; all other shipping charges are to be borne by the Government. The clause also provides that the guaranty shall continue as to the corrected or replaced supplies for one year after the date of their delivery. It is interesting to note that the experience of the Department of the 

Navy, in formally advertising for supplies on the basis of the above “Guaranty" clause or alternatively on a "no-guaranty" basis, has indicated that in the vast majority of cases little, if any, additional cost of the Government is occasioned by the imposition of the standard "Guaranty" clause currently in use.

Where the specifications to which the supplies are to conform set forth the characteristics to be met rather than the method of meeting them, it is of extreme importance that such supplies be of a suitable design. Consequently, in such cases the mere replacing or correcting of non-conform- 

76 NPD 7-103 (May 27, 1957). 556

MARKING OF SHIPMENTS 

$ 9.34 ing articles may not be satisfactory. Provision may therefore be made, in the "Guaranty" clause used in such cases, that failure of some or all of the supplies to meet the specifications is conclusively presumed to necessitate a complete redesign of the supplies, and that the contractor in that event will, at its own expense, replace all supplies with those of an approved redesign. This provision, though seemingly costly, has resulted in considerable overall saving to the Department. 

In the case of cost-reimbursement type contracts, correction or replacement costs under any "Guaranty" provision generally constitute "Allowable Costs" thereunder, unless such correction or replacement is due to fraud, lack of good faith or willful misconduct on the part of any of the contractor's directors or officers, managers, superintendents, or other equivalent representatives, if such person has supervision or direction of (i) all or substantially all of the contractor's business, or (ii) all or substantially all of the contractor's operations at any one plant or separate location in which the contract is being performed, or (iii) a separate and complete major industrial operation in connection with the performance of the contract. It is expressly provided in the contract that fraud, lack of good faith or willful misconduct on the part of any of such supervisory personnel shall be deemed to include the selection of individual employees or the retention of employees after any of such supervisory personnel has reason to believe that such employees are habitually careless or otherwise unqualified.

The "Guaranty" clause in the case of cost-reimbursement type supply contracts is contained in the "Inspection of Supplies and Correction of 

Defects" clause prescribed by ASPR 7-203.5 (Jan. 28, 1958) for such contracts. The correction of defects portion of this clause provides that not later than six months (unless a different period is provided elsewhere in the contract) after final acceptance of all the supplies, the Government may require the contractor to remedy by correction or replacement, as directed by the contracting officer, any supplies which at the time of delivery thereof are defective in material or workmanship or otherwise not in conformity with the requirements of the contract. $9.34.
