For fiscal control purposes, all cost-reimbursement type contracts contain a provision enabling the Government to be informed of the extent of the total cost of such contract and to limit the extent of its monetary obligation thereunder. In the case of cost-type supply contracts, these objectives are achieved by a "Limitation of Cost" clause (ASPR 7-203.3, May 

14, 1958). This clause requires the contractor to notify the Government of the revised estimated total cost of the contract, whenever he has reason to believe such cost will be substantially greater or less than the estimate set forth in the contract, and in any case when he believes he will have spent within the succeeding 30-day period 85 percent of the estimate set forth in the contract. This clause also provides that the Government shall not be obligated to reimburse the contractor for costs incurred in excess of the estimated cost set forth in the contract unless and until the contracting officer shall have increased said estimate (and then only to the extent of the revised estimate), and that the contractor shall not be obligated to continue performance under the contract in excess of the contract estimate except to the exent such estimate is revised. $9.36. Records

All cost-reimbursement type contracts contain a clause regarding the accounts and records to be maintained thereunder by the contractor. 

Such clause requires the contractor to keep books, records, documents, and other evidence (collectively referred to as "the records") bearing on its costs and expenses under the contract, and to use approved accounting methods.

Unlike the earlier Navy "Records" clause, which required the contractor to furnish to the Government upon request such of the records as may be required by the General Accounting Office, the "Records" clause 558

GOVERNMENT PROPERTY 

$ 9.37 prescribed by ASPR 7-203.7 (Nov. 3, 1958) for all cost-type supply contracts requires the records to be made available to authorized representatives of the Department or of the Comptroller General at the office of the contractor except in the case of documentary evidence in 'support of transportation costs, which are the only records to be delivered to the Government by the contractor if required by the Comptroller General. 

This modification was made possible by the institution of "on-site" audits by the General Accounting Office, a practice which became a standard one for cost-type contracts entered into after September 2, 1952.78 This change in record requirements reduces auditing and clerical expenses and leads to better relations with contractors.79 The new "Records" clause obligates the contractor to preserve and make its records available for a six-year period after submission of the final invoice. Records relating to appeals under the "Disputes" clause, litigation, claims or exceptions taken by the Comptroller General to costs of the contract are to be retained by the contractor until such matters have been disposed of, though a longer period than six years may be involved.

Like the old "Records" clause, the contractor is required to insert a similar "Records" clause in each subcontract which is on a cost, costplus-a-fixed-fee, time-and-material, or labor-hour basis. In regard to other types of subcontracts the contractor agrees to insert the clause discussed in § 9.17 of this chapter.

The Armed Services Procurement Regulation requires the inclusion of prescribed "Government Property" clauses in all cost-reimbursement type contracts for supplies and services. These clauses, set forth in Section XIII of the Regulation, contain provisions concerning title, risk of loss, use and disposition of contractor-acquired and government-furnished property used in the performance of the contract. ASPR 13–503 (May 14, 1958) sets forth the general clause for all supplies and services except for experimental, developmental, or research work with educational or nonprofit institutions where no profit to the contractor is contemplated. 

ASPR 13-506 (Dec. 23, 1955) prescribes the clause for the excepted class.

The "Government Property" clauses provide that title to all property acquired for the performance of the contract, and for the cost of which

Insurance

Early in World War II, the Department of the Navy established, with respect to its procurement contracts, the policy of assuming the risk of loss of or damage to government property, as well as certain liabilities to third persons arising out of the performance of cost-reimbursement contracts. This assumption is independent of the negligence of the con- 560

INSURANCE 

$ 9.38 tractor or its employees, and in effect is in the nature of a self-insurance plan. Its purpose was the same as that which prompts private contractors to establish self-insurance plans-namely, to save the cost of insurance premiums. This policy, with minor revision, has been extended throughout the armed services and is reflected in the clauses prescribed by the Armed Services Procurement Regulation for use in negotiated contracts. With respect to government property, these clauses are entitled "Government-Furnished Property" in the case of fixed-price contracts and "Government Property" in the case of cost-reimbursement contracts. In regard to third-party liability under cost-reimbursement contracts, the clause is entitled "Insurance-Liability to Third Persons." 

The policy of the Department in the case of formally advertised procurements is for the contractor to assume the risk of loss of or damage to government-furnished property. 

The assumption of risk by the Government under fixed-price contracts extends to all risks customarily covered by insurance unless the managerial personnel of the contractor are guilty of willful misconduct or lack of good faith. In the case of cost-reimbursement contracts, the 

Government assumes all risk of loss except that which results from willful misconduct or lack of good faith upon the part of the managerial personnel of the contractor. Under both clauses, however, the contractor has an express obligation to maintain and protect government property in accordance with sound industrial practice. Indicative of the types of risk so assumed by the Government are those covered by the following types of insurance: windstorm, flood, fire, earthquake, hail, explosion, riot, vandalism, smoke damage, aircraft damage, transportation, and aircraft flight and crash insurance. The clause entitled "Government

Property," approved for cost-reimbursement type contracts, applies to all government-owned property acquired by or furnished to the contractor under the contract; it deals with risk of loss of or damage to such property solely from an insurance standpoint. On the other hand, the clause entitled "Government-Furnished Property," approved for fixedprice contracts, covers only property furnished to the contractor by the Government under the contract, this being so because such property generally is the only property to which the Government has or acquires title prior to the completion of the contract. This fixed-price clause deals with all risks of loss of or damage to such property, and also with other obligations of the contractor and the Government with respect to such property. Only the provisions of this clause pertaining to insurance and risk of loss are discussed herein; its other provisions are discussed in § 9.40 of this chapter. 

A. Government Property (ASPR 13-503, May 14, 1958)-This clause, used generally in cost-reimbursement contracts, provides that the contractor is not to be reimbursed for, nor include as an item of overhead, 561

$ 9.38

any insurance against any form of loss of or damage to governmentowned property acquired by or furnished to the contractor under the contract. Notwithstanding the foregoing assumption of risk, the contractor is expressly made responsible for any loss or damage which results from willful misconduct or lack of good faith on the part of any of the contractor's directors, officers, or any of its representatives having supervision or direction of all or substantially all of the contractor's business, or of all or substantially all of any plant used by the contractor in the performance of the contract. The clause further provides that the contractor is also responsible for such other loss of or damage to the foregoing property as it is expressly made responsible for elsewhere in the contract; for example, a responsibility is frequently imposed on the contractor for loss or damage resulting from the contractor's failure to comply with any directions received from the Department as to measures to be taken with respect to government-owned property for the purpose of protecting such property.

Insofar as repair and replacement of government-owned property is concerned, the clause requires the contractor to make such repairs and renovations at government expense as the contracting officer directs. 

B. Government-Furnished Property (ASPR 13-502, May 14, 1958)— 

This clause, used in fixed-price contracts, provides with respect to insurance that the prices stipulated in the contract do not include the cost of insurance, nor any provision for a reserve, covering such risks of loss of or damage to government-furnished property as are assumed by the Government thereunder. It further states that the Government, unless the managerial personnel are guilty of bad faith or willful misconduct, assumes the risk of loss of or damage to the government-furnished property occasioned by: (1) fire, lightning, windstorm, cyclone, tornado, hail, explosion, riot, riot attending a strike, civil commotion, vandalism and malicious mischief, sabotage, aircraft or objects falling therefrom, vehicles running on land or tracks (excluding vehicles owned or operated by the contractor or any agent or employee of the contractor), smoke, sprinkler leakage, earthquake or volcanic eruption, flood (meaning thereby the rising of a body of water), hostile or warlike action (including action in hindering, combatting, or defending against an actual, impending or expected attack by any government or sovereign power, de jure or de facto, or by any authority using military, naval or air forces, or by an agent of any such government power, authority, or forces); or (2) other perils customarily covered by insurance. The clause provides that in the event the contractor is reimbursed or compensated for loss of or damage to government-furnished property caused by a risk assumed by the Government, it shall equitably reimburse the Government. This clause does not relieve subcontractors from liability for loss of or damage to the government-furnished property unless the subcontract, with the prior 562

$9.38

approval of the contracting officer, relieves the subcontractor of such liability. Such approval would be conditioned upon adequate consideration flowing to the Government and only if in the interests of the Government. 

The terms of the subcontract clause would have to be consistent with the "Government-Furnished Property" clause of the prime contract. 

C. Insurance-Liability to Third Persons (ASPR 7-203.22, March 17, 1958)—This clause, entitled "Insurance Liability to Third Persons” and approved for use in cost-reimbursement type contracts, expressly requires the contractor to procure and thereafter maintain, with respect to the work under the contract, workmen's compensation, employer's liability, comprehensive general liability, comprehensive automobile liability, and such other insurance as the Government may require-all such insurance to be in the form and amount, for the periods of time, and with the insurers required or approved by the Department. The clause further provides that the contractor shall be reimbursed for the allowable cost of the foregoing. It expressly states that the Government will also reimburse the contractor for liabilities to third persons (including expenses incidental thereto), for loss of or damage to property (other than the contractor's property or property in the custody of the contractor), and for death or bodily injury not compensated by insurance or otherwise. These liabilities must arise out of the performance of the contract and are reimbursable whether or not such liabilities are caused by the negligence of the contractor, its agents, servants or employees. However, to be reimbursable, such liabilities must be represented by final judgments or by settlements approved in writing by the Department. Reimbursement is expressly disallowed for liabilities (i) with respect to which the contractor has failed to insure as required or approved by the Department, (ii) for which the contractor is made responsible by other provisions of the contract, or (iii) which result from willful misconduct or lack of good faith on the part of any of the contractor's directors, officers or any of its other representatives having supervision or direction of all or substantially all of the contractor's business, or of all or substantially all of any plant or separate location or separate and complete major industrial operation used by the contractor in the performance of the contract. 

To the extent that third-party claims against the contractor are covered by insurance, such claims do not generally concern the Department since it has no liability in that regard (the insurance carrier having the responsibility for settling or defending such claims). However, if the amount of such claims exceeds the amount of the insurance coverage and if the Government is obligated to reimburse the contractor for the amount of such excess, it has an interest in collaborating with the insurance carrier in settling or defending such claims. Consequently, the clause entitled "Insurance-Liability to Third Persons" expressly provides that the contractor shall authorize representatives of the Government to col- 563

$9.39

laborate with counsel for the insurance carrier in the settlement or defense of such excess claims. If the liability is not covered by insurance and if the cost is reimbursable under the contract, it is reasonable that the Government should, if it so desires, assume complete control in the defense or settlement of such claims by representing the contractor therein; and hence this clause expressly requires the contractor, if so requested by the Government, to authorize the Government to do so. The 

Department has consistently refused to permit the contractor to deprive the Government of this right of election, but it does permit the contractor at its own expense to associate itself in the litigation or settlement. 

Whether or not the Government elects to assume control with respect to the defense or settlement of a claim is a matter determined by the Department of Justice since that agency represents the Government in all such actions.

It should be noted that although the Government does not assume the risk of loss with respect to the contractor's property or property within its custody over which the contractor is responsible to someone other than the Government, the clause does expressly provide that the contractor is to be reimbursed for the allocable portion of the reasonable cost of insurance covering the aforesaid property, to the extent that such property is used or to be used in the performance of the contract. 

The "Government-Furnished Property" and "Government Property" 

clauses used in fixed-price and cost-reimbursement type contracts provide that when aircraft are to be furnished under the contract, any loss of or damage to such aircraft or to other government-furnished property which may occur in connection with the operations of the aircraft is to be governed by a separate "Flight Risks" clause to be included in the contract. $9.39. Priorities, Allocations, and Allotments

It is the policy of the Department of Defense to require contractors to use ratings and allotment authority to support military procurement; this is done in the interest of maintaining a minimum priorities and allocations system as a mobilization preparedness measure. The military departments are required to comply with the priorities and allocations program set forth in the Defense Department Priorities and Allocations Manual and the rules and regulations established by the Business and 

Defense Services Administration (BDSA). 

In order to aid effectively in the use of priorities, allocations, and allotments, ASPR 1-308.2 (Feb. 5, 1958) requires the contract clause set forth in ASPR 7-104.18 (Sept. 18, 1958) to be inserted in all fixed-price or cost-reimbursement type ratable contracts, except purchase orders of less than $5,000. Under this clause the contractor agrees to comply with the provisions and rules and regulations of the Business and Defense 564

GOVERNMENT-FURNISHED PROPERTY 

$ 9.40

Services Administration, including Defense Materials System Regula tions. Each ratable contract, defined as those contracts for supplies which are required to be supported with rating and allotment authority, must include a statement of the Defense Materials System classification and certification.

A contract is rated by including in the contract the required delivery date, the specific DO rating and allotment number (consisting of the capital letter and digit program code symbol identifying the appropriate 

Department of Defense Claimant Program) and a certification. 

Every rated order must specify delivery or performance on a particular date or dates or during a particular month, which, in no case, may be earlier than required by the person placing this order, and any order failing to comply with this requirement is not to be treated as a rated order. Generally, every order bearing a rating must be accepted and filled regardless of existing contracts, except under certain circumstances set forth in BDSA Regulation No. 2.81 The delivery date specified in a rated contract becomes a part of the priority and in case of a production conflict in a manufacturer's plant between two rated orders received at the same time, the required delivery dates govern the producer's scheduling.

The Business and Defense Services Administration of the Department of Commerce has been delegated authority under Title I of the Defense Production Act 2 for establishing the basic priorities and allocations to support defense programs with the least disruption to the national economy. BDSA Regulation No. 2 93 is the basic regulation for the priorities system; it concerns such matters as the kind of orders which are rated orders, the placing of rated orders and their preference status. 

The Department of Defense has been delegated certain responsibilities by BDSA for administering the priorities and allocations system and has issued the Priorities and Allocations Manual prescribing the regulations concerning that subject for use in the Department of Defense.

The policy of the Department of Defense with respect to the furnishing of government property to contractors for use in the performance of procurement contracts, set forth in Section XIII of the Armed Services Procurement Regulation, varies with the type of property involved. For this purpose, the regulation classifies property into three types. The first type is "material," like raw and processed material, parts and assemblies, which comprises property that may be incorporated into or attached

The general policy of the Department of Defense requires contractors to furnish all materials required for the performance of government contracts.84 Exception to this policy is permitted when for reason of economy, standardization, expediting production, or other circumstances, a procuring activity determines that the furnishing of government material will be in the best interests of the Government. There is no clear-cut distinction between an "escalation" clause and a "price redetermination" clause. In fact, the Navy's present forms of escalation clauses are an outgrowth of certain types of price redetermination clauses used prior to World War II. Generally speaking, however, "price redetermination" clauses are used in situations in which the contracting officer is not satisfied that the contractor's quoted price is a reasonable one and desires to make provision for a downward "repricing" on the basis of cost data to be submitted by the contractor after it has partially performed the contract." "Escalation" clauses, on the other hand, are generally used in place of contingency allowances added to the

ESCALATION 

$ 9.42 price to cover possible increased labor or material costs (usually up to a maximum amount).

Although clauses have been used in Navy contracts for many years to protect contractors against specific contingencies, it was not until about 1940 that the escalation problem became generally acute. The first general attempt to meet this problem was a "labor and material index" type of clause. This clause provided that the percentage of changes in specified labor and material indices should be applied to a contractor's actual expenditures. Since actual expenditures presumably already reflected the increase, the result was an increase on an increase. Fortunately, the clause reserved the right in the Navy Department to prescribe changes in the method of escalation where the method prescribed would not reflect equitably the contractor's increased costs. Also some early labor-index clauses provided that adjustments in prices with respect to labor costs would be made on the basis of the index of average hourly earnings of employees in the contractor's industry, as compiled monthly by the Bureau of Labor Statistics, Department of Labor. However, since premium compensation for overtime work was generally included by the Bureau of Labor Statistics in computing these indices, the application of such indices to labor costs resulted in the allowance of unwarranted margins of increases. The Bureau of Labor Statistics was accordingly requested to furnish to the Navy Department indices which did not include premium compensation for overtime, and steps were taken to amend then existing contracts under an escape provision to substitute the indices of straight-time average hourly earnings for those specified in the contract. A modified version of this clause is still used in the Navy's contracts for the construction of ships. 

Soon after the creation of the Office of Price Administration and the establishment of maximum prices, contractors demanded protection in the event of OPA action increasing ceiling prices. Many and varied clauses were developed providing for either the negotiation of new prices or an automatic escalation in case of changes in the OPA maximum price. Similarly, after the National War Labor Board was created, contractors requested protection against increases in costs resulting from changes in labor costs due to government action. Accordingly, in July 

1944, there was approved a clause (commonly referred to as the "Forrestal" clause) under which the contractor warranted that it had excluded from its contract price all contingency allowances for wage increases, salary increases, and adjustments in other terms and conditions of employment, but which also provided that if the contractor was ordered or authorized by a "duly authorized agency of the federal government" to make such changes in its wages, salaries, or other terms and conditions of employment as would substantially affect the cost of performing the contract, the contract price could be adjusted by mutual agreement. Con- 569

$ 9.42

tractors continued to request price adjustments after the abolition of the National War Labor Board and its successor, the National Wage Stabilization Board, but such requests were uniformly denied on the theory that the order or authorization by a duly authorized agency of the Government was a "condition precedent" to any adjustment in price.' 

After World War II, unsettled market conditions resulted in the demand by contractors for protection against rising costs and prices. Accordingly, the Navy prepared and offered two escalation clauses, one for labor and one for materials. The former provided for a single upward escalation (after the contract was completed) of direct labor on the basis of agreed estimates of average hourly wage rates and total hours of labor, with a fixed dollar ceiling on the price adjustment; and the latter provided for a single upward escalation (also after the contract was completed) of material prices on the basis of agreed estimates of quantities and prices of raw materials, subject to a fixed dollar ceiling on the price adjustment. These clauses were later revised to permit downward as well as upward adjustments and are still authorized for use in Navy contracts. However, because of detailed information which was required to be provided by the contractor, as well as the exclusion from adjustment of indirect labor and indirect material, such clauses found little favor with industry. Consequently, simpler and broader escalation clauses were developed by the Navy. Four of these clauses were subsequently adopted throughout the Department of Defense and are discussed below. The policy of the Navy with respect to escalation clauses is to keep their use at a minimum consistent with the best interests of the Government. Generally, escalation is not used in contracts which provide for relatively short-term delivery and for relatively small amounts (less than six months, or less than $5,000).

Four escalation clauses set forth in ASPR cover basic steel, aluminum, bronze or copper mill products (ASPR 7-106.1); non-standard steel items (ASPR 7-106.2); standard supplies (ASPR 7-106.3); and semi-standard supplies (ASPR 7-106.4). All of these clauses allow for both upward and downward price adjustments based upon changes in contractors' established prices and fix a maximum as to the amount of upward change. 

The ASPR 7-106.1 (July 15, 1958) escalation clause for basic metal mill products is used in both advertised and negotiated fixed-price supply contracts with producers of such products when an established price exists for the particular product being procured. It furnishes a method for lowering or raising the contract price in proportion to changes in the contractor's established price. In the event that a requested upward adjustment in any contract unit price is not acceptable to the contracting

$ 9.43 officer and the parties do not reach agreement with respect to a price increase, the contract may be terminated without cost or liability to either party for further performance.

The ASPR 7-106.2 (March 17, 1958), covering escalation of non-stand ard steel items, allows for price revisions which result from changes in the cost of both labor and steel. It is used in both advertised and negotiated fixed-price supply contracts for those non-standard steel items for which the contractor does not have an established or published price, such as projectile heads and armor plate, where the contractor is both a steel producer and the actual manufacturer of the item being procured. Price revisions on account of changes in labor or steel costs are determined by reference to a base labor index and to a base steel index. A dispute as to the allowability of an increase is treated as a dispute concerning a question of fact within the meaning of the "Disputes" clause. 

The ASPR 7-106.3 (March 17, 1958) escalation clause for standard supplies is used by the Navy in negotiated fixed-price supply contracts only when a substantial portion of the contractor's business is with purchasers other than the Government, when established prices exist, when the total contract price is over $5,000, and when delivery is not to be completed within 6 months after the contract date. The clause permits decreases and increases in the contract unit prices to the extent that there have been decreases and increases in the established price for identical supplies. Like the "basic steel" clause, it provides that in the event a requested upward adjustment is unacceptable to the contracting officer and the parties are unable to reach an agreement, the contract may be cancelled without liability to either party for further performance. 

Insofar as escalation is concerned, semi-standard supplies are treated much the same as standard supplies. The ASPR 7-106.4 escalation clause is similar to ASPR 7-106.3 and may be used when the prices of the semistandard supplies can be reasonably related to the prices of nearly equivalent standard supplies for which established prices exist. 

A fifth escalation clause, set forth in ASPR 7-107 (Jan. 28, 1958), provides for the negotiation of an equitable adjustment in the contract unit prices based on increases or decreases in certain labor rates or unit prices for materials identified in the contract as being subject to such adjustment. This clause may be used in negotiated fixed-price supply contracts over $50,000 where the period of performance exceeds six months and the item being procured is of stable design. The clause provides that disputes concerning price adjustment shall be deemed disputed questions of fact within the meaning of the "Disputes" clause. $9.43. Liquidated Damages

In addition to the standard clause relating to "Termination for Default" (discussed in § 9.28, supra), it is also desirable to provide for 571

$9.43

liquidated damages in certain contracts so as to protect the Government against the failure of a contractor to prosecute the work diligently to completion. While such failure often results in loss or in inconvenience to the Government, the damages are frequently difficult to ascertain in amount. For this reason, contracts for the construction or repair of public buildings or public works generally include a liquidated damages clause. In addition, supply contracts in which the time of delivery is of the essence often contain such a provision. 

It is well settled that where proof of actual damage for delay in performance of a contract is impracticable or difficult, courts look with favor upon reasonable agreements for liquidated damages made by the parties.2 

However, if the amount stipulated as liquidated damages is so disproportionate to the amount of the probable loss as to show that compensation was not the object of the liquidated damages clause, the clause will be regarded by the courts as an agreement for a penalty and will not be enforced. Whether a provision is one for liquidated damages or for a penalty is to be decided on the basis of conditions existing as of the time the contract is made, not at the time of the breach. The standard liquidated damages clause for fixed-price supply contracts (set forth in ASPR 7-105.5, Sept. 18, 1958) provides in substance that if the contractor refuses or fails to make deliveries of any of the articles called for in the contract at the times specified, the contractor shall pay to the Government, as fixed, agreed and liquidated damages for each calendar day of delay in making delivery, an amount specified therein. Contracting officers are instructed to provide in the contract an amount for liquidated damages which bears a reasonable relation to the probable damage the Government would suffer; and in the case of a contract for more than one type of article, an amount for each type. The contractor is not charged, however, with liquidated damages if the delay in delivery is due to causes beyond its control and without its fault or negligence. 

This clause forms a part of the "Default" clause of the contract, and provides that in the event of a termination for default, the contractor shall be liable for liquidated damages in addition to the excess costs provided for elsewhere in the clause. This overcomes the effect of the holding of the Supreme Court in the case of United States v. American Surety 

Company that the termination of a contractor's right to proceed operates as a waiver of liquidated damages.5 

While one might conclude that a liquidated damages clause adequately protects the Government against default by the contractor and hence

It may on first impression appear that the provision for the assessment of excess costs under the "Default" clause, when added to liquidated damages, is, inequitable and imposes a hardship on the contractor. However, the use of the liquidated damages clause is limited to contracts where time of performance is of first importance; and since the contractor makes its bid or proposal with that clause in contemplation, the use of both clauses is for the purpose of accomplishing the desired result of delivery or performance within the time required." "Liquidated Damages" clauses are rarely used in cost-reimbursement contracts, or in maximum-price contracts subject to redetermination, since the contractor would undoubtedly incur any and all costs to avoid the payment of liquidated damages, and these costs would in turn be borne by the Government either as allowable costs under a cost-reimbursement contract or as part of the redetermined price of the maximum-price contract.

In conclusion, it should be noted that a contractor is protected against the possibility of harsh treatment in the administration of a "Liquidated Damages" clause. 10 U.S.C. § 2312 authorizes and empowers the Comptroller General, on the recommendation of the agency concerned, to remit the whole or any part of the liquidated damages assessed against a contractor.7 

$ 9.44. Military Security Requirements 

All contracts which are classified "Confidential" (including "Confidential-Modified Handling Authorized"), or higher, or the performance of which requires access to matter of such classification, are required to contain certain provisions with respect to the safeguarding of classified security information. These security provisions are set forth in a contract clause entitled "Military Security Requirements." To safeguard classified information required to be furnished contractors for bidding purposes, prospective contractors are required to enter into a formal security agreement with the Government (DD Form 441) and to abide by the provisions of the "Industrial Security Manual for Safeguarding Classified Information" issued by the Department of Defense (DD Form 

441 Attachment). Once executed such agreement continues in effect until terminated as provided therein.

While there is some variation in the provisions of the clauses set forth in the Armed Services Procurement Regulation for various types of contracts, they generally provide for the Government to notify the contractor of the security requirements of the contract and any elements thereof, and of any subsequent revisions in their security classification, by the use of a prescribed Security Requirements Check List (DD Forms 254 and 

254-1). This method of pinpointing the classified portions of the contract limits the application of security regulations only to classified matter and effectively destroys any idea that a security classification assigned to a contract applies equally to all phases of the contract. 

The contractor is obligated by the "Military Security Requirements" clause to safeguard all classified elements of the contract and to provide and maintain a system of security controls within its own organization in accordance with (i) requirements of the "Department of Defense Indus trial Security Manual for Safeguarding Classified Security Information" 

in effect on the date of the contract, (ii) any subsequent amendments to said Manual determined by the Government to be required by the demands of national security, notice of which has been furnished to the contractor by the Government, and, except in non-profit contracts with educational institutions, (iii) those provisions of written security agreements (DD Form 441) entered into between the parties, and modifications thereto, which pertain to the adaptation of the Manual to the contractor's business. The Manual establishes the general requirements for the safeguarding of official information the unauthorized disclosure of which would or could harm, tend to impair, or otherwise threaten the security of the nation. These requirements reflect the provisions of applicable federal statutes and executive orders. The Manual sets forth in some detail applicable definitions; requirements and procedures for the handling of classified information; qualifications for, and restrictions on, access to such information; control of areas in which classified matter is located; regulations with respect to visitors; clearance and selection of, and action by, subcontractors; and application of the Manual with respect to cryptographic information and the graphic arts. With respect to access to classified information, the Manual sets forth in some detail additional requirements for the clearance of foreign nationals and immigrant: aliens.

The "Military Security Requirements" clause gives the Government the right of inspection, at reasonable intervals, of the procedures, methods and facilities utilized by the contractor in complying with the requirements of this clause; it provides further that, in the event of noncompliance, the Government shall advise the contractor in writing of the proper action to be taken to effect compliance. The prime contractor is charged with the responsibility for determining that a security clearance of subcontractors has been granted before they are accorded access to classified 574

MILITARY SECURITY REQUIREMENTS 

$ 9.44 3 1 security information. The clause also requires the insertion in all subcontracts, regardless of tier, which involve access to classified security information provisions conforming substantially to the language of the clause in the prime contract.

Since the Government has the right to make changes in the security requirements and classification under a contract, subsequent to the date thereof, without the consent of the contractor, provision is made in the contract clause for an equitable adjustment in the contract price or the estimated cost and fixed fee, as the case may be, to reflect any increase or decrease in costs occasioned by such changes, in the same manner as if such changes were directed under the clause in the contract entitled "Changes." In the case of nonprofit contracts with educational institutions, the security clause provides that in the event that a security classification is upgraded either from nonclassified to classified or from a lower to a higher security classification, the contractor is to exert every reasonable effort compatible with its established policies to continue performance in compliance with the security change. However, if the contractor determines that continuance of performance is not practicable because of such change, it shall so notify the contracting officer in writing, whereupon the contracting officer is to investigate the circumstances and endeavor to work out a mutually satisfactory method whereby the contractor can continue performance. If, upon the expiration of 15 days after receipt of such notice by the contracting officer, the application of the security change to the contract has not been agreed upon, the contractor may request the contracting officer to terminate the contract, which he shall do; and such termination shall be deemed to be a termination under the provisions of the clause of the contract entitled "Termination for 

Convenience of the Government."

Along with the "Military Security Requirements" clause, the patent clause, entitled “Filing of Patent Applications" (ASPR 9–106, Oct. 15, 1958), should also be considered. $10.59.

Recordation of Facilities Contracts $ 10.1. Introduction: What Are "Facilities" 

The term "facility" means, generally, anything which is useful in producing, repairing, maintaining, or storing something else. As used in 

Navy contracting, it is given a slightly more restricted meaning, and has become a word of art, under the rubric "industrial facility." This phrase is in substance defined in the Armed Services Procurement Regulation as follows: 

Industrial facility means property, other than material and special tooling, of use for the performance of a contract or subcontract, including real property and rights therein, buildings, structures, improvements, and plant equipment.' 

There are several things worth noting about this definition : (a) It is limited to property used for the performance of contracts or subcontracts for supplies or services. Hence the term "industrial." (b) Subject to this limitation, it includes all kinds of property, real or personal, large or small. Most industrial facilities are, however, relatively large (buildings, machine tools, vehicles, and the like). (c) It does not include "material." This is property which is expected to be used up in the performance of a contract or subcontract for supplies, or incorporated in the end product delivered under such a contract or subcontract.2 "Material" is used in, not for, the performance of a contract. (d) It does not include "special tooling," which is property or equipment of a highly specialized nature, useful for the production only of particular supplies or the performance of particular services.³ 

An industrial facility is intended for general purposes and for a variety of uses, and unlike material or special tooling is usually of long-term duration. From an accounting standpoint, it is property of a capital nature.

Under the above definition, an industrial facility is a facility owned by a contractor, or owned by the Government and provided to a contractor for use in production. In a broader sense, the term also includes a facility owned and operated by the Government at one of its own plants, for example at a naval shipyard or ordnance plant. No attempt is made herein to draw a sharp distinction between the two usages; the context will normally indicate in what sense the phrase is being used. 

1 ASPR 13-101.6 (Nov. 3, 1958). 

2 ASPR 13-101.4 (Nov. 3, 1958). 

3 ASPR 13-101.5 (Nov. 3, 1958). For a discussion of "special tooling," see § 9.41 supra. 579

$ 10.

FACILITIES 

$ 10.2.

Why the Navy Is Concerned With Facilities 

It sometimes happens that the supplies or services required by the Navy cannot be produced with existing facilities. Often, because the supplies or services are primarily for military application, with little or no commercial usefulness, private concerns are not equipped to perform the work. While this situation occurs even during peacetime and periods of reduced military appropriations, the greatest demand for additional facilities occurs during war or a national emergency, when the quantity and variety of supplies required for national defense increase immensely. 

During such period the existing facilities of the nation are frequently unable to turn out the larger quantities of supplies at the rate required, or to manufacture the new weapons and devices developed by scientists and engineers. It therefore becomes necessary to create additional industrial capacity by the addition of new facilities. 

A period of very great facilities expansion for military purposes occurred during World War II. Another period of expansion occurred during the Korean hostilities. Between such periods, the creation of new facilities may be reduced in volume but, because new techniques in warfare as well as new techniques of production are constantly developed, new facilities continue to be required. Moreover, planning for industrial mobilization sometimes requires the construction of additional facilities to be held on a standby basis against emergency needs. 

Once facilities have been acquired, the owner (whether the Government or a private contractor) has to face the problems of their proper management, use, maintenance, and ultimate disposal. Accordingly, this chapter is addressed broadly to the legal problems incident to the life cycle of facilities. 

I. THE CREATION AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW FACILITIES 

$10.3. Introduction

Assuming that, in order to produce a particular military item in the quantity or at the rate required to accomplish the Navy's mission, it is necessary to expand or augment existing facilities, what courses of action are available?

A. PRIVATE EXPANSION OF FACILITIES $10.4. Acquisition, Construction and Installation of Facilities by Con tractor Without Direct Reimbursement by the Government If private enterprises having the necessary skills to produce military items will acquire the necessary facilities at their own expense, the total cost to the Government of the supplies will ordinarily be less than if the Government were to pay not only for the supplies but also for the 580

PRIVATE EXPANSION OF FACILITIES 

$ 10.4 additional facilities needed to produce them. Moreover, future expenses of maintaining, administering and disposing of the facilities would be the responsibility of the private concern rather than the Government. 

The desirability of having the necessary facilities provided by private manufacturers is reflected in the following statement of policy found in the ASPR: 

It is the general policy of the Department of Defense that Contractors will furnish all facilities required for the performance of Government contracts. However, subject to and within the limitations of existing authority, facilities may be provided by the Government for use by Contractors when such providing is considered necessary to meet essential production or program schedules, or when otherwise considered by the Secretary of the Department concerned to be in the best interest of the Government.4 

Private concerns, however, are often reluctant if not unwilling to invest their own capital in new facilities required for military production. 

Frequently, the additional facilities are not adaptable for use in regular commercial business and the military demand might be too uncertain to assure an adequate return on the capital investment involved. To en- courage private investment in additional facilities under these circumstances, various means have been made available from time to time by the Congress.

Certain priorities have been established in this respect. Thus, the governing Navy directive, after reiterating the above general statement of policy, states that before a procuring activity decides to acquire new facilities with government funds, the following alternatives will be thoroughly considered: (a) Availability of existing government-owned facilities; (b) Use of other suppliers or sources; (c) Better utilization of the contractor's industrial facilities, management, material and manpower; (d) More effective use of subcontractors; (e) Leasing by contractor of industrial facilities from private owners; (f) Acquisition of industrial facilities by the contractor with private capital; (g) Conversion of civilian production capacity to military production capacity (for mobilization requirements); (h) Loans by government agencies under applicable provisions of law; (i) Certificates of Necessity permitting accelerated amortization of cost of industrial facilities for federal tax purposes and contract pricing.

The policy is reiterated that direct government financing under a facilities contract is the least desirable means of acquiring industrial facilities. 

Methods (a) through (d) above do not concern us directly in this chapter. The remaining methods will be discussed below. In addition, brief mention will be made of two other devices which have been used in the past for facilities expansion but which are not now favored for that purpose, namely, guaranteed loans and Emergency Plant Facilities contracts. 

$10.5. Expansion of Facilities With Private Capital 

This method, which is by far preferred, envisages the wholly private financing of facilities construction or expansion. The contractor may build the facilities itself, with its own or borrowed funds, or may lease them from private sources. This does not mean that the Government pays nothing. A factor for normal depreciation, or an appropriate use charge, will be recognized as a proper element of cost entering into the price of the supplies manufactured with the aid of such facilities and sold to the Government. Beyond this, however, the Government assumes no responsibility for facilities so financed and acquires no interest therein. This method therefore presents no special problems which require further consideration in this chapter. $10.6.

Accelerated Amortization 

This method was devised during the defense build-up preceding Pearl Harbor, was widely used during World War II, and was revived during the Korean emergency. It takes the form of a tax incentive to encourage contractors to build emergency facilities which they might otherwise be reluctant to undertake because of the uncertainty as to their economic usefulness once the emergency had passed. In brief, it permits the contractor to amortize for tax purposes all, or a portion of, the cost of such facilities over a period of five years, instead of the normal ten, fifteen, or twenty year, or even longer, period. Such rapid amortization results in higher tax deductions and hence lower taxes for the contractor during the period of emergency, when income from military orders would presumably be highest and most certain, and when tax rates (both normal and excess profits) would presumably be highest. It was, and is, available only as to those facilities certified by the appropriate defense authorities as necessary for emergency defense purposes; hence the term "certificates of necessity." Even then, the certificate of necessity may cover only a portion of the cost of the facilities. This was occasionally 

6 See Bordner, Defense Department

Policy in Use of Accelerated Amortization As a Cost in Contracts, 95 J. ACCOUNT- 

ANCY 179, at 181-82 (1953). 582

DIRECT LOANS 

$ 10.7 the administrative practice during World War II,7 and has been followed as a regular procedure authorized by the statute in effect since Korea. 

Attractive as accelerated amortization is, it has certain disadvantages from the contractor's standpoint, which make it less than a perfect solution to the problem of facilities expansion: (a) It confers primarily a tax benefit. The increased deduction allowed for tax purposes is not necessarily recognized as an allowable item of cost entering into the price of supply contracts. During 

World War II the latter continued to be computed at the so-called "normal" rate of depreciation. The present policy is somewhat more liberal, in that it allows "true" depreciation for pricing purposes, which recognizes a factor for prospective economic obsolescence.? 

Even so, "true" depreciation only rarely equals the full accelerated amortization allowed for tax purposes. (b) In a sense, accelerated amortization is a form of insurance based on the assumptions that income earned by the facilities after the period of emergency will be less and that income tax rates will go down. If either assumption is false, the benefits are that much less.

In fact, if tax rates should go up and income remain high, the contractor might well lose, since he would no longer have the benefit of a depreciation deduction on that portion of his costs which has been fully amortized. (c) Finally, as pointed out above, it is the usual practice to allow accelerated amortization only on a percentage, less than 100 percent, of the entire cost of the facilities. As to the balance, the contractor has to take depreciation at the "normal” rate.

For these, and possibly other reasons, it often becomes necessary to provide other inducements to the expansion of facilities by contractors. $10.7. Direct Loans

Guaranteed Loans 

To overcome the reluctance of private financing institutions to lend the necessary funds for construction or expansion of emergency facilities (occasioned by the same factors which discourage industry from risking its own capital), the Government is empowered to guarantee private loans for this purpose. Authority for this is found in section 301 (a) of the 

Defense Production Act.13 Executive Order No. 10480 14 delegates to the Department of Defense and the military departments the authority to enter into guarantees under this statute. 

However, although guaranteed loans are theoretically available for facilities construction or expansion, they are not commonly so employed, and present policy precludes their use solely for this purpose.15 Rather, they are used primarily to provide working capital or otherwise to finance performance of contracts for supplies and services, or to finance contract terminations. Moreover, the Government rarely guarantees more than 

90 percent of any such loan, requiring the private bank to assume the risk as to the balance.16 Hence, this device is of limited usefulness for facilities expansion. 

$10.9. Emergency Plant Facilities Contracts 

This was a device used during the early days of World War II prior to Pearl Harbor to encourage private financing of facilities expansion.

ROLE OF THE NAVY LAWYER 

$ 10.10

Although it met an emergency need, it proved to be cumbersome and complicated, and today it is chiefly of historical interest. Briefly, it took the form of a contract between a private manufacturing concern and the Army or Navy under which the private concern agreed to construct the needed additional facilities at its own expense, and the Navy agreed to pay to the private concern the cost of the expansion in 60 monthly installments. Upon completion of such payments, the Government was entitled by the contract to own the facilities if the Contractor did not elect to buy them.

Many legal complications arose. It became necessary to amend the statutory prohibitions against the assignment of government contracts 17 so as to enable private lending institutions to provide the necessary capital on the security of the so-called Emergency Plant Facilities (EPF) contract. The form of contract used, providing for repayment by the 

Government over a period of years, involved the creation of a sort of divided ownership, under which the private concern held legal title, while the Government held an equitable interest by virtue of provisions in the contract for acquisition of legal title by the Government when it had paid the cost of the plant expansion. Owing to the relative complexity of these contracts, as well as other factors, the Navy had by mid-1941 virtually discontinued their use (except for the Bureau of Aeronautics, which continued until later in World War II to employ a similar arrangement under which the Defense Plant Corporation contracted with the private concern). Instead, the Navy turned to the use of arrangements under which facilities expansions were contracted for, controlled and financed directly by the Government. $ 10.10. Interest of the Navy Lawyer in Privately Financed Facilities

Expansion 

As can be seen from the foregoing outline, the Navy's participation in privately financed facilities expansion is at best an indirect one (except in the unusual case of a guaranteed loan). The primary responsibility for issuing certificates of necessity for accelerated amortization, or for granting direct loans, rests with civilian agencies such as the Office of 

Civil and Defense Mobilization or the Treasury Department. Neverthe less, these agencies look to the military departments for information and recommendations on such questions as the need for the proposed facilities, and the extent to which the requirements of national defense justify the type of governmental aid requested. Since the Navy lawyer is normally consulted before such recommendations are made, it behooves him: (a) to be familiar with the governing statutes and regulations; 

17 REV. STAT. § 3477 (1875). Amended by the Assignment of Claims Act of 1940, 54 Stat. 1029, as amended, 31 U.S.C. § 203 (1952). 585

$ 10.11

FACILITIES 

(b) to be informed as to overall Government and Department of Defense policies in this area; and (c) to exercise an informed judgment in reviewing applications for such assistance and proposed Navy recommendations.

Here, as elsewhere, the Navy procurement lawyer is looked to for expert advice on the legal aspects of these complicated matters, for assistance in drafting, and for counselling on the policy implications of each application and proposed recommendation.

B. ACQUISITION OF FACILITIES AT GOVERNMENT EXPENSE 

$10.11. Introduction

When incentives such as have been discussed above fail to persuade a private concern to invest its own funds, or to borrow on its own credit, to provide needed facilities, the Navy may find itself faced with the alternatives of arranging for the provision of the necessary facilities at government expense or of foregoing the desired supplies. When military necessity will not permit the latter course, the services of the Navy lawyer become important in developing and advising as to means of accomplishing the acquisition and installation or construction of facilities at government expense. 

1. FINANCING BY GOVERNMENT CORPORATIONS § 10.12. Financing Through Defense Plant Corporation Contracts 

The Defense Plant Corporation was established on August 22, 1940, as a subsidiary of the Reconstruction Finance Corporation, pursuant to the authorization contained in section 5 of the Act of June 25, 1940.18 

As amended by section 4(b) of the Act of June 10, 1941,19 this legislation authorized the Reconstruction Finance Corporation to make loans to any corporation for plant construction or expansion, and further authorized RFC, either directly or through subsidiaries, ". . . to purchase and lease land, purchase, lease, build, and expand plants, and purchase and produce equipment, facilities, machinery, materials, and supplies, for the manufacture of strategic and critical materials, arms, ammunition, and implements of war," 20 and so on, conferring very broad powers. Such increased plant capacity was authorized to be leased or otherwise made available to private corporations for the manufacture of arms, armaments, and war supplies. 

The machinery employed by the Army, Navy, RFC, and DPC, aided by the Army-Navy Munitions Board, under the Act of June 25, 1940, as

DEFENSE PLANTS CORPORATION CONTRACTS 

$ 10.12 amended, enabled a contractor to construct or purchase industrial installations and machine tools as an agent of DPC, and provided that DPC would pay for such facilities either directly or through reimbursement of the contractor. With respect to DPC contracts sponsored by the Navy, the Navy obligated itself (by what was commonly termed a "take-out agreement") to reimburse DPC initially for 40 or 50 percent of the cost and to reimburse the balance if and when funds were appropriated by Congress for that purpose. In each case, interest was charged at the rate of 12 percent per annum. Rentals and proceeds of sales received by 

DPC were credited against the Navy's obligation under its take-out agreement.

From an overall standpoint, this was only an internal bookkeeping arrangement, since both the Navy and DPC were arms of the United States Government. However, the Navy, as a part of the Executive 

Branch, can obligate and spend only such funds as are appropriated by Congress, usually on an annual basis. Any funds paid over to it must usually be deposited in the Treasury. The DPC, as a government corporation and a subsidiary of the RFC, although it also had funds appropriated to it, was able to lend money, and to collect and retain rents and repayments of loans, without regard to fiscal year limitations, and in general to conduct its financial operations in much the same manner as a private corporation.

There were both advantages and disadvantages to DPC financing. 

Aside from the fact that obligations and expenditures were not initially charged against the Navy's limited appropriations, the program saved the Navy a considerable amount of administrative work. In addition, facilities financed by the DPC could be disposed of by that organization once they had outlived their usefulness, with no disposal burden placed on the Navy.

On the other hand, the arrangement involved bookkeeping and administration on the part of two government agencies as well as the private concern. The Navy as sponsoring agency was removed from direct supervision and control of the project and also over the use and operation of the new or expanded facilities. As soon, therefore, as the military services were granted adequate authority and funds to permit them to contract directly with private concerns for industrial facilities expansion, most branches discontinued use of the DPC arrangement. Since that time, the Navy has followed the pattern of direct financing of facilities expansions required for its purposes. It seems doubtful that any extensive use of the DPC or equivalent arrangement will be made in the future. 587

FACILITIES 2. DIRECT FINANCING THROUGH GOVERNMENT-OWNERSHIP CONTRACTS § 10.13. Authority 

It must first be realized that direct financing by the Government of facilities construction or expansion is dependent upon the existence of adequate legal authority therefor. For all practical purposes, the Navy's authority to acquire, construct or install facilities must derive from legis lation enacted by the Congress. 

$ 10.14. Congressional Control Over Facilities Construction: Express Authorization and Appropriations 

Congress has traditionally exercised close control over the construction of public buildings and works and the acquisition of land therefor. The 

United States Code is studded with provisions, many of them deriving from laws over half a century old, imposing restrictions or conditions in this regard.21

Such congressional control is further exemplified by the long-established practice of authorizing public works expressly by "substantive” legislation which authorizes the head of the department concerned to carry out a specific project or projects, described in the law and normally identified therein at least by location, intended purpose, and total authorized cost. Frequently, such legislation goes into greater detail. 

In addition to this type of "substantive" legislation (commonly referred to as a "military construction authorization act" or "public works act"), it becomes necessary to secure separate legislation appropriating the actual funds to finance the construction previously authorized. While as a strict matter of law the latter is sufficient authority, if enacted,22 it is subject to a "point of order" while on the floor of the Congress and may therefore be defeated if any member of Congress objects to such a shortcut.23 As a practical matter, both types of authorization, substantive and appropriation, are usually obtained. One important difference between the two is that while in bill form they are considered by different committees, the former by a subcommittee of the Senate or House Armed Services Committee (in the case of military construction), the latter by a subcommittee of the Senate or House Appropriations Com-

Such legislation is normally submitted by the sponsoring military department to the Congress via the Department of Defense and the Bureau of the Budget. Reviews of the projects requested are conducted at various levels. Hearings are held by the congressional committees concerned with the operation of the armed services and with appropriations. 

By the time the bill or bills are enacted many months may have elapsed from the date on which the projects were initially sponsored by the requiring service, bureau, or agency. 

$ 10.15. Relaxation of Congressional Control During World War II 

The time ordinarily consumed in obtaining authority for a facilities project by a public works authorization bill (apart from the additional time involved in obtaining the necessary appropriations) is such that, during war or national emergency, the requirements of national defense necessitate the relaxation by the Congress of some of its control by broader grants of authority to the executive departments. Operational requirements, for example, may develop overnight which in turn demand a tremendous and unanticipated increase in the quantity of particular weapons or other supplies which must be delivered to the fleet. Even before Pearl Harbor, in June 1940, Congress recognized the need for broader powers by granting the Secretary of the Navy general authority to acquire machine tools and other production equipment.24 A little later, by section 1(a) of the Act of July 2, 1940, the Secretary of War was granted broad authority to provide facilities, including authority to construct buildings and other works, and to acquire the necessary land therefor.25 The authority of the Secretary of War under the latter act was extended to the Secretary of the Navy by Executive Order No. 9262, dated November 5, 1942.26 Thereafter, the Act of December 17, 1942, granted similar authority directly to the Secretary of the Navy." 

The broad authorizations of the Act of December 17, 1942, and of the Act of July 2, 1940, as made applicable to the Navy by Executive Order No. 9262, provided the basic continuing or "permanent" war-time authority of the Navy to acquire, construct and install facilities.28 The Act of December 17, 1942, required that the Secretary of the Navy find it "impossible" to make contracts or obtain facilities.29 The Act of July

$ 10.16. The Korean Hostilities: Emergency Powers 

World War II was followed by a period of relative military quiet. 

This meant the disposal (rather than new construction) of facilities. 

But then the United States became engaged in the Korean action. A new national emergency was declared by the President on December 16, 1950.32 

Congress took steps to continue in effect certain statutory provisions, notwithstanding the official termination of World War II and of the prior national emergencies declared by the President in 1939 and 1941, pending the completion of study as to which of the emergency powers previously granted should continue in effect. These interim extensions of war powers were reflected in the Emergency Powers Continuation Act, approved July 3, 1952,33 which continued the effectiveness of certain statutory provisions for the duration of the national emergency proclaimed by the President on December 16, 1950, and six months thereafter, but not beyond April 1, 1953. This date was later extended to August 1, 1953.34 

The Emergency Powers Continuation Act liberalized the Act of De cember 17, 1942,35 so as to make it applicable to facilities expansion in connection with "the maintenance of the national defense," as well as the prosecution of war. This made it appropriate to exercise the authority of that act during the Korean conflict. The new act also made a direct statutory grant to the Secretary of the Navy of the authority originally conferred only on the Secretary of the Army (formerly the Secretary of War) by the Act of July 2, 1940,36 thus eliminating the need for reliance upon an Executive Order in this respect. 

Although, as pointed out above, the Emergency Powers Continuation Act was twice extended beyond its original expiration date, such exten-

The failure of Congress to extend the Act of July 17, 1953, beyond its last expiration date, as noted above, has left a serious gap in the general substantive authority of the Navy to expand industrial facilities, although the gap is partially filled by appropriations which have been made in general terms for facilities expansion.39 Congress has been asked to enact permanent legislation, which would take the place of the special war-time statutes and of the 1953 Act, but as of this writing, it is not possible to say what action will be taken. $10.18. Facilities for Research and Development

The authority granted by the Act of July 17, 1953, was to provide facilities "necessary for defense production or mobilization reserve purposes." It would appear that facilities needed for research or development were by implication excluded.40 The successful accomplishment of many important types of research and development work often requires the construction of special facilities, such as towers and abutments for guided missile testing ranges, or special-purpose structures to serve as targets, to hold test instrumentation, or to protect personnel and instruments from blast damage or the elements. With the cessation of World War II hostilities, the emphasis in defense procurement shifted from production to research and development, and the question of the authority of the Navy to provide facilities therefor became an important one. Major new installations for research and development were sometimes covered by public works authorization bills granting specific authority for particular projects. Often reliance was placed upon annual appropriation acts expressly providing funds for the purchase of equipment and machine tools and the installation thereof in public or private plants, and in some cases for erecting specialized housing for special devices. However, when it became necessary to construct buildings or other specialized structures for research and development, the authority most widely used was the "minor construction" provisions of annual appropriation acts, discussed below in § 10.20. But as will be seen, this authority was severely limited, both in applicability and in dollar amount. $ 10.19. 

General Authorization for Research Facilities for Contractors 

Considerable relief from the difficulties imposed on prosecuting research and development work by the limited authority to construct facilities therefor was provided by the Act of July 16, 1952.41 Section 4 of that act (as now codified in 10 U.S.C. § 2353) provides in effect that a contract of a military department for research or development may provide for the acquisition or construction by, or furnishing to, the contractor of such research, developmental or test facilities and equipment (including specialized housing therefor) as may be determined by the Secretary concerned to be necessary for the performance of the contract. 

The act specifically excludes from its authorization new construction (or improvements) having general utility. Specific requirements are imposed to safeguard the interest of the Government in facilities placed on property not owned by the Government which would not be readily removable without unreasonable expense or loss of value. This act is interpreted as making funds appropriated generally for research available for the acquisition, construction and installation of facilities determined by the Secretary of the Navy to be needed for the performance of Navy research or development contracts.42 The authority granted by this statute apparently does not extend to facilities needed to carry out work being conducted by civil service personnel of a naval establishment, rather than under private contract. MINOR CONSTRUCTION AUTHORITY 

$ 10.20 1 ble as permanent statutory authority for the construction of research and development facilities. $ 10.20. The "Minor Construction" Authority

The "minor construction" provisions previously referred to have been enacted annually for a number of years. They have taken the form of provisions in the annual appropriation acts to the effect that funds otherwise available to the Department of Defense for construction or maintenance shall be available for "minor construction (except family quarters), conversion of and extensions to existing structures, and improvements, at facilities of the Department concerned." 43 The legal effect was to provide general authorization for construction projects which qualified as being "minor" within the contemplation of the statute and were otherwise within the limitations prescribed. Consequently, a wide variety of such projects could be undertaken, with the use of general construction or maintenance funds, without the necessity of obtaining specific congressional authorization for each one.

There were three important limitations on this authority. One was a dollar ceiling. Secondly, the project had to be located at a facility of the department concerned.44 This excluded projects for improvements of contractors' plants. Thirdly, new construction of family quarters was expressly excluded. 

Despite these limitations, this type of provision proved extremely helpful in empowering the Navy to build many small facilities, including research facilities, at its various activities. In recent years, the authority was broadened to include conversions of and extensions to existing structures, as well as new construction. Although this included conversion of other structures to family quarters (as opposed to new construction of family quarters, which was expressly excluded), such conversions were closely controlled. 

In 1956 Congress gave this type of authority permanent statutory sanction (as opposed to a mere general provision in an annual appropriation act) by enacting section 408 of the Act of August 3, 1956.45 This section, as now codified in 10 U.S.C. § 2674, authorizes the establishment and

3. RESTRICTIONS ON GOVERNMENT EXPANSION OF FACILITIES 

$10.21. In General

The emphasis of the discussion up to this point has been on the affirmative authority to undertake facilities projects, and the restrictions thereon have only been noted in passing. It seems desirable at this point to outline the more important of the various restrictions and limitations which do exist. For present purposes, such restrictions may be divided into those imposed by law and those imposed by administrative authority. It is difficult to categorize these restrictions, however, and a discussion by way of introduction and example, such as appears below, cannot serve as a substitute for current familiarity with the stream of legislation and administrative regulations. 

§ 10.22. Statutory Restrictions: Approval of Land Titles 

Historically, there has long been a statutory requirement that before any land is acquired by or for the Government, the title must be approved by the Attorney General.48 The importance of this restriction was greatly reduced in the case of land acquisitions for facilities construction under the Act of July 17, 1953, discussed above in § 10.16, by a provision thereof which waived the requirement in the case of land acquisitions under that statute.49 Now that that statute has expired, if the land is being acquired under some other authority, it will become necessary to have the title approved by the Attorney General (unless 46 Section 511 of the Military Construction Act of 1958 supra provides that "no determination that a project is urgently required shall be necessary for projects, the cost of which is not in excess of $5,000."

Contracting Authority of Navy or Other Agency 

It may become necessary to inquire whether the statutory authority for the proposed acquisition or construction permits the Navy itself to make the purchase, or whether some other agency must be brought into the picture. For example, as to some types of general purpose facilities, the appropriate agency to make a purchase or a lease, or to construct a building, will be the General Services Administration, established under the 

Federal Property and Administration Services Act of 1949.51 No simple rule can be laid down here. In each case the governing statutes and regulations must be carefully scrutinized. $ 10.24. Special Restrictions

In any given case, there may be special restrictions in the statute conferring the substantive authority, or in the appropriation legislation, or in both. For example, the acquisition, construction, or operation, within the continental United States, with the use of Department of Defense funds, of new facilities or equipment for metal scrap baling or shearing, or for melting or sweating aluminum, is prohibited unless the Secretary or an Assistant Secretary of Defense determines that the operation of such a facility is in the national interest.52 The military departments are not allowed to establish bakeries, laundries, or dry-cleaning plants, unless the Secretary of Defense certifies that the products or services involved are not obtainable at reasonable rates from commercial sources.53 

Coming down to equipment and fixtures which might be required for use in connection with a particular facility, there are important restrictions on the purchase of passenger vehicles,54 furniture,55 and typewriters.56

$ 10.25. Cost Limitations 

In terms of cost, any proposed project must be within the financial limitations imposed by the substantive authorizing legislation, or by the appropriation involved, or both. In the case of public works authorization bills, projects are usually authorized on an itemized basis, with a specified dollar maximum or ceiling placed on each project, subject ordinarily to minor escalation at the discretion of the Secretary concerned." 

Where, however, a general authorization, such as that contained in the Act of July 17, 1953,58 is granted, the availability of the overall appropriation made for projects fitting the description of those authorized is not controlled by any individual project ceilings. 

That portion of appropriation legislation which actually sets forth the amounts appropriated for facilities construction usually speaks in terms of a total, without allocation of specific amounts or sub-totals for individual projects or categories of projects. Hence, the law on its face is ordinarily so broadly worded as to make any part of the appropriation available for any project of the kind described, and it will normally be unnecessary to look behind the language of the law as written. Nevertheless, since the budget justifications submitted to the congressional committees in support of the appropriations requested usually contain fairly detailed breakdowns, it is unwise to depart too greatly from such estimates without at least consulting informally with the congressional committees concerned.59 $ 10.26. 

Congressional Committee Clearance 

Apart from informal consultations of the nature just described, there is a very important requirement for formal congressional committee clearance in connection with all major facilities projects. U.S.C. § 2662 sets forth detailed requirements for "coming into agreement" with the Armed Services Committees of the Senate and the House of Representatives with respect to any proposed acquisition or disposal by a military department of real property by lease, purchase or sale, or by transfer from or to other government agencies (including transfers between military departments), which involves more than $25,000 in price, rental, or estimated value.
