Quite evidently the Congress has no intention of giving up this control. There is some administrative burden but not an insuperable one. 

$10.27. Administrative Restrictions: Navy Department Requirements 

A discussion of restrictions imposed by administrative regulation or directive, rather than by statute, can appropriately begin with mention of the approvals required within the Navy. The basic policy is that there will be added to the already enormous industrial and non-industrial facilities and establishments of the Navy only such additional government-owned facilities and property as are essential to carry out the Navy's mission. The directives applicable from 1952 to 1955 required review and approval by the Assistant Secretary of the Navy of (i) any proposed acquisition of real property, (ii) any project involving the procurement and installation of plant equipment or machine tools where the combined cost of procurement and installation exceeded $50,000, and (iii) any construction of buildings or other improvements to real property, or alterations of, or extensions to, existing structures (other than projects falling within the "minor construction" authority and not requiring Secretarial approval under the terms of that authority).64 The substance

Other Administrative Reviews 

From time to time, administrative regulations have required the Secretary of the Navy to seek approval of certain proposed facilities projects by authority outside the Navy. For example, during World War II the shortage of materials for construction and for the manufacture of tools and machinery resulted in competition for materials between facilities expansion and the production of end products. This, together with the need for allocating materials and labor to the most urgent projects, regardless of which government agency might be sponsoring them, resulted in the imposition of requirements that any new facilities project costing over $100,000 be submitted to a Facility Review Committee established by the War Production Board and be approved by such Committee prior to going forward. In addition to the requirement for approval by the Secretary of Defense of industrial facilities projects costing over $1,000,000, noted above, present regulations require approval by the Secretary of Defense, or an Assistant Secretary of Defense, of any proposed project for the construction, at a new location, of wholly governmentowned commercial or industrial-type facilities." Counsel's Responsibility To Know Current Facilities Direc tives.

The detailed methods of seeking the administrative and other approvals discussed above, and the channels through which requests for approval are forwarded, are the subject of numerous and constantly changing directives. Familiarity with these directives is essential to the Navy lawyer charged with any responsibility in this area, not only from the standpoint of obtaining the required clearances, but of sound timing of related contractual action. It might be noted here that, in order to expedite review of projects submitted for approval by eliminating or reducing the need for further legal review at high levels, the Chief of Naval Material in 1951 required that all Bureau requests for approval of facilities projects incorporate a statement to the effect that Counsel for the Bureau had approved the legal aspects of the proposed project."⁹ 

4. TYPES OF ARRANGEMENTS UNDER WHICH GOVERNMENT-OWNED FACILITIES MAY BE ACQUIRED, CONSTRUCTED OR INSTALLED 

$10.30. In General

Once it is ascertained (i) that the Navy has the necessary substantive authority to provide the facilities involved in a particular project, (ii) that the necessary funds have been appropriated and are available, and (iii) that all necessary approvals have been obtained, the next step is to enter into arrangements for the acquisition, construction or installation of such facilities. A number of methods are available, the choice of which will be controlled by the circumstances of each case. 

$ 10.31. Facilities at Government-Operated Plants 

Where the facilities are to be located at a government-owned and operated plant, and any substantial amount of construction work is involved, the Navy usually contracts for such construction with outside contractors. 

The contracts for such work are normally placed by the Bureau of Yards and Docks, which has been given broad authority over both the contractual and engineering aspects of all such construction.70 The technical bureau concerned, however, will normally consult with the Bureau of Yards and Docks to explain its specialized requirements and to be sure that they are met.

The question might be asked why it should be necessary to contract with private parties, rather than have the work performed by the Navy itself. 

For policy reasons, the use of uniformed personnel to perform construc- 

68 See § 10.24 supra for other applications of this policy. 

69 NPD 13-402f.3 (Aug. 1, 1955). 

70 NPD 13-1501 (May 23, 1958). 599

$ 10.32

FACILITIES 

tion work within the continental United States has been administratively limited to the performance of construction incident to emergency or disaster relief (such as erection of levees required to prevent imminent flood damage) work required for military training of personnel, and projects restricted by security. While at most naval shore establishments there are civil service station maintenance forces, qualified to carry out small construction projects and the installation of equipment, these forces are not as a rule qualified or prepared to carry out major construction projects. The extent of construction work by station maintenance forces is further limited by administrative directives which limit civil service personnel to the performance of maintenance work, and repairs and rehabilitation closely akin to maintenance, recognizing the claims of industry in the area of new construction."1

Where, however, the project involves only the procurement and installation of production equipment (e.g., machine tools) at a naval station, the policy restrictions against the use of station maintenance personnel do not apply and it may be possible to accomplish the installation work by the use of station forces. Even here, however, it is usually necessary to contract for the manufacture (as opposed to the installation) of such production equipment, since naval shore establishments are not normally equipped or staffed for the actual fabrication or manufacture of machine tools or other production facilities. 

$ 10.32. Facilities at Privately Operated Plants 

In many cases the purpose of a facilities project is to increase capacity, not at a Navy-operated production facility, but at a plant operated by a private concern. There are two possible approaches. One, which is available principally when the project consists in the purchase and installation of production equipment, is for the Government to buy the equipment and furnish it to the supply contractor, for installation by the latter under such terms as may be worked out. This method, although used by some agencies, is rarely followed by the Navy. The other and more common method, applicable to any type of facilities project, is for the Navy to place a contract with its supply contractor, under which the latter agrees to purchase and install the necessary machine tools, or to construct the necessary buildings or structures, for the account of the Government. In the latter situation it is customary for the supply contractor to subcontract the actual construction work to a firm accustomed to handling that type of work. 

71 SecNav Circular Letter (OIR 211: 

mp Sept. 14, 1950), transmitting DOD policy governing procurement of services for the maintenance, repair, alteration and new construction of real property. 600

TYPES OF CONTRACTUAL ARRANGEMENTS 

$ 10.33 $10.33. Types of Contractual Arrangements 

Where only a minor amount of construction or installation is involved, it may be possible to provide for it by appropriate provision in the supply contract or contracts which make the expansion necessary. The installation or construction costs would then be recognized as reimbursable items (where a cost-type contract is involved), or as elements properly entering into the price of the supplies (where a fixed-price contract is involved). At best, however, this is a makeshift approach which leads to confusion, both as to the pricing of the supplies, and as to the title to, and accounting for, the facilities involved. 

Accordingly, the Armed Services Procurement Regulation provides that, wherever the cost of procuring and installing or of constructing facilities exceeds $50,000, a separate contract, distinct from the supply contract, will ordinarily be used.72 Such a contract is known as a "facilities contract." (The latter term is also used, as will be explained later, for a contract under which facilities already constructed or installed are provided to a supply contractor for his use. Often, the same "facilities contract" will provide both for the construction, or acquisition and installation, of the facilities, and for their furnishing and use.) 

Where construction of buildings is involved, there are additional reasons which exist for providing for such construction under a contract separate from the related supply or service contract. Certain federal statutes and administrative regulations require the inclusion in any government contract providing for construction of buildings, or the like, of special provisions designed to assure that such contracts will not be performed at substandard wages or under substandard labor conditions.73 

The Government is also required to include in such contracts provisions designed to assure, not only that the laborers on the project will be paid by the Government's prime contractor, but that laborers or materialmen who have supplied work or materials to the project will have substantially the same rights as are normally accorded them under state laws.74 These statutory and regulatory stipulations are not normally required in supply or service contracts, and incorporation thereof in such contracts presents awkward problems of draftsmanship and of contract administration. 

Ordinarily, such contracts for the procurement and installation of production equipment, or construction of buildings, at privately owned plants are negotiated directly with the supply contractors concerned.

FACILITIES 

One of the factors militating against the use of advertised bids is the fact that the Government has no right (short of the use of extraordinary powers in the nature of condemnation) to authorize any third person to enter and perform work on privately owned property without the consent of the owner. Moreover, even if this difficulty were overcome, there remain for resolution complex problems concerning the mutual rights and obligations of the parties in the event of damage to the supply contractor's property, injury to its personnel, or interference in its production operations by the third party. Negotiation of the facilities contract directly with the supply contractor owning the plant avoids delay. It permits the Navy to hold a single party responsible both for the construction or installation of the facilities and for the production for which they are required. Another factor favoring negotiation with the supply contractor is the fact that the latter is normally best qualified to determine what type of installation or construction is best suited to its needs. 

Facilities contracts are customarily of the cost-reimbursement type. 

The use of this method of contracting must be justified under 10 U.S.C. § 2306 (c).75 It is usually impracticable or impossible to ascertain, in advance of the work, the precise nature and extent of the facilities and work which will be required. 

Facilities contracts normally provide for reimbursement of cost alone, without fee. This provides a means of implementing the Navy policy against allowing a profit for work of expanding facilities when (as is usually the case) the contractor will use the facilities to earn a fee or profit under a supply or service contract. 

Wherever the Government reimburses the contractor in full for the cost of acquiring equipment, or of constructing buildings, the contract provides that title to such facilities vests in the Government. A fortiori, this is the case when the facilities are acquired directly by the Government and furnished to the contractor. This has at least three important consequences: 

(a) The provisions of Section XIII and of Appendix B (or C) of the Armed Services Procurement Regulation become applicable and must be complied with; (b) Such government-owned facilities are exempt from the direct imposition of State and local taxes; (c) The Government's interest must be protected upon ultimate disposal of the facilities.

These problems will be taken up, along with others, in the remaining parts of this chapter.

THE USE OF FACILITIES 

$ 10.34

II. PROVISIONS GOVERNING THE USE OF FACILITIES 

$10.34. In General

In the preceding sections consideration has been given to the means by which new facilities may be established. But the only purpose of creating additional facilities is to use them to produce supplies or perform services for the Navy, or at least to hold them in standby for such use in the event of future emergency.

The actual operation of the facilities will either be by government personnel (where the facilities are established at a government-operated plant) or by private parties (where the facilities are to be used by a private manufacturing company holding contracts for services or supplies). 

Even though a contractor has to acquire additional facilities in order to perform a prospective contract, there is no question as to the authority of the Navy to award such contract on the basis that the contractor will acquire the necessary facilities on its own account and will include in the contract price an amount representing normal depreciation on such facilities, allocable to the supply contract, plus amounts representing a properly allocable portion of his expenses for taxes, insurance, and other items of overhead in respect of the facilities. But where the Government furnishes the necessary facilities, there should be eliminated from the contract price any amounts for depreciation and similar items of overhead (except that if rental is charged, as explained hereafter, it becomes an item of reimbursable cost). 

There flows by implication from the Navy's basic authority to procure supplies and services the authority, when necessary, to make available government-owned facilities to private contractors for their use in performing service or supply contracts." As mentioned above, this is done by an instrument labeled a "facilities contract." When governmentowned facilities are thus provided to a contractor, the contractor's authority to use them is limited substantially to such use as is necessary to perform the government supply or service contracts concerned. The transaction is essentially one in the nature of license or permit, analogous to a bailment of personal property. Accordingly, it is considered that the contractor acquires no property interest in the facilities. The transaction is to be distinguished from a lease of the facilities, under which the Government conveys to the lessee a recognized property interest and may clearly authorize the lessee to use the facilities for purposes other than the performance of Navy or government work." Admittedly, however, the distinction is often a fine one, especially in a case where the facilities contract provides for the payment of rental or of a "use charge." 

76 Many of the statutes discussed above in 88 10.15-10.19 expressly so provided. 

77 See §§ 10.37, 11.84-11.87 infra. 603

$ 10.35

FACILITIES 

Where facilities are established at government-owned plants, they remain in the possession of the Government and their proper use and management, as well as their eventual disposition, may be provided for by administrative regulations binding upon the government officers or employees who are in immediate charge of the facilities. Such is not the case, however, where the facilities are installed or constructed at a private plant, or are otherwise made available to a private concern for performing Navy supply or service contracts. Unless some agreement is reached between the Navy and the contractor governing the use and eventual disposition of the facilities, the rights and obligations of the parties are determined by whatever rules may be established under applicable statutory or common law. The difficulty of determining readily such rights and obligations, even assuming that they adequately protect the interests of the Government and the contractor, indicates the desirability of a written contract which will state the terms and conditions under which the facilities are put in the contractor's possession. 

$10.35. Contractual Provisions Required by Regulations 

Applicable regulations require that every facilities contract include provisions covering the following, among others: measures to be taken for proper maintenance and protection of the facilities while in the contractor's possession; the extent to which either party is to assume the risk of loss of or damage to the facilities; the uses to which the contractor may put the facilities; and the rights of the Government to terminate the arrangement and repossess the facilities.78 As pointed out above, the agreement setting forth such terms and conditions is commonly referred to as a "facilities contract," whether or not it is combined in a single document with provisions for the initial acquisition and installation or construction of the facilities. During World War II the various Bureaus of the Navy each devised forms of facilities contracts which were basically similar in purpose and scope. Nevertheless despite centrally imposed controls over the wording of such provisions, there were some differences in policy and practice as among the Bureaus, and considerable differences between the Navy and the War Department. In some cases this resulted in a single contractor having similar facilities furnished to him under quite dissimilar terms and conditions. In March 1951, Section XIII of the Armed Services Procurement Regulation was promulgated. Part 4 of this section sets forth the substance of certain major provisions which are made mandatory for inclusion in contracts under which industrial facilities are provided to supply or service contractors. 

The required provisions include the following:

Space does not permit a detailed discussion of all the provisions outlined above, or of the other paragraphs of Part 4 of Section XIII of ASPR which affect the work of the Navy lawyer in the area of facilities, but some of them will be discussed below. 

$ 10.36. Additional Contractual Provisions: Deviations From Regulations 

It must be borne in mind that the circumstances of the case will often necessitate the inclusion of provisions additional to those required by section XIII of ASPR. In most cases such additional provisions have to do with the protection of the Government's interest upon disposal of the facilities. These will be discussed later. But here may be noted the advisability of including such provisions as one granting the Government the right to enter premises owned or controlled by the contractor for the purpose of inspecting the facilities or of removing them. 

Furthermore, it should be borne in mind that it is impossible to draft a regulation having the scope of section XIII of ASPR which will fit every situation that may arise. Although deviation from the requirements of ASPR will be granted only when adequate justification exists, the requirements of Part 4 as written are not inflexible rules. When the necessity for a deviation appears, the Navy lawyer will be expected to know whether and to what extent each of the required provisions is based on requirements or limitations of law on the one hand, or upon considerations of policy on the other hand. Such knowledge is essential to determine the extent to which deviation from the required provisions is legally feasible and, if policy considerations underlie the requirement, how serious the result of the contemplated deviation may be as a policy matter. 

Moreover, the lawyer's training in applying legal principles and in analyzing and interpreting the language of statutes, contracts, and other legal documents, will be of great help to him in solving problems which arise in the course of negotiations. If the circumstances of a particular case make it impossible or impracticable to arrive at an agreement with the contractor consistent with the exact letter of section XIII of ASPR, but an agreement can be reached under which the substance of the rights intended to be protected will be enjoyed by the Government, then a deviation may be appropriate."

PRIVATE USE OF GOVERNMENT FACILITIES 

$ 10.37 

§ 10.37. Authority for Private Use of Government Facilities 

Where the facilities are furnished to a contractor primarily for the purpose of enabling it to perform certain Navy supply or service contracts, it is usually unnecessary and inadvisable to grant the contractor the right to use the facilities for other purposes. In some cases, however, it may be desirable to authorize the contractor to use the facilities for the performance of other government contracts or subcontracts. In either case, the ASPR requires that the facilities contract specify, or otherwise identify, the supply or service contracts for which the facilities may be used.80

Sometimes, however, it becomes desirable, in the interest of both parties, to permit the use of the facilities for commercial work in which the Government has no particular interest. An example might be where government machine tools are placed in a production line along with machine tools owned by the contractor. If the contractor is to operate efficiently and economically, he must be able to run all his production of a certain type, whether government or commercial, through this particular line. 

The question then arises as to the authority of the Navy to permit the use of government facilities for private, non-governmental purposes. It is recognized that the Secretary has a certain inherent, though limited, authority to make naval property available for private purposes when it is in the public interest to do so. Aside from this, Congress has expressly granted authority to the Secretary of the Navy to lease facilities for commercial purposes. One such grant of authority is found in the 

Military Leasing Act of 1947,82 which will be discussed at greater length below. Another was contained in the Act of July 17, 1953,83 discussed above in connection with the question of authority to construct and provide facilities. It seems fair to say that both these statutes, and especially the former, contemplated primarily a lease in the conventional sense of the word, including the execution between the Navy and the lessee of a document in the usual lease form. Such a transaction is particularly appropriate when the facilities involved are not currently devoted to governmental use, and are being leased for commercial purposes. 

Although some Defense Department agencies have made leases under the Military Leasing Act of 1947 in order to place in the hands of private concerns government facilities for the primary purpose of performing supply or service contracts, this has not been the general practice of the. 

Navy, which prefers to use the device of a facilities contract, as explained above. But where facilities have been made available under a facilities contract for performing government work, and it is desired to authorize

$10.38. Rental or Use Charge 

Where the authority of a contractor to use the facilities is limited to the performance of work to be paid for directly or indirectly by the Government, the Government cannot expect to realize any net return to the Treasury from rentals charged for the use of such facilities. This is because the contractor, in order to recover the amount it must pay out for rental, will include a corresponding amount as an element of cost or price to the Government under the supply or service contract in the performance of which the facilities are used. Indeed, since rental is normally an overhead charge, general and administrative expense as well as profit may be calculated by the contractor, in addition to the direct rental cost, resulting in a net out-of-pocket loss to the Government.85 Nevertheless, the general policy is to charge rental for the use of government-owned facilities when necessary to avoid giving contractors who have been furnished government-owned facilities an unfair competitive advantage over other contractors who provide their own facilities and who, therefore, are risking their own capital and must absorb costs of ownership (depreciation, taxes, insurance and the like). This policy is recognized by ASPR 

13-407 (Sept. 18, 1958). However, contracting agencies are authorized to waive rental for the use of government-owned facilities in the performance of government work if "the user is not thereby placed in a favored competitive position . . . and . . . the Government receives adequate consideration through reduced cost for the supplies or services or otherwise." 87 The intention of this language is simply to insure that there 86

It does not mean that other legitimate costs of the contractor must be reduced in return for permission to use the government-owned facilities. 

The principal reason for the rule which generally requires the payment of rental is, as explained above, the desire to put all suppliers on an even basis and to prevent one from having an unfair competitive advantage over others. Moreover, in non-rental situations it is sometimes difficult to police the arrangement to insure that the contractor's prices properly reflect the elimination of amounts for rental and overhead and profit based thereon. In the case of subcontractors it is even more difficult to do so. $10.39. Maintenance and Protection

ASPR 13-408 (Sept. 18, 1958) states that each facilities contract, shall require the contractor, without cost to the Government under the facilities contract, to protect, preserve, maintain, and repair the facilities, in accordance with sound industrial practice, until relieved of responsibility therefor. This means that maintenance costs are, in general, expected to be recovered as a charge to the supply or service contracts for the performance of which the contractor has been furnished the facilities. 

Where the facilities are being used to capacity by the contractor for performing government work, this will have no abnormal effect on prices. 

But where there is a high proportion of government-owned equipment in a particular plant, difficulty may be experienced during any period of low production, when a relatively small number of orders must bear the expense of maintaining a large quantity of idle government facilities. 

It is true that under ASPR 13-413.2 (Sept. 18, 1958) the contractor is granted a right to terminate the facilities contract (and, accordingly, its obligation to protect and maintain the facilities), but such right is of limited value since the contractor must exercise it as to all, or a substantial portion, of the facilities in its possession under the contract, and since such termination does not relieve the contractor of its obligation to perform its supply or service contracts. Consequently, especially in cases where the Navy desires to keep the facilities available at the contractor's plant as mobilization reserve capacity, the point will be reached sooner or later when it is no longer feasible or fair to require the contractor to look to government supply or service contracts for reimbursement of its maintenance costs, and some new arrangement must be entered into. The solution may be a complete assumption by the Government of maintenance and protection costs under a contract so providing, or a lease of the facilities, or some combination of the foregoing. This will be dis- 609

cussed later on in more detail in connection with the subject of reserve facilities. 

$10.40. Property Accounting and Record Keeping 

ASPR 13-409 (Sept. 18, 1958) requires the inclusion in each facilities contract of a provision that the contractor will maintain, without cost to the Government under the facilities contract, adequate property control records and a system of identification of the industrial facilities furnished thereunder. Again, the contractor may recover the cost thereof by appropriate charges to its supply and service contracts. 

Apart from the inherent desirability of such a requirement from the standpoint of good administration, it is made necessary by section 410 of the National Security Act of 1947, as amended, which requires the Secretary of Defense to cause property records to be maintained in the three military departments, on both a quantitative and monetary basis, of the fixed property, installations, and major items of equipment, as well as the supplies, materials, and equipment held in store by the armed services, and to report annually thereon to the President and to Congress. 

The detailed regulations for such property accounting are set forth in 

ASPR, Appendix B, "Manual for the Control of Government Property in Possession of Contractors," applicable to commercial contractors, or Appendix C, applicable to non-profit research and development contractors. One or the other of these, as appropriate, is to be incorporated by reference in every facilities contract.

Space does not permit a detailed discussion of the requirements of these manuals. In general, reliance is placed on the contractor's own property accounting and record-keeping systems, provided these meet certain minimum standards. The standards set are, so far as possible, those recognized by sound industrial practice. Government property must be so marked. The records kept must be such that at any given time it may be determined what government property the contractor has and where it may be located. Provision is made for the regular taking of inventories. So far as possible, in accordance with the requirements of the statute, records are kept both on a quantitative and a monetary basis. 

Separate records of industrial facilities (land, buildings, production equipment, and the like), and of special tooling and material, are required to be kept. $10.41. Risk of Loss

As pointed out above, each facilities contract is required to include a provision substantially absolving the contractor from liability for loss 

88 61 Stat. 495 (1947), as amended, now codified as positive law in 10 U.S.C.

THE MILITARY LEASING ACT OF 1947 

$ 10.43 or damages to the facilities provided thereunder.89 At first blush, this may seem a strange provision for the Government to require. But the reason is simple. If a risk of loss is placed on the contractor, the latter will take out insurance and the cost thereof will be reflected in the price of its products sold to the Government. But the Government is such a large property holder that it is cheaper for it to self-insure than to pay the cost of insurance premiums. (The term "self-insure" is used here in the broad sense of assuming the risk, not in the technical sense of setting up a funded program of self-insurance in the strict sense of the word.) 

Accordingly, the Government assumes all risk of loss or damage to the facilities, and expenses incidental thereto, which is normally insurable.90 

This includes loss or damage to the facilities caused by the contractor's negligence, because that is normally insurable. It does not, however, include the risk of loss or damage resulting from willful misconduct or lack of good faith on the part of the contractor's top management." 

Examples of the latter would be rare.

In any particular case, however, where special circumstances might necessitate it, the Government may require the contractor to take out insurance on the facilities, and the contract clause will so require.⁹2 In that event, or if insurance is being carried for any other reason, the contract will provide that the proceeds of such insurance will inure to the benefit of the Government.93 $ 10.42. III. RESERVE FACILITIES 

Most of the foregoing discussion has centered around the problem of acquiring and furnishing facilities for current production. Of almost equal importance, however, is the problem of maintaining sufficient standby or reserve capacity for use in the event of emergency. 

$ 10.43. The Military Leasing Act of 1947 

At the end of every period of large-scale mobilization, there is considerable pressure on the Government to cut down its operations and dispose of its huge inventories and its industrial plants and equipment. But such disposal is often at sacrifice prices. If a few years later the same facilities have to be acquired anew, at great cost, the Government will have proved itself the victim of false economy. 

89 ASPR 13-411 (Sept. 18, 1958). 

90 For the proposition that the Government may act as a self-insurer as to its own property, even though in the possession of another, see Newport News Ship building & Dry Dock Co. v. United States, 

34 F. 2d 100, 106 (4th Cir. 1929), cert. denied, 280 U.S. 599 (1929).

On the policy problems involved, see

18, 1958).

93 See ASPR 10-601 (Sept. 18, 1958). 611

$ 10.43

FACILITIES 

This was realized after the end of actual hostilities in 1945, and various steps were taken to avoid too rapid a dissipation of the nation's military production facilities. The first such measure was the Military Leasing 

Act of 1947,94 which has already been mentioned in § 10.37. This statute made it practicable for the military departments to lease to commercial users plants and other facilities which, although not surplus to the overall needs of the Government, were not for the time required for public use. It thus accomplished the twofold purpose of making such facilities available for commercial production, while at the same time assuring that they would be available to the Government when needed. 

From this standpoint, the two most important provisions of the act were those relating to maintenance and to termination. Under prior legislation, it was not permissible for the Government to lease property except for a full cash rental; the lessee's agreement to maintain the property could not be counted as part of the consideration. This made it difficult, if not impossible, for the military departments to lease facilities and have any assurance that they would be maintained in such manner that upon repossession they would still be suitable for defense purposes. For obviously there would be no incentive to a commercial user to pay a full cash rental and to assume over and beyond that any maintenance obligation, other than what was essential for his own immediate purposes. This was changed by section 1 of the Military Leasing Act of 1947, which stated that any lease thereunder might provide for the maintenance, protection, repair, or restoration by the lessee of the property leased (or of the entire unit or installation where a substantial portion thereof was leased), as a part or all of the consideration of the lease. 

Another basic requirement, from the standpoint of national defense, is that property leased be available to the Government when needed. 

Accordingly, the act provided (i) that any lease thereunder should be for not more than five years, and (ii) that each such lease should contain a provision permitting the Secretary to revoke it at any time. Upon a determination that it would promote the national defense or be in the public interest, the Secretary may make a lease for a longer term, or may omit the clause reserving the right of absolute revocation, but in the latter case he must reserve at least the right to revoke the lease during a national emergency proclaimed by the President.

Although designed primarily for the purpose explained above, the Military Leasing Act of 1947 is not limited thereto. It authorizes lease for any purpose, so long as the requirements of the statute are met. Thus, as mentioned above, leases may be made for current production. The act was later broadened to permit long-term leases under the Wherry

$10.44. The National Security Clause 

Another device for keeping reserve facilities available is by sale subject to a "National Security Clause." This means that the plant or other facility is actually sold to a private party, but the purchaser agrees, under the terms of the so-called National Security Clause, (i) to maintain it, (ii) not to make any alterations which would interfere with the intended mobilization use of the property, unless they could be removed and the property restored within 120 days, (iii) not to sell or transfer the property, or remove any important production equipment, without the Government's consent, and (iv) to allow the Government to repossess the plant upon payment of evacuation expenses, rental for the period of repossession, and expenses of reconversion at the end of such period. The obligations of the National Security Clause normally run for 20 years in the case of buildings and improvements, and 10 years in the case of machinery and equipment.

When first devised, the National Security Clause was simply inserted in contracts disposing of facilities by administrative decision, without benefit of statutory authorization. However, section 5 of the Military 

Leasing Act of 1947 % gave statutory recognition to and authorization for the use of the National Security Clause. This section was repealed in 1948, and a comprehensive statute, the National Industrial Reserve Act of 1948, enacted in its place. This act is still in effect. The Department of Defense has issued detailed regulations under it, including the text of various versions of the National Security Clause for use with different types of facilities." Problems concerning the validity and enforcement of the National Security Clause are discussed in Chapter 11, along with the validity of similar restrictions sometimes attached to the sale of other types of property.

TAXATION OF CONTRACTOR'S INTEREST IN FACILITIES $10.49 IV. TAXATION OF GOVERNMENT FACILITIES 

$10.47. In General

Mention has already been made of the fact that a contractor having government facilities often enjoys certain tax advantages which should be taken into account in arriving at a fair price for his product, and in comparing his prices with those of his competitors who use their own facilities. The reason is that federal property is constitutionally exempt from direct state and local taxation, without the consent of Congress. 

However, certain recent decisions of the Supreme Court, while leaving this basic doctrine intact, have upheld some kinds of local taxes on contractors using government facilities. These decisions will be discussed below. $ 10.48. Federal Tax Immunity

For many years the leading tax case in the facilities area was United States v. County of Allegheny.10 In that case the contractor had been furnished government-owned machine tools, which it had installed in its factory. The local Pennsylvania taxing authorities, in accordance with their usual practice, had added the value of these machines to the assessed value of the contractor's real estate. A majority of the Supreme Court held that this amounted to an unconstitutional attempt to levy an ad valorem general property tax on property owned by the United States. 

The Allegheny County case stands generally for the proposition that the states and municipalities may not levy direct ad valorem property taxes on government-owned property. But in other respects there is no such exemption. The contractor's income derived from the use of government facilities is subject to local taxation." A state may impose a tax on sales of property from a subcontractor to a prime contractor, even though the full cost of such purchases is reimbursed to the prime contractor under a cost-type contract and even though title to the property vests immediately in the Government.12 The rule is otherwise, however, where the prime contract expressly makes the prime contractor the Government's "agent" to effect such purchases.13 $10.49. Taxation of Contractor's or Lessee's Interest in Facilities

An important qualification of the principle forbidding direct taxation by the states of federal property is the rule that a state may tax the possessory interest of the private contractor in government-owned facili-

ties. There is a dictum in the Allegheny case 14 that this might be done. 

But how far this qualification could go did not become apparent until 1958, when the Supreme Court decided the cases of United States and Borg-Warner Corporation v. City of Detroit 15 and United States et al. 

(Continental Motors Corporation) v. Township of Muskegon.16 

In the Borg-Warner case, the contractor had leased a governmentowned plant at a stipulated rental for use in its private manufacturing business. A Michigan statute 17 provides that when tax-exempt real property is used by a private party in a business conducted for profit, the private party is subject to taxation to the same extent as though he owned the property. Acting under this statute, the City of Detroit imposed a tax on the lessee, based on the value of the property leased and computed at the rate used for calculating real property taxes. Under the terms of the lease, the amount of such tax, if finally upheld, was deductible from the annual rental. The economic burden of the tax therefore fell upon the United States. 

By vote of 7 to 2, the Supreme Court upheld the tax,18 holding that the tax was imposed on the lessee, as its personal obligation, and not on the United States as owner, and pointing out that the property did not become subject to a lien if the tax was unpaid. The fact that the tax was measured by the value of the fee was not regarded as changing the nature of the tax: it was still a tax on the lessee in respect of its beneficial use of the property, and not a tax on the property itself. The Court held that the Allegheny case was not controlling, because there the tax had been construed as imposed on the property itself and not on the contractor's beneficial interest.19 The Court further held that the tax was not discriminatory, being levied in respect of all exempt property used by private parties in business conducted for profit, and not merely property owned by the United States.20

The dissenting justices thought this tax "even more nebulous" than the other. The result of these cases,23 especially the former, had been foreshadowed by a 1956 decision of the Court construing section 6 of the Military Leasing Act of 1947, which read, in pertinent part, as follows: "The lessee's interest, made or created pursuant to the provisions of this Act, shall be subject to state or local taxation. . This circumstance was enough to convince the majority of the Court that the valuation used by the local authorities was fair and reasonable, and that the tax was on the lessee's interest only. It is apparent that these cases, while they render obeisance to the doctrine of immunity, as a practical matter reduce very substantially its operation in the facilities area. Nevertheless there are limitations: (a) The taxing statute must be non-discriminatory in operation. An attempt to single out government property, for use of which the contractor or lessee is taxed, while continuing to exempt similar use of state or municipal property, would probably violate this requirement.29 (b) There must be a reasonable basis for the valuation placed upon the contractor's right of use. An attempt to value this at the full assessed value of the property, where the contractor or lessee held the property under a one-month lease, for example, might not be sustained.30 (c) The tax, under the precise terms of permissible construction thereof," must be levied on the contractor's or lessee's possessory interest, and assessed against him. Government property itself may not be directly taxed, nor may the tax be levied against the Government, nor may any lien be asserted against the Government property. (d) Finally, the contractor's or lessee's possessory interest must be property of a kind taxed by the state or local statute. Failure of a state statute to meet this test resulted in the recent invalidation by the New York Court of Appeals of an attempt to tax the lessee's interest in government property leased under the Military Leasing Act for Wherry Housing purposes.32 The sole basis of the assessment was the New York tax on real property.33 New York has no tax on personal property. Applying the ancient rubric that a leasehold interest is a chattel real, or personal property, the New York court held that a tax on real property could not touch it. The court held, however, that this applied only to the leasehold interest in the fee; the lessee's ownership of the buildings and improvements could be taxed under the New York statute. The case is of interest as the first state court decision applying the doctrine of the Borg-Warner case to a statute of a state other than Michigan. $10.50. Congressional Consent to Local Taxation

$ 10.50 property. This possibility was recognized in the remainder of section 6 of the Military Leasing Act of 1947, which now reads, in part, as follows: 

A lease under this section shall provide that, if and to the extent that the leased property is later made taxable by State or local governments under an act of Congress, the lease shall be renegotiated.34 

It is important to note that this is not itself a consent to local taxation. 

It is merely a provision as to what shall happen if at some subsequent date Congress should grant such consent. The reason for the renegotiation provision is to permit an equitable adjustment of the rental (presumably downward), if at a later date the lessee should, as a result of congressional permission, be required to pay local taxes to which he was not subject when the lease was made. It should be noted that there is no requirement that the rental be renegotiated should the state or local authority merely tax the lessee's interest (as it did in the Supreme Court cases discussed above).

Congress has in the past given its consent to state and local taxation of federally-owned facilities. It did so in the case of facilities owned and furnished by the Reconstruction Finance Corporation or its subsidiary, the Defense Plants Corporation.35 When these facilities were transferred from R.F.C. or D.P.C. to the Armed Services or to General 

Services Administration, they became immune from state and local taxation. There was considerable feeling that this was inequitable. As a result, in 1955 a statute was enacted which made all property so transferred after January 1, 1946, subject to payments by the federal government to state and local authorities in lieu of the taxes which had previously been payable.36 It has been proposed that this be extended to cover all industrial facilities acquired by the Government since the beginning of World War II, in view of the large amount of such holdings and the potential tax revenues lost to local governments thereby, and that to compensate the states therefor the federal government should “inaugurate a broad system of payments in lieu of property taxes to State and local governments." 37

$10.51

FACILITIES V. DISPOSAL OF GOVERNMENT FACILITIES 

$10.51. In General

The subject of disposal of government property, including facilities, is treated in detail in Chapter 11 of this text. But there are certain disposal problems relating to facilities which may arise long before the time for actual disposal arrives, and which have to be considered when the facilities contract is first placed. It will be convenient to treat of these now. Usually these problems arise from a situation where buildings or other non-severable facilities are attached to land not belonging to the Government. $ 10.52. Authority for Disposal

As will be brought out in Chapter 11, the Constitution vests in Congress full and complete authority over the acquisition, holding, and disposition of property by the federal government.38 This has been interpreted to mean that no federally-owned property may be disposed of without express authorization of Congress. The basic statute now in effect is the 

Federal Property and Administrative Services Act of 1949,39 which authorizes the General Services Administration to dispose of all excess and surplus property. But this statute is geared to the problem of disposing of property after it has outlived its usefulness to the particular agency or to the Government as a whole. Moreover, it requires generally that all sales be by formal advertising; negotiated sales to a particular contractor are permitted only under unusual circumstances.40 It is not very helpful in solving problems which arise at the outset, and which look toward the future disposal of facilities currently being acquired or installed.

The Act of July 2, 1940,41 discussed above in § 10.15, authorized the 

Secretary of War (such authority being later extended to the Secretary of the Navy by Executive Order) to lease, sell, or otherwise dispose of plants and facilities, including land, constructed or acquired under that act. The Act of July 17, 1953,42 omitted these disposal provisions, except that it permitted leases.43 The failure to include disposal provisions in the more recent legislation has undoubtedly been prompted by the belief in some quarters that the Federal Property Act is adequate for the purpose. But this is not always so. 

Section 4 of the Research and Development Act of July 16, 1952,4 

44 authorizes the sale at fair value to a contractor of facilities acquired or

By implication, this would seem to authorize a sale. But this authority is limited to facilities for research or development, or both. 

Occasionally, reliance has been placed on Title II of the First War Powers Act,45 to authorize sales of property to contractors, or more commonly, to authorize inclusion in a facilities contract of option or other provisions giving the contractor a right to acquire the facilities at a later date. $10.53. Non-Severable Facilities: Definition 

As mentioned above, the problem of disposal arises principally in connection with "non-severable facilities" installed on land not belonging to the Government, since other types of facilities can be disposed of without too much difficulty in the ordinary manner. The term "non-severable industrial facility" is defined in ASPR 13–101.8 (Nov. 3, 1958) as “an industrial facility which, after erection or installation, cannot be removed without substantial loss of value or damage thereto, or to the premises where installed." $ 10.54. 

Protection of Government's Interest 

ASPR 13-406 (Sept. 18, 1958) states the policy that non-severable industrial facilities may be located on land not owned or controlled by the Government only where the head of the procuring activity determines that it is necessary, and that location on government land is not feasible. 

In any such case, unless the facilities are disposable for commercial or industrial purposes to parties other than the contractor, there must be an agreement by the contractor that he will (to the extent authorized by law) purchase the facilities, at or before the expiration of the facilities

The same paragraph of ASPR also provides that in any case of nonseverable facilities the Government shall reserve the right to abandon the facilities in place and shall not assume any obligation to restore or rehabilitate the premises, unless the head of the procuring activity personally approves a clause providing otherwise. Experience has shown that where a contractor has a right to require restoration (which is usually very expensive), he can use this as a bargaining weapon to force sale to him of the facilities at a sacrifice price. But even this is not altogether satisfactory, because abandonment is itself a form of disposal and probably requires statutory authority.50 

Somewhat similar provisions, as mentioned above, are contained in section 4 of the Research and Development Act of July 16, 1952,5¹ except that there is no mention of abandonment. 

$10.55.

Title to Underlying Land 

Where facilities are to be installed or constructed at a contractor's plant, it is advisable to ascertain what rights the contractor has in the underlying land, for, if it is occupied by the contractor under a shortterm lease from a third party, the establishment even of removable production facilities may be found inadvisable. Again, even if the term of the lease is adequate, examination of its provision may disclose requirements, such as for restoration of the premises by the contractor-lessee and forfeiture to the lessor of property not removed upon expiration of the lease, which are not consonant with proper protection of the Government's interest in the facilities and the policy against obligating the Government to pay for restoration. But even if the contractor owns the premises where the facilities are to be installed, it is possible that a mortgagee of the realty might successfully claim that the facilities, when installed or constructed, became subject to the mortgage. 

Some protection against these possibilities can be obtained by inclusion in a facilities contract of the following: (a) a representation by the contractor regarding the nature of its rights in the land; 

49 See also § 10.56 infra. 

50 See 88 11.117-.121 infra. 

51 See § 10.52, n. 44 supra. 622

CONTRACTUAL PROVISIONS FOR DISPOSAL 

$ 10.56 (b) a provision to the effect that no part of the government-owned facilities shall be deemed to become a part of the realty, but shall be considered personal property; and (c) a provision under which the contractor agrees that the title to the facilities shall be kept free from any encumbrances. 

It may also be appropriate, if the land where the facilities are to be installed or constructed is leased or mortgaged, to require the contractor to obtain from the lessor or mortgagee, as the case may be, an agreement as in (b), above, together with an agreement that the facilities shall not be subject to any right of the lessor or mortgagee. 

§ 10.56. Contractual Provisions for Disposal 

Apart from meeting the minimum requirements of statute and regulation outlined above, it may become necessary or desirable to provide in the facilities contract for more comprehensive provisions relating to disposal of the facilities. Thus the contractor may desire an option to purchase the facilities, either at a stated price, or at "fair value," or at cost less depreciation. Such an option, giving him the right to purchase the facilities, in some respects goes further than an obligation on his part to purchase only if the Government does not wish to, or cannot, make other disposition. Often, he will be unwilling to accept the facilities contract on any other terms, because of his understandable desire to protect the marketable title of his plant, free from any encumbrance created by the existence of a government-owned structure on the premises. 

During World War II, facilities contracts frequently included a crossoption arrangement, under which the Government was granted an option to buy the land underlying a government-owned non-severable facility, if the contractor failed to exercise an option granted to it to purchase the facility. This provided an equitable and advantageous means of assuring in advance that the Government would either receive a fair return upon sale of the facilities or would obtain clear title to property saleable to third persons as a unit. Statutory authority to enter into such arrangements at the time facilities projects are in the stage of planning and negotiation would do much to facilitate the negotiation of facilities contracts consistent with the best interests of the Government. 

About all that can be done at the present time, unless the Research and Development Act is applicable, is to make any such provisions for ultimate disposal subject to the availability of statutory authority, and await the event. When the time comes, it may be possible to negotiate a sale under the Federal Property and Administrative Services Act.52 

52 While § 203 (e) (3)(b) of the Fed eral Property Act, 72 Stat. 288 (1958),

VI. OTHER MATTERS $ 10.57. Role of the Lawyer: Participation in Contract Negotiations 

Although it is important in nearly all fields of Navy contracting for the lawyer to be familiar with, if not a participant in, negotiations preceding the award or execution of a contract, such participation is particularly important where facilities are concerned. Where the providing of facilities is necessary to enable a private concern to perform a contemplated supply contract, the award of the supply contract will normally be dependent upon the feasibility and time of such assistance. 

This in turn will involve such matters as ascertaining the existence of adequate authority to provide the facilities, as well as the existence and effect of any restrictions upon the exercise of such authority, and determining whether authority to agree to particular proposed terms and conditions exists. During the negotiations, the lawyer must look beyond the time when the facilities have performed their immediate purpose of producing the supplies to be delivered under the contemplated supply contract, and must take into account the problems which will arise when the facilities must be disposed of. If retention of the facilities at the contractor's plant as standby capacity for production in the event of mobilization is desired, the lawyer must be prepared to guide negotiations toward that end. $ 10.58. 

Drafting Problems 

The preceding portions of this chapter indicate that the lawyer dealing with facilities will often be confronted with the problem of drafting contractual documents. Part 4 of Section XIII of ASPR does not set forth prescribed clauses, but merely the substance of provisions which are to be included when facilities are provided by the Government to a contractor. Part 5 of Section XIII sets forth certain standard clauses on government-furnished property and special tooling for use in contracts for supplies. Some of the language of these clauses (which, although complicated, has been carefully thought out) can be adapted for use. 

But, in general, the actual wording in facilities contracts of clauses implementing the requirements of Part 4 of Section XIII is largely in the discretion of the attorneys concerned. fair market value of the property and other satisfactory terms of disposal can be obtained by negotiation," this authority applies only to surplus property so that the Navy at the time of acquisition of non-severable industrial facilities can give the owner of the underlying land little assurance of when the property will be in fact declared surplus by the 

General Services Administration.

RECORDATION OF FACILITIES CONTRACTS 

$ 10.59

As has previously been pointed out, it is common practice to incorporate in a single contractual document both an agreement for the construction, or the acquisition and installation, of facilities and an agreement covering the use of the facilities for their intended purpose after such construction, or acquisition and installation. This dual nature of many facilities contracts requires that the drafter consider what provisions must be inserted as common to both aspects of the transaction, and that he avoid conflict between those provisions which are peculiar to the construction, or acquisition and installation, phase and those which are peculiar to the use phase. 

Additional complications may be introduced because of the continuing nature of facilities contracts. Facilities once set up at a contractor's plant may remain there for many years, inactive, partly active, or, when it is necessary to retain them in place, as part of the mobilization reserve, wholly inactive. Because of the requirement of ASPR 13-403 (Sept. 18, 1958) that, in general, all industrial facilities provided by a procuring activity for use by a contractor at any one plant or general location shall be governed by a single facilities contract, amended from time to time as necessary, provision for additional facilities will frequently take the form of an amendment to an existing contract. Each such amendment will have to reflect revisions in contract language brought about by intervening changes in law or regulation. 

$10.59. Recordation of Facilities Contracts 

During World War II, the Navy adopted the practice of having a copy or abstract of each facilities contract, including schedules listing the facilities included, placed on public record by the Department of Justice in the office or offices of record for the county or counties in which the facilities were located. Since few states have enacted any statute under which contracts such as facilities contracts may be recorded, with the effect of giving constructive notice to third parties, most of the Navy's war-time facilities contracts were actually recorded as though they were mortgages or contracts of conditional sale, so as to fit into the normal categories of recorded instruments. Although it may be questioned whether such recordation operated to give valid constructive notice of government ownership, the recording did provide some opportunity for actual notice to a third party contemplating a purchase or mortgage of a contractor's plant. 

Much may, therefore, be said in favor of recording, particularly where the facilities provided by the Government consist of structures on or improvements to land or plants owned by private contractors. But where the facilities consist solely of machinery or other movable personal property, and the Government's ownership is prominently disclosed by markings on the property, there seems little reason to fear that a purchaser or mortgagee could successfully establish lack of notice of the Govern- 625

$ 10.59

FACILITIES 

ment's interest. In any event, since the above-mentioned war-time arrangement with the Department of Justice is no longer in effect, any such recording must now be accomplished either by the Navy, or by the contractor pursuant to a contractual requirement that he do so. 626

INTRODUCTION 

$ 11.1 $11.1. Introduction

The other chapters of this text have dealt, in the main, with the procurement of supplies and services by the Navy. This chapter deals with the converse situation, the disposal of property by the Navy. 

The term "disposal" is often used in a broad sense to include all transfers of property within and without the federal government. However, under current technical usage having its origin in the Federal Property and Administrative Services Act of 1949 (hereafter called the "Federal Property Act"),' the term "disposal" is generally limited to transfers of property outside the Government by sale, lease, bailment, donation, abandonment, or destruction; while the term "transfer" is generally reserved for transfers of property from one federal agency to another, and the term "reassignment" is used to refer to transfers of property from one activity to another within a federal agency." "Transfers" between agencies and "reassignments" within an agency are jointly referred to as "property utilization."

Most of the property disposed of by the Navy falls into the categories of "excess" or "surplus" property, the former being defined as "property under the control of any Federal agency which is not required for its needs and the discharge of its responsibilities, as determined by the head thereof," whereas the latter is "excess property not required for the needs and the discharge of the responsibilities of all Federal agencies," as determined by the Administrator of General Services. The generation of excess and surplus property which originally cost the Government billions of dollars presents the military departments with a major disposal problem, especially since the Departments of the Army, Navy and Air Force generate and dispose of approximately ninety percent of government excess and surplus personal property. 

Besides the categories of excess and surplus property, the Navy disposes of other property which does not come strictly within these technical statutory definitions. These other types of disposal are also taken up in this chapter.

In the main, this chapter deals with the disposal of Navy personal property, but some attention will be given to the disposal of real property, especially in the form of industrial facilities, although certain of the special problems incident to disposal of the latter are treated in Chapter 10.5

 I. AUTHORITY TO DISPOSE OF NAVY PROPERTY 

$11.2. Constitutional Authority

Article IV, section 3, clause 2 of the United States Constitution provides: 

The Congress shall have Power to dispose of and make all needful Rules and Regulations respecting the Territory or other Property belonging to the United States; . . . (Emphasis added.)

This constitutional provision is the foundation upon which rests the authority to dispose of government property, and it also constitutes a basic limitation on such disposal. For in construing it, the courts have held that the power of Congress over the disposal of the Government's property is absolute, and that in order to justify a sale of such property, there must be an act of Congress to support it. As recently as 1941, the 

Supreme Court reiterated this rule, saying: 

Power to release or otherwise dispose of the rights and property of the United States is lodged in the Congress by the Constitution. 

Art. IV, §3, Cl. 2. Subordinate officers of the United States are without that power, save only as it has been conferred upon them by Act of Congress or is to be implied from other powers so granted.' 

The constitutional phrase "Territory or other property" is not restricted to territory, but includes "all other personal and real property rightfully belonging to the United States." 

$11.3. Statutory Authority To Dispose of Property 

Prior to 1944 there were innumerable statutes on the books which affected in some measure the disposal of government property. These had been enacted to meet the particular situations of the various agencies, and it was often difficult to ascertain the precise application of a given statute to a particular agency.

But the generation of enormous surpluses toward the end of World War II prompted Congress to pass a comprehensive disposal statute, the 

Surplus Property Act of 1944.9 Under this act, a Surplus Property 

Board (later known as the Surplus Property Administration) was established in the Office of War Mobilization to supervise and handle the surplus property generated by the war.10 Somewhat later, the War

STATUTORY AUTHORITY TO DISPOSE OF PROPERTY 

$11.3 

Assets Corporation (later War Assets Administration) was set up to take the place of the Surplus Property Administration." Over the period from 1944 to 1949, these agencies disposed of personal property and capital assets having an original cost of over 182 billion dollars.12 

In 1948, however, the Surplus Property Act was in effect repealed by a statute making it inapplicable to any property not declared surplus by June 30, 1948, and providing that any surplus property disposed of after that date should be disposed of "in accordance with the terms of other existing law." 13 This made it necessary to fall back on such of the older disposal statutes as were still in effect. So far as the Navy was concerned, the only general authority to sell surplus property to the public was found in two old statutes which were still law but which were rarely used, viz, the Act of August 5, 1882,14 and the Act of June 30, 1890.15 

But this period of hiatus was relatively brief. In 1949 Congress passed a comprehensive peacetime disposal statute, the Federal Property and Administrative Services Act of 1949 (hereafter referred to as the Federal 

Property Act).16 This statute created the General Services Administra tion, at the head of which was to be an Administrator whose duty, among other things, was to prescribe policies and procedures for the utilization and disposal of government property. The statute required that each federal agency (i) maintain adequate inventory controls and accountability systems for property in its custody; (ii) continuously survey property to determine what was excess and report such excess promptly to the Administrator; (iii) perform the function of caring for and handling excess property under its control; and (iv) dispose of excess property as rapidly as possible in accordance with authority delegated and regulations prescribed by the Administrator." Section 502 of the 1949 Act ¹8 repealed many of the old disposal statutes, but those not repealed continued to cause confusion. In 1951 Congress amended the act to repeal many more of the old statutes, and provided that certain others not repealed were to be subject to applicable regulations of the Administrator.' 19 The Federal Property Act and regulations issued under it control the vast bulk of the disposal of naval excess and surplus property. There are exceptions, in that certain types of property, such as facilities, combatant vessels, personal effects, and some others, are subject to special statutes, which will be discussed in Parts IV through VIII of this chapter.

 $ 11.4. Regulations Governing Disposal 

Pursuant to sections 202 and 203 of the Federal Property Act,20 the Administrator of General Services has issued regulations dealing with the utilization of excess government property and the disposal of surplus property.21 These regulations deal in detail with property subject to the act, and set forth the policies and procedures to be followed in order to achieve maximum utilization and effective disposal. A very important feature of these regulations is that, subject to the broad policies therein set forth, the operating authority to make actual disposals is very largely delegated to the agencies themselves, including of course the Department of Defense.22 

Within the Department of Defense, policy statements have been issued in the form of Department of Defense directives which affect the three military departments and delegate to them most of the operating authority. In the Navy, control of disposal policy has been delegated by the Secretary to the Chief of Naval Material, who has promulgated, with the approval of the Secretary, the Navy Property Redistribution and Disposal Regulation No. 1 (hereafter NPR&D Reg. II. TRANSFER OF PROPERTY AMONG GOVERNMENT AGENCIES 

$11.5. In General

Before taking up the subject of disposal of surplus property by sale to the public, it seems desirable to take up the subject of intra-governmental transfers. Such transfers may take one of two forms: (i) reassignments of non-excess property within a particular agency; (ii) transfers of excess and non-excess property from one agency to another. $11.6. Reassignments of Non-Excess Property Within the Department of Defense 

Section 202 (c) of the Federal Property Act provides that each executive agency shall, as far as practicable, reassign property among its component activities when that property is no longer needed for the purposes of the appropriation from which it was purchased.25 Under the authority of section 621 of the National Military Establishment Appropriation Act, 1950 (which was permanently codified),26 property may be transferred from one naval activity to another and between the military departments without reimbursement of funds, i.e., without charging an appropriation therefor. An exception to this non-reimbursement rule is found in the case of property financed by working capital or revolving funds." In that case the agency receiving the property must reimburse the appropriation (unless the property is surplus and has no resale value). 

The Navy Stock Fund, successor to the Naval Stock Account established in 1921,28 is an example of such a revolving fund.

Another statute, which parallels and to some extent overlaps the statute just mentioned, permits the transfer of military stores, supplies and equipment of every character, including real estate, between the Army, Navy, Air Force and Coast Guard, upon the request of the head of one service and with the approval of the head of the other service.29 Reimbursement is not required. $11.7. Transfer of Excess Property to Other Government Agencies 

If property is reported as excess to a particular Navy bureau or office, it is first "screened" by the Armed Forces Supply Support Center of the Department of Defense for possible utilization by other bureaus or activities within the Department of Defense, and reassignment thereto in the manner described in § 11.6 supra.30 If there is no requirement for it within the Department of Defense it is declared excess to that Department and reported as excess to the General Services Administration, 25 63 Stat. 384 (1949), as amended, 40

The 

Formerly, any such transfer (with a few exceptions) from the Department of Defense to another federal agency had to be on a reimbursable basis, that is the receiving agency had to pay the fair value thereof by a charge to its appropriation.32 The term "reimbursement" was a misnomer, however, because except in certain unusual cases, such as where a reimbursable appropriation or revolving fund was involved, the proceeds were paid into the Treasury as "miscellaneous receipts." 33 reason for the rule was to prevent "augmentation of appropriations" by permitting agencies to obtain property without a charge against their appropriations. The requirement proved impracticable, however, in that it discouraged transfers within the Government and promoted wasteful practices. For the potential transferee agency would reason that if it had to pay "fair value" for used items, it might just as well pay a little more and get new ones.

For this reason, the requirement has now been relaxed and by an amendment to the statute,34 the Administrator of General Services with the approval of the Director of the Bureau of the Budget may, with a few exceptions, authorize transfers without reimbursement. To implement this, the Administrator has issued regulations which permit transfers without reimbursement in a wide variety of cases, although he has retained the requirement in others.35 

In addition to this general authority of the Administrator, there are a number of specific statutes which authorize transfers without reimbursement. For example, the military departments, with the approval of the Bureau of the Budget, may transfer without reimbursement excess equipment and supplies to the Weather Bureau for the establishment, maintenance, and operation of arctic weather stations.36 Similarly, excess land, improvements, equipment, materials or furnishings useful for veterans' housing may be transferred to the Housing and Home Finance Administrator without reimbursement, and excess equipment, material and supplies may be transferred without reimbursement to the Department of the Interior for operations conducted in the administration of the Territories and the Trust Territory of the Pacific Islands.38

TRANSFER OF NON-EXCESS PROPERTY 

$ 11.8 $11.8. Transfer of Non-Excess Property to Other Government Agencies 

Beside the authority discussed above in § 11.6 to make transfers of nonexcess property within the Department of Defense, there exist certain statutes which authorize transfers of such property outside the Department as well. For some years, Department of Defense Appropriation 

Acts have permitted the transfer of vessels between the Departments of Commerce, Army, Navy, and Air Force without reimbursement.39 The 

Department of Defense may transfer without reimbursement aeronautical and space vehicles and supplies and equipment (other than administrative supplies and equipment) to the National Aeronautics and Space Administration.40 The heads of executive departments may transfer or loan aircraft and aeronautical equipment without charge to the Smithsonian Institution for exhibition, historical, or educational purposes.41 Other examples are the transfer of facilities, equipment and supplies to the Veterans Administration for the care of veterans; 42 and the transfer of airport property outside the continental United States to the Federal Aviation Agency and of meteorological facilities outside the continental limits to the Weather Bureau.43 By regulation, however, the Navy has limited non-reimbursable transfers of this nature to excess or surplus property.44

Under section 601 of the Economy Act of 1932,45 the Department of the Navy may furnish to other federal agencies materials, supplies, equipment, work, or services of any kind upon payment of the estimated or actual cost. Transactions under the Economy Act relate to current stock and not to excess property. Payment for the property or service is credited to the appropriation or applicable working fund, unless it is determined that replacement of the property is unnecessary, in which case the payment (except in the case of Navy Stock Account Material) is "covered" into the United States Treasury as miscellaneous receipts. 46 Transfers of property by one federal agency to another on a temporary or loan basis have long been recognized. Until recently, the rule has been that where one agency lends property to another it may not charge for the use or depreciation thereof, or require that lost or damaged property be replaced or repaired by the borrowing agency."

III. DONATIONS 

$11.9. In General

If, after screening, property is found to be surplus to the needs of the Government as a whole, it becomes available for disposal to the public. While the normal method of disposal is by sale at the best price obtainable, in some situations donations to certain types of institutions take priority. It seems desirable, therefore, to take these up at this point and at the same time, for the sake of completeness, to discuss other categories of donable Navy property. $ 11.10.

Donations to Service Educational Activities
