Importance of Donation Program

Although donations bring no direct financial return to the Government, and although they are only collaterally related to the subject of Navy contract law, it is important for the lawyer dealing with disposal matters to be thoroughly familiar with this subject. Some idea of its importance can be gathered from the fact that from 1919 to 1955, over a billion dollars in acquisition cost of government surplus personal property has been the subject of donation, $800 million of it since 1946. 

Of this amount about 80 percent has been donated for educational purposes, and 20 percent for public health purposes.68 As pointed out above, the possibility of donation must always be considered before disposal by sale can be effected. This means that the Navy lawyer must understand the many rather complex statutes and regulations on the subject. Finally, of particular interest from a legal and contractual point of view, are the restrictions which are often placed upon the use of property by the donee after receipt thereof. These will be discussed, along with other types of restrictions, in Part X of this chapter.

A. METHODS OF SALE $11.17. Approved Sales Methods 

As in the case of procurement, formal advertising is the rule and negotiation the exception for most sales of surplus property.69 But unlike formally advertised procurement which is conducted exclusively by sealed bids, the Federal Property Act and regulations of the General Services Administration authorize formal advertising-or "public advertising" as it is called-incident to the sale of surplus personal property to be conducted in any one of three ways: sealed-bid sales, spot-bid sales, and auction sales.70 These will now be discussed in more detail. Negotiated sales of surplus property are considered in § 11.21 infra. $11.18. 

Sealed-Bid Sales

This is the normal method of disposing of large quantities of surplus property, where the acquisition cost and probable sales return justify the preparation and issuance of adequate commercial descriptions." The ordinary rules of contracting by formal advertising, as explained in Chapter 2 of this text, apply to such sales, except, of course, that the award is ordinarily made to the highest rather than the lowest responsible bidder whose bid conforms to the invitation for bids.

Paragraphs (3) and (5) deal with negotiated sales and are considered in § 11.21 infra. Section 203 (e) (7) provides that "section 3709, Revised Statutes, as amended (41 U.S.C. 5) shall not apply to disposals or contracts for disposals made under this subsection."

AUCTION SALES 

$11.20 $11.19. Spot-Bid Sales

The site or spot-bid sale is used to sell expeditiously small quantities of usable property having commercial demand, salvage items, and sometimes other types of surplus.72 Under this method, bidders are furnished with bid forms (one for each lot or unit to be separately sold), and the official in charge requests bids on items or lots, after announcing, identifying by number, and briefly describing them. Awards are made, or bids rejected, immediately following the offering of each item or lot. Sometimes mailed written bids under seal will be received.73 Among the special features which distinguish spot-bid sales from formal sealed-bid sales are: (a) shortened sales period; b) condensed descriptions; (c) emphasis on inspection; (d) simplified bid formats; e) deposits not required.74 $ 11.20. 

Auction Sales

The GSA regulations permit the sale of surplus personal property at public auction.75 Such auctions may be conducted either by qualified government personnel or by public auctioneers. The Navy practice is to employ a professional auctioneer, his compensation to be an agreed percentage of the gross return to the Government. Detailed procedures for selecting and contracting with qualified auctioneers are set forth in 

NPR&D Reg. No. 1.76 

The latter regulation requires that sales by auction be approved in advance by the Commandant of the Marine Corps or the Chief of the Bureau of Supplies and Accounts." They are used primarily to dispose of large quantities of surplus materials having wide commercial application.78 They have been used extensively in the case of surplus machine tools and other production equipment, although this has drawn some criticism." On the whole, however, the Navy's experience with auction sales has been very successful and the future will probably see increased use of this method.

Negotiated Sales

The Federal Property Act as originally enacted in 1949 permitted the disposal of surplus property to be "made without regard to any provision of existing law 83 for advertising until 12 o'clock noon, eastern standard time, December 31, 1950," "unless the Administrator shall determine that disposal by advertising will in a given case better protect the public interest." 84 By 1949 disposal of World War II surplus property had by no means been completed and Congress wished to continue the broad authorization for the negotiated disposal of wartime surplus that it had granted under the Surplus Property Act of 1944.85 It was thought that by December 1950 disposals of surplus property would revert to the traditional pattern of competitive bidding and award to the highest bidder." 

But the Korean War intervened and disrupted the World War II surplus disposal program. This in turn led to a number of extensions of the temporary negotiation authority conferred by the Federal Property Act, the last extension having been to July 31, 1958.87

§ 11.22. Reviewing Authority 

The GSA regulations require that before any proposed award is made, approval by a reviewing authority within the holding agency be obtained whenever the acquisition cost (actual or estimated) of the personal property involved amounted to: (a) $1,000 or more in the case of a negotiated sale; or (b) $10,000 or more in the case of a competitive bid sale.¹4

B. STANDARD FORMS AND CLAUSES $11.23. Standard Forms for Property Disposal Contracts 

In sealed bid sales of surplus personal property, executive agencies are required to use Standard Form 114 (Sale of Government Property, Invitation, Bid, and Acceptance) and Standard Form 114a (Continuation Sheet). In auction, spot-bid, and negotiated sales, the General Sales 

Terms and Conditions printed on the back of Form 114 are used, plus other parts of the form as deemed appropriate. Agencies may also include special terms and conditions deemed necessary, provided they are not inconsistent with Form 114.16

The text of these forms is set forth in the NPR&D Reg. No. 1.17 In general, these forms parallel those used for advertised procurement. 

There are however certain provisions peculiar to disposal contracts, some of the more important of which will be discussed below. $11.24. Disclaimer of Warranty

The General Sale Terms and Conditions in Standard Form 114 pro vide that all property is offered "as is" and "where is," and without recourse against the Government. The provision goes on to state that the description of the property is based on the best available information, but that the Government makes no guaranty, warranty, or representation, 12 H.R. REP. No. 1763, supra, § 11.21, n. 

96, at 8.

express or implied, as to quantity, kind, character, quality, weight, size, or description of any of the property, or its fitness for any use or purpose, and that no claim will be considered for allowance or adjustment or for rescission of the sale based upon failure of the property to correspond with the standard expected. Finally, the provision states that "this is not a sale by sample." 

As might be anticipated, such a sweeping disclaimer of any liability whatsover for failure of the goods to meet the description has given rise to a good deal of litigation between the Government and disappointed purchasers. On the whole, the courts have enforced the disclaimer clause as written and have held buyers to the strict rule of caveat emptor." 

After all, the Government is not in the merchandising business. In disposing of surplus, a good deal of which is used property, it is not performing its primary function. Buyers are expected to know this, and to realize that they are taking their chances: they may lose, but they may strike an unexpected bargain." Normally, the buyer is given an opportunity to inspect the goods, and the general rule is that he will be held to what such an inspection would have disclosed, whether or not he avails himself of such opportunity.20 $11.25. Exceptions to General Rule of Caveat Emptor

GROSS MISREPRESENTATION

$ 11.26. 

Gross Misrepresentation

Where the description of the property offered for sale varies so greatly from the property actually delivered that it can fairly be said that there is almost a total failure of consideration, or a mutual mistake as to subject matter, even though the misrepresentation by the Government was unintentional, the buyer will be allowed to rescind, or the Government will be held liable for breach, or an adjustment of the purchase price will be ordered. An interesting recent case illustrating this principle is In dustrial Salvage Corporation v. United States.21 The War Assets Ad ministration had offered for sale all the underground electric cable underlying a discontinued navy yard. Prospective bidders were furnished with drawings showing the location of all the cable, discontinued ends of which protruded above ground at numerous points. The plaintiff spent four days inspecting the yard. Wherever the drawings showed a projecting cable end, the inspection confirmed the fact that it was there. 

The yard was overgrown with weeds and gave no evidence of having been disturbed since its discontinuance. Estimating the quantity of removable cable at 375,000 pounds of copper, the plaintiff accepted an offer from the War Assets Administration to take it all (plus certain other items) for $50,000. When the plaintiff went to remove the cable, it discovered that each protruding cable end extended only a few feet underground. The balance had been skillfully removed, the ends left in place, the earth re‘ored, and weeds allowed to grow, so as to give the impression that the whole cable system had never been disturbed. Instead of the estimated 375,000 pounds of copper, the plaintiff recovered less than 120,000 pounds. Plaintiff filed a claim for $30,000. The Government defended on the ground that it had sold the property "as is" and "where is," with no warranties of any kind. The Court of Claims overruled this defense and allowed the plaintiff to recover $30,000, on the basis of the 

Government's misrepresentation.

In another case, the War Department invited bids on surplus property described as "Wheels, GP 1015, 16″ drop center." It was agreed that this was technical language meaning jeep wheels. The invitation for bids contained the usual broad disclaimer of warranty and urged bidders to inspect. The defendant submitted a bid without inspecting. Defendant's bid was accepted and he paid the purchase price. The Government then found that what it had really meant to sell was a quantity of obsolete discs and rims from old gun carriages. The contracting officer allowed the defendant to rescind and refunded him his money. Subsequently, the 

21 122 Ct. Cl. 611 (1952). 651

$ 11.27

Government attempted to enforce the purported contract by suing for the purchase price. The court held for the defendant and denied recovery.22

In still another case, the Government offered for sale, "as is" and "where is," a crawler shovel powered by a "general motor 6 cycle diesel engine." The claimant's bid, accompanied by a deposit, was accepted. 

It was then discovered that the engine to the crawler had been removed. 

The Comptroller General ruled that, even though the sale was "as is" and the bidder had been urged to inspect, it would be unconscionable, in view of the gross misdescription, for the Government to retain the deposit and force the property on the bidder.23 

On the other hand, it has been held that where a specific lot of material, described simply as "Head Harnesses," was sold "as is" without any representation of quantity, the presence in the lot of a substantial quantity of foreign matter not conforming to the description did not give the buyer, who had accepted delivery, the right to demand a price adjustment for shortage of quantity, although he would have had the right to reject the shipment and rescind the contract if he had acted promptly upon discovery of the admixture.24 $11.27. "Used" Versus "Unused"

Government surplus should never be described as "new," since by definition it has been in the supply system for at least some time subsequent to its initial procurement. At best it may be described as "unused." 

Cases have arisen in which property described as "new" or "unused" has turned out to be "used." The results have not been completely consistent. In one case, where the purchaser bid on a quantity of service hats which appeared from the sample to be unused and were so described by the auctioneer, he received a quantity of used hats along with the others and worth substantially less. The written contract of sale described the hats as "unused." A local "board of sales control," established by the Secretary of War to supervise sales of surplus after World War I, adjusted the price on the used hats from 44 cents to 12 cents each. Later the board attempted to rescind this action and the General 

Accounting Office held the purchaser to its bid price of 44 cents. A federal district court held that this was improper and allowed the pur-

The cases can be distinguished on the ground that in the former the court thought that the bidder had no genuine opportunity to inspect the goods, whereas in the latter he apparently could have inspected but failed to do so. Nevertheless in both cases bidders were urged to inspect, and in both cases there were disclaimers of warranty. The cases are difficult to reconcile. It is believed, in the light of the more recent cases, that if this situation were to arise today the courts would probably hold the Government to its obligation to deliver unused material, where it is so described."7 $ 11.28. 

Alterations by Government

If, after the invitation for bids and inspection (or opportunity to inspect), the Government intentionally or otherwise changes the material offered for sale in any substantial degree by adding different material, or removing material, the purchaser may rescind the contract (or treat it as never having been consummated) and obtain a refund of his bid deposit 28 or, in an appropriate case, may sue for breach and recover loss of profit on that portion of the goods covered by the contract but not actually made available to him.29 $ 11.29. Specific Warranty

It goes without saying that if the Government, acting through a duly authorized agent, does make a specific warranty, it will be held to it. 

Thus, where the War Assets Administration sold certain surplus electric generator sets on a written representation that they were new and in good condition, the purchaser was allowed to recover damages for breach when it turned out that the generators were all in poor condition and needed substantial repairs before they could be resold.38 The measure of damages was the difference between the market value of the generators as actually delivered and the market value they would have had if they had been as warranted. 

§ 11.31. Limitation of Government's Liability 

Absent any special provision limiting its liability, the measure of damages for breach of a sales contract by the Government is the difference in market value between the property as represented by the contract and as actually delivered.39 To avoid this result, the General Sales Terms and Conditions attached to Standard Form 114 include the following limitation of liability clause: 

In any case where liability of the Government to the purchaser has been established, the extreme measure of the Government's liability shall not, in any event, exceed refund of the purchase price or such portion thereof as the Government has received.40

§ 11.32. Failure To Make Payments or Remove Goods 

The General Sales Terms and Conditions attached to Standard Form 114 provide that if the buyer does not pay the full purchase price, or fails to remove the property from the place designated for delivery within 30 days from the date specified for such removal, the Government reserves the right, upon notice, to resell the property and charge the buyer with the loss, if any, plus any costs of storage, handling, and moving.43 The validity of this provision has been upheld by the

Provision for Liquidated Damages.

The ordinary measure of damages which may be collected by the Government against a defaulting buyer is the difference between the contract price and the market value of the goods, which is normally determined by resale on the open market.46 (The latter is specifically made the measure of damages by the contractual provisions noted in the preceding section.)

Sometimes, however, the Government inserts a provision for liquidated damages, and this is the usual practice of the Navy in effecting sales of surplus. A standard clause imposing liquidated damages, in the amount of 20 percent of the purchase price, is required by the Bureau of Supplies and Accounts Manual to be used in all contracts for sale by formal advertising. Such a clause is valid and enforcible, unless the amount of liquidated damages is so large as to amount to a penalty." 48

C. OTHER CONSIDERATIONS APPLICABLE TO DISPOSALS BY SALE 

$11.34. In General

Except to the extent that special rules of government contracts, as explained elsewhere in this text, may apply, and except to the extent that specific provisions of the contract, such as those outlined in sections 11.23 through 11.33 above, may be controlling, government sales contracts are subject to the general law of contracts and of sales.50 No attempt is made herein to outline those general rules, which may be found in any of the standard treatises on these subjects. But there are a few problems which might be deserving of special comment. $11.35. Impossibility of Performance; Supervening Illegality; Hardship 

If performance of a disposal contract should become impossible (within the meaning of that term in the law of contracts) or illegal, performance may be excused, or the terms of the contract modified. Thus, where the Government contracted to sell petroleum at prices which were in excess of a subsequently promulgated maximum price regulation issued by the Office of Price Administration, the Comptroller General ruled that the contract would have to be amended to the lower price until such time as the price ceiling might be removed; otherwise there would no longer be any binding legal obligation on the parties under the contract.51 

But mere hardship caused by subsequent legislation does not provide an excuse for non-performance. Thus, where a contractor agreed to buy certain surplus materials from the Government at fixed prices, a subsequent order from the Office of Price Stabilization reducing the ceiling prices on such materials gave the contractor no ground for relief, where the contract prices were still below (or not subject to) the ceilings, but imposition of the ceilings allegedly made resale unprofitable.52 

The Korean War gave rise to claims of impossibility of performance, particularly in running-term waste disposal contracts. Hog farmers who purchased food waste from military installations were hardpressed when the number of men subsisted at such activities increased to such an extent that the farmer could not carry off all the refuse. When this happens, and where no fault can be imputed to the contractor, it is suggested that the contractor is entitled to modification or rescission of his

Co., 205 U.S. 105, 120-21 (1907).

§ 11.36. Delivery and Shipment 

Although many government agencies sell surplus property "where is," and impose on the buyer the obligation and expense of removing the property,54 the Navy, for administrative reasons, prefers to sell F.O.B. carrier.55 This means that title and risk of loss pass upon delivery to the carrier, but the Government has the obligation of placing the goods "free on board" the cars, trucks, vessel, or other carrier designated, without expense to the buyer.56 In such a case the Government cannot, absent a contract provision to the contrary, assess a loading charge against the buyer.5 57 In one interesting case the Government's Foreign Liquidation Commission sold certain surplus war equipment located in Noumea, New Caledonia, to the plaintiff, a naval officer who was en route to the United States for separation. The contract was "F.O.B. shipside, Auckland, New Zealand." When the goods arrived at Auckland, the Government insisted that the plaintiff pay the freight from New Caledonia to New Zealand, which came to $918.70, and refused to deliver the property until the freight was paid. Because of this dispute, plaintiff was unable to use or sell the goods to advantage, and was finally forced to sell them at a sacrifice. The Court of Claims held that the Government's refusal to pay the freight was a breach of contract which made it liable to the plaintiff for damages of over $3,000,58 $11.37. Fraud

Importance of Disposals by Sale

The foregoing discussion gives some idea of the variety and complexity of the problems faced by the lawyer working in the area of property disposal. The importance and magnitude of the program can be gauged from the fact that during the four fiscal years from 1951 through 1954, federal agencies disposed of surplus property having an aggregate acquisition cost of $2,602,200,000, and in fiscal 1954 alone of $1,240,500,000.64 

Of these totals, 95 percent was disposed of by the military services.65 

While these figures apparently include donations, it is fair to assume that at least two billion dollars of the amount shown represent disposals by sale.66 $ 11.39.

$11.40. Statutory Provisions for Disposal of Foreign-Excess Property 

The Federal Property Act makes each executive agency responsible for the disposal of its own foreign-excess property, in conformity with the foreign policy of the United States.69 Disposal may be by sale, exchange, lease, or transfer, for cash, credit, or other property, upon such terms as the head of the agency deems proper, or for foreign currencies or credits, discharge of claims, or other benefits, whenever the head of the executive agency deems it in the interest of the United States. Negotiation is permitted, where the head of the agency finds it most practicable and most advantageous to the Government. Abandonment, destruction, or donation of property having no commercial value, or where the estimated cost of care and handling would exceed the estimated proceeds of sale, is authorized. Any sale must be on a condition prohibiting importation into the United States, except in certain circumstances.70 

Any proceeds in, or reduced to, United States currency are normally covered into the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts. Proceeds in foreign currencies or credits are administered in accordance with procedures established by the Secretary of the Treasury."

The act makes provision for delegation and redelegation of authority from the head of each executive agency, for employment of personnel, and for annual reports to Congress of all foreign disposals.72 

§ 11.41. Administrative Regulations: In General 

The NPR&D Reg. No. 1 provides that, in general, Navy foreign-excess personal property shall be disposed of in a manner similar to domestic surplus property. However, foreign-excess property is not reportable for screening to the General Services Administration, is not subject to screening by the Department of Health, Education, and Welfare for donation, and is not subject to the ordinary limitations on sale by negotiation.73 Foreign-excess property is, however, subject to screening by the

Redistribution and Screening 

Under the direction of the Chief of Naval Operations, each area commander is responsible for reviewing property under his control to determine what is excess to the needs of the area, and for reporting and redistributing activity-excess property to other Navy and Marine activities in the area, and to local Army and Air Force commands. Where feasible, property excess to the needs of the local military is to be offered to other federal agencies in the area, prior to sale or other disposal.75 

Control Lists of property desired for United States use have been established by each bureau and supply-demand control point and transmitted to area commanders. If property excess to the area appears on such a list, it is to be returned to the United States.76 

Certain other categories of area-excess property, not on the control lists, are required to be reported for screening, in some cases by a bureau or supply-demand control point, in others by the Armed Forces Supply Support Center.77 After such screening, if required, and after local screening with other federal agencies in the area, the property becomes available for disposal.

Sometimes military aircraft, as such, as well as commercial aircraft, may be sold, loaned or donated to friendly foreign governments under statutory authority such as the Mutual Security Act.10 Otherwise, a military type aircraft must be demilitarized before it can be donated, sold, or otherwise disposed of outside the United States Government."

SALES TO FOREIGN NAVAL VESSELS § 11.61 D. PETROLEUM, FUEL, AND SUPPLIES $11.59. Sale of Fuel and Supplies: For Aircraft 

Under the Air Commerce Act of 1926, as superseded by the Federal Aviation Act of 1958,17 fuel, oil, equipment, supplies, services, and other assistance may be sold or furnished at any airport or emergency landing field owned or operated by the United States to any aircraft, if by reason of emergency it cannot make its way to the nearest airport operated by private enterprise. The sales price must be the fair market value prevailing locally. So much of the receipts from the sale as represents the cost to the Government may be credited to the appropriation from which such cost was paid. The balance, if any, is covered into the miscellaneous receipts of the Treasury.

It is difficult to generalize as to what constitutes an emergency within the meaning of this act. The Attorney General, while warning that each case must be considered in the light of its particular facts, seems willing to interpret the act liberally.18 In effect, under his view, any circumstance which disables an airplane from flying would seem to provide sufficient justification of "emergency" to permit sales under this authority, provided the need has a reasonable relation to an actual and definite flight. $ 11.60. 

To Merchant Vessels 

Recent legislation permits the sale, at prices considered reasonable by the Secretary of the Navy, of fuel and other supplies to a merchant ship, where such fuel and supplies are not procurable locally, and provided that without such fuel and supplies the vessel could not proceed to the nearest port without endangering the safety of the ship, the health and comfort of its personnel, or the safe condition of the property carried on it.19 Sales of this kind must be on a cash basis, or such other basis as will reasonably assure prompt payment. Receipts may be credited to the current appropriation concerned. § 11.61. 

To Foreign Naval Vessels 

The Secretary of the Navy may furnish to foreign naval vessels, on a reimbursable basis, fuel, provisions and miscellaneous supplies, routine port services, and repairs and installations.20 Payment need not be made in advance. The funds received in payment for such supplies and services may be credited to current appropriations.

TYPES OF CONTRACTOR INVENTORY 

$11.73 end product and the disposal of any material left over is his own risk and responsibility. But in many cases, the Government owns or has an interest in the unfinished materials. For example, the Government generally acquires title to such materials under the progress payment clauses commonly used; it may furnish government-owned property to the contractor for use in the performance of the work; and under the standard termination clauses, the Government has an option to acquire title to uncompleted materials. In such cases, upon termination of the contract or change in the work by change order or otherwise, it becomes necessary to dispose of the unfinished materials expeditiously and economically in order to clear the contractor's plant and also to minimize the overall cost to the Government. The normal disposal procedures are not adequate for this purpose and, accordingly, special provisions of law and regulations have been enacted and promulgated for the handling of this type of property, known as "contractor inventory." $ 11.72. 

Definition

The Federal Property Act defines the term "contractor inventory" as follows: 

The term "contractor inventory" means (1) any property acquired by and in the possession of a contractor or subcontractor under a contract pursuant to the terms of which title is vested in the Government, and in excess of the amounts needed to complete full performance under the entire contract; and (2) any property which the Government is obligated or has the option to take over under any type of contract as a result either of any changes in the specifications or plans thereunder or of the termination of such contract (or subcontract thereunder), prior to completion of the work, for the convenience or at the option of the Government.55 

The same definition appears in the GSA regulations 56 and the ASPR,57 except that the words "(including Government-furnished property)" are added after the words "in the possession of a contractor or subcontractor." $ 11.73. 

Types 

The most common type of contractor inventory is termination inventory, which is defined in ASPR as "any items of physical property purchased, supplied, manufactured, furnished, or otherwise acquired for performance of the terminated contract which are properly allocable to the terminated portion of the contract." 58 Property, the disposition of which is governed by a separate contract or contract clause (e.g., facilities, special tooling), is excluded from this definition.

The next most common type is contractor inventory arising out of change orders. ASPR authorizes the use of the same procedures in the disposal of this (and any other) type of contractor inventory as are set forth for the disposal of termination inventory.59 Accordingly, the Navy has prescribed that the policies set forth in ASPR Section VIII, Part 5, with respect to termination inventory, shall be followed in respect of contractor inventory generally.60 Hence whatever may be said hereafter concerning disposal of termination inventory applies to other types of contractor inventory as well.

$11.75. Relation of the Disposal of Contractor Inventory to the Disposal of Excess and Surplus Property 

Considerable confusion and misunderstanding have grown out of the widespread belief that contractor inventory is just another species of government surplus property, and should, therefore, be subject to the same stringent rules on disposal. Actually it is not "surplus property" (in many cases it is not government property at all), but is a special category of property, both by statute and under the regulations, and is subject to entirely distinct, and considerably more liberal, rules as to disposal.

The Government may, under the applicable contract clause, elect to take over the contractor inventory, upon reimbursement to the contractor of the cost thereof, plus any applicable charges. If it does not so elect, the contractor may elect to "retain" the property at cost (unless it was government-furnished to begin with). This simply means that the con- 

59 ASPR 8-000 (d) (Sept. 5, 1958).

ASPR 8-000 (c) provides that the disposal of contractor inventory arising out of any change order under a cost-reimbursement type contract shall be in accordance with the ASPR provisions applicable to the disposal of termination inventory. 

60 NPR&D REG. No. 1 ¶ 409 (July 1, 1958). 

61 See also GSA REG. 1-III-304, 1–IV- 

304 (March 1, 1955). 

62 NPR&D REG. No. 1 1 409 (July 1, 1958). 672

IMPORTANCE OF PROBLEM 

$ 11.76 tractor elects to keep the property as his own and not put in any claim for it. Since in most cases, except for the Government's title under progress payment clauses, the property has belonged to the contractor all along, it is obviously his prerogative to do this (so long as the Government has not exercised its option to acquire the property), even where it has appreciated in value. By an extension of this reasoning, the contractor is given the same privilege with respect to property acquired by him under a cost-type contract or fixed-price contract with provision for progress payments even though title thereto has vested in the Government), with a re-vesting of title in the contractor and any sums previously reimbursed to the contractor on account thereof being repaid or credited back to the Government. But it has been felt that this could not possibly be stretched to include government-furnished property, title to which had been in the Government all along. Hence "retention at cost" is not available as to this latter type of property.63 

It is only if neither of these options is exercised that the problem of disposal enters in. Disposal is made the initial responsibility of the contractor.64 But the Government has an interest because it is obligated to reimburse the contractor for the original cost of the property, and the higher the net return on disposal, the less the overall cost to the Government. Hence the Government reserves the right to approve all disposals.65 

Ordinarily, disposal should be on competitive bids, but the contractor himself may submit a bid on the same conditions as others." By statute 67 and regulation 68 the proceeds of any such disposal may be credited against the amount due to the contractor under the contract, and need not be covered into the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts. $11.76. Importance of Problem

Disposal of contractor inventory is essentially a problem of contract administration, especially administration of terminations. It is related only collaterally to normal excess and surplus property disposals. It is important however. $11.77. Definition

B. GOVERNMENT-FURNISHED PROPERTY ASPR 13-101.2 (Nov. 3, 1958) sets forth the following definitions: 

Government property means all property owned by or leased to the Government, or acquired by the Government under the terms of a contract; except that property to which the Government has acquired a lien or title solely as a result of partial, advance or progress payments shall not for the purpose of this Section be classified as Government property. With this exception, Government property includes both Government-furnished property and contractor-acquired property as defined below: (i) Government-furnished property is property in the possession of or acquired directly by the Government and subsequently delivered or otherwise made available to the contractor; and (ii) Contractor-acquired property is property procured or otherwise provided by the contractor for the performance of a contract, pursuant to the terms of which title is vested in the Government. 

The term "provide," as used in the context of such phrases as "Government property provided to the contractor" and "Governmentprovided property," is intended to include both Governmentfurnished property and contractor-acquired property. 

$11.78. Contract Clauses 

Government-furnished property is normally found in the case of a fixed-price contract, contractor-acquired government property in the case of a cost-type contract. The standard contract clauses are found in 

ASPR 13-502, 13–503, 13–505, and 13-506. These clauses are discussed in sections 9.37 and 9.40 of this text. This material will not be repeated here, but some mention will be made of the problem of disposal. 

§ 11.79. Disposal of Government-Furnished and Contractor-Acquired Government Property 

The standard property clauses for supply contracts provide that, upon completion of the contract (or prior thereto if so specified by the contracting officer), the contractor will submit inventory schedules listing all government-owned property not consumed in performance of the contract (including resulting scrap) and still in the possession of the contractor. 

The contractor must deliver or make other disposal of such property as the contracting officer may direct. The net proceeds of any disposals may be credited against the contract price or otherwise paid as the contracting officer may direct.70 

70 ASPR 13–502 (h) (Aug. 1, 1957), 13-503 (i) (Sept. 18, 1958). The clauses prescribed for research and development contracts with non-profit institutions provide that such property shall be disposed of as elsewhere provided in the contract with respect to termination inventory. 

ASPR 13-505 (i) (Dec. 23, 1955), 13-506 (k) (Dec. 23, 1955). 674

$11.81

As noted above in § 11.73, such property may be disposed of like other contractor inventory (except that in the case of government-furnished property the contractor does not have the option of "retaining" such property at cost). Or it may be returned into normal government supply channels, in which case any subsequent disposal would be in accordance with normal procedures relating to excess or surplus property. A third alternative would be to leave it in the possession of the contractor for use on a subsequent contract, in which case it would become subject to the Government-Furnished Property clause of that contract. 

C. SPECIAL TOOLING 

$11.80. In General

Special tooling is specialized property designed for a specific end product and often usable only with the specific machines of a particular contractor (a technical definition is given in the next section). It may be furnished by the Government, in which case it is controlled by the standard Government-Furnished Property clause." Or it may be acquired by the contractor under a cost-reimbursement type contract, in which case it is controlled by the standard Government Property clause.72 Or it may be required as an end product to be delivered under the contract, in which case ordinary principles of supply contracting govern. Most commonly, however, it is acquired by the contractor in the course of performing a fixed-price supply contract, the entire cost thereof (or substantially so) entering into the contract price. For this reason the Government obtains certain rights in the use and disposition of such tooling. $11.81. Definition 

ASPR 13-101.5 (Nov. 3, 1958) gives the following definition:

Special tooling means all jigs, dies, fixtures, molds, patterns, special taps, special gauges, special test equipment, other special equipment and manufacturing aids, and replacements thereof, acquired or manufactured by the contractor for use in the performance of the contract, which are of such a specialized nature that, without substantial modification or alteration, their use is limited to the production of such supplies or parts thereof, or the performance of such services, as are peculiar to the needs of the Government. The term does not include: (i) items of tooling or equipment theretofore acquired by the contractor, or replacements thereof, whether or not altered or adapted for use in the performance of the contract, (ii) consumable small tools, or (iii) general or special machine tools, or similar capital items. 

71 ASPR 13-502 (May 14, 1958). 

72 ASPR 13-503 (Sept. 18, 1958). 675

$11.82

 § 11.82. Standard Clause 

In the case of a fixed-price contract where (i) the special tooling, if any, is usable solely for the production of supplies or parts, or the performance of services, peculiar to the needs of the Government, and (ii) the entire cost, or a substantial portion thereof, has been taken into account in arriving at the contract price, but (iii) the special tooling is not to be delivered as an end item, the standard contract clause set forth in ASPR 13-504 (Sept. 18, 1958) is to be used.73 This clause is discussed above in section 9.41 of this text. Suffice it to say here that it gives the 

Government an option to acquire such special tooling, when no longer needed for purposes of the contract, without further cost to it, except for shipping and handling. If the Government does not exercise this option, the problem of disposal arises. 

$11.83. Disposal of Contractor-Acquired Special Tooling 

If the Government does not wish to exercise its option to acquire the special tooling, the contractor may (i) offer to take it over, free and clear of any government interest, upon credit or reimbursement to the Government of its then fair value, (ii) offer to retain it for further work on additional contracts, or (iii) hold it for disposal instructions. If (iii), the Government may then direct that it be sold, or disposed of as scrap. 

Any proceeds may be credited against the contract price.74

Although differing in detail, this method of disposing of special tooling is similar to that outlined above with respect to contractor inventory, and rests on the same statutory basis. The principal difference is that the situation generally arises independently of termination or change order, upon completion of the contract. Also the Government does not have to reimburse the contractor further, having already done so in the contract price.

In this part we shall discuss briefly its applicability to other leases, especially of personal property.

$11.85. Principal Provisions of the Military Leasing Act of 1947 

The statute authorizes the Secretary of each military department, when he considers it advantageous to the United States, to lease to such lessee and upon such terms as he considers will promote the national defense or be in the public interest, real or personal property which is under the control of his department, which is not for the time required for public use, and which is not excess property within the meaning of the Federal Property Act. A lease entered into pursuant to this statute may be for a period not exceeding five years, unless the Secretary determines that a longer period will promote the national defense or will be in the public interest. The Secretary may also give the lessee the first right to buy the property if the lease is revoked to allow the United States to sell the property under any other provisions of law. Furthermore, each lease must contain a provision permitting the Secretary to revoke it at any time, unless he determines that the omission of such a provision will promote the national defense or will be in the public interest, in which case the lease must in any event permit revocation by the Secretary during a national emergency proclaimed by the President. 

In addition, the lease may authorize the lessee to maintain, protect, repair or restore the leased property, or of the entire unit or installation where a substantial part of it is leased, as a part or all of the consideration for the lease. Money rentals received by the United States for property leased under this act must be covered into the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts, although payments received for utilities and services furnished to the lessee under such a lease may be deposited in the Treasury to the credit of the appropriation or appropriations from which the cost of furnishing such utilities and services was paid. The statute does not apply to oil, mineral, or phosphate lands. The statute also includes certain tax provisions, which are discussed above in sections 10.49 and 

10.50 of this text. $11.86.

Administrative Procedures 

The procedures for leasing real property under the Military Leasing 

Act are set forth in NPR&D Reg. No. 2, Chapter 6 (June 1, 1953) and other Navy directives. They will not be discussed further herein. 

The procedures for leasing personal property are set forth in NPR&D 

Reg. No. 1, paragraph 305 (July 1, 1958). Ordinarily, any proposed lease must be submitted via the cognizant Bureau, the Chief of Naval Operations, and the Chief of Naval Material, to the Secretary for approval and the necessary authorization. Actual execution of the lease is by the Chief of the cognizant Bureau or his duly authorized representative. 677

$ 11.87

Each lease shall ordinarily be for a term not to exceed five years, and shall be revocable by the Secretary at any time. It shall ordinarily provide for the payment of a fair and reasonable rental for the use of the leased property. The lessee must maintain, protect and repair the property at his expense. Upon termination of the lease, the property shall be returned to the Government in as good condition as when received, reasonable wear and tear excepted. The requirement for a fair and reasonable rental may be waived when the property is to be used solely in government work, when the contractor is not placed in a favored competitive condition, and the Government receives an equivalent consideration by way of a corresponding reduction in the price or cost of the goods or services to be produced for or furnished to the Government with the use of the property leased. When scientific or technical equipment is leased, it may be decided that a fair and reasonable rental therefor may take the form of a scientific or technical report covering research performed with the aid of such equipment, and the granting of irrevocable, non-exclusive and royalty-free licenses under all inventions conceived or first actually reduced to practice in the course of the work in which such equipment is used. 

In addition to the specific requirements of the statute, the administrative officials of the Department must consider the advisability of insurance coverage during the period of the lease, and the desirability of a performance bond to protect the interests of the Government. 

§ 11.87. Leases of Machine Tools and Production Equipment 

Under NPR&D Reg. No. 1, the Secretary of the Navy has issued a blanket approval under prescribed terms and conditions for the leasing of machine tools and other items of production equipment, primarily to government contractors and subcontractors for use in the performance of government work.76

IX. SALE OF INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES § 11.88. Basic Statutory Authority 

The only general authority for the disposal of industrial facilities, whether plant or equipment, is the Federal Property Act. The disposal of industrial facilities under this authority has been considered in sections 10.51-10.56 supra. Beside the Federal Property Act, there are some other provisions of law which relate to the sale of industrial facilities. These will be discussed in the following sections. 

76 NPR&D REG. No. 1 ¶ 305-7 (July 1, 1958). 678

THE NATIONAL INDUSTRIAL RESERVE ACT OF 1948 $ 11.90 $11.89. Disposal Provisions of Military Leasing Act 

The Military Leasing Act of 1947 77 authorizes the inclusion in any lease made under that act of a provision giving the lessee the first right to buy the property if the lease is revoked to allow the United States to sell the property under any other provision of law." Two things should be noted about this: (a) It does not in itself constitute authority to dispose of the property leased; such authority must be found in some other law, such as the Federal Property Act; (b) It does not authorize the giving of an option, but only of what is sometimes called a "right of first refusal."

A right of first refusal is similar to an option, but is not quite the same thing. It merely means that the holder thereof has the right to meet the best offer of any third party, and be preferred over him, if the owner elects to sell. An option gives the holder a right to purchase, and if it is exercised in accordance with its terms, the owner must sell to the optionee. 

Since, as pointed out above, the actual authority to sell must be found in some other statute, and the necessary conditions for disposal must be met, any lease in which the lessee is given a right of first refusal should be most carefully considered. The exercise of such right must be conditioned upon the Government then having the requisite authority to effect a sale, and it is preferable that the lease so state. 

$11.90. The National Industrial Reserve Act of 1948 

This act is discussed above in Chapter 10, sections 10.44 and 10.45. 

Again, it is important to note that this statute by itself confers no disposal authority. It authorizes the inclusion in disposal contracts or leases of the so-called National Security Clause (see section 10.44), but it is contemplated that the disposal itself has taken place under the Surplus Property Act, or takes place under the Federal Property Act, or some other statute.

The National Security Clause, as formulated by the Secretary of De fense for insertion in instruments of sale of industrial property, is a statement of terms and conditions designed to preserve the potential productive capacity of the industrial facility for national defense purposes. More specifically, the basic purpose of the clause is to insure that the productive capacity of certain strategic plants will not be lost, despite the sale of such plants to private business interests. 

The National Security Clause requires the purchaser to maintain and preserve the capacity of the plant, not only for the current requirements of the purchaser but also for possible future government requirements, 77 Discussed in § 11.85 supra. 

78 10 U.S.C. § 2667 (b) (2) (1958). 

79 62 Stat. 1225 (1948), as amended, 50 

U.S.C. 88 451-462 (1952). 679

$ 11.

80 including capacity excess to present needs of the purchaser. The purchaser agrees not to make any alterations which would prevent reconversion of the plant to its original purpose within 120 days. He agrees not to sell or transfer the plant, and not to sell, transfer or remove any important production equipment in the plant, without the consent of the Governmen. Finally, the Government reserves the right to recapture the plant for a period up to five years (which period is renewable), upon paying reasonable rental to the purchaser, plus its expenses of clearing the plant and of converting it back to commercial production at the end of that period. These restrictions are for a period of twenty years in the case of buildings, ten years in the case of machinery and equipment. They usually result in a substantial reduction in the sales price of the plant, compared with the price which it would bring if sold free and clear. 

While it is possible to estimate what the amount of this price concession should be, and while this is usually done for the purpose of evaluating bids, in the final analysis it is determined by what a bidder is willing to pay for a plant with these restrictions attached. In determining the price at which an industrial property is sold subject to the National Security Clause, consideration is given to the additional costs to the purchaser occasioned by the requirements for maintenance, the disadvantages occasioned by the restrictions on improvements and the restraints on alienation, the possible future value of the plant to the purchaser, and the benefits the purchaser may receive by furnishing future government requirements. 

The National Security Clause is considered to be a series of covenants running with the land. It is of course a restraint on alienation, and thus presents a situation at variance with the general policy of the common law. The validity of such a restraint in this connection will be considered in Part X of this chapter. 

The National Security Clause has on occasion appeared in contracts of lease, and existing regulations under the National Industrial Reserve Act require that a form thereof be included in leases of property held and administered by the General Services Administration under the authority of that act.81 The wisdom of inserting such a clause in a lease is open to question. A simple provision in a lease to the effect that the 

Government may terminate it in the event of war or national emergency, plus the customary provision for maintenance, should be enough to insure a rapid return of the facility to Government use. The presence of more complicated provisions, containing what appear to be unreasonable limitations, and subjecting the Government to unnecessary costs, can and has given rise to expensive and avoidable litigation.82

B. RESTRICTIONS ON USE OR RESALE BY TRANSFEREE 

$11.97. In General

It is not unusual, in disposals of surplus property, to impose conditions and restrictions upon the use or further transfer of the property by the donee, purchaser, or other transferee. Some of these have been mentioned briefly in the preceding sections. Some are required or authorized by statute; others by administrative regulation. They take various forms. 

Not all have been tested in the courts, and the results of those that have have been varied. In the following sections we shall discuss some of the more common of the restrictions and some of the more important court decisions. $11.98. Restrictions: Donations for Education and Research

In donating surplus property to educational or other nonprofit institutions for educational or research purposes, it is customary to obtain an agreement from the donee that the property will be so used and will not be sold to others, except as scrap, for a certain period, without the consent of the disposal agency. The purpose of course is to prevent donees from taking advantage of the donation program and realizing windfalls at the expense of the public treasury. In the early days of the donation program under the Surplus Property Act there were many abuses. Some property was donated which had no conceivable educational or health use, such as machine tools and heavy roadbuilding and maintenance equipment. Some property was channeled through state institutions to dealers in war surplus. Some of these irregularities were corrected administratively, and there were some criminal proceedings for fraud.

But certain of the initial attempts to enforce by civil proceedings in the courts the restrictions against resale embodied in the instruments 4 ASPR 8-501.2(d) (Sept. 5, 1958).

Property Sold Subject to National Security Clause 

As explained above in sections 10.44 and 11.90, the National Security 

Clause consists of a series of covenants included in certain instruments for the sale or lease of industrial property. One of the most important of these is an agreement by the transferee that he will not sell or transfer the property, or any important part thereof, for a certain period of time without the consent of the Government. When included in an instrument of sale, this is a restraint on alienation. At common law it would be bad, regardless of (i) its reasonableness, (ii) its limited duration, or (iii) the fact that alienation could take place with the consent of the grantor.14

So far as known, the National Security Clause has only been tested once in court, and has been upheld. In 1950 the United States District 

Court for the Northern District of California granted an injunction against the unauthorized removal of machine tools located in a former government-owned shipyard, where both the yard and the machinery and equipment therein had been sold subject to the National Security Clause.15 This was in the face of an argument that the California Civil 

Code and cases thereunder made void all "conditions restraining alienation, when repugnant to the interest created." 16 

This result finds support in the following reasoning. The Constitution gives Congress exclusive authority over the disposal of property belonging to the United States," and provides that the Constitution and the laws of the United States made in pursuance thereof shall be the supreme law of the land, anything in the Constitution or laws of any state to the contrary notwithstanding.18 A federal statute, the National Industrial Reserve 

Act of 1948," authorizes the inclusion of a National Security Clause in the sale of certain types of government-owned industrial property. The 

Supreme Court has held that in the acquiring, holding or disposing of government property, federal policies prescribed or authorized by Con-

Disposals of Foreign-Excess Property 

As pointed out above in section 11.40, the Federal Property Act requires that sales of foreign-excess property be on a condition prohibiting importation into the United States, unless the Secretary of Agriculture or the Secretary of Commerce, as the case may be, has determined that the importation of such property would relieve domestic shortages or otherwise be beneficial to the United States.22 Certain general exemptions to such import restrictions which have been granted by these officials are listed in the NPR&D Reg. No. 1, which also sets forth the procedure for obtaining specific exemptions.23

In addition, the Navy requires a special warranty that foreign-excess property will be used only in the country in which sold or will be exported only for use and to a destination acceptable to the United States.24 The purpose of course is primarily to prevent resales to persons in or representing Soviet-dominated countries, or other resales which might be prejudicial to American foreign policy.25 $11.102. The legal effect of such a scrap warranty has been recently considered by the Court of Claims.28 In 1943 the United States sold the historic old battleship Oregon to the plaintiff Ricker. The contract contained a warranty (in somewhat different form from that described above) under which Ricker undertook to scrap the vessel within six months. After scrapping operations had commenced, and without notifying the United States, Ricker decided to convert the hull into an unpropelled barge. In 

1944, the War Shipping Administration requisitioned the hull from plaintiff pursuant to section 902 of the Merchant Marine Act of 1936.29 The suit involved a dispute concerning the proper method of computing just compensation to the plaintiff for the taking of his property. The plaintiff's position was that he should be paid for the property in accordance with its value at the time of the requisition, i.e., as a barge. The Government, on the other hand, maintained that compensation should be determined by the scrap value of the property, because plaintiff was contractually obligated to scrap the vessel. The court agreed with the Government's position. The effect of this decision would seem to be that a scrap warranty is valid and will be enforced by the courts.30

 ABANDONMENT AND DESTRUCTION A. ABANDONMENT BY THE GOVERNMENT § 11.117. Property Subject to the Federal Property Act 

The Federal Property Act provides that the Administrator of General Services may authorize the abandonment, destruction, or donation to public bodies of property which has no commercial value or of which the estimated cost of continued care and handling would exceed the estimated proceeds from its sale.54 The implementing Navy regulation is set forth. 

in NPR&D Reg. No. 1 and 2.55 

$11.118. Procedure

Property may be determined to be valueless by a formal offering for sale, or it may without such an offering be reasonably believed to be valueless or uneconomical to sell even as scrap. Bureau Chiefs and Commanding Officers are authorized to appoint a representative to make the necessary findings as to value, and a reviewing authority of one or more persons to approve such findings in cases where review is required. No abandonment or destruction is to be made in a manner which is detrimental to public health or safety or which will infringe the rights of others.56 

$11.119. Abandonment of Destruction: Without Notice 

Property may be abandoned or destroyed without notice upon a written finding, approved by the reviewing authority, that immediate abandonment or destruction is necessary or desirable because of the nature of the property, or the expense or difficulty of its care and handling. Examples would be (i) military necessity, (ii) considerations of health, safety, or security, or (iii) value so little or cost of care and handling so great that retention for advertising for donation or sale would not be justified.

Property at one location having an acquisition cost of less than $100 may be presumed to fall under (iii) above.57 $ 11.120.

Authority under the Federal Property Act to abandon, destroy or donate property does not apply to U.S. Navy battleships, cruisers, aircraft carriers, destroyers, or submarines, since they are excluded from the definition of "property" under that act. The provisions in the NPR&D 

Reg. No. 1 on abandonment and destruction are not so limited, yet it is difficult to apply them to vessels which have been wrecked and are sunk below the surface of the sea. Wherever feasible the Navy undertakes salvage operations of such vessels, either itself or by contract with a private salvor. But some known wrecks have been under the ocean for many years without having been successfully salvaged. Sometimes a commercial salvor will request permission to salvage such a vessel in return for a certain percentage of the salvage value. The Navy then has to determine (i) whether it wishes to permit such operations under the terms proposed, or (ii) whether it can properly take the position that the Government has no further interest in the vessel. Since there is no statute on the subject 62 and since the controlling precedents are very few, this is an extremely difficult problem. On the one hand, the 

Navy has no right to give up government property which may have a value. On the other hand, continued "ownership" of such vessels, some of which were sunk fifty or more years ago, is an administrative burden

B. ABANDONMENT TO THE GOVERNMENT 

$11.122. In General

On occasion, the Government comes into possession of property which it did not originally purchase or own. Property is frequently left on naval premises, or is seized by security or health authorities. When property has thus been abandoned, forfeited or seized on naval premises, disposal action must be taken, and the nature of the property may dictate the method of disposing of it. 

§ 11.123. Statutory Provisions 

The Federal Property Act authorizes the Administrator of General Services to take possession of abandoned property on premises owned or leased by the Government, to determine when title thereto vested in the United States, and to utilize, transfer, or otherwise dispose of such property.64 Former owners are given three years within which to file claims for the proceeds or the fair value of such property, depending upon whether it has been sold, transferred, or used, less the cost of care and handling.

The Act of April 14, 1949, authorizes the Secretaries of the military departments, and the Secretary of the Treasury, to dispose of, by public or private sale or otherwise, all lost, abandoned, or unclaimed property in the possession of their departments, not less than one year after receipt thereof at designated storage points.65 Diligent effort is to be made to locate the true owner, his heirs, or legal representatives, and at least 120 days' notice of any proposed disposition must be sent to the last known address of such owner, heirs, or representatives, if determined. Net proceeds are to be covered into the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts. 

The true owner, his heirs, or representatives, have five years from the date of disposition within which to file claims for such proceeds with the General Accounting Office, after which all claims are barred.

Checks and Balances 

It seems appropriate that this final chapter should be devoted to an explanation of the practical operation of Navy procurement. The earlier chapters, with the possible exception of Chapter 1 which was principally historical in approach, have dealt at some length with the legal aspects of various phases of Navy procurement and property disposition. At the expense of concluding this book with a purely factual and non-legal chapter, a description of the procurement organization of the Naval Establishment would seem to be as necessary as an understanding of the legal restrictions woven about Navy purchasing. A knowledge of “how it is done" is no less important than "how to do it." 

A salient characteristic of the Navy's procurement organization is its consciously developed system of checks and balances. No one individual, below the level of the Secretary himself, carries the entire responsibility for the many steps required by the procurement cycle. Thus, the contracting officer who makes the contract is not the one who certifies it for payment; that responsibility resides in the technical inspector who has to *This chapter of the 1949 edition was prepared by Hudson B. Cox, formerly 

General Counsel for the Department of the Navy, in collaboration with other members of the Office of the General Counsel, and was revised for this edition by John Green, Member of the Armed Services Board of Contract Appeals. 

697

$ 12.

certify that the items called for have been delivered and accepted. After certification as to quality and quantity has been made, still another individual, the disbursing officer, makes the payment. This division of responsibility plays a far more important role than solely that of insuring against an improper use of authority: it insures that technically qualified and trained personnel carry the responsibility for that phase of the procurement cycle for which they are best fitted. Actually, the Navy's system of checks and balances is carried far beyond contracting, inspection and disbursing. For example, in all negotiated purchases of any significant size, a series of individuals and offices contribute toward safeguarding the Government's interest. The negotiating officer, usually aided by a price analyst and a lawyer, will work out with each of several qualified suppliers the best transaction, contract and price-wise, that he can obtain. That deal which appears to be most advantageous to the Government will be approved by him and submitted to the Office of Navy Material for its approval of the basic terms proposed. This "business clearance" at a departmental level provides a review backed by the experience of past purchases of the same or similar items and a knowledge of at what prices and from which suppliers other procuring activities of the Navy Department may have been buying similar commodities. If approved by the 

Office of Naval Material, Counsel for the Bureau or other Navy procuring activity making the procurement will prepare or approve the contract, aided materially in that respect by having participated in the negotiations for the purchase. The contract is then reviewed and signed by an authorized contracting officer for the Bureau or other Navy procuring activity concerned.

The administration of the contract at that point passes to production experts who follow and inspect the work as it progresses: the Inspectors of 

Naval Material, Inspectors of Ordnance, Supervisors of Shipbuilding, Inspectors of Machinery, or Bureau of Aeronautics Representatives, as the case may be. If the determination of costs of production is germane to the 

Government's interest, as when the contract calls for reimbursement of the contractor's costs, still another group, the Contract Audit Division of the Office of the Comptroller of the Navy, assumes responsibility for the audit and approval of costs of performance. Finally, if the items properly meet the specifications of the contract and are accepted on delivery, upon certification of the technical inspector, and of the cost inspector where necessary, another individual, the disbursing officer, will make payment under the contract. In this manner the Government's interests are carefully safeguarded at every stage of the procurement cycle. 

Because of the existence of this system of checks and balances with the opportunity it affords for review, the Navy policy is to vest wide discretion and scope for the exercise of judgment in its contracting and negotiating officers, subject to the generally broad guidelines set forth at the depart- 698

THE NAVY PROCUREMENT ORGANIZATION- -CONTRACTING $ 12.2 

mental level, primarily (i) in the Armed Services Procurement Regulation (ASPR), which is developed through the joint efforts of the three Military Departments and the Office of the Secretary of Defense, and (ii) in the Navy Procurement Directives (NPD), which affords Navy implementation of the Armed Services Procurement Regulation and which also deals with subject matter not covered therein. 

The actual procurement organization of the Navy Department can best be considered in terms of its three main components: contracting, fiscal, and legal. 

$12.2. The Navy Procurement Organization-Contracting 

Improvements in the procurement organization of the Navy Department developed rapidly as World War II legislation opened the way for simplified methods of placing contracts. Today, the organization is flexible and could expand quickly to meet any emergency. As always, ultimate procurement authority and responsibility are in the Secretary and radiate from him down to the Assistant Secretary (Material), the Office of Naval Material, the various Bureaus and other Navy procuring activities, the field offices, and to the contracting officers who actually sign the contracts. However, responsibility has been spread along functional lines to prevent bottlenecks and facilitate expansion. 

Except for "single department" and "plant cognizance" procurements and for procurements made under "single manager assignments,” discussed in § 12.9 infra, purchasing for the Navy is performed by the individual procuring activities and the field purchasing activities. On them falls the responsibility of filling the procurement needs of the Naval Establishment. Technical and large scale purchases are generally handled by the procuring activities and the principal field purchasing activities. Other shore activities, having a regularly organized supply department, procure some items for the use of the particular local activity of which they are part. 

The return to post-World War II procurement did not alter significantly the Navy's wartime procurement organization. In broad outline, present organizational lines of responsibility were formalized in December 1942 when the Secretary vested the principal Navy Bureaus with contracting authority to procure the material for which they had procurement responsibility, and in August 1945 when the Secretary abolished the Office of Procurement and Material, transferred its functions to the Assistant Secretary, and established the Material Division in the Office of the Assistant Secretary. On March 5, 1948, the Material Division became the Office of Naval Material,' but by administrative delegation 

1 Act of March 5, 1948, 62 Stat. 68, now codified as 10 U.S.C. § 5111 (1958). 

699

$ 12. 

the Assistant Secretary of the Navy (Material) continues to be the Secretary's alter ego with respect to procurement matters. $ 12.3.

The Office of Naval Material As the head of the Office of Naval Material, the Chief of Naval Material has the statutory responsibility, under the Secretary of the Navy, to "effectuate policies of procurement, contracting, and production of material throughout the Department, and plans therefor "2 In practice, however, the Chief of Naval Material is under the direction of the Assistant Secretary (Material) and has much broader functions than those outlined in the statute. His office has the responsibility for making and implementing policies, coordinating procurement activities, and standardizing procedures in all matters connected with the procurement, production, inspection, and control of Navy material, and in the utilization of production facilities. It also renders assistance to procuring activities and performs operational functions common to two or more procuring activities or offices in the Navy which can be more effectively performed under a single administration, such as the clearance of contracts and inspection of material. 

Of the several divisions which comprise this Office (the Administrative Division, the Production Division, the Field Services Division, the Material Control Division, and the Procurement Division) the last is most closely connected with the operational functions of the procuring activities and the field offices. Potentially, the Production Division could also assume a somewhat close relationship with the operational procurement activities in the event materials become subject to government allocation. 

While the Field Services Division has a close affinity to procurement in the areas of inspection and contract administration, it is not concerned with the placing of contracts, except for performing pre-award surveys when requested by contracting officers.

As Director of the Procurement Division, the Assistant Chief of Naval 

Material (Procurement), by virtue of a delegation of authority from the Chief of Naval Material, has jurisdiction over policies and procedures relating to the procurement of supplies, facilities and services, and is charged with the responsibility of assuring compliance by the Navy procuring activities in this connection. Integration of the Armed Services has imposed upon him an additional responsibility of coordinating the procurement activities in the Navy with the overall policies and pro cedures of the Department of Defense.

Navy Procuring Activities 

Evolution to the present operational organization began with Secretary Forrestal's directive of December 13, 1942, which decentralized operational procurement functions, transferring them in large part from the Bureau of Supplies and Accounts to the other contracting Bureaus and Navy procuring activities. (See § 1.7 supra.) In order to achieve administrative flexibility, the directive refrained at that time from imposing any rigid delineation of responsibility and simply authorized the Chief of each Bureau to determine the extent to which contracts for material and services under his cognizance would be negotiated, prepared and executed either by his Bureau or by the Bureau of Supplies and Accounts. At the present time, the United States Navy Regulations, 1948 (as amended), delineate 701

Navy Field Purchasing Activities 

As noted above the procurement responsibilities of the Bureau of Supplies and Accounts are discharged entirely through the field purchasing activities of the Navy which are under the technical or management control of that Bureau. In exercising administrative control over field purchasing activities, the Bureau issues procedural instructions, assigns certain requisitions for purchase action, reviews certain proposed contracts and documents designated for field action so as to insure conformance with procurement policies, and acts as liaison between field purchasing activities and the other Bureaus and Offices of the Navy Department. 

In all, the Bureau of Supplies and Accounts has over fifty major field purchasing activities with authority to make purchases in unlimited dollar amounts within the general fields of their assigned procurement responsibility. The remaining field purchasing activities are authorized to make purchases at least up to $100, and generally up to $2,500 in the case of Navy field activities having a regularly organized supply department.

Certain of the major field purchasing activities accomplish centralized area buying, ordinarily embracing requirements originating within a naval district or river command, and include the Navy Purchasing Offices at New York, Washington (D.C.), Los Angeles, London, and Pearl

Harbor. Other of the major field purchasing activities accomplish cen- 704

$ 12.6. The Navy Procurement Organization-Fiscal: The Office of the 

Comptroller of the Navy

The fiscal aspects of the Navy's procurement organization are under the overall jurisdiction of the Office of the Comptroller of the Navy. As discussed more fully in Chapter 4 supra, the Office of the Comptroller has the responsibility within the Navy of making, supervising and coordinating the policies and procedures affecting the budgeting, reporting, finance, accounting, and auditing activities of the Navy Department. The Office prescribes the type and content of all accounting and financial records maintained by the Bureaus and Offices of the Navy Department, prepares statistical fiscal status reports, rules on appropriation availability, arranges financing of departmental programs, administers advance and progress payments and guaranteed loans in connection with Navy procurement contracts, and, through its Contract Audit Division, determines the allowability of reimbursable costs under cost-type contracts and conducts advisory audits in connection with the final pricing of certain kinds of contracts and with the settlement of certain termination claims. The 

Comptroller maintains fiscal liaison with the other military departments, the Department of Defense and with other government agencies, and is responsible for translating the program of the Chief of Naval Operations into the formal budget for submission to the Secretary of Defense, the Bureau of the Budget, and Congress. The Office of the Comptroller has three main divisions: Budget and Reports, Accounting and Finance, and Audit. 705

$ 12.7

1. The Budget and Reports Division, in addition to its budget function, prepares recurring reports on the status of Navy appropriations and funds, and points out trends which call for remedial action. 

Current and historical fiscal statistics are maintained by this division, and statistical service is provided to the various Bureaus and Offices within the Navy. 

2. The Accounting and Finance Division is responsible in general for coordinating fiscal policies and practices among the Bureaus and Offices with respect to fiscal operations, and also coordinates fiscal matters with other government agencies. This division develops Navy fiscal standards for the management of various funds, and for contract termination and property disposition; is responsible for the administration of advance payments and guaranteed loans to contractors, and is charged with supervision of progress payments. In addition, the Accounting and Finance Division issues the instructions governing Navy disbursing officers attached to the various Navy
