The Audit Division has the function of designing, improving and standardizing the systems and procedures that affect Navy internal accounting and auditing activity and the Navy's audit function with respect to Navy contractors, the latter function being administered by the Contract Audit Division. The Contract Audit Division, formerly the Cost Inspection Service of the Bureau of Supplies and Accounts and later transferred to the Office of the Comptroller of the Navy, conducts audits of the books and records of Navy contractors to determine the accounting accuracy of amounts claimed by the contractors where costs are the basis of payment. The Contract Audit Division, at the request of a contracting Bureau or other procuring activity, also carries out unit cost studies and cost analyses in connection with price redeterminations, and special studies in connection with fixed-price negotiated contracts. It conducts accounting reviews of termination claims, audits of rentals paid under facilities contracts, audits under royalty agreements, audits and reviews in connection with controlled bank accounts and advances to contractors, and performs accounting reviews of special claims, special investigations for the Office of the Naval Inspector General, and other miscellaneous work. $ 12.7.

$12.8. The Navy Procurement Organization-Legal: The Office of the General Counsel 

In the first chapter, brief mention was made of the origin in 1941 of the Office of the General Counsel ("OGC") as a part of the procurement organization of the Naval Establishment during World War II. Gen erally, this Office is charged with the responsibility for all legal matters (with certain exceptions) pertaining to the field of business and commercial law within the Navy, as distinguished from matters pertaining to military law and discipline and those connected with the administrative and internal affairs of the Department. Excepted from OGC responsibility are tort and admiralty claims arising independently of contract, and matters relating to the Naval Petroleum Reserves. 

Doing business with American industry on an annual billion dollar scale gives rise to an urgent need for lawyers with a sound commercial and business law background to counsel and assist the procuring Bureaus and activities in the infinite variety of day-to-day problems to be met with. It was realized that to be of greatest service the lawyers should be physically located in the Bureaus and Offices that were actually engaged in procurement, property disposition, contract termination and the other aspects of Navy contract activity. This was in keeping with the Navy's policy, established during World War II, of decentralized procurement, with the various technical Bureaus and procuring activities being responsible for the purchase of the material under their particular cognizance. 

The lawyer called upon to draft a contract embodying the terms under which atomic-powered ships are to be built and paid for by the Navy could not be expected to do an adequate job unless he has actually partici-

Navy in the Field of Business Law, 4

PRAC. LAW. No. 6 at 38-52. (Oct. 1958). 

707

$ 12.8

pated in the negotiations and knows at first hand the various agreements that have been reached and the problems that have been discussed. 

From its inception the Office of the General Counsel has operated on a decentralized basis, with Offices of Counsel established, at the present time, in each of the Navy procuring activities, for the Office of the Comptroller of the Navy, for Headquarters Marine Corps, and for the several single manager agencies under Navy management control, namely, the 

Military Petroleum Supply Agency, the Military Medical Supply Agency, and the Military Sea Transportation Service. In addition, the Office of the General Counsel presently has several field offices, including a New York and a European (London) Branch Office, as well as field counsel located in various parts of the United States, including Philadelphia, Dayton (Ohio), Los Angeles, Oakland, and Seattle, and overseas in Spain, Hawaii, Guam, the Philippines, and Japan.

Again, as is true of the procurement function itself, decentralization of operation requires centralized coordination and policy control. This is effected through the General Counsel, two Deputies General Counsel, and a small group of attorneys in the Executive Office of the Secretary. The principal function of this group is to secure uniformity of approach among the several Bureaus and procuring activities to the many legal problems that are of common interest, and to recommend to the Secretary and to the Chief of Naval Material policy decisions which appear to be necessary or desirable in the procurement and property disposal fields. 

To the fullest extent practicable in a military organization, the concept of the attorney-client relationship is maintained between the Office of the General Counsel and the procurement and other officials of the Navy whom OGC serves. Just as a law firm is a service organization to its corporate clients, so the Office of Counsel for a technical Bureau or procuring activity is not a policing agency, dictating what may and what may not be done, but rather an office whose function it is, in the procurement field, to counsel and guide its client as to the appropriate and best means of accomplishing its desired and legitimate ends. 

The maintenance of an attorney-client relationship of this nature is made possible in no small measure by the fact that the Office of the General Counsel is free from the staff concept which is properly and necessarily inherent in a military organization. Comprised as it is of civilian lawyers, problems of rank and military channels present no obstacles to the independence of expression and individual responsibility which the profession demands of a lawyer. This freedom from lines of military responsibility renders possible the decentralization of the Office and the furnishing of legal counsel and advice at the operating levels of the Navy's procurement 4 A list of the principal field offices of the Office of the General Counsel is set forth in the Appendix to this chapter. 708

Coordination of Procurement Among the Services 

Emphasis throughout the previous chapters of NAVY CONTRACT LAW 

has understandably been on the procurement practices and problems of the Navy with little or no mention of any relationship with the procurement of the Army, the Air Force or other agencies of the Government. It might be thought that in its purchase activities and in the expenditure of many billion dollars a year for procurement the Navy acted as an independent autonomy, without regard to the other Services or to other government agencies. Nothing could be further from the truth. Actually, there is probably a greater degree of coordination and inter-Service relationship in the field of procurement than in any other activity of the Armed Services, and this has long antedated the National Security Act of 1947.

World War II scarcities and the existence of a strong seller's market during the war compelled a close collaboration between the War and Navy Departments and a reconciliation between the demands of each. 

In part, this was effected through the medium of such World War II expedients as allocations of materials, preference ratings, the Controlled Materials Plan, and priorities (dictated in large part by agencies, such as the War Production Board, which were independent of the Military Services). This process was further accelerated during the Korean emergency by the similar government controls put into effect at that time. 

For the most part, just as World War II was a centripetal force welding the various Bureaus and procuring activities of the Navy Department into a homogeneous unit, so did World War II and the Korean emergency necessitate an increasingly close coordination and integration of procurement activities and requirements among the Armed Services themselves. 

The Army-Navy Munitions Board, which had been established as early as 1922, originally was the instrumentality through which this coordination was largely effected. Prior to the National Security Act of 1947, in addition to resolving conflicting demands between the Services for scarce materials, the Army-Navy Munitions Board developed various means of eliminating duplication and overlapping procurement functions between the two Services and of putting an end to extravagant competi- 709

$ 12.10

tion between them in the wartime seller's market. Thus, a central procuring agency for lumber was created to purchase the lumber requirements of the Army, Navy and the Maritime Commission. Procurement of food products (so-called “subsistence items") for the personnel of both Services was assigned to the Army. Requirements for aircraft and major components were assigned between the Services on a plant allocation basis; thus, for example, the Navy purchased the entire output of 

Pratt and Whitney both for itself and for the Army Air Force. There were a large number of other items so assigned for "single department" or cross-service procurement. 

$ 12.10. Regulations Governing Procurement 

The enactment of the Armed Services Procurement Act in 1948 has provided new impetus to post-war coordination of procurement among the Services. By section 10 of that act, the Services were authorized to agree upon the performance of procurement functions and responsibilities by one Service for the others, and were also authorized to create joint or combined offices to exercise procurement functions and responsibilities. That this authority has been widely used is evidenced by the fact that at present a very substantial portion of the dollar volume of procurement of the three military departments is subject to either (i) single department procurement, where one Service is responsible for the purchase of the requirements of all three, either on the basis of product assignment or plant cognizance, or (ii) single manager assignments, where a single manager agency buys, and performs certain supply management functions with respect to, certain common-use supplies and services for all three Departments.

Coordination between the Services in procurement matters, however, is by no means confined to the assignment of purchase responsibilities. 

While during World War II there was little consciously developed uniformity of approach between the Army and Navy in their respective procurement practices and procedures except in the fields of renegotiation and contract termination, since 1946 large strides have been made toward unifying the procurement policies and practices of the three Services. Having for the first time in history a common and uniform statutory basis for procurement under the Armed Services Procurement Act, there has developed among the procurement personnel of the three Services a sense of collaboration, interchange of ideas and common approach. Notable in this respect has been the development of the Armed 

Services Procurement Regulation, discussed below.

Shortly before the effective date of the Armed Services Procurement Act on May 13, 1948, the Departments of the Army, Navy and Air Force jointly issued the first three sections ("General Provisions," "Procurement by Formal Advertising," and "Procurement by Negotiation") of the "Armed Services Procurement Regulation" (ASPR), for the purpose of providing new procurement policies and practices under and in implementation of that statute. The regulation implemented in particular the new requirements of that act with respect to procurement by negotiation. To the extent that existing departmental procurement direcives were inconsistent with ASPR, the latter was to control. 

The regulation was originally effective May 19, 1948, and was formally adopted as part of the directives system of the Secretary of Defense on

Generally, all of the ASPR sections were originally prepared by working subcommittees comprised of department specialists in their particular fields; and thereafter these sections were submitted for consideration and comment to the respective Departments and to representatives of various industrial groups, prior to final review by a special editing subcommittee and intermediate approval by a specially designated ASPR Committee, composed of representatives of the military departments and presently including those of the Department of Defense. Originally, final approval was obtained from the Procurement Secretaries of the respective Departments (now called Materiel Secretaries) and the final drafts were cleared with the Munitions Board and its Procurement Policy Council. At the present time, approval of the ASPR Committee is sufficient without the necessity of further referral, except with respect to major policy matters or where there is disagreement within the ASPR Committee. In such instances, the matter is referred to the Assistant 

Secretary of Defense (Supply and Logistics) for resolution in coordination with the Materiel Secretaries of the Departments.

$ 12.11. How a Negotiated Procurement Works THE NEED 

As a finale to NAVY CONTRACT LAW, it may be interesting to pursue, step by step, a hypothetical purchase by the Navy Department. We will assume that the Bureau of Aeronautics wants to buy some highly specialized radar sets for a definite and vital purpose. We will call this radar equipment the XYZ-20 and will assume that it is to be furnished to the airframe manufacturer by the Government for installation in planes being manufactured.

Strategic concepts have their origin in the Joint Chiefs of Staff, and from time to time the Navy is assigned certain tasks to execute. One task so assigned is the responsibility for anti-submarine warfare measures. 

Upon receiving such assignment, the Chief of Naval Operations determines what aircraft and what aircraft equipment are needed to carry out the mission. This original determination is in terms of required perform- 712

$ 12.ance only; for instance, it may call for an airborne radar that will detect submarines up to a certain range. Having determined performance characteristics, the Office of the Chief of Naval Operations directs the Chief of the Bureau of Aeronautics to develop and test such a piece of equipment. This the Bureau of Aeronautics will do through the medium of a research and development contract with the ABC Corporation; and the piece of equipment so developed is designated the XYZ-20. The equipment is deemed satisfactory by the Chief of Naval Operations, and his office then issues a directive that anti-submarine warfare airplanes shall be equipped with the XYZ-20. Sometime thereafter, CNO and the 

Chief of the Bureau of Aeronautics decide to purchase a quantity of antisubmarine warfare aircraft, equipped with the XYZ-20 radar. The Chief of the Bureau of Aeronautics thereupon directs the appropriate offices and divisions of the Bureau to purchase a specified quantity of such type of airplane from an aircraft manufacturing company. The Production 

Division of the Bureau of Aeronautics, which has responsibility for the procurement of items of government-furnished equipment for installation in new aircraft, then goes into action.

THE PROCUREMENT REQUEST The Production Division prepares a Procurement Request which con tains quantitative radar requirements, specifications, delivery dates, place of delivery, and other pertinent information. This Procurement Request is then approved by the Program Officer and forwarded to the Contracts 

Division. The Contracts Planning Branch convenes a Procurement Re view Board (PRB) meeting. The PRB is composed of procurement, technical, small business, legal, and other specialists; and this Board coordinates the procurement to insure that departmental policies and procedures are followed, that all potential suppliers are given an opportunity to participate in the procurement, that all company proposals are given adequate consideration, and that a recommendation of award is made which is in the best interests of the Navy. 

In our hypothetical case, the Procurement Review Board decides that only the ABC Corporation, which had developed the XYZ-20 under the research and development contract, should be solicited for a proposal. 

This decision to procure by negotiation, rather than through formal advertising, and then to confine such negotiation to one company can be justified under 10 U.S.C. § 2304 (a) (14)-Technical Equipment Requiring Substantial Initial Investment or Extended Period of Preparation for 

Manufacture. The minutes of the Board are carefully documented on

the Procurement Request form and the facts pertaining to the justification for negotiation are set forth. 

NEGOTIATION CLEARANCE 

Before requesting the contractor to submit a proposal, the Contracts Division prepares a Negotiation Clearance Memorandum of the pertinent facts of the procurement and the justification for the use of non-competitive negotiation. This Negotiation Clearance Memorandum, together with the accompanying Determination and Findings, is reviewed by Counsel as to form and legality and, if proper, is forwarded to the Assistant Secretary of the Navy (Material) for approval and signature under exception (14) used as the negotiation authority for this specific procurement. As indicated above, that particular section authorizes the use of negotiation if the Secretary determines the supplies are of a technical or specialized nature requiring substantial initial investment or an extended period of preparation for manufacture and if the Secretary further determines that formal advertising (and competitive bidding) would result in duplication of investment or would unduly delay the procurement of the required items. Upon completion of the negotiation process, a copy of the Negotiation Clearance Memorandum will accompany the request by the Bureau for "business clearance" or final approval by the Office of Naval Material, discussed below. 

THE REQUEST FOR PROPOSAL 

The Request for Proposal, a standard Department of Defense form, is then prepared by the Contracts Division and forwarded to the ABC Corporation. It contains a complete and specific description of the items to be procured, together with all applicable specifications, quantities, time and place of delivery, method of shipment, specifications for preservation and packaging, technical instruction books required, and the material, if any, to be furnished by the Government. The manufacturer is requested to submit a quotation on a fixed-price basis for undertaking the work, supported by a complete cost breakdown on the form enclosed. The 

Request also states that the Government is not committed to pay any costs incurred in the submission of such quotation or in making necessary studies or designs for the preparation thereof, or any other costs incurred by the offeror in connection with the proposed procurement for which the quotation is being requested. Approximately thirty days are allowed the company to prepare and submit its proposal. 

In this case, since only the ABC Corporation has been requested to quote, the proposal will be opened when received. A second PRB meeting is then called to review the proposal to ascertain if it is responsive to the requirements of the procurement, and to determine whether, if the proposal is not acceptable as submitted, it can be corrected through negotia- 714

$ 12.tion. The recommendations of the Board are again documented and the necessary funding papers are prepared by the Production Division. 

The Procurement Request is then sent to the Comptroller Division of the Bureau for commitment of funds, and is then forwarded through the chain of command, for the required approval of the purchase decision. 

The proposal from the ABC Corporation, accompanied by the Procurement Request, is also reviewed by Patent Counsel, and recommendations are made for the proper patent clauses to be included in the final contractual document. Following this, the Services Branch of the 

Contracts Division assigns a contract number. 

NEGOTIATING THE CONTRACT 

Meanwhile, the Negotiator proceeds with an analysis of the proposal submitted by the ABC Corporation, aided, as necessary, by cost analysts. 

In accordance with the original solicitation, the ABC Corporation has proposed a fixed-price contract and has submitted a cost breakdown on the standard form showing the amounts estimated for material, subcontracted parts, shop labor, production engineering labor, tooling, overhead, and profit. The Negotiator consults with technical personnel to find out how the XYZ-20 radar set compares with similar equipments which have been purchased. From them he ascertains the reasonableness of the amounts estimated for the material and the subcontracted parts. He discusses with them the estimated hours of direct shop labor necessary for manufacturing the equipment and the estimated hours of production engineering labor required to put this newly developed piece of equipment into production. He questions them regarding the estimated amount of tooling to determine whether, on the one hand, the contractor is contemplating the use of more tooling than is justified by the number of sets presently being procured, or whether, on the other hand, additional tooling will result in overall saving to the Government through reducing the amount of direct labor.

Next, the Negotiator compares the hourly labor rates and the overhead rates used in the cost breakdown with similar data available from previous negotiations with ABC Corporation and other manufacturers of similar equipment. In addition, since ABC Corporation developed the 

XYZ-20 radar set under a cost-plus-fixed-fee contract with the Bureau of Aeronautics, an inquiry may be made as to the labor and overhead rates then prevailing at the contractor's plant. On the basis of this past record and his knowledge of current business trends, the Negotiator is able to determine the reasonableness of the projected labor and overhead rates which have been used by the contractor in its cost breakdown. 

The Negotiator's investigation, comparison and analysis in this case results in the conclusion that the proposed price is fairly reasonable but that the manufacturing overhead rate is somewhat too high and that the 715

$ 12. 

figures apparently include too generous an amount for contingencies. 

Having decided that the proposal is not acceptable as submitted, the Negotiator requests ABC Corporation to send a representative to Washington to discuss the proposal further. At the conference the Negotiator first goes into the high overhead figure. The representative of ABC 

Corporation shows the Negotiator how the rate was worked out and what assumptions were made in projecting the rate into the future. As a result of discussions on these points, the contractor agrees that he may have been overly pessimistic about his expenses and that he will reduce the percentage used in calculating the manufacturing overhead. The 

Negotiator then indicates that, although no other single factor seems excessively far out of line, the final price appears high in comparison with that of other recently procured radar sets. The contractor stresses the numerous unpredictable expenditures likely to be encountered in putting a new item into production and argues that reductions in any of the items of the cost breakdown would involve too great a risk. He agrees, however, that it is entirely possible that such difficulties may not eventuate and states that although he wants protection against them he is not aiming at an excessive profit. Since it is the type of situation for which a price-redetermination type contract is adapted, the Negotiator suggests the use of such a contract, explaining that it will operate to reduce the agreed fixed price only in the event that ABC Corporation's cost experience in the early phases of the contract indicates total costs lower than those now anticipated.

After agreement on the use of redetermination, the only remaining item to be negotiated is that of the profit component to be included in the price. 

In cost-plus-fixed-fee contracts, where the contractor is taking a minimum of risk, the maximum rate of profit or fee is limited by law. In the firm fixed-price contract the contractor takes a greater risk and is entitled to a higher profit rate than in CPFF work. In the redeterminable fixedprice contract, the contractor theoretically has the possibility of experiencing just as large losses as under a fixed-price contract, but will have any large profits reduced through the operation of the price redetermination clause. Accordingly, the contractor arguably would be entitled to even larger rates of profit in this type of contract except for the fact that he is frequently given the benefit of the doubt on conjectural costs because of the later possible reduction in price, and hence the possibility of loss is reduced. Final agreement on a rate of profit in this particular case would be reached only after weighing these various factors. 

BUSINESS CLEARANCE 

The points at issue, so far as the negotiation is concerned, have now all been decided. As a final step, the Negotiator prepares for the approval of the Contract Clearance Branch of the Office of Naval Material a "busi- Sta red the co d of 

The bjed 716

$ 12.ness clearance" request. This includes a brief description of the material and its use, the final breakdown of costs used as a basis for establishing a contract price, a discussion of the various factors in the breakdown, and recommends approval of a contract for 500 XYZ-20 radar sets at prices and on the terms negotiated. 

EXECUTING THE CONTRACT 

After the proposed procurement has been approved by the Contract 

Clearance Branch of the Office of Naval Material, the Procurement Request and all of the supporting papers, including the contract clearance, are forwarded to the Documents Section of the Contracts Division of the Bureau for the preparation of the contract. This preparation is done with the advice and assistance of the Bureau Office of Counsel. In difficult or unusual circumstances, the complete preparation of the contract will be done by the Office of Counsel.

The contractual document itself consists essentially of two parts: the 

Schedule, which contains the particulars of the procurement and special clauses; and a printed set of General Provisions or contract clauses, together with such additional general provisions as necessary, both commonly referred to as the "boilerplate." The Schedule states, among other things, the number, kind, specifications, prices, and delivery dates of the radar sets. It also may include such special provisions as the price redetermination clause, and sets forth any omissions from or modifications of the General or Additional General Provisions. The General and Addi tional General Provisions consist of standard clauses designed to fit the majority of fixed-price contracts, including those contract clauses required by statute (see Chapter 9 supra). When prepared, the contract is sent to the ABC Corporation for execution in triplicate and for return to the Bureau. When the three copies are signed and returned by the contractor, they are presented to a duly authorized contracting officer for execution on behalf of the Government. One of these executed copies is then returned to the contractor, one is retained in the files of the Bureau of Aeronautics, and one is forwarded to the General Accounting Office in conformity with its regulations. In the Bureau of Aeronautics, the Bureau's executed copy, before being filed, is sent to the Bureau's Comptroller Division, where the obligation created by the contract is recorded against the appropriation charged. A number of conformed copies of the contract are made and distributed to all persons having an interest in the administration of the contract, such as the technical desks, the disbursing officer, the Bureau of Aeronautics Representative, the Comptroller Division, Bureau Counsel, and others.

PERFORMING THE CONTRACT-INSPECTION 

The contract provides that all articles, materials and workmanship are subject to inspection and test, by an inspector representing the Navy 717

$ 12. 

Department, to the extent practicable at all times and places including during manufacture, and in any event prior to final acceptance. In the case of the XYZ-20, inspection will be conducted at the plant of ABC Corporation; there will also be "source inspection" at the plants of subcontractors supplying materials and major components. Inspection performed in the factory of the ABC Corporation will be carried out by the cognizant Inspector of Naval Material. However, if this contract were being performed at an aircraft factory under the cognizance of the Navy Department, and in certain other cases, the inspection would be done by the Bureau of Aeronautics Representative (BAR), an aeronautical engineer who has an office and staff located at the particular plant under his cognizance.

As the Inspector's main job is to see that the Government gets exactly what the contract calls for, down to the most minute specifications, he is guided in detail by his copy of the contract, including a complete set of the documents incorporated in it by reference, such as the "General Specifications for the Inspection of Material" and the drawings and detailed specifications for the equipment itself. The Inspector also performs such duties as providing government bills of lading for the shipment of finished goods, and the establishment and enforcement of security regulations in the plant. 

ACCEPTANCE 

When the radar sets are considered completed, the manufacturer tenders delivery of them to the Inspector, who has authority on behalf of the Navy Department to accept or reject them. He may return the article for rework; or, if so instructed by the Bureau of Aeronautics, he may accept articles deviating from the specifications within authorized tolerances, in which event the contract price would be reduced. By means of stamps, stencils or other appropriate means, he will mark the results of his inspection on the articles submitted. The Inspector will also check the packing of the finished products, the method of loading for shipment, and the means of transportation. Preliminary inspection of the instruction manuals will be made by the Inspector, but final inspection and acceptance will be made by the Publications Division of the Bureau of Aeronautics. 

DELIVERY 

The radar sets and spare parts will be delivered f.o.b. a common carrier at the contractor's plant, suitably packed for domestic shipment, on government bills of lading, some to the plant of the aircraft manufacturing company for installation in the aircraft, and the spares to appropriate naval installations. If both ABC Corporation and Aircraft 

Manufacturing Company adhere to their respective schedules, the sets will not accumulate at the plant of the airframe manufacturer prior to installation, nor will there be any delay in the assembly of the aircraft 718

$ 12.while waiting for delivery of the sets. The instruction manuals will be shipped directly to the Publications Division of the Bureau of Aeronautics for distribution to the field activities which will have occasion to use or service the radar sets.

PRICE REDETERMINATION 

In accordance with the terms of the particular price redetermination clause used, after delivery of 60 percent of the radar sets, ABC Corporation will submit to the contracting officer a breakdown of the costs. incurred and estimated to be incurred in the performance of the contract, together with such further relevant information as the contracting officer may request. This information will be analyzed, by the individual who negotiated the original contract, in substantially the same manner as the contractor's original cost breakdown was analyzed. In addition, the 

Contract Audit Division of the Office of the Comptroller of the Navy may be requested to make a spot audit to verify the costs submitted. The 

Negotiator and the contractor will then agree upon a redetermined price for the equipment delivered and to be delivered under the contract. The 

Negotiator will prepare another business clearance for approval by the Office of Naval Material. After such approval is granted, an amendment to the contract will be prepared revising the contract prices in accordance with the new agreement and this amendment will be executed for the Government by the contracting officer and signed by the contractor. 

PAYMENT 

As the radar sets are delivered to the carrier, the contractor will prepare invoices therefor. These invoices will be submitted to the Inspector for certification by him as to receipt and acceptance of the items listed thereon. The Inspector will then forward these invoices to the appropriate Navy Regional Accounts Office where contracts of the Bureau of Aeronautics are paid. The Disbursing Officer will prepare public vouchers based upon the invoices, and mail checks in payment to the contractor. Prior to redetermination of the contract price, the Disbursing Officer withholds a certain percentage (which is stipulated in the redetermination clause) of each payment. After redetermination, the 

Disbursing Officer will pay the redetermined contract price, adjusted to cover any underpayment or overpayment on previously delivered sets. 

The invoices for the instruction manuals will be submitted to the Publications Division of the Bureau of Aeronautics, via the Inspector; and the Publications Division will certify concerning receipt and acceptance of the manuals, and transmit the invoice to the Disbursing Officer for payment.

And thus with the delivery of the last item of XYZ-20 radar equipment and payment of the final invoice, this hypothetical procurement and this final chapter of NAVY CONTRACT LAW are completed.
